News.title: Zack Polanski says he'll run for former PM Starmer's seat in by-election
News.content:
Green Party leader Zack Polanski has confirmed he wants to stand in the by-election brought about by Sir Keir Starmer's resignation as an MP.

Polanski, who is currently a London Assembly member but not a member of Parliament, said he was "so excited by the prospect" of being the first Green MP for Holborn and St Pancras.

The Greens are targeting the seat, until now a Labour stronghold, after coming second to Labour in the area in local elections earlier this year.

Sir Keir announced on Tuesday that he was quitting as MP for the London constituency, two months after he stood down as prime minister, setting up a challenging by-election for his successor Andy Burnham.

In comments to the Camden New Journal, external on Thursday morning, Polanski said: "I have lived and worked in this community over many years, I know it well and I love it.

"It represents so many of the things that make London so special. I am so excited by the prospect of representing this place in Parliament."

He added: "It's a clear fight between Labour and the Green Party."

The Green Party currently has five MPs.

In order to officially be the Green candidate for the seat, Polanski needs to be selected by local party members - something his comments suggest will happen.

But there have been reports in recent days of splits among local Green activists, some of whom are said to favour a Palestinian candidate or a pro-Gaza independent.

Andrew Feinstein, the independent runner-up to Sir Keir in the constituency at the 2024 general election, said he believes Polanski will be an "excellent candidate".

Writing on X, Feinstein said: "Unfortunately I am not in a position to stand this time round."

He said the Camden People's Alliance will meet next week to formally decide its position, adding: "This is a crucial time for progressives in Camden and across the country to be united."

A date has not yet been set for the by-election.

The stakes were already high for Labour at this by-election, because it offers an early test of Burnham's ability to stave off the Green threat in inner-city constituencies.

With Polanski's candidacy, the stakes are even higher for the Greens, to see whether they make good on their leader's oft-stated ambition to replace Labour.

Polanski said a Green victory would be a "clear message that we won't sit by as we get poorer and extreme wealth is concentrated at the very top".

The London Assembly, on which Polanski currently sits, is an elected body of 25 representatives who scrutinise the policies of the mayor of London.

News.title: Households warned gas price spike could pile fresh pressure on energy bills
News.content:
Households across the UK are being warned to brace for higher energy bills this winter as European countries scramble to replenish their natural gas stores before the weather dips.

Wholesale natural gas prices are already at three-year highs, which could lead to increased energy bills for businesses and consumers.

Europe, which delayed its summer stockpiling due to high wholesale costs sparked by the Iran war, had been gambling the conflict would end before winter and prices would in turn fall.

Storage levels are significantly lower than usual for this time of year, with countries facing the prospect of rushing to buy gas now or paying potentially higher prices when the winter comes.

The European benchmark natural gas price topped â¬75/MWh on Wednesday, its highest level since late 2022, the tail end of a spike caused by Russia's invasion of Ukraine. Natural gas prices in the UK this week topped 185p per therm, also the highest since late 2022.

The price has jumped in the past week amid a return to hostilities between the US and Iran, with analysts fearing the renewed fighting will keep the key Strait of Hormuz closed even longer. Typically, around a fifth of the world's oil and liquefied natural gas (LNG) is transported through the waterway.

Hamad Hussain, senior climate and commodities economist at Capital Economics, said he did not expect the waterway to begin reopening until early 2027.

Even then, there will be a lag before energy is flowing freely through the strait and pressure on energy prices are eased.

"The risks to gas prices are definitely tilted towards the upside," Hussain told the BBC, warning that the gas price would top â¬80 by the end of this year.

Hussain recalled interviews with gas storage operators at the outbreak of the US-Israeli war in Iran saying they would wait three to four months for the crisis to ease before stocking up.

"We are about six months into the strait being effectively closed and that obviously has not happened," he added.

Higher wholesale gas prices feed through to household energy bills by helping determine regulator Ofgem's price cap.

The energy price cap rose in July, and will increase by 4% in October, leaving a typical household paying Â£1,723. But analysts at the energy consultancy Cornwall Insight have forecast domestic energy prices could rise a further 9% in the new year, bringing renewed concern to households during the coldest months.

Dr Craig Lowrey, principal consultant at Cornwall Insight, told the BBC on Thursday a fresh increase in wholesale prices would "increase pressure on our January price cap forecast".

However, he cautioned that there was "plenty of time to go" and a fall in wholesale prices could ease the pressure.

News.title: Four to face trial accused of murdering baby
News.content:
Four people accused of murdering a newborn baby found dead at a house in Sheffield are to stand trial next year.

The baby girl, who suffered 33 wounds in 15 separate stabbings, was found at a house in Holywell Heights, in the Wincobank area of the city, on Sunday.

Andrea Skopova, 20, Peter Horvath, 19, Peter Horvath, 38, and Nina Horvathova, 37, appeared at Sheffield Crown Court charged with murdering the child, named only as Baby S. A 15-year-old girl also appeared in court charged with perverting the course of justice.

The adults, all Slovakian nationals, were remanded into custody until the next hearing on 2 October. The girl was remanded into youth custody.

Horvath Jnr, Horvath Snr and Horvathova, all of Holywell Heights, and Skopova, of Robey Street, Grimesthorpe, Sheffield, are also charged with causing or allowing the death of a child, and perverting the course of justice by cleaning the scene of the alleged crime.

On Wednesday, prosecutor Luke Hopkinson told Sheffield Magistrates Court the baby's body was found on top of a washing machine in an outhouse at the property in Holywell Heights.

News.title: Watch: BBC witnesses 'taxi boat' picking up migrants multiple times in a day
News.content:
A BBC investigation has found smuggling gangs are running low on small boats, forcing rival gangs to have to work together to meet demand for crossings.

With crossings at a six-year low, it includes loading more migrants on larger vessels, as the 'mega-dinghies' that were first seen last month.

The gangs claim more are being prepared.

News.title: Amelia Dimoldenberg to close doors of Chicken Shop Date
News.content:
"To me the show is my very own rom-com and I have loved creating so many stories for you to watch," she wrote.

"I am so grateful to everyone who has followed me on this journey and found some joy in these episodes.

"I never thought I'd stop Chicken Shop Date, I thought maybe it would be a part of me forever, and in some way it always will, but I feel like it's now time to move on from this adventure and on to a new one."

Dimoldenberg insisted just months ago she had no plans to end Chicken Shop Date, and said she planned to carry on until she met her "one true love".

Her most recent interviewees have included music heavyweight Paul McCartney, Swedish pop star Zara Larsson and US television host Conan O'Brien.

The presenter has long said her dream guest, external would be Drake and fans will be speculating if she's managed to bag the Canadian rapper for one of her final episodes.

And thousands of supportive comments have been left under the announcement post.

Radio 1 presenter and podcaster Jamie Laing wrote: "The G.O.A.T."

Author and broadcaster Elizabeth Day wrote: "Knowing when to stop - and leaving on such a high, after shaping the culture - is the quintessential power move."

Rapper Tinie Tempah commented: "Smashed it!"

Dimoldenberg previously told the BBC how Chicken Shop Date had grown out of a series of interviews with grime artists she conducted as a teenager for culture magazine The Cut.

"I started Chicken Shop Date as part of a youth club, and we made a magazine, and everything I learned there, the connections I made, the mentoring I got, set me up for the career that I have today," she said.

News.title: Pupil who stabbed teacher in head given four-year detention order
News.content:
A pupil who stabbed a teacher in the head with a kitchen knife after asking her to check his homework has been sentenced to four-and-a-half years in youth detention.

The 16-year-old boy followed Vicki Williams into her empty classroom at Milford Haven Comprehensive School, Pembrokeshire, after asking for help with his work on 5 February.

The teenager pulled a knife from his bag and lunged at her, Swansea Crown Court previously heard, with Williams saying she feared she would die.

After the trial in July, he was found not guilty of attempted murder but guilty of wounding with intent.

On Thursday, Judge Thomas told the court there was a "significant degree of planning" and that "time stood still" for Williams.

During the trial, Williams said the attack "came out of nowhere" after the boy - who cannot be named due to a court order - asked her for help with his work at the end of the school day.

He closed the classroom door behind him and Williams noticed him looking through his bag as he asked her if his work "was correct".

She said he suddenly pulled a large kitchen knife from the bag, and stabbed her in her head.

Williams grabbed the knife, pushed the boy back with her legs, and screamed.

She had injuries to her head, back and hands and said the boy looked at her with "pure hatred".

News.title: 'Naive' police staff who leaked information jailed
News.content:
Prosecuting, Helen Rodger said each had a sexual relationship with men involved in crime, and should have known that these were "disclosable associations".

The first time Doherty accessed information about an incident and passed it on to Robbie Braddock, with whom she was said to be in a relationship, was in December 2023, roughly two months after she completed her control room training.

Doherty shared details about the incident, a fight in which another male had smashed a window, with Braddock.

Rodger said a second incident involving Doherty on 6 March 2024, saw her access details about a search warrant being executed and pass on details about it to the same man as before.

Doherty viewed the details of the incident several times before also checking who was in custody at Ripley custody suite.

Fitzhugh, who was also said to be in a relationship with a man with a criminal record, looked up incidents in spring 2024, out of what the judge called "idle curiosity".

The two women, who met while both working at McDonald's before starting with the force, sat apart in the dock and were accompanied in court by their families.

Spencer speculated that maybe their "friendship has not survived this case" and said "I have little doubt that it will haunt you for the rest of your days".

He said: "It's impossible to recognise the young women who I read about, with such positive qualities, in the women who committed these offences."

Defending Fitzhugh, Elizabeth Power said she had a "lack of awareness" about the "severity of the breaches that she made".

Lowri Butterworth, for Doherty, told the court that she was "acutely aware" and had been using her time since to "give back" to her community.

Both women were charged in April following an investigation led by the Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) after conduct referrals.

Emily Barry, from the IOPC, said Doherty admitted supplying information to a man with known links to crime within a few months of her joining the force.

"Call handlers are privy to sensitive information and have access to confidential data on police systems," she added.

"It's incumbent on them not to inappropriately disclose information and to only access material for policing purposes."

Barry said the pair were likely to be barred from working in policing again following respective misconduct hearings.

News.title: Arboretum's name change faces veterans' backlash
News.content:
There are 420 memorials at the 150-acre site, which honours the service and sacrifice of the armed forces, emergency services and other civilian organisations, including the Sands charity's baby loss memorial.

Cornhill said enduring the loss of a stillborn baby had been difficult, but he described the Sands memorial as "a good place to go for a think and sit down and talk and have a bit of a cry even".

The petition claimed the arboretum's name change "undermines its rich heritage and the deep emotional connections many have with it".

David Willis, a Royal Navy veteran of 39 years from Polesworth, Warwickshire, said he visits to remember patients he treated as a medic.

"There are a lot of names of friends and former colleagues on the walls.

"There are also names of patients, I remember their names, on the walls as well, who we battled to save their lives but unfortunately passed away.

"Quite often I just touch their names when I'm there. It gives me comfort," he said.

And added: "To change it to 'memorial gardens' hasn't got that grandeur."

News.title: Sex offender ran into sea to escape officers during arrest
News.content:
A sex offender who ran into the sea to escape being arrested has been jailed, South Wales Police has said.

Gavin Bennett, 45, ran into the water off Porthcawl, Bridgend County, at night after sending inappropriate messages to a girl he believed to be under 16.

In a video, two officers are seen wading into the Bristol Channel with torches at about 21:45 on 22 October 2025 and pulling Bennett out.

He was charged with two counts of attempting to engage in sexual communication with a child.

The force said he pleaded guilty at Cardiff Crown Court, and was sentenced on Tuesday to three years and eight months, and handed a 10-year sexual harm prevention order.

The sentence also covered two counts of sexually assaulting a female, relating to a separate incident spanning two years.

News.title: Dad and daughter who dumped body in canal convicted
News.content:
On the opening day of the trial, the court heard Bailey was last seen on the afternoon of 27 September.

Police said CCTV footage revealed Bailey had entered Anslow's home on Stour Street in West Bromwich on that day, after the pair met on Great Bridge Street.

West Midlands Police said her body was later found on 7 October.

Opening the case, prosecutor Michael Duck KC told the court the victim was a vulnerable individual who lived alone in Tipton, and had been leading "something of a chaotic lifestyle".

She had occasionally been a sex worker in the area, Duck said.

He added that while it was not clear exactly what happened inside Anslow's property, the evidence suggested he had attacked her inside his bedroom.

"During that attack she sustained a number of facial fractures, bruising to many parts of her body [and] was ultimately strangled and very likely bitten to intimate parts of her body", Duck said.

Police said the assault led to her death and described how the following morning, Anslow had cancelled his community carers and called his daughter for help.

Ferguson travelled to her father's address in a taxi with slabs and claimed she was helping in him with his garden, the West Midlands force added.

The 42-year-old returned in the early hours of 29 September when the pair were caught on CCTV as they moved Bailey's body in Anslow's "distinctive wheelchair", police said.

The force added that the father and daughter then dumped the victim's body in the canal known locally as "eight locks".

News.title: Production ends at historical Kellogg's factory
News.content:
Production at the Kellogg's factory in Greater Manchester has come to an end after almost 90 years, with the loss of about 360 jobs.

The site in Trafford Park was one of the largest cereal factories in Europe when built in 1938 but production is being transferred to the company's site in Wrexham, north Wales.

A spokesperson for owners Kellanova said the site has been a crucial part of its success for decades, adding: "We thank everyone who has worked there, as well as the suppliers, partners and local community who have worked alongside us."

Mick Murray from retail union Usdaw said it was "a sad time" after working to "try to secure the best possible outcome for our members".

In 2024 Kellanova announced that production of breakfast cereals would move to Wrexham, saying the investment required to maintain the factory was not viable.

It came after the end of three-month talks with union and employee representatives.

Marking the last week of production on site, a company spokesperson said: "A significant milestone was reached this week, as operations across production and packing came to an end."

They said their priority through the transition has been to "support colleagues and the wider community through this period of change".

News.title: Scottish Holocaust victim recognised at Auschwitz
News.content:
The name of a Scot who died in the Holocaust after refusing to abandon Jewish children in her care has been added to a special memorial wall at Auschwitz.

Jane Haining is recognised in a renewed section of the Auschwitz Birkenau Memorial and Museum's main exhibition - devoted to hundreds of prisoners for whom no registration photographs were taken.

The new name plaques adorn the wall of a long corridor and are displayed next to many images of prisoners dressed in striped shirts with shaved heads.

Haining's death certificate said she died in hospital on 17 July 1944, aged 47, but it is widely accepted she died in a gas chamber and her remains are on the Auschwitz site.

News.title: College lecturer admits killing husband and wife in drink-drive crash
News.content:
At the time Jatinder Kaur was driving the family's Volkswagen Polo, making deliveries with her husband and their children in the car.

The family ran the Keystore grocery store in Kirkcaldy.

The couple's 19-year-old daughter Parveet was in the front passenger seat and their son Princedeep, 10, was sleeping in the back seat beside his father.

The advocate depute added: "The accused's vehicle crashed head-on, which caused both vehicles to come to a stop."

Other drivers who witnessed Hynd's erratic driving stopped to try and help, with police and paramedics arriving a short time later.

Rodger said that at the scene police observed that Hynd "smelled of alcohol and appeared to not know she had been in a collision".

Kaur was unresponsive and was pronounced dead at the scene. Satwant Singh was taken to hospital where he died two days later.

Hynd was arrested and charged in May this year.

Defence lawyer Ewen Roy said that she recognised that her actions had "devastating consequences which weigh on her heavily".

Judge O'Grady told Hynd: "You understand the charge you have pled guilty to is very grave indeed.

"You have left in your wake a dead husband and wife."

In a statement, the family said "we will miss them more than words can express".

They added: "Mum was always there for us, whether we needed her advice, reassurance or someone to talk to, she always made things better.

"Nothing was ever too much trouble for Dad, he loved Mum and us more than anything.

"It's incredibly difficult to accept they won't be there to share the important milestones in our lives."

The case is due to call again in October.

News.title: Stacey Solomon and Joe Swash issue major life update with change ‘imminent’
News.content:
Stacey Solomon and Joe Swash have issued a major life update, announcing that change is "imminent" for their family.

In an Instagram video posted on Wednesday (2 September), the pair explained that they would be leaving Pickle Cottage – the Tudor-style house they have lived in since 2021.

The TV presenters, who began dating in 2016 and married at the property in 2022, have documented their refurbishments to the house over the last few years.

"We’ve always been thinking if there was ever a chance to move further out and get a bit more land then we would consider it," Solomon explained.

J. Peterman, the quirky catalog retailer that became a pop-culture fixture thanks to “Seinfeld,” appears to have quietly closed after nearly four decades in business.

The company’s website has been shut down, displaying only a message that reads, “This store is not currently taking orders.” The same goes for its companion brand, Territory Ahead, while phone numbers for J. Peterman’s corporate office and customer service have been deactivated.

The apparent closure comes as the Ohio-based company faces allegations of violating consumer protection laws. In a lawsuit filed August 17, Ohio Attorney General Andrew Wilson alleges that J. Peterman failed to deliver some orders, issue refunds for canceled orders and returned merchandise, and, in some cases, honor its own refund policies. The state also alleges that customers struggled to reach the company’s customer service team.

The filing disclosed J. Peterman’s “retail business” as “no longer in operation.”

Retail Dive reported the apparent closures Wednesday and said the company had not responded to the allegations. Founder John Peterman, who is listed as chairman, and his son Tim Peterman, a former CEO and CFO, also did not respond to the outlet’s requests for comment.

open image in gallery John O’Hurley, who played the eccentric J. Peterman on ‘Seinfeld,’ later became a part-owner of the real company ( NBC/Youtube )

The Independent has reached out J. Peterman for comment.

Fans of the 90s sitcom “Seinfeld” may remember the company-inspired eccentric character J. Peterman, played by John O’Hurley, who became Elaine Benes’ (Julia Louis-Dreyfus) boss when she took a job writing for the catalog.

The real J. Peterman catalog was known for its unusual, highly detailed descriptions, which turned clothing into romantic tales of travel and adventure rather than simply listing fabric, color and size. “Seinfeld” exaggerated that signature style, portraying Peterman as a wealthy, dramatic adventurer who spoke about everyday clothes as though they had emerged from some grand expedition.

The character became so closely tied to the real company that O’Hurley eventually became a part-owner after investing in J. Peterman during its 2025 revival.

The company itself has had a turbulent history. John Peterman founded it in 1987, and the catalog business grew rapidly, bringing in tens of millions of dollars in sales by the mid-1990s.

open image in gallery The real John Peterman (pictured) founded the company in 1987 ( Kelsey246!/CC BY-SA 4.0 )

But an expansion into brick-and-mortar stores helped push the company into Chapter 11 bankruptcy in 1999. Peterman bought back the company’s intellectual property in 2001 and revived the brand.

The comeback continued for years, but the financial challenges remained. In 2023 filings, the company reported net losses of $3.6 million in 2021 and $5.7 million in 2022 and warned that it expected to continue losing money. It had also considered going public, though that plan did not materialize, according to Retail Dive.

Peterman acknowledged the difficulty of operating the smaller company in a 2018 interview with Retail Dive, telling the publication, “We’re too small to make a lot of money.”

The Athletic has determined that former NFL reporter Dianna Russini violated newsroom standards with her relationship with Mike Vrabel, the head coach of the New England Patriots.

On Thursday, The New York Times-owned Athletic released the findings of the newspaper’s internal investigation into 51-year-old Vrabel and 43-year-old Russini’s relationship. The report comes after Russini resigned from her role in April following outrage over pictures that emerged of her and Vrabel — who are both married to other people — hugging and holding hands.

Although the review concluded that Russini violated its conflict-of-interest rules by not disclosing her relationship with the coach, the investigators did not find any inaccuracies in her reporting about Vrabel or his teams.

The investigators reviewed 903 articles, 204 podcast episodes, and 77 videos, and interviewed 14 staffers at the paper to come to their conclusion.

“Russini's relationship with Vrabel was in clear violation of The Athletic's standards,” the report said. “Regardless of whether the relationship was romantic, it was a breach and should have been disclosed.”

Dianna Russini was found to have violated ‘The Athletic’ newsroom standards over her relationship with Patriots head coach Mike Vrabel ( Getty )

The findings continued, “I've not found a clear link to conclude that Russini used her platform to help promote Vrabel or help his teams during her time at The Athletic.”

A pregnant woman in a black dress stood at the head of her 21-year-old husband’s casket Tuesday in Kyiv, mourning the man she met when they were both soldiers fighting Russia's full-scale invasion of their country.

Yeva Smyrnova and Danyil Smyrnov both joined the army in 2023, at 18, and married two years later, in July 2025. Young as they were, decided they needed to hurry and start a family.

“We dreamed of this child, but because we were both always at war, it was very difficult,” said Smyrnova, who serves as a drone pilot under the call sign “Yunha.”

Danyil Smyrnov was killed in action on Aug. 28, 2026, on the Sumy front in northeastern Ukraine, one of a group of four soldiers killed in action serving with military intelligence. He held the rank of junior sergeant, served as a reconnaissance operator, and helped train recruits.

“This month our son is due to be born — the son Dania dreamed about so much. He dreamed of being the best father," Smyrnova told The Associated Press.

But instead of choosing a name for her firstborn child, she and hundreds of others came to say goodbye to her husband at St. Michael’s Golden-Domed Monastery.

In the days after Smyrnov's death, his wife wrote online that their son would be “his continuation.”

The monastery, where Ukraine typically holds funeral services for soldiers killed in the war, was packed. Mourners of all ages came to pay their respects, including fellow soldiers holding bouquets of roses.

When Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022, Smyrnov was 16 and finishing high school. He went on to study psychology at a university in Lithuania but did not stay long — fighting had intensified around Bakhmut, where his uncle was serving at the time, and the young man left his studies. As soon as he turned 18, he signed a military contract.

“He … called me that evening, very happy, and said, ‘Sorry, Dad, I signed the contract. I forged your signature. Forgive me,’” recalled his father, Oleksandr Smyrnov, his voice shaking. He struggled to speak about his son, but embraced his daughter-in-law, saying he also found some comfort in the grandson soon to arrive.

Danyil Smyrnov went on to command an assault group in the 3rd Separate Assault Brigade. He was wounded by shrapnel in both legs and underwent rehabilitation, then returned to service, later transferring to Ukrainian military intelligence. Many knew him by his call sign, “Surfer” — from the age of 6, he had flown to visit his mother in Bali every summer, where he became a skilled surfer.

“Despite all the horrors of war, Dania managed to find his treasure — his girlfriend, and later his wife, Yeva,” read a passage from the eulogy at the monastery, as explosions echoed through the city. “Their relationship changed them both. They were both fighting for life, for a shared future.”

Now his wife is left alone, widowed at 21.

“He wanted all of us to be able to live in peace,” she said. “And in the end, he paid for that with his life.”

Smyrnov often wrote about the war on his Instagram, an account that holds mostly photos from his military life — himself in uniform, at different positions — with his most recent photos showing him with his wife, who is also pictured in military fatigues.

In an earlier post, written around his 20th birthday, he wrote: “In my 20 years, I’ve understood one thing: people don’t value life until they feel its edge. … War is not romance. It’s an experience that strips you down to what’s real,” the message said. “The choice is simple: who will you be — a victim, or someone who takes responsibility?”

___

Alex Babenko contributed to this report.

A commercial airplane crash can change how people behave long after the immediate tragedy. News outlets replay the images, people affected share their harrowing stories, and an extraordinarily rare event becomes easy to imagine. Some travelers cancel trips; others drive to their destination instead.

These choices may feel cautious. Statistically, the alternatives people switch to may come with greater risk.

Commercial airline crashes command attention because they are rare, catastrophic and beyond a passenger’s control. But the choice to avoid flying does not eliminate risk. As a new report from our research team at Embry-Riddle Aeronautical University outlines, skipping a flight and opting to drive instead is typically much riskier, even if it doesn’t feel like it.

Airline travel is safer than headlines suggest

People tend to respond strongly to events that are vivid, while paying less attention to familiar hazards – the risks of which manifest more frequently but less visibly. As a result, efforts to avoid one danger can create another.

open image in gallery The fatality risk is about 626 times higher in a passenger car or truck than on a commercial airline ( AFP via Getty Images )

In our recent peer-reviewed report, prepared with support from Embry-Riddle Aeronautical University’s Boeing Center for Aviation and Aerospace Safety, we compared fatality risk in U.S. commercial aviation with other transportation modes, recreational activities, household hazards and occupational risks. While the Boeing Center receives some funding from The Boeing Company, it operates independently.

We focused on commercial Part 121 airlines operating in the U.S. and analyzed data from 2016 through 2025. Part 121 carriers generally include large U.S. airlines and regional carriers that operate scheduled passenger service. Because fatal accidents are so rare, data from a single year would not have provided a stable risk estimate.

Across several measures of risk exposure, including distance traveled, individual boardings, hours spent traveling, annual risk and lifetime odds, the data consistently shows that U.S. commercial aviation is exceptionally safe.

For the same distance traveled, we estimated the fatality risk as about 626 times higher in a passenger car or truck than on a commercial airline. The risk associated with motorcycle travel was more than 22,000 times higher than commercial airline travel. Even highway bus travel, itself a relatively safe option, carried about nine times the risk of commercial airline travel over the same distance.

When risk is measured per passenger boarding, the numbers remain striking. From 2016 through 2024, the long-run estimate was approximately one passenger fatality per 97.7 million boardings on commercial airlines.

These numbers do not mean flying is risk-free, just that the risk is small enough that researchers need many years and enormous amounts of exposure to estimate it. Across the 10-year study period, 73 people died in accidents involving commercial airline travel in the United States.

These findings complement earlier research. A peer-reviewed 2013 study comparing U.S. transportation modes examined data from 2000 through 2009 and also identified commercial aviation as the safest way to travel. A 2018 study using data from the same period similarly ranked commercial aviation as the safest mode.

About the authors Mihhail Berezovski is an Associate Professor of Mathematical Sciences, Embry-Riddle Aeronautical University. Alex Chaparro is a Professor of Human Factors and Behavioral Neurobiology, Embry-Riddle Aeronautical University. This article was first published by The Conversation and is republished under a Creative Commons licence. Read the original article .

More recently, a 2022 study analyzed U.S. news coverage, travel patterns and accident data from 1996 through 2017. It found that increased news coverage of aviation accidents was associated with more road traffic and more fatal road accidents in subsequent months.

The 9/11 aftermath and the risk of avoiding risk

The aftermath of the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks provided a powerful example of how behavior can shift risk from one setting to another. Air travel declined sharply after the 9/11 attacks. Subsequently, researchers were able to investigate whether fear of flying led to additional deaths on the road.

Psychologist Gerd Gigerenzer analyzed traffic patterns for the final three months of 2001 and estimated 353 excess road deaths nationwide. He characterized many people’s decision to drive rather than fly as an attempt to avoid a “dread risk”: a low-probability event in which many people could die at once.

Transportation researchers Michael Sivak and Michael Flannagan later reanalyzed the period. They used road fatality trends from the first eight months of 2000 and 2001 to estimate how many deaths would normally have occurred during the final three months of 2001. They then compared that estimate with the number actually recorded in the past three months and calculated 1,018 additional road fatalities from October 2001 through December 2001.

But their findings complicated the idea that people who avoided flying merely drove to the same distant destinations. Much of the increase occurred on local roads, not interstate highways, and pedestrians and bicyclists experienced a disproportionate share of fatalities. This pattern suggests that travel behavior may have changed more broadly after the attacks, perhaps because people canceled longer trips, stayed closer to home or changed their daily routines.

It is hard to pin down how much of this increase was related to people changing their travel patterns in response to the 9/11 attacks, since these studies cannot track each individual’s transportation decisions.

But both studies suggest that a collective effort to avoid a highly visible danger can increase exposure to ordinary hazards whose victims are less visible. When more people choose to drive rather than fly, the roads become busier and the number of traffic deaths can rise.

The question shapes the risk estimate

One reason discussions about risk become confusing is that there is no single way to measure it. The answer to the question “Is it safe?” depends on what you measure.

open image in gallery An average of 2.48 million travelers passed through TSA screening each day in 2025 ( AFP/Getty )

How much risk does a person face for each mile traveled? What is the risk of one trip? How much risk accumulates during one hour of travel? What is the chance of dying from this cause in a year or over a lifetime?

These are legitimate questions, but to make a valid comparison, you need to look at the same measure of risk for both types of transportation. Comparing the risk of one flight with the annual risk of driving, for example, mixes unlike quantities.

A traveler deciding whether to fly or drive between two cities can compare the two modes over the same trip or distance. This comparison provides a clearer perspective than comparing a highly visible plane crash with a familiar daily routine.

Time matters too. In our estimates, an hour in a passenger car or truck carried about 74 times the fatality risk of an hour aboard a commercial aircraft.

Feeling in control is not the same as safety

Driving gives people a steering wheel, a brake pedal and the belief that their skill can protect them. Flying asks passengers to place control in the hands of pilots, airlines, regulators, air traffic controllers and a complex technical system. Psychological research has linked a stronger sense of agency – the feeling that people control their actions and their outcomes – with greater risk-taking. That difference in perceived control helps explain why a rare aviation disaster can feel more threatening than routine road travel.

Media attention also matters. A major airplane crash is treated as news of national or international importance. Road deaths occur across many locations and at different times, so the public does not see the cumulative toll.

The emotional intensity of coverage does not mean journalists are wrong to cover crashes. It just means audiences need context alongside the images.

Crafting better risk communication

Telling anxious travelers that flying is “safe” is rarely enough. Research on risk perception shows that people do not judge danger through statistics alone. Fear and vivid images also shape how risky an event feels. But providing more context about the risks from other forms of transportation can still help.

Effective communication about risk does not minimize tragedy or dismiss the real fear people may feel. But it can help people understand that when millions of travelers shift from one type of transportation to another, the risk moves with them.

For travelers, the practical question is not whether an option has zero risk. No option does. The question is whether a choice reduces their total exposure to risk or merely replaces a frightening, highly visible risk with a greater one that feels routine.

To put the rarity of fatal airline events into perspective, an average of 2.48 million travelers passed through TSA screening each day in 2025. Modern commercial aviation in the United States has achieved a safety record that is difficult to grasp precisely because fatal events are so unusual.

When fear leads people away from that system, the safest-feeling decision may not be the safest decision at all.

Dame Joanna Lumley has described the flash flood in Nepal as "heartbreaking", suggesting the disaster "could have maybe been predicted" as she attended a vigil for those affected.

The 80-year-old actor, who has visited Nepal frequently and maintains strong links with the Gurkha community, said that seeing the flood sweep through the country's northern region last week "broke her heart".

Dame Joanna joined members of London’s Nepalese community for a candlelit service at Panas Gurkha Restaurant in Blackheath, south-east London, on Thursday afternoon.

Around 50 people gathered at the venue to light candles, observe a minute of silence and pray for affected communities.

“The sense that it could have maybe been predicted by all the people who understood that by human activities somehow the world seems to be changing, seems to be getting warmer.

“These catastrophes, the great Himalayan glaciers melting, isn’t something that we haven’t heard of and thought of before.

open image in gallery Around 50 people gathered at the venue to light candles, observe a minute of silence and pray for affected communities ( PA )

“When you see the catastrophic outcome, I think we feel completely hopeless every day we look in the papers.”

On Thursday, Nepal’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs confirmed 1,252 deaths recorded since the flash flood on August 26.

It added that approximately 4,200 people remain missing, including 590 foreign nationals from 34 countries.

On Tuesday, Foreign Office minister Lord Wood of Anfield told the House of Lords that 36 British people are currently unaccounted for, up from the previous total of 33.

During the vigil, Dame Joanna said: “I think, actually, in this country and around the world our hearts have been absolutely broken by what happened in Nepal.

The United States Geological Survey (USGS) said a magnitude 5.2 seismic event occurred near the border between Nepal and China.

It added that a “glacial collapse and debris flow” caused “subsequent catastrophic impacts downstream”.

Rescue efforts had previously been hampered by fears of more flooding from a lake formed by the glacier collapse which sparked the flooding.

open image in gallery A drone view of excavators clearing mud to make way for a road after flash floods and a mudslide, in Trishuli, Nuwakot district, Nepal ( Reuters )

Dame Joanna said having visited and travelled in the country, “it breaks my heart because I know how difficult it is to get around”.

“It seems that we have been warned about this over the years,” she added.

“Now, there are two camps, as we both know: there is the people who believe that climate change is largely affected by mankind and those who just say that it’s completely a natural phenomenon.

“I belong to the first camp, which is that I do believe that what we do here, and the fossil fuels we burn and the plastic waste in the sea and so on, I do believe that is making the world a sicker place and a weaker place.

“And the places which are melting fastest are the high mountains and places, and so the Himalayas are there.”

Dame Joanna is the patron of healthcare charity Doctors for Nepal and vice patron of The Gurkha Welfare Trust, which provides aid to Gurkha veterans who served in the British Army.

Her father served in the 6th Gurkha Rifles, a regiment of the British Indian Army, during the Second World War.

Also present at the vigil on Thursday were Vice Lord-Lieutenant Colonel Jane Davis, former Coronation Street star Sally Lindsay, drummer Steve White and Greenwich mayor David Wardrop.

Investigators on Thursday were scouring the scene of the downtown Minneapolis shooting that left three people dead, including the suspect, and five others injured.

Dozens of law enforcement officers were at the apartment building where the shooting occurred Wednesday evening, along with a mobile crime scene unit from the Minnesota Bureau of Criminal Apprehension, the state investigative agency.

The five wounded by gunfire included two Minneapolis police officers, while a sixth person, another officer, suffered other injuries, police Sgt. Garrett Parten said at a Wednesday news conference. The three officers were hospitalized but expected to make full recoveries, said Interim Police Chief Bill Peterson.

A 911 call about shots fired at the building came in just after 4:30 p.m. Officers were inside the building within two minutes and quickly found victims, Peterson said.

Officers heard more gunshots and followed them to a higher floor, where they found “a haze that significantly limited their visibility,” he said. Peterson did not provide additional details about the haze.

One officer was shot in the leg and another was shot twice in the abdomen, he said.

Authorities did not provide any details about the suspected shooter but said they were familiar with the person before the shooting.

One victim was fatally shot at the scene, and one died after arriving at the hospital, he said. It was not immediately clear how the shooter died, he said.

Resident Julius Bailey was sitting with a friend just outside the building entrance when he heard gunshots and saw a man he recognized as another resident holding a pistol. Bailey said he heard a woman screaming and immediately started running, counting eight shots as he headed for safety.

Bailey said the man with the gun was well known in the building for his belligerence and showing off his weapon. Bailey, who moved into the building in June, said he went out of his way to avoid the man.

“I could tell he was trouble,” he said.

Chris Miller, who also lives in the apartment building, said he heard a rapid succession of gunshots and quickly ran outside for safety. He said he believed he knew who carried out the shooting and that he encountered someone in the hallway with a handgun earlier this week and reported that person to management.

Associated Press reporters Mark Vancleave, Hallie Golden in Seattle, Safiyah Riddle in Los Angeles and Josh Kelety in Phoenix contributed to this report.

News.title: The Ukrainian children struggling to survive alone in Europe
News.content:
Every day begins and ends in the same way for Arsenii, 17: calling his mum back home in Kyiv. A year ago he moved from Ukraine to a school boarding house in Slovakia. One night he fell asleep before phoning. When he woke, his mobile was flooded with messages from the few adults his mum knew in the country: the dorm security guard and agent she paid to become his temporary legal guardian. “She woke up everybody,” he says, still with a sense of guilt. She had been trying, agonisingly, to account for her son from over 1,000km away.

Russia’s unprovoked full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022 triggered Europe’s largest displacement of children since World War II. More than 1.8 million crossed into neighbouring countries in the first month – 90 per cent of them with their mothers or other female relatives. But as bombardments battered the country in the following four years, children continued to leave – only without their relatives.

A year-long investigation by the Telegraph has discovered thousands of Ukrainian children are living in Europe alone in the hope of a better life. Some have adapted to independent living, studying and learning the local language. Others have fallen into illegal work, experienced insecurity and discrimination. A few attempts end in tragedy.

The exact number of Ukrainian children who are now living alone in Europe is unclear. Data collected by EU statistical database Eurostat suggests the total cases since 2022 could be almost 23,500. It shows that 19,580 unaccompanied Ukrainian minors in European Union (EU) countries received EU Temporary Protection Status (TPS) between March 2022 and July 2026.

Non-EU countries offer parallel protection schemes. Eurostat data revealed that in the same time-frame, Liechtenstein, Norway and Switzerland granted their protection status to an additional 3,905 unaccompanied Ukrainian minors.

However, the data is incomplete. Only 20 out of 27 EU members declared their numbers. Among those missing are key Ukrainian refugee destination countries, such as Germany and Poland. Poland alone issued 42,332 temporary guardian orders to Ukrainian minors between 2022 and 2025, according to Polish Ministry of Justice data requested by The Telegraph.

In theory, any child granted TPS protection should have a locally appointed legal guardian to sign their papers. However, our investigation revealed loopholes in the system, leaving this category of children vulnerable to abandonment or poor guardianship arrangements.

Arsenii is among at least 1,024 Ukrainian children aged 14 to 16 who have evacuated to Slovak school boarding houses, according to a snapshot 2025 survey by the Slovak Children’s Commissioner. The real figure is likely to be thousands higher, as this research covered just over half of secondary schools in five of the country’s eight regions. It concluded some 5,000 Ukrainian minors in Slovakia have no responsible adult “close to them”, of whom around 1,000 have no legal representative at all.

News.title: Zika virus mosquitoes breed in Britain for first time
News.content:
Mosquitoes capable of spreading the deadly Zika virus, dengue and yellow fever have been found breeding in Britain.

Aedes aegypti mosquitoes, which typically live in Africa and Asia, have been discovered with larvae in east London by the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA).

The agency has deployed specialist teams to destroy the insects in an effort to prevent them from settling in the capital and spreading. The species has been detected in Britain before, but this is the first time a reproducing colony has been found.

Although the exact location of where the mosquitoes are has not been released, images shared with The Telegraph suggest that at least one of the residential properties where they were found is a middle-class, Victorian home with a well-kept garden, including potted tomato plants.

The colony is likely to have been found through a tip-off from a homeowner via a mosquito submission website operated by the UKHSA.

Dr Jolyon Medlock, head of medical entomology and zoonoses ecology at the UKHSA, said in a statement: “It is expected that in a warming climate, we will continue to see incursions of invasive mosquitoes, and increased reports of them being able to survive in the UK.”

News.title: Burnham risks Truss moment, warn bond traders
News.content:
Andy Burnham risks a Liz Truss-style market meltdown unless he presents a credible plan to pay for his agenda, bond traders have warned.

Investors said the Prime Minister faces further spikes in borrowing costs unless he outlines tax rises or spending cuts to fund his major policies.

UK borrowing costs have surged to multi-decade highs this week amid a global bond market sell-off. However, investors are particularly concerned about Mr Burnham’s fiscal agenda before his first Budget next month.

Al Cattermole, a portfolio manager at Swiss private bank Mirabaud, said investors were “unclear” about the Prime Minister’s plans and how he would pay for them.

He said: “If you have a lack of credibility about your spending plan and how that will be funded, then you would get spikes in yields similar to [what] we saw during the Liz Truss episode.

“That was about unfunded fiscal spending. And if you get that again, then there is concern about that.”

Mr Burnham refused to rule out increasing borrowing during his first Prime Minister’s Questions on Wednesday despite recent market turmoil.

Jim Athey, a portfolio manager at Marlborough Investment, said: “Spending cuts are the thing the market wants to hear.

“It would go a long way if this Government were to recognise that it is a challenge that needs addressing – that the path we are on in terms of welfare spending is completely unsustainable.”

He added: “The market knows that, and the market wants to hear that the Government understands that.”

Lord Jim O’Neill said earlier that the Prime Minister must “get real” and cut public spending in order to ease pressure in the bond market.

The cost of long-term government borrowing hit its highest level since 1998 on Wednesday, increasing the strain on the public finances as John Healey, the new Chancellor, prepares for the Budget.

The 10-year gilt yield – a benchmark for what the Treasury pays to borrow money – has risen to its highest point since 2007.

News.title: H5N1 hits US mink farms, sparking calls for an urgent cull
News.content:
H5N1 has been detected on a US mink farm for the first time, igniting fears the infected animals could present a human pandemic risk.

The bird flu virus, which has “jumped” from birds to numerous mammal species and infected hundreds of people in recent years, was detected in at least six mink on a farm in Utah in mid-August, according to a notification from the US Department of Agriculture (USDA) released over the weekend.

Mink in captivity have previously been described as pandemic “time bombs”. The size and density of the farms gives invading viruses a perfect environment in which to mutate. Mink also have strikingly similar respiratory systems to humans, which greatly increases the human risk.

The animals are farmed for their fur, which is then typically exported to fashion manufacturers in China, Hong Kong, and Russia and used in items like coats and scarves.

Scientists have long warned that if H5N1 acquires the ability to spread efficiently between people, it could trigger a human pandemic.

“Avian influenza viruses tend to replicate pretty poorly in humans and don’t really have the right sort of properties that allow them to transmit from person to person.

“If H5N1 were to cause a pandemic, it would need to make quite a lot of changes, and there’s a real concern that mink, particularly farmed mink, have a lot of the features that could drive the evolution of H5N1,” Dr Tom Peacock, a virologist at The Pirbright Institute, told The Telegraph.

News.title: Collapsing child vaccination in South Africa ‘a public health emergency’
News.content:
Plummeting child immunisation rates are now a public health emergency in South Africa and risk causing outbreaks of preventable but potentially deadly childhood diseases, the government has said.

The proportion of children under one who have received no vaccinations has trebled in the past decade to nearly a third of infants in South Africa.

Mistrust of vaccines and growing ignorance about the benefits of childhood immunisations risk undoing years of progress made by one of the continent’s most effective health systems.

Outbreaks of measles, diphtheria and whooping cough this year have all been linked to poor immunisation rates and are evidence that herd immunity is breaking down, officials warned.

An alert from the department for health said the proportion of unvaccinated infants had hit 36.3 per cent in the first four months of 2026, up from 12.1 per cent in 2017.

The department warned the jump was “effectively tripling the number of completely unvaccinated children and leaving hundreds of thousands of infants at risk of life-threatening illnesses”.

Coverage of the six-in-one hexavalent infant vaccine that protects against diphtheria, tetanus, whooping cough, polio, meningitis, and hepatitis B declined from 87 per cent to 60.5 per cent over the same period.

Officials said the shortfall was caused by a lack of people coming forward to bring their children for jabs and was not due to any shortage of vaccines.

Dr Nonhlanhla Ndlovu, deputy director general of South Africa’s health department, told the state broadcaster that parents had a poor understanding of the public health benefits of childhood jabs.

She said: “The second one that comes out is the issue of public trust, in terms of the safety of the vaccines, but also the trust in terms of our systems.”

“Theses vaccines are very safe and we have seen the gains that we have had in our years before and now that is changing.

“The benefit of vaccines far outweigh anything we can talk about in public health. We need them to come back and bring the children for immunisation.”

News.title: Man City sign Enzo Fernandez for £125m to end transfer saga of the summer
News.content:
It is expected to be another busy deadline day in the Premier League, with many clubs still hoping to finalise deals before the transfer window shuts at 11pm. Here, Telegraph Sport identifies 10 potential high-profile moves that could yet go through.

Julian Alvarez to Barcelona… or Arsenal

This has been the most dramatic and relentless saga of the European transfer window. The situation, as far as we understand it, is as follows: Barcelona want Alvarez and Alvarez wants Barcelona, but Atletico Madrid refuse to sell him to Barcelona. Arsenal want Alvarez, and Atletico are more open to selling him to Arsenal, but Alvarez only wants Barcelona. For a move to happen, it will require one party to change their mind. Either Atletico decides to sell to Barcelona, or Alvarez decides he will join Arsenal.

Enzo Fernandez to Manchester City

Another long-running saga. Chelsea are well aware of City’s interest in Fernandez but want a massive fee for the Argentina international, having initially valued him at £120m. City have the cash and the space in the squad after saying goodbye to Rodri, Tijani Reijnders, Nico Gonzalez and Bernardo Silva this summer. Fernandez has not featured in Chelsea’s last two games.

Lamine Camara to Chelsea

As reported by Telegraph Sport last week, Chelsea have identified Monaco midfielder Camara as a target amid the uncertainty over Fernandez’s future. French reports on Monday suggested the move may have stalled, however. The clock is ticking.

Iliman Ndiaye to Manchester City

Spurs had been working on a deal to sign Ndiaye from Everton but they now appear to have fallen behind City in the race for the winger, as a consequence of City failing in their attempt to sign Cody Gakpo from Liverpool. City are ready to complete the hijack on deadline day.

Ismaila Sarr to Liverpool

A deal that, as of Monday night, is regarded as unlikely to happen. As with their interest in Brighton’s Yankuba Minteh, Liverpool have so far been unable to strike a deal with Crystal Palace for Sarr, who scored 21 goals in 45 games last season. Liverpool would only allow Gakpo to leave if a replacement, such as Sarr, can be signed.

News.title: Borrowing cost surge leaves Healey with £10bn headache
News.content:
Britain’s borrowing costs have surged at one of the fastest paces in the world in a move that threatens to blow a near £10bn hole in Chancellor John Healey’s fiscal plans.

Interest rates on 10-year gilts, a benchmark for Treasury borrowing costs, rose to the highest level since 2008 on Tuesday amid a global bond market rout.

Britain’s cost to borrow over 20 years rose to its highest level since 1998, signalling growing stress in the market.

Government borrowing costs around the world have climbed sharply in recent weeks, amid concerns about unsustainable debts and persistent inflation.

However, Britain suffered the biggest increase in bond yields in the G7 on Tuesday as economists warned that investors were particularly nervous ahead of Mr Healey’s first Budget.

Sports.title: Hamilton reveals hope of becoming first black Ferrari driver to win in Italy
Sports.content:
Lewis Hamilton says he has been considering the magnitude of potentially becoming the first black Ferrari Formula 1 driver to win a home race for the team, ahead of this weekend's Italian Grand Prix.

The seven-time world champion has enjoyed a much improved second campaign in red, with a first Grand Prix win for the team in Barcelona in June helping to keep him in title contention, as he trails Mercedes' Kimi Antonelli by 59 points with 11 rounds remaining.

Hamilton's hopes of claiming victory in Monza have been boosted by the fact Antonelli will start from the back of the grid as he serves a penalty for exceeding his engine-part allowance.

Asked what a prospective 107th career Grand Prix win would mean to him, Hamilton said: "I've really thought coming into this weekend, as I pondered, just thinking of the sheer magnitude of the concept that I'm coming to this Grand Prix, I didn't even know that I had I was equal with Michael [Schumacher] on [five Monza] wins, for example.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton claimed his first win in red at the Barcelona-Catalunya Grand Prix.

"But the thought that there's a first ahead of me, in the sense that potentially, if I was to win, you go into new territory.

"Winning in Monza for the first time with Ferrari is something I've witnessed Charles [Leclerc] win in 2019, when I was on the podium with him. But to do it while I'm here would be phenomenal.

"And the thought of if I did do that, probably I would be the only black driver to ever do that for Ferrari in Italy probably in history, maybe, and so just like a lot of those thoughts have been through my mind.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Lewis Hamilton and Charles Leclerc were greeted with a big reception as Ferrari fans gathered in Milan to cheer on the F1 stars at a House of Peroni Nastro Azzurro 0.0% event.

"The pressure is high. You also want to deliver for the team. There's all those people at the factory, many of them will get to come to this race, the Tifosi, who come in huge numbers and the passion is unmatched, and you want to deliver for them as well.

"And my mum's here this weekend because I don't think she's been to Monza, but also particularly on a Ferrari weekend. I wanted her to experience that and you know bring any of the lucky dust she can bring."

Engine upgrade won't recover 'whole gap'

Hamilton's hopes of victory should be boosted by the arrival of Ferrari's second engine upgrade of the season.

The team confirmed on Wednesday that they have taken up the second of two opportunities they've been granted to improve their engine during their 2026 campaign.

Perhaps Ferrari's biggest weakness this season has been having a weaker power unit than Mercedes, who also supply McLaren with their engines.

Hamilton said: "Every little helps, and I think up until this point of the year we've been losing, even in the last race on such a short circuit we were losing four tenths a lap through the race. That's a huge deficit and we've carried that through the year to this point.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Speaking on the F1 Show podcast, Harry Benjamin believes Lewis Hamilton can take positives away from the Dutch Grand Prix, despite a frustrating result.

"What I can say is I'm really proud when I go back to the factory and see how hard everyone is working. They're really just heads down, and everyone's so enthusiastic.

"I see a different focus this year to last year. Last year, I felt like there wasn't really a north star. We were doing the best we could, but not really knowing exactly what we were trying to aim for. Now we have a north star, and we know where we need to work towards.

"I think they've done a tremendous job to really pull together and deliver. This is a step forward, it's not the whole gap that we need but we knew that would be the case.

"But to see bits coming each weekend, adding to the car, it's exciting to see that we are pushing and I strongly still believe that we've got what it takes to win."

Sports.title: British NFL player Traore: I'll do what I need to do to make Dolphins impact
Sports.content:
You may have heard Seydou Traore's story before. The likelihood is that you'll hear it many more times throughout his NFL career.

Despite the recent successes of Jay Ajayi, Efe Obada and Jermaine Eluemunor, it is still rare to see a British player in the NFL, and Traore is already on a unique journey

By being selected in the 2026 NFL Draft (fifth round, 180th overall), Traore became the first player to have attended London's NFL Academy and later be drafted to the NFL - after taking part in trials as a 16-year-old at Tottenham Hotspur Stadium all the way back in 2019.

After moving to Florida to seek a college scholarship, he played two seasons at Arkansas State before transferring to Mississippi State, sitting out a year, then putting together two more seasons that caught the eyes of NFL scouts.

Since being drafted, he has made Miami's initial 53-man roster, but there is a lot more work to do. Traore spoke to Sky Sports this summer about the draft, landing in Miami, and his future in the league...

The NFL Draft experience

It was a long road from the NFL Academy to having his name called and walking across the stage in Pittsburgh, and Traore said the draft-day experience was "everything I expected and more".

He said: "Having my mum and my sister there with me meant a lot. Being able to reap the rewards of the years of hard work and the years they haven't been able to see me and be around me. As much as it was for me, it was for them.

"Heading on to that stage is an amazing feeling. I was speechless when I got out there, but yeah, it was amazing."

Unsurprisingly, Traore said he was inundated with "a bunch" of messages from people involved in the International Player Pathway programme, whether players, coaches or staff.

"Everyone from back home was checking up on me, congratulating me and just wishing me the best, saying they've either seen the videos or read this," he said.

"I was more than happy to go through each one and just connect with people and say thank you."

Life in Miami

Image: Traore faces a long road to make an NFL impact

After spending five years in what he called the "countryside" of Arkansas and Mississippi, Traore is back in a lively city.

However, he didn't have much time for exploring. First up was training, conditioning, film, playbook and importantly: forming connections.

The Dolphins are coming off a disappointing 7-10 season, their second straight losing campaign. That meant the end of the Mike McDaniel era and a fresh start in Miami.

For new head coach Jeff Hafley, new general manager Jon-Eric Sullivan, and new quarterback Malik Willis, the main goal is bringing the team together.

"The first thing is connection," Traore explained.

"Connection between the whole team and teammates and everything.

"We'll be eating; no one's on their phones. When they're in this building, people are trying to get better and connect with teammates.

Image: Traore played college football for Mississippi State

"So at the door, you understand once you get in here, you're coming in with a purpose.

"Everything outside, you can put on pause for a few hours, but get to know the people you're going to be with the whole day. Because those are the people that are going to have your back on the field."

What does the future hold?

Traore could offer something to a Miami team lacking offensive weapons right now, but it's a long road ahead.

Tight ends rarely make an instant impact, and fifth-round picks face a fight each and every year to make a team.

The 24-year-old understands his situation and knows his career won't be defined by year one.

"It's such a long process," Traore said. "So you've got to look at the far picture."

In his rookie campaign, his plan is "learning, soaking up as much as I can this first year and showing when I do have those chances, showing the ability to make a play."

"If the play is out there, make it."

He has no specific goals or milestones but Traore knows what he can offer to the league, now and in the future.

He said: "I'm versatile. Not just on the field - as a person as well. I adapt pretty well to different stuff.

"I'm a team player. I am willing to do what I need to do for the team's success.

Sports.title: Graffard's Drazinda faces Armor Supreme
Sports.content:
Lingfield, Southwell, Newcastle and ParisLongchamp are the venues for today's action - live on Sky Sports Racing.

2.40 ParisLongchamp - Listed winners Drazinda and Armor Supreme lock horns

Listed winners Drazinda and Armor Supreme lock horns in the Group three Prix d'Arenberg.

The Francis-Henri Graffard-trained Drazinda has improved with each run this season after a nice debut win. After chasing down Victorious and Senorita Bonita in the Queen Mary when drawn on the wrong side, she placed second in a Listed race before going one better last month.

A quality-looking edition of the Group 1 Prix Morny was a step too far, but this Sioux Nation filly still ran creditably and can continue her progression down in grade.

She just about sets the standard, although Diego Dias' progressive filly Armor Supreme beat the former in the Queen Mary when drawn on the quicker side. She then franked the form when scoring at Listed level impressively over at the Curragh last time out. She should be primed for a big run and these two should be closely matched.

Grayrobin won two on the bounce since moving to Kate McGivern before finishing just over a length behind the aforementioned Armor Supreme. She should go close again, albeit the winner was well on top at the line that day.

Archie Watson's Vollering and Valentina Bella round off the field of five, but both will need to improve a fair bit to feature at the front end.

4.55 Lingfield - Highly tried Kamaal drops in class against Mouj Albuhoor

On home soil, the highly-tried Kamaal drops in class against Arqana Series fifth Mouj Albuhoor in the Sky Sports Racing Sky 415 / EBF Novice Stakes.

Jack Jones' son of Minzaal sets a solid standard with an eye-catching 10th in the Coventry Stakes at Royal Ascot. He then took a step backwards when eighth in the Rose Bowl but the ground may have been a touch too quick that day for a sharp six furlongs at Newbury. He shaped as if seven furlongs could suit when staying on at the Royal meeting and as a half-brother to Breeders' Cup Juvenile Turf third North Coast, who ran his best at two over a mile, this lad can get back on track down in grade and up in trip.

The opposition is not without potential, with the Richard Hughes-trained Mouj Albuhoor clearly well thought of having gone off a short-priced favourite in the valuable Arqana Series Stakes at Deauville last month. He raced too freely to win that day but ran creditably in fifth and could be quite a nice type going forward.

The fourth-placed Munch came out and ran well in another novice, with seventh-placed Catch My Eye very much franking the form when improving markedly to beat promising juveniles Charged and Katon.

Ralph Beckett fields 125,000gns two-year-old Saturn Star, who contains more of a middle-distance-based pedigree. Any market clues will be informative for this debutant.

6.10 Southwell - Godolphin's Castlemont returns following striking debut success

Godolphin's Castlemont returns in the bettingsites.co.uk Novice Stakes following striking debut success.

A full-brother to Bay Bridge, Charlie Appleby's gelding put up a taking display when winning a fair novice at Windsor in July. He overcame inexperience when looking green a few furlongs out, but did his best work late to win with plenty in hand.

The step up in trip should only be an advantage judging by both pedigree and his debut performance, and he should prove tough to beat.

Walking On Stars is going the right way for Sir Mark Prescott and gets 12lbs from Billy Loughnane's aforementioned mount, whilst Maestro Del Mar and Liam Mera Kai set a fair standard with creditable runs this season. However, they will have to improve quite markedly to reach the level of Castlemont as long as the Godolphin contender runs to form.

Best of the rest...

At Lingfield, Hamdania bids to make it two from two Download The At The Races App Fillies' Restricted Novice Stakes but may need the run returning from a break. Andrew Balding's Mystic Music looks to be the best of the opposition, having chased home Moonswept at 50/1 the last day. Later on the card, Wyle Cop aims for a course and distance hat-trick in the Free Tips On attheraces.com Handicap (4.20pm).

At Newcastle, Norfolk Stakes third Mussab looks to bounce back in the 3.59pm Admiral Race To Riches Novice Stakes having disappointed in the Gimcrack the last day. A step into calmer waters down in class should suit. Southwell's 5.05pm bettingsites.co.uk Novice Stakes sees the Amo-owned Black Orchid attempt to turn three seconds into a first success.

Back in France...

Impressive the last day at Dieppe, Daryoura seeks to back up that debut win against Juddmonte's Maintain and Prix de Diane fifth Evita in the Prix de Liancourt at ParisLongchamp. In the following Prix Joubert, Charlie Appleby's Ribbon Of Sea steps up in class, with stablemate Tribal Queen also in situ.

Godspeed, Braida and Fortuna Diamond clash in the Prix de la Cochere (4.25pm), with representatives from the Jack Channon and James Fanshawe yards also present.

Sports.title: The WSL returns bigger than ever and with a mouthwatering title race
Sports.content:
It has been a summer of change for women’s football in England, with expansion of the Women’s Super League to 14 teams bringing three new sides into the fold, huge transfers hitting the headlines, changes to the League Cup and a new name on the WSL trophy as we prepare for kick-off on Friday.

Players have had a proper break over the summer, with no major international women’s tournament for the first time in six years (Covid delays pushed back the Tokyo Olympics to 2021 and the European Championship to 2022, followed by the 2023 World Cup, 2024 Paris Olympics and Euro 2025). As a result, managers have had a full pre-season with all available players for the first time in more than half a decade, too.

In many respects, this is the most mouthwatering and unpredictable WSL season of recent years. At the top end, the title race is wide open from the outset. The holders, Manchester City, have perhaps the most settled squad and a potent attack spearheaded by the winner of three back-to-back Golden Boots, Bunny Shaw. However, they will also be juggling their league and FA Cup title defences alongside Champions League football, which they avoided last season through a fourth-place finish in the league the preceding year. That will be counteracted somewhat by Champions League teams no longer competing in the rebranded League Cup, which also opens the door to domestic silverware for those outside the top three.

Arsenal and Renée Slegers have no excuses for a poor season, after two disappointing and costly starts to WSL campaigns were somewhat understandable due to the tight turnarounds following the major tournament exploits of many players, and Champions League qualifying campaigns in the 2022-23 and 2023-24 season. The Gunners have overhauled the squad in the summer and lowered the age profile, adding experienced top-level talent such as Georgia Stanway, Ona Batlle, Géraldine Reuteler and Selina Cerci.

Chelsea have embarked on their own squad evolution, after a transitional season where they sought to strike the balance between making changes and retaining that winning spirit synonymous with the side. Some hugely influential and longstanding players have departed in Millie Bright, who has retired, Guro Reiten, Sam Kerr, Catarina Macario, Johanna Rytting Kaneryd and Niamh Charles.

Melvine Malard, who has reunited with Sonia Bompastor having played under her at OL Lyonnes, has already hit the ground running with two goals from the bench in the team’s 5-2 win against Real Sociedad in the first leg of their Champions League qualifier. Where playing in Champions League qualifiers was a burden in seasons following major international tournaments, this campaign it could be an advantage for the Blues who have a chance to shake off any rust before they kick off their title challenge.

It perhaps feels a little unfair to drop Manchester United out of the title challengers and to place them in with “the best of the rest” but, with a nine-point gap between them and Chelsea last season, a lack of serious backing from the club and a so far underwhelming transfer window, this season could be a tough one for the Red Devils.

Marc Skinner’s exit after a frustrating five years in Manchester was welcomed by sections of their fanbase but the manager arguably helped the side to punch well above their weight, with a comparatively small wage bill despite a competitive turnover. Eva Olid is an exciting young manager, having led Hearts from the bottom of the Scottish Women’s Premier League (with the team avoiding relegation only because of league expansion) to the title before her exit at the end of last season. However, if fans are hoping for a fresh start they should perhaps temper their excitement, with the club leaning into Olid’s reputation for player development and their four summer recruits so far not doing anywhere near enough to offset the loss of their outgoing players.

View image in fullscreen Eva Olid talks to the media on the eve of the new WSL season. Photograph: Poppy Townson/MUFC/Manchester United/Getty Images

They could be troubled by a chasing pack who have invested shrewdly, in the case of Tottenham, Everton, Liverpool and Brighton, or boldly, in the case of London City Lionesses.

United’s first challenge is against Michelle Kang’s big-spending side as they open the WSL season on Friday night, when the two-time Ballon d’Or winner Alexia Putellas will answer the question of whether she can “do it on a Friday night in Bromley”.

The London City manager Eder Maestre has the enviable job of being able to put together his dream team, but the unenviable job of trying to gel a side that have had 13 departures and eight players coming in. The decision to remove the manager that led them into the WSL, Jocelyn Prêcheur, was billed as a purely football one by sources, with the club sixth in the league in their first season in the top flight. That decision, though, shows Kang will not accept mediocrity and the patience required by Maestre may not be forthcoming.

Tottenham and Brighton are two other teams aiming high. Martin Ho’s Spurs are the league’s not-so-dark dark horses, with a hugely impressive debut season for their manager followed by an astute and targeted transfer window, which has included the recruitment of the third-highest scorer in the league last season, the midfielder Kirsty Hanson, and the club-record signing Alice Sombath from OL Lyonnes.

The impact of the shock departure of Dario Vidosic from Brighton, with his move to the NWSL side Angel City announced soon after, will be fully known when the season gets under way, but they have recruited a very promising young replacement in Arturo Ruiz and their squad has huge potential after a strong window.

Everton, Liverpool and West Ham could all prove to be surprise packages this season after similarly impressive transfer windows as the middle-lower end of the table ups its game.

View image in fullscreen Everton will be looking to make an impact in the top half this season. Photograph: Tony Smith/Alamy

Aston Villa have recruited 10 to replace the nine departed players but the fear will be that the incoming players struggle to fill the hole of players such as Hanson, Ebony Salmon and Gabi Nunes.

Of the newcomers to the WSL, Birmingham and Crystal Palace have overseen similarly large squad turnovers, with some top-level talent brought in to attempt to ensure they avoid the drop back down to WSL 2 such as Millie Turner and Lisa Naalsund for the former and Bethany England for the latter.

Charlton have not been able to recruit so ambitiously in the summer, though eight new players have arrived to help the manager, Karen Hills, and her side hoping to leave egg on the faces of many who will have put them as favourites to go down.

Predicting results or the outcome of the season is nigh on impossible though, and that will be the hope: that the expanded league delivers surprises.

Sports.title: Andoni Iraola defends transfer strategy and reveals Liverpool turned down options
Sports.content:
Andoni Iraola has defended Liverpool’s summer transfer strategy and said the club’s priority was to sign quality over quantity.

Liverpool had the highest net spend in the Premier League, with Bradley Barcola, signed for a potential £123m, added to a front line that includes the £125m Alexander Isak and £116m Florian Wirtz. Barcola could make his debut at Ipswich on Friday, despite not featuring for Paris Saint-Germain before his move on Monday.
