World.title: Is Quebec actually the most taxed jurisdiction in North America?
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

With the rising cost of living front and centre in the Quebec election campaign, a familiar refrain has emerged: Quebec is the most taxed jurisdiction in North America.

Conservative Party of Quebec Leader Éric Duhaime is leaning on that claim to justify his promise of deep income and corporate tax cuts to help address the cost of living.

"Quebecers face the highest tax burden in North America. It is now the government's turn to tighten its belt,” Duhaime said in a news release last Friday.

He repeated that point during a news conference the same day, saying Quebec is "the worst one" among 60 states and provinces across Canada and the U.S.

But is the claim actually true? We took a closer look.

An overall heavy burden

The short answer is yes — with an asterisk. It depends on what exactly is being measured, according to Luc Godbout, a professor and the research chair in taxation and public finance at the Université de Sherbrooke.

One way to answer this question is through what economists call the "overall tax burden." This involves adding up all taxes paid to federal, provincial and local authorities by individuals and businesses, and then expressing that as a percentage of the gross domestic product (GDP).

By that measure, Quebec does indeed have the highest taxes among all 10 Canadian provinces, sitting at 38.6 per cent of its GDP for 2024, according to an annual study prepared by Godbout and other researchers at the university.

Quebec also has a higher overall tax burden than the United States and Mexico.

As this chart shows, the province's tax burden sits closer to the average of advanced countries in the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD).

Another way to measure the tax burden is by analyzing it at the individual level and looking at personal income taxes, social contributions and consumption taxes, Godbout explained to CBC News.

On that front, Quebec’s gross individual tax burden is heavier than all other provinces except one: Nova Scotia, Godbout pointed out.

On the whole, if Nova Scotia's tax system were applied to Quebecers, they would actually pay more.

LISTEN | This is Montreal: Should Quebec cut taxes to tackle the cost of living?: This is Montreal 15:16 Should Quebec cut taxes to tackle the cost of living? It’s often repeated that Quebecers pay the highest taxes of any jurisdiction in North America. CBC reporter Ben Shingler breaks down how the tax burden on Quebecers compares to elsewhere and what we get for it. And we’ll hear why some economists are saying that any government intervention to help with the cost of living needs to be targeted to the people who need it the most.

Taxes shrink wealth gap

The picture becomes more nuanced when evaluating what's called the "net tax burden."

This measure takes into account not only what individuals pay in taxes, but also what they get back through refundable tax credits and family allowances paid directly to households.

By this metric, the tax system in Quebec actually results in a lighter burden for individuals than in four of the nine other provinces. Nova Scotia, Prince Edward Island, Newfoundland and Labrador, and New Brunswick all have a higher net tax burden, Godbout pointed out.

For example, a single-parent family earning $56,714 (which is two-thirds of the average wage) in Quebec gets back 12 per cent more in government transfers than they pay in total taxes — the lowest net burden in Canada, according to the annual study.

On the flip side, high-income earners with no children are heavily taxed in the province.

A single person earning $141,362 (which is two-thirds more than the average wage) faces a net tax burden of nearly 35 per cent, the highest in the country.

As the chart below illustrates, Quebec's tax system significantly shrinks the wealth gap.

Before taxes, Quebec's Gini coefficient, which measures inequality, is 0.43, but government transfers drop it to 0.27, leaving the province with some of the lowest income inequality in the country.

Colin Pratte, a researcher at the Institut de recherche et d’informations socioéconomiques (IRIS), argues higher tax collection in Quebec serves as an effective mechanism for wealth redistribution.

He points to the latest numbers from Statistics Canada, that show Ontario’s poverty rate is 50 per cent higher than in Quebec.

“It is actually the main tool for a given government, a given society, to make sure that wealth is well distributed among people of that society,” he said.

So, while Duhaime’s campaign rhetoric rings true for corporations, high-income earners, and childless individuals, Quebec's system of government transfers means lower-income families actually face some of the lightest net tax burdens on the continent.

World.title: Vaccine-preventable illnesses on the horizon again as Canadian kids head back to school
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

With millions of Canadian kids heading back to school and temperatures set to drop, it’s time to brace for another fall of seasonal illnesses — and medical experts say staying healthy takes more than just a flu shot.

The latest federal surveillance report , which tracks influenza, COVID-19 and respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), shows it’s likely the calm before the storm, with low and stable levels of all three respiratory threats that are set to come roaring back in the months ahead.

“As we transition to colder weather and we’re inside more, that’s when the bugs spread … and that’s when we see our emergency department visits start to go up, and then kids in the hospital more,” said Saskatoon-based pediatrician Dr. Ayisha Kurji, an assistant professor at the University of Saskatchewan.

McMaster University immunologist Matthew Miller says Canadians should already start assessing their options to get seasonal vaccines. For flu specifically, he noted that last year included a “really unusual severe early peak” in influenza circulation.

“We saw really high case counts in … early December, which is about a month in advance of when we normally see flu season peak,” Miller said.

“What that means is that it's really important to be immunized in a timely manner in the fall to ensure that our immune systems have time to respond to the vaccine and mount that protective immunity.”

It typically takes around two to four weeks for the body to hit a peak immune response to the shot, he said.

And Miller stressed that a fall flu shot — which is recommended for all Canadians aged six months and up — is just one piece of the “suite of vaccines” families should consider.

Measles, for example, has continued circulating, and this fall may see further spread.

“Coming out of the summer months where families have often travelled ... puts everybody at increased risk when the school year starts again,” said Miller, “and all these young children, who have been to all kinds of different places, are now in close quarters again in classrooms.”

WATCH | Mother urges parents to vaccinate kids after daughter's measles death: Mother urges parents to vaccinate kids after daughter’s measles death | Duration 2:07 Measles may start like a bad cold — with symptoms like a high fever and cough — but in rare cases, it turns deadly. For one child, complications emerged about a decade later, robbing her of speech, movement and, eventually, her life.

Flu, COVID, RSV shots available for fall

Canada’s national vaccine advisory body recommends a COVID shot for higher-risk individuals , including older adults 65 and up and anyone who is pregnant or has underlying medical conditions.

“I still recommend the COVID vaccine because it’s still something that’s around, and still sends people into hospital,” said Kurji.

RSV vaccines are also available for older adults and pregnant individuals, to combat what Miller called an “extraordinarily dangerous virus to newborns.”

Real-world research has shown these relatively new shots are making a huge difference in serious RSV-related illness, with one large study showing the vaccine given during pregnancy cut babies’ hospital risk by more than 80 per cent .

“It's really having a profound impact on reducing rates of infection and particularly severe infection in these age groups — older adults and, in particular, newborns,” Miller said.

Beyond seasonal vaccines, experts stress Canadians need to stay up to date on their routine shots as well, given the resurgence of a range of vaccine-preventable diseases like measles, which can lead to flu-like symptoms and a blotchy rash, or in more serious cases, pneumonia, brain swelling, or even death.

“We have seen, since the pandemic, a decrease in uptake in the basic regular childhood vaccines,” said Dr. Joss Reimer, Canada’s chief public health officer.

“The recent spread of measles really shows us exactly what we need to be worried about,” she added.

“As soon as our numbers dip below a certain level, we do start to see these viruses come back and put children at risk, especially those kids who are either too young or, for some other health reason, can't get vaccinated.”

WATCH | Calls for B.C. to adopt universal infant RSV immunization program: Group calls on B.C. government to adopt a universal infant RSV immunization program | Duration 3:32 A national organization of women physicians is calling on B.C. to adopt a universal infant RSV immunization program ahead of this year's cold and flu season. Currently, pregnant people can elect to get the maternal RSV vaccine but they must pay out of pocket. The Federation of Medical Women of Canada is calling for a provincial program that would cover the costs for all. We spoke with Dr. Shelley Ross, who co-chairs the RSV task force.

Measles resurgence across Canada, U.S.

Just 85 per cent of two-year-olds in Canada were fully vaccinated against measles, mumps and rubella by the end of 2025, federal data shows — a far cry from the 95 per cent medical experts say is needed population-wide to keep measles at bay.

The same data shows less than 80 per cent of children that age were fully vaccinated with the shot targeting diphtheria, tetanus, and whooping cough.�

Middling vaccination rates in recent years have contributed to an explosion of measles, one of the world’s most contagious viruses, across North America.

The U.S. has seen 37 new outbreaks so far in 2026, involving thousands of cases, while Canada lost its official measles elimination status last November after racking up more than 5,000 infections since late 2024, and more than 1,000 new cases just this year.

B.C.'s provincial health officer Dr. Bonnie Henry recently said most of the 30 people hospitalized since the start of that province's outbreak last year have been unvaccinated children.

“It’s sad to me that’s that where we are,” Kurji said. “Measles is an illness that is highly preventable [through vaccines]… one dose is great, two doses is almost perfect.”

Most modern clinicians haven’t even witnessed a real measles infection in their lifetime, Kurji added, which means cases can be tougher to spot and precautions to prevent onward transmission may not be put in place fast enough.

World.title: Saint John police apologize after woman told to cover up at beach
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A Saint John woman who was told by police to cover up while topless at a city beach this summer has received a formal apology from the Saint John Police Force.

Lacey Tompkins was at Dominion Park Beach on July 25 when she took off her bikini top while sunbathing. She said a lifeguard approached her and told her to cover up.

When she declined, a police officer also told her she needed to alter her attire.

Tompkins said she was surprised by the request because she understood that women can be topless in public in Canada.

“I was a little shocked and a little bit confused,” she said.

Tompkins eventually complied with the officer’s request but later filed a service complaint with the New Brunswick Police Commission on July 27.

Dominion Park Beach is a popular beach on the St. John River on the west side of Saint John. (CBC)

In an Aug. 11 letter to Tompkins, Neal Fowler, the acting chief of the Saint John Police Force, said the incident was reviewed.

The review included police records, a call to police for service, and body-worn camera footage from responding officers.

“Based on the available evidence, it was determined there was no legal basis requiring you to alter your attire,” Fowler wrote. “In these circumstances, the direction provided to you was not supported by the applicable law.”

Police said officers had been called to the beach following concerns raised by lifeguards. An officer then approached Tompkins and advised her that she was required to alter her attire.

According to the review, Tompkins questioned the basis for the direction and remained respectful throughout the interaction. No enforcement action was taken, although she complied with the officer’s request.

The police force said the incident identified a need for additional education about the applicable law and relevant case law.

The responding officer received immediate guidance from a supervisor. Frontline members and supervisors also received further education about Criminal Code provisions relating to indecent acts.

Fowler acknowledged that being directed by police to do something Tompkins believed she was not legally required to do would be concerning.

“As a police organization, we have a responsibility to ensure our members are properly informed, trained, and equipped to apply the law appropriately and consistently when responding to calls for service,” Fowler wrote.

“Please accept my apology on behalf of the Saint John Police Force for the interaction and the concern it caused.”

Tompkins said she welcomed the response.

“I think it’s a really good thing,” she said. “It just shines a light on people being aware of what they are permitted and not permitted to do.”

What does the law say?

The legal question goes back to a 1996 decision by the Ontario Court of Appeal. The court considered whether then-student Gwen Jacob's removal of her shirt while walking on a Guelph street in sweltering weather had constituted an indecent act under the Criminal Code.

The court found that toplessness, on its own, does not make a woman’s conduct an indecent act. The circumstances of the conduct are relevant, including whether it is sexual in nature.

Howard Sapers, executive director of the Canadian Civil Liberties Association, told CBC News earlier this summer that municipalities cannot change how the Criminal Code is interpreted.

“The simple answer is no. A municipal bylaw can’t alter the way the Criminal Code is interpreted,” Sapers said.

For Tompkins, the issue is also about equality and the different standards applied to men’s and women’s bodies.

“We tend to lean towards sexualizing women’s bodies,” she said. “We are not applying the same standard to everyone.”

Tompkins has since returned to Dominion Park Beach and continues to go topless.

“Nothing happened,” she said. “I was there and I sunbathed and then I was left alone.”

She said she hopes other women will be able to exercise the same right without having to go through a similar experience.

World.title: Gloria Steinem, leading U.S. feminist and author, dead at 92
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Gloria Steinem, the celebrated U.S. author and activist who became one of the most potent voices of the feminist movement, has died. She was 92.

Steinem, a co-founder of Ms. magazine, was a hugely recognizable presence wherever she went. And she went everywhere: Much of her life as an advocate was spent on the road, speaking at college campuses and community centres, at rallies and marches.

She died Wednesday at her home in New York City, according to her foundation's social media pages.

"Gloria's greatest gift was her ability to listen to others, to make others feel seen and heard," the posts said. "Her words, actions, and example gave people permission to be their truest selves. Gloria lived true to her independent spirit, always with curiosity and a great sense of humour."

Steinem enjoyed writing and spending time in the community in recent years, the posts said. She also hosted talking circles for hundreds of people in her home. She died just before a planned memoir was to be released this fall.

In a 2019 interview with CBC News, Steinem said she had not seen as much grassroots activism in all of her years advocating for feminist issues as she had during U.S. President Donald Trump's first term.

My role is to listen to younger women and to say, 'What can I do to help?'" she said, when she was asked about the broader backlash from other activists amid a push for intersectional feminism.

"It's not to tell anybody what to do, that's ridiculous. It's to listen."

WATCH | Steinem speaks to CBC News in 2019: ‘I’ve never seen more activism in my life’: Gloria Steinem | The Weekly with Wendy Mesley | Duration 6:30 Feminist icon Gloria Steinem reflects on the evolution of the women’s movement and the rise of grassroots activism in the age of U.S. President Donald Trump.

She began her career as a journalist, notably one who reported, in 1963, on degrading conditions in Hugh Hefner's Playboy empire, an undercover assignment she came to later regret. She credits a meeting six years later, where women spoke out boldly in favour of abortion rights, with changing her career path.

"That speak-out was the beginning of activism for me," Steinem, who had undergone a secret illegal abortion herself at age 22, told The Associated Press in an email in 2022, reflecting on the reversal of Roe v. Wade. "Either our control over our own bodies is equal, regardless of sex or race, or we're not living in a democracy."

Activism spanned decades

Though she soon became a known activist, those who watched Steinem denounce discrimination for so many years likely never suspected that she'd had to overcome a deep fear of public speaking. She would have simply stuck to writing, she said, if only editors at the time had been willing to let her write about the women's movement.

But they weren't interested, she told The Associated Press in 2015.

"So I ended up going out and speaking, which was my nightmare," she said. "I mean, I was terrified. But I'm grateful, even though I still get scared even now."

In this Nov. 21, 1979, photo, American attorneys and politicians Bella Abzug, left, and Patsy Mink sit next to Gloria Steinem during a speech in Washington where they warned presidential candidates that promises about women's rights would not be enough to get their support in the next election. (Harvey Georges/The Associated Press)

Time hardly slowed Steinem down; well into her 80s she was traveling the globe and speaking out on issues of importance to her. These included everything from genital mutilation to Korean reconciliation, but it was equality for women that took precedence.

"Being a feminist means that you see the world as whole instead of half," she once said. "It shouldn't need a name, and one day it won't."

A few days after her 85th birthday, she was leading a women's "talking circle" at an off-Broadway play celebrating her life, where one by one, women in the audience — many fighting tears — rose to thank her and tell their own stories of discrimination.

In 2020, her life was the subject of a feature film: The Glorias, A Life on the Road, based on her 2015 memoir and starring Julianne Moore.

And at 91, she collaborated on a picture book with Liberian peace activist and Nobel laureate Leymah Gbowee aimed at inspiring young people to change the world. Rise, Girl, Rise: Our Sister-Friend Journey. Together for All was published in February 2026.

The constant visibility came with a price. Even into her older years, Steinem expressed frustration that despite her accomplishments, she was often described as beautiful or glamorous (A 1992 Vanity Fair profile noted her "spectacular racehorse legs.") It was a label she said unfairly detracted from her message.

"Nobody ever called me beautiful until I was publicly a feminist, and that was in my mid-30s," she said. "It was clear that label was being assigned to me. The most hurtful part is that you work very hard, and people say it's because of your looks."

Steinem also had to deal with hostility, which sometimes came from surprising places.

Steinem is pictured during a visit to Toronto on Sept. 28, 2011. (Chris Young/Canadian Press)

Appearing on Larry King's talk show on CNN in 1990, she was visibly stunned when a female caller greeted her cheerfully, then told her to "rot in hell" because she had ruined "the beautiful American family."

But by then, she noted, at least people were taking feminists seriously. That wasn't the case in 1972 when she co-founded Ms. magazine and many commentators — especially male — dismissed it as ridiculous, predicting an early demise. (The magazine continues to this day, published by the Feminist Majority Foundation.)

Among Steinem's detractors was then-president Richard Nixon, who was caught on an Oval Office tape ridiculing both her and the "Ms." title. The ridicule was mutual: In a 1972 National Press Club speech, Steinem called Nixon "the most sexually insecure chief of state since Napoleon."

It was just one example of Steinem's trademark wit. Before she married at 66, she often explained her singlehood by saying "I can't mate in captivity."

Laughter, she wrote, was "the only free emotion — the only one that can't be compelled."

World.title: 'Choppy McChopface' among favourite suggested helicopter names, N.S. documents show
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Name suggestions for Nova Scotia's four new helicopters ranged from imitative to imaginative, according to the full list of recommendations obtained exclusively by CBC News.

Among the favourites, the most common was a combination of "Choppy McChopface" and variants of the same theme.

That suggested naming format mimicked the winner of a British vessel naming contest in 2016 , when U.K. officials stepped in to reverse the outcome, asserting "Boaty McBoatface" was too informal.

Nova Scotia government list curators seemed to lean toward conventional names as well.

After the list of nearly 10,000 suggestions in the naming competition was collected, the provincial government asked the public to vote for one of four groups of names, based on local beaches, birds, landmarks or trees.

In July, the fleet of helicopters was unveiled with the names Spirit of the Osprey, Spirit of the Falcon, Spirit of the Hawk and Spirit of the Eagle.

WATCH | Here are some of helicopter names that didn't make the cut: Donair Force One? We got the full list of names suggested for new N.S. helicopters | Duration 1:38 Choppy McChopFace, Owlexander Graham Bell and Houston Herc were among the list of 10,000 name suggestions for a new fleet of helicopters in Nova Scotia. The CBC's Brett Ruskin shares some of the names that didn't make the cut.

After some online outcry about the final result, CBC News filed freedom of information requests seeking documents related to the naming process. The province released hundreds of pages of emails and internal documents.

The government's list shows "Osprey" as the top suggestion. But the list also reveals the recurring push for "Choppy McChopface" and similar suggestions such as "Chopper McChoppyface," "Choppy Mc Flys A Lot" and others with slightly different spellings.

While those names owe their origin to the British contest a decade ago, Nova Scotians also showed creativity with other ideas.

Notable locals suggested

There were repeated suggestions to name the helicopters after iconic Nova Scotians such as Anne Murray, Douglas McCurdy, Maud Lewis and Viola Desmond.

More than one person proposed naming the helicopters after Nova Scotia Premier Tim Houston, including a pitch to name one the "Houston Herc," an alliterative reference to the Hercules military transport aircraft.

Some ideas combined notable names with avian wordplay, such as "Jacob Shaffelbird" and "Owlexander Graham Bell."

Contestants also submitted the names of Nova Scotian athletes Sidney Crosby, Nathan MacKinnon, Ellie Black and Blayre Turnbull, as well as characters from the TV series Trailer Park Boys: Ricky, Julian, Bubbles and Mr. Lahey.

"The trailer park boys transcends the global audience," one person wrote. "This show is a phenomenal that has fans all over the world. Their status is legendary. They are one of the few things that I can say I'm proud of about this province."

Another entry proposed "Air Nova," offering the rationale: "Because it's a helicopter in Nova Scotia. So Air Nova makes sense."

'An asinine practice'

Some suggestions showed a range of humour and eccentricity, while others indicated a disdain for the process itself.

One contestant suggested "Heloblue 55284," explaining that it combined the word "helicopter," the blue of the Nova Scotia tartan, and the total land mass of the province in square kilometres.

Another proposal, "4 blade delivering water," reflected the helicopters' firefighting capabilities, while "BlackRocks Down" seems to combine references to the black rocks at Peggys Cove and the movie about two American Black Hawk helicopters shot down by Somalian forces in 1993.

Some entries read more like customer service complaints. One person wrote: "Stop naming things off of people it's an asinine practice."

Another lengthy submission included: "How bout you survey nova scotiams on thi gs that really matter. Like the stupid pickerel and bass cull, or your plans do destroy our outdoors with mining and fracking. This is 100% ridiculous."

One commenter summarized the process succinctly.

"If you ask the internet to name your thing, you will get exactly the stupid name you deserve."

MORE TOP STORIES

World.title: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy expected to visit Canada next week: sources
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy is expected to visit Canada next week, according to sources that spoke to Radio-Canada.

The visit, which was first reported by the Globe and Mail, has been confirmed by two independent sources.

The sources say the visit to Canada could include two stops.

Zelenskyy’s last visit to Canada was in December, when he met with Prime Minister Mark Carney in Halifax before travelling to the U.S. to meet with President Donald Trump for talks aimed at ending the Russia-Ukraine war.

The Prime Minister's Office declined to comment on the expected visit.

News of the visit comes as Russian President Vladimir Putin said a number of countries, including the U.S. and China, were ready to support a peace settlement between Russia and Ukraine.

"Ultimately, however, the problem must be resolved by the countries involved in the conflict — Russia and Ukraine," he said.

"We are ​grateful to everyone attempting to contribute to a settlement. Is there ​a chance? In my view, yes, there is."

Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha told reporters in Kyiv: "I believe that we will now have a new dynamic in the peace efforts, with the return of ​this active phase of political and diplomatic engagement in many capitals around the world."

He did not ⁠elaborate further, telling reporters to "follow the ⁠news."

After 4½ years of Europe's deadliest ‌conflict since the Second World War, it is rare for either side to offer an upbeat assessment of peace prospects.

They last met for U.S.-mediated talks in February.

World.title: Giorgia Meloni is Italy's longest-serving postwar leader. Will that stability last?
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

On Friday, on a quay in the southern Italy port city of Bari, more than 10,000 supporters will have room to celebrate a number that once seemed about as likely as an Italian putting ketchup on spaghetti: 1,413.

That is how many consecutive days Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni's government will have survived on Sept. 4, overtaking the record set by Silvio Berlusconi's second administration to become the longest-lasting government in the postwar history of the Italian Republic.

The milestone is being marked with a rally organized by Meloni's Brothers of Italy party at Bari's port, where the prime minister will be joined by ministers, lawmakers and other supporters for what's being billed as a celebration of the government’s record longevity.

For a country that has cycled through 68 governments in the 80 years since the end of the Second World War, the record may say more about Meloni than Italy.

Italy's first female leader rose to power with a public persona constructed around combat and defiance.

Raised largely by her mother in Rome's working-class Garbatella neighbourhood after her father left, Meloni, 49, entered politics in the 1990s through the youth movement of the post-fascist Italian Social Movement.

A self-described "underdog," she describes resistance as a main source of her motivation, recently telling the New York Times, "a 'No' is one of the things that most mobilizes me."

Meloni arrives for an EU summit at the European Council building in Brussels on June 29, 2023. (Geert Vanden Wijngaert/The Associated Press)

Her political communication is similarly personal. The rally cry that helped make her famous — "I am Giorgia, I am a woman, I am a mother, I am Italian, I am Christian" — was catchy enough to be turned into a dance remix .

Governing by coalition

But for someone who built her image on fighting, it is caution, not confrontation, that has most marked her governing style.

While Italian politics is littered with the wreckage of male leaders undone by overreach, Meloni has built her staying power on knowing when not to push her luck.

It's patience she displayed even before reaching office. When almost every major party entered Mario Draghi's broad coalition government in 2021, Meloni kept her small, outlier Brothers of Italy party alone in opposition.

Outgoing Italian Premier Mario Draghi, left, hands over the cabinet minister bell to Meloni during a ceremony in Rome on Oct. 23, 2022. (Andrew Medichini/The Associated Press)

After the 2022 collapse of Draghi's government, Meloni claimed power, heading a three-party, right-wing coalition that gave her a clear parliamentary majority. The politician who had railed against Brussels now largely toed the European Union's fiscal rules , remained steadfastly pro-Ukraine and fell silent on earlier talk of challenging the euro.

She's also managed to keep together that sometimes-fractious alliance with Matteo Salvini's anti-immigration, pro-Russia League and Antonio Tajani's centre-right Forza Italia.

That combination — fiery political identity, pragmatic governing — has helped her beat the odds.

Lorenzo Pregliasco, a head pollster with YouTrend , calls Meloni's durability "highly unusual." Brothers of Italy is polling slightly above its 2022 election result right now, in a country where governing parties typically start losing support within months.

But Pregliasco said that shouldn't be mistaken for an overwhelming love of the party's leader.

"Meloni's strength in the polls doesn't reflect a genuine, overwhelming support for a government," he said. "The key issue here is how much Meloni is seen as credible, as opposed to the alternative."

That alternative — an opposition led by the Democratic Party and populist Five Star Movement that has shifted left — remains divided. Meloni, meanwhile, remains politically dominant within her own coalition, with Brothers of Italy polling well ahead of both the League and Forza Italia.

Her governing style also involves knowing when rhetoric and policy can quietly clash.

Migration is a case in point. Meloni campaigned vociferously on stopping migrant arrivals by sea to Italy — numbers that have sharply fallen from their 2023 peak — and built controversial offshore migrant processing centres in Albania.

Yet at the same time, her government has authorized almost half a million legal entries for non-EU workers between 2026 and 2028 to fill severe labour shortages driven by Italy's aging population.

The same pragmatic compromise has marked her foreign policy.

The only EU leader to attend Donald Trump's inauguration, Meloni was widely cast as Europe's natural bridge to the U.S. president. But building that bridge to Trump proved akin to engineering one across an Italian fault line: the relationship buckled over the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran and Trump's attacks on Pope Leo .

WATCH | Giorgia Meloni fires back at Donald Trump: Italy's Meloni tells Trump to focus on his own popularity | Duration 2:57 Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni fired back at U.S. President Donald Trump after he suggested she was trying to repair ties with Washington to boost her approval ratings. The exchange comes days after Trump claimed Meloni had 'begged' him for a photo at the G7 summit in France.

That ability to adapt without appearing to abandon her political identity helps explain the credibility voters still give her, Pregliasco said.

She still talks about nation, family, motherhood and traditional values. She has tightened the rules around same-sex parenthood, and criticized feminists for focusing on gender quotas and symbolic battles over language, saying real equality meant a woman being free to become prime minister in the first place.

It's language that speaks squarely to a conservative electorate in one of the world's oldest countries.

Stability vs. growth

But economist Veronica De Romanis, with Rome's Luiss University, says the same caution that has shielded Meloni politically has also held back deeper structural change in a country whose debt-to-GDP ratio is second only to Greece in the EU.

"Stability is an instrument," she said. "The goal is growth, economic growth, and we haven't seen that."

De Romanis credits the Meloni government with fiscal discipline, but adds its leader has failed to exploit four remarkably stable years to tackle weak productivity, low education spending or the precarious foothold women and young people have in Italy's labour market.

In a country where female employment hovers around 53 per cent, Meloni has pledged to boost that figure to both support growth and counter Italy's demographic decline. (Remo Casilli/Reuters)

Higher female employment rates and higher fertility are positively correlated across Europe, she said, pushing back against the idea that getting more women into the workforce worsens Italy’s demographic problem.

"We cannot afford having one out of two women at home," she said.

Pressure from the right

As elections approach next year, a stagnant status quo is not Meloni's greatest threat. The outsider who built her career attacking the political establishment is now experiencing what it means to become the target.

Former general Roberto Vannacci, positioning himself to Meloni's right after breaking off from Salvini's League, is now trying to outflank her on immigration, security and social issues, including his opposition to 2SLGBTQ+ and abortion rights.

Vannacci gives Meloni something she has long avoided, Pregliasco said: "An opposition from the right which can basically speak the language of her electorate."

After a record 1,413 days in power, Meloni has demonstrated a rare instinct in modern Italian politics: knowing when to fight, when to back down and when to wait it out.

But whether Italians believe Meloni can transform political stability into lasting change may be a question they decide at the polls next year.

World.title: Interior design: A new angle on tile
World.content:
Article content

Tile is breaking out of the kitchen and bathroom. The familiar finish is moving into living rooms, bedrooms, home offices and entertaining spaces, proving its potential extends far beyond traditional wet zones. With an extraordinary range of colours, formats and tactile effects available, it can anchor a room, define its architecture or introduce a quiet layer of personality. Its durability adds another compelling advantage, meeting the growing desire for interiors that feel elevated yet can handle the realities of daily life.

World.title: Weaponizing oil against U.S. will go ‘badly’: Heather Exner-Pirot
World.content:
Article content

Amid the debate over how or whether Canada should escalate its trade dispute with the United States, there’s been a push from some Canadian leaders to consider using energy exports as leverage. The premiers of both Alberta and Saskatchewan have warned against the idea of an oil export tax or restrictions on Canadian oil exports, and have faced accusations of being out of step with a so-called “Team Canada” approach. In this interview, Rob Breakenridge is joined by Heather Exner-Pirot of the Macdonald-Laurier Institute, who lays out the risks and downside of weaponizing Canada’s energy exports. Exner-Pirot argues that any attempt to inflict economic pain on the U.S. could backfire on Canada, hurting domestic oil producers, disrupting supply chains, and inviting further American retaliation. Such a move could also undermine Canada’s aspirations to be seen globally as a stable and reliable supplier of energy.

World.title: De la Espriella claims Colombia’s military killed 23, arrested 6 EMC guerrillas
World.content:
President Abelardo de la Espriella claimed Wednesday that Colombia’s armed forces killed at least 23 members of FARC dissident group EMC and captured another six.

In a video, De la Espriella said that “Operation Azarias,” targeted the EMC’s Carolina Ramirez Front and killed one of its commanders, a man called “Tigre” or “Pintado,” in the south of the Guaviare province.

A second guerrilla commander, “Victor,” was among the six alleged EMC members who were arrested during the operation, which included air strikes.

The president claimed that Victor carried out attacks against the military “during the elections, as part of the ‘gunpoint vote’ strategy launched by the previous regime to skew the popular verdict.”

That narcoterrorist, whom we have now taken out of circulation, carried out attacks against members of the National Army and the Navy. During the elections, as part of the “gunpoint vote” strategy launched by the previous regime to skew the popular verdict, this criminal ambushed a unit that was on the move precisely to protect citizens’ right to vote freely. President Abelardo de la Espriella

There is no evidence to suggest that De la Espriella’s predecessor, former President Gustavo Petro, employed illegal armed groups to coerce voters into voting against his would-be successor.

One minor allegedly survived the attack and was surrendered to family welfare agency ICBF. The Medical Examiner’s Office is expected to investigate how many minors were among the alleged “narcoterrorists.”

At least three minors were killed in a previous operation in Guaviare that killed at least nine alleged members of the EMC’s main rival, FARC dissident group EMBF, the Medical Examiner’s Office said earlier this week.

Air strikes against illegal armed groups are controversial as they could imply the blanket killing of victims of child recruitment, a war crime according to international humanitarian law.

The government has long insisted that those recruiting children and minors are responsible for the deaths of their victims.

World.title: 1 killed, 15 injured in northeast Colombia car bomb attack on police station
World.content:
At least one person was killed and another 15 injured in a car bomb attack on a police station on the outskirts of Cucuta, the capital of Norte de Santander.

According to the National Police, the bomb exploded on Monday evening outside of the police station in Los Patios, a municipality that is part of Cucuta’s metropolitan area.

Apart from the casualties, the blast also damaged buildings and vehicles that were parked near the police station, police told local media.

In an initial response, President Abelardo de la Espriella said on social media platform X that he had convened a security council meeting “with the entire top brass of the security forces.”

“Wherever the terrorists try to sow fear, that is where the State will be with all is might,” said De la Espriella.

We will pursue with an iron fist those who threaten Colombians, until we capture them, dismantle their networks, and restore peace to our communities. Abelardo de la Espriella

In the region around Cucuta, guerrilla organizations ELN and EMBF have been fighting each other. Organized crime groups operate mainly inside the urban area of the capital of the Norte de Santander province.

No group immediately claimed responsibility for the attack.

World.title: Vote to move Uribe’s massacre probe to Congress triggers infighting among Colombia’s left
World.content:
Internal fractures within Colombia’s leftist opposition burst into the open following a vote by five representatives of the Historic Pact (PH) party to transfer a criminal investigation against former President Alvaro Uribe to Congress’ Accusations Commission.

The controversy erupted after the five PH members of the committee backed a motion of Uribe’s Democratic Center (CD) party to assert legislative jurisdiction over long-standing criminal cases against Uribe, including investigations into the massacres of El Aro (1997) and La Granja (1996), and the 1998 assassination of human rights defender Jesus Maria Valle.

PH members

David Alejandro Toro

María del Mar Pizarro

Heráclito Landínez

Jorge Bastidas

Gabriel Becerra

As the former governor of Antioquia, Uribe would have been in on the massacres carried out by the Bloque Metro and AUC paramilitary groups, according to the Prosecutor General’s Office, which refused to turn over the investigations.

The commission claimed jurisdiction over the Uribe file because the paramilitaries didn’t demobilize until after 2002, when he became president.

Critics of the decision, including the prosecution and PH Senate chief Ivan Cepeda, argued that Uribe’s alleged involvement in the crimes happened years before he was granted presidential immunity.

Cepeda spent much of his career fighting Uribe in court over his alleged ties to the AUC.

Because of the committee vote, the Constitutional Court will have to rule on who gets to investigate Uribe’s alleged crimes against humanity, which could delay the investigation.

Journalists who reported on the PH support for the fabricated conflict suggested that this may be part of a political deal between congressmen political deal between Uribistas and Petristas, supporters of former President Gustavo Petro.

Becerra, who is close to Cepeda, said in a statement that there “existed nor will there exist any political deal that would compromise justice, truth or the rights of victims.

According to the house representative, the PH lawmakers “initially considered it reasonable and legally appropriate to clarify the jurisdiction of the authority responsible for conducting the investigation,” but changed their mind in response to the controversy and calls for their resignation.

Lawyer Miguel Angel del Rio, the victims representative in the Uribe case, told Tercer Canal that “the ethic committee of the Historic Pact should investigate these five congressman,” adding that “what we have here is solidarity with impunity and this cannot be allowed.”

The Historic Pact became Colombia’s largest political party after congressional elections in March, but has seen an increase in internal tensions after Cepeda’s failure to win the presidential election in June.

World.title: Finance minister presents Colombia’s $203B budget proposal
World.content:
Colombia’s Finance Minister Miguel Gomez presented a budget proposal of COP634.9 trillion ($203 billion) for the coming year, a 14% increase compared to last year.

Much of the increase is due to the government’s debt obligations, which went up 55% to 155.4 trillion ($49.8 billion), almost a quarter of the entire budget.

At a presentation, Gomez told press that an earthquake that left tens of thousands homeless in western Colombia earlier this month also forced the administration of Abelardo de la Espriella to increase spending.

In a video, the finance minister also said that the government “has taken deci

The budget bill, a revision of the one that was presented by the former government of former President Gustavo Petro, will have to be approved by Congress before October 20 or be issued as a decree.

The government will also present a Finance Bill, which determines how the government plans to pay for its spending, before December.

World.title: Colombia claims killing eight suspected EMBF guerrillas
World.content:
President Abelardo de la Espriella said Thursday that Colombia’s armed forces killed eight guerrillas of FARC dissident group EMBF in a joint operation.

In a post on social media platform X, De la Espriella said that the military offensive targeted “camps used by structures of the Jorge Suarez Briceño Block,” a unit of the EMBF, in a rural part of El Retorno in the Guaviare province.

In a precision airstrike followed by an operation carried out by our commandos, the preliminary tally shows that 8 terrorists have been killed so far, 11 rifles and 5 machine guns have been seized, along with a large amount of logistical supplies. President Abelardo de la Espriella

De la Espriella said that “Colombia must know we are going on the offensive” against organized crime and illegal armed groups that are all deemed “narco-terrorist” organizations by the government.

“Major ringleaders and their criminal organizations will find no hiding place or sanctuary anywhere in the country,” the president added.

De la Espriella took office earlier this month, vowing to end peace negotiations with illegal armed groups and go on a military offensive with the help of the US military instead.

One of the groups that was negotiating peace with the administration of former President Gustavo Petro was the EMBF, led by former FARC commander “Calarca.”

The group, together with FARC dissident group EMC, controls large swathe of territory in southern Colombia and along the border with Venezuela.

World.title: De la Espriella calls for “iron fist” against crime in Colombia
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella called on the security forces to impose the law “like a giant with an iron fist, the iron fist of the State.”

During a meeting with commanders of the security forces, De la Espriella stressed that security “is the cornerstone of our government and the most forceful government policy.”

The president urged the security forces to confront crime with an iron fist and stressed that “our soldiers and police officers have the full and unconditional support of this government. Never again will they be mistreated or forced to bow down to crime.”

Here we must act like a giant with an iron fist—the iron fist of the state. And that ability to convey a sense of unity is what has a psychological impact on crime and sends a clear message to citizens: we are here to protect you, to look out for you, but also to enforce the law. President Abelardo de la Espriella

De la Espriella called to erase the distinction between organized crime and illegal armed groups, and “treat them all under a single designation, which is that of terrorist groups,” claiming they are interconnected.

We have to stop treating these criminals differently. We must treat them all under a single designation, which is that of terrorist groups, because the criminal pyramid we have in Colombia—whose base is drug trafficking, followed by illegal mining, extortion, and smuggling—is all perfectly interconnected. The foundation of all crime and the primary source of all forms of violence is drug trafficking. President Abelardo de la Espriella

“When it comes to fighting crime, there are no differences—neither in the state’s actions nor in its response and certainly not in the categorization” that allowed peace talks with groups like the FARC and ELN, according to the president.

“That is over in this administration. They are all terrorists, and we are going to treat them as such, no matter what happens,” said De la Espriella.

World.title: De la Espriella claims 123,700 barrels stolen monthly from Colombia’s state oil company
World.content:
Oil thieves from north Colombia would be stealing at least 123,700 barrel of gasoline, diesel and naphtha, a month, claimed President Abelardo de la Espriella.

According to De la Espriella, the theft of the refined oil products that wee imported or produced by state-owned oil company Ecopetrol “is utterly alarming, and demands an immediate and forceful response from the State.”

Every month, approximately 123,700 barrels of refined products—gasoline, diesel, and naphtha—imported or produced by Ecopetrol would be stolen. This would occur solely on a 14-inch pipeline that connects Pozos Colorados, in Santa Marta, to the interior of the country, and the losses are concentrated mainly in Cesar and Magdalena. President Abelardo de la Espriella

“We would be talking about more than 1.5 million barrels a year, with losses exceeding $500,000 million for Ecopetrol and, therefore, for the nation,” the president said in a post on social media platform X.

De la Espriella added that “these fuels are used as raw materials in the illicit processing of cocaine” by illegal armed groups that operate in the country’s periphery.

If we confirm that a large portion of this fuel is being used to power cocaine production facilities, then we are not only dealing with a massive theft from Ecopetrol: we are dealing with a criminal network that may be linking the theft of hydrocarbons to drug trafficking and the financing of armed terrorist organizations. President Abelardo de la Espriella

The president ordered a “joint operation” of the military, police, prosecution and administrative authorities “to comprehensively combat this criminal economy” led by Defense Minister Jorge Eduardo Mora.

“I want results and periodic report on progress,” said De la Espriella.

Organized crime and illegal armed groups have been involved in fuel theft for decades.
