World.title: Is Germany's economic slump finally over?
World.content:
Despite a slew of negative headlines, the German economy has posted its best figures in years. There are reasons for optimism, but structural issues remain.

The German economy is showing tentative signs of recovery after a prolonged period of gloom. Europe's largest economy is on track for its strongest GDP growth since 2022, while business sentiment is finally trending upwards again after a lengthy spell in the doldrums.

The country's official statistics office reported last week that the economy grew by 0.3% in the second quarter of 2026, beating estimates and building on robust figures for the previous two quarters.

Several others have revised their forecasts upwards. The Ifo Institute, Kiel Institute for the World Economy and the Leibniz Institute for Economic Research are all now predicting growth of 1.3% or more for 2026.

Meanwhile, the Ifo business climate index — a key barometer of the country's corporate mood — returned its highest reading in a year for August.

"It's more than a flash in the pan," Clemens Fuest, president of the Ifo Institute, told DW. "It could be a recovery."

"The momentum is positive and the economy has shown a better-than-feared level of resilience," said Carsten Brzeski, ING's global head of macro research.

However, he cautioned against too much cheer, saying some of the economy's fundamental problems remain. "In order to really transform this into a longer-term recovery story, we still need more," he said.

Where has the good news come from?

The positive figures come as negative headlines related to Germany's economy continue to stack up.

Volkswagen, one of the country's most iconic companies, is in the midst of a bitter downsizing — reflecting a wider restructuring across the country in the face of competition from China and other global headwinds.

This summer, record low water levels on key German waterways such as the Rhine and Danube significantly disrupted trade and economic activity while the war in Iran continues to drive energy prices upwards.

Low water levels on the Rhine hit economic activity this summer Image: Dominik Bund/IMAGO

Yet part of the reason for the upturn relates to how the German economy has handled some of those challenges, notably the closure of the Strait of Hormuz as a result of the Iran war.

Germany's exports and industrial base have powered GDP growth, with new orders increasing for the third month in a row, leading to the strongest production growth since early 2022. The VDMA, which represents the German mechanical and plant engineering sector, reported a 2% increase in foreign orders for July year-on-year.

Brzeski says many German manufacturing firms, especially in energy-intensive sectors such as chemicals, have benefitted from the closure of the Strait of Hormuz. They have increased orders and taken some market share from Asian suppliers who were more severely dependent on Middle Eastern oil.

"There was a bit of a re-channeling of industrial orders away from Asia to Europe and Germany," he says.

The German Federal Ministry for Economic Affairs and Climate Action itself identifies this factor in its August statement, saying Asian rivals "were more affected by price increases and supply bottlenecks."

It says that the multiple shocks of recent years have led German companies to diversify supply chains.

"Many companies have altered their transport logistics in recent years, are maintaining larger stocks, and are using a variety of transport routes in order to make their supply chains more resilient," it added.

Can the German government take some credit?

Analysts also think Chancellor Friedrich Merz's government deserves some credit for the turnaround, despite it hitting historic levels of unpopularity in 2026.

"It's driven by government demand and debt-financed spending, particularly in defense," says Fuest.

German industry shifts to defense production amid job losses To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The government's economic plans are built around a €500 billion ($580 billion) infrastructure investment drive, a massive increase in defense spending and a major reform proposal aimed at boosting competitiveness.

It has also introduced some energy price relief measures and a €10 billion tax relief plan for lower-income households. "Companies are more optimistic and a big part has to be the stimulus," says Brzeski. "It is gradually reaching the economy."

Germany's structural problems remain

Despite the positive data, many of the issues which have dogged the German economy in recent years remain.

The recent uptick is driven by export demand, with practically no increase in domestic demand. According to the Federal Statistical Office, public and private consumption spending was flat, while investment declined.

"Even though everyone is happy that we have some positive news, we need to watch out and not fall into the trap of thinking that now 'everything is fine,'" says Brzeski, noting that the factors undermining German competitiveness persist.

"Chinese competition is still there," he says. "The long loss in international competitiveness in the automotive industry and other industries is still here," he added, stressing that these structural challenges would be difficult to alter or reverse.

Tentative optimism among Germany's businesses

Yet the positive sentiment remains. Indicators for the third quarter of 2026 suggest significant optimism among business leaders about the future, while overall German growth is now on track for a 1.2% increase for 2026. That puts it ahead of other European countries such as France, the UK and the Netherlands.

In the wake of the war in Ukraine, Germany's economy fell into a sustained slump from which it has struggled to emerge since 2022. While other economies showed signs of recovery, Germany remained in the doldrums.

For some analysts, the recent positive data reflects a sense that things had reached a natural "bottoming out" and that a return to growth was inevitable.

Germany's industrial backbone remains intact Image: Oliver Berg/dpa/picture alliance

"It could hardly have gotten much worse," says Brzeski. "We're bouncing back from low levels. This is not wirtschaftswunder 3.0, we have to keep that in mind."

He also thinks part of the optimism is related to corporate Germany finally accepting some harsh truths about how it had fallen behind in key areas such as innovation and digitalization, and belatedly trying to improve.

"They realize they simply have to embrace technological change, AI and so on, and have to start investing," he says. "They are no longer waiting for what's happening in Berlin in terms of reform packages; it's a question of survival."

For Fuest, the data suggests Germany's "industrial core" remains intact. He says that three-quarters of German manufacturing companies are still expanding, but warns that the recovery will be short-lived unless bigger change follows.

"It is urgent to allow for structural change and to find new areas where German companies have competitive advantages," he says.

Edited by: Rob Mudge

World.title: Malaysia's middle path between China and US faces new tests
World.content:
The prime minister's comments on Taiwan and US-backed military facilities near Sabah have revived questions over Malaysia's non-aligned foreign policy.

Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim has spent much of his time in office insisting that Kuala Lumpur will not be forced to choose between the United States and China.

But two sets of comments last month have raised questions about how sustainable that position is as rivalry between the two superpowers increasingly spills into Southeast Asia.

"I see Taiwan as part of China, period," he said in an interview with news outlet Al Jazeera that aired on August 16.

Beijing considers democratically governed as Taiwan part of its territory. While Chinese leaders say they favor "peaceful reunification," they have never ruled out using force to bring the island under Beijing's control.

More controversially, Anwar appeared to accept Beijing's argument that force could be necessary.

"If one province decides to break away. Do we use force? I think I will, [to] protect the sanctity and unity of the nation," he said.

China's gray zone warfare in the Pacific To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Regional concerns

The comments drew an enthusiastic response from Beijing, while Taiwan's Foreign Ministry accused Anwar of effectively legitimizing the use of force against the islandand warned that his "one-sided support for China could negatively impact Taiwanese businesses' confidence in investing in Malaysia," including in the country's strategically important semiconductor sector.

Two days after his comments on Taiwan aired, Anwar argued that Malaysia should strengthen its defenses in Sabah, citing the expansion of US-backed military facilities on the nearby Philippine island of Balabac.

The Philippines is upgrading facilities on Balabac, roughly 50 kilometers (31 miles) from the Malaysian islands of Banggi and Balambangan.

Balabac was one of four additional locations added in 2023 to the Enhanced Defense Cooperation Agreement, which allows US forces to access designated Philippine military facilities, construct infrastructure and pre-position equipment.

Taken together, Anwar's comments raised concerns that Malaysia is growing warmer toward Beijing while becoming more suspicious of Washington's military footprint in the region.

A fundamental realignment?

Kuala Lumpur has also been one of the region's strongest critics of Israel's actions in Gaza. Anwar has repeatedly accused the United States and European governments of hypocrisy and double standards for championing democracy and international law while failing, in his view, to hold Israel sufficiently accountable.

But Malaysia experts warn against interpreting Anwar's rhetoric as evidence of a fundamental strategic realignment.

"Malaysia still maintains very good relations with the US and other Western countries," Ngeow Chow Bing, director of the Institute of China Studies at Universiti Malaya, told DW.

Those ties may sometimes be less visible than Anwar's increasingly warm public rhetoric towards Beijing, Bing said, but the underlying relationship remains strong.

"It is certainly true that the space for maintaining its traditional balancing act between China and the US is narrower than before, but that space remains, and Malaysia will continue to operate within it," Bing added.

Philippine island on edge amid fear of China-Taiwan conflict To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

A shift in tone, not strategy

Anwar's comments about the Philippine military buildup are much more about an ongoing territorial dispute between Kuala Lumpur and Manila, Chee Meng Tan, assistant professor at the University of Nottingham Malaysia, told DW.

The Philippines maintains a territorial claim over Sabah, which became part of Malaysia when the federation was formed in 1963. Malaysia rejects the claim and regards its sovereignty over the state as indisputable.

Those tensions resurface regularly, and in August Kuala Lumpur lodged a fresh objection with the United Nations over a Philippine submission about its continental shelf.

"A neighbor that claims part of your territory is building a military base 20 minutes offshore — any government would react," said Tan.

Anwar called for the strengthening of Malaysia's own defenses, not for Chinese help, "and he went out of his way to say relations with Manila remain good," Tan added.

Anwar also sought to lower the temperature over Taiwan after his initial comments. Speaking to Malaysian media after the event, he stressed that Kuala Lumpur wanted a peaceful resolution to cross-strait tensions and insisted that Malaysia's position had not changed.

Malaysia has formally followed a "One China" policy since establishing diplomatic relations with Beijing in 1974.

Chinese state media quickly interpreted Anwar's remarks through Beijing's preferred terminology, with Xinhua reporting that the Malaysian leader had "reaffirmed the one-China principle," something Malaysian analysts said isn't true.

Malaysia has not abandoned its traditional position, but Anwar's rhetoric "has sometimes been more accommodating towards Beijing than necessary," Khoo Ying Hooi, associate professor of international relations at Universiti Malaya, told DW.

"That can create the perception of a tilt even when Malaysia's wider strategic behavior remains more hedged and pragmatic," she added.

Malaysia has less room to hedge

The prime minister faces mounting political pressure after his Pakatan Harapan coalition suffered three consecutive setbacks in state elections.

The defeats have intensified tensions within Anwar's broad governing alliance and speculation that he could call a snap general election.

Yet beyond Anwar's rhetoric and domestic political calculations lies a more structural problem for Malaysia.

Its longstanding strategy of hedging between the United States and China is becoming more difficult as Beijing's economic and military weight grows and Washington takes an increasingly transactional approach to foreign relations.

How much leverage does the US have over its adversaries? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

"Malaysia is not abandoning its traditional balancing strategy, but the space for ambiguity is narrowing," said Hooi.

Anwar is expected to visit China in late September, his first trip there in more than a year. He is reportedly due to attend the Global Digital Trade Expo in Hangzhou and hold talks with Chinese Premier Li Qiang as Kuala Lumpur seeks to deepen economic ties with its largest trading partner.

But closer relations with Beijing do not remove Malaysia's dependence on Western markets, investment and technology, or its own differences with China.

Despite warm political ties, Kuala Lumpur continues to reject Chinese maritime claims in the South China Sea that overlap with waters Malaysia considers its own.

In February, Foreign Minister Mohamad Hasan reiterated that Malaysia would not recognize Chinese claims that conflict with its maritime boundaries in the South China Sea, while Anwar has recently insisted that Malaysian oil and gas exploration will continue in the waters despite objections from Beijing.

For Tan of the University of Nottingham, Malaysia's ability to continue balancing the two powers ultimately depends less on Anwar's rhetoric than on Malaysia remaining valuable to both.

"China wants friendly neighbors to keep trading with, and America needs Malaysian factories, where a big share of the world's chips is tested and packaged," said Tan.

"Neither gains from pushing Malaysia toward the other."

Edited by: Ole Tangen Jr

World.title: Iran bets on shadow networks to evade US sanctions
World.content:
To circumvent US sanctions, Iran has spent decades building a complex network of businesspeople and companies. A billionaire once sentenced to death is now back at its center.

With its toughest sanctions yet, the administration of US President Donald Trump is seeking to force Iran's leadership into submission.

The measures, dubbed "economic D-Day" sanctions, are intended to achieve what military pressure since February has failed to accomplish.

In addition to targeting Iran's key sources of revenue and trade, including oil, banking, gold, shipping, aviation and certain technology sectors, US authorities are increasingly focusing on cryptocurrencies.

Digital currencies such as bitcoin, which operate outside the traditional banking system and dollar-based financial networks, are being used by Iran for money transfers, trade transactions and, increasingly, oil-related business.

An opaque network to help Tehran bypass sanctions

Iran also appears to be exploring cryptocurrencies as a way to secure oil shipments passing through the Strait of Hormuz.

According to the Fars News Agency, which is close to Iran's Revolutionary Guards, the idea was proposed by Babak Zanjani.

The 53-year-old billionaire was released from prison last year and remains one of the most prominent figures in a network that has grown over decades and helped Iran navigate international sanctions.

In 2016, Zanjani became entangled in Iran's internal power struggles and was sentenced to death Image: Tasnim News/AFP

Individuals within these networks enjoy support and protection from influential figures inside the Islamic Republic. In return, they are believed to share part of their profits with powerful patrons within the system.

"Among these people, Zanjani belongs to an economic elite with innovative ideas and has repeatedly demonstrated his capabilities in the past," said Behzad Ahmadinia, an Iran-born journalist based in Cyprus who specializes in the oil and energy sector.

"It appears that the regime has decided to overcome internal rivalries and rely on professionals and experts who can work more efficiently than others and take over key positions."

Selling oil barrels on the black market

Iran can draw on decades of experience in operating under sanctions. The system extends far beyond individual businessmen and includes a vast network of companies, financial channels and personal connections.

Corruption and a lack of transparency are widely regarded as structural problems within Iran's political and economic system. Transparency International's Corruption Perceptions Index 2025 gave Iran a score of 23 out of 100 and ranked it 153rd out of 182 countries, indicating a very high perceived level of public-sector corruption.

Zanjani reportedly controlled a business empire of around 60 companies, including entities in Malaysia, Tajikistan, Turkey and the United Arab Emirates.

Many of these firms were later sanctioned by the United States. Through this network, Zanjani began selling billions of barrels of Iranian oil on the black market during the presidency of Mahmoud Ahmadinejad, while also importing a wide range of goods, including aircraft, into Iran.

Is Iran set to become an economic outcast? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

In 2016, however, he became entangled in Iran's internal power struggles. Authorities accused him of failing to return around $2.6 billion (€2.24 billion) in oil revenues to the Iranian state.

After a highly publicized trial in one of the country's biggest corruption cases, he was sentenced to death. For years, he disputed claims over the missing funds and negotiated with Iranian authorities.

US gains insight into sanctions evasion routes

A key link in this network was Turkish-Iranian businessman Reza Zarrab. He was arrested in the United States in 2016 while on vacation and accused of money laundering and violating US sanctions on Iran.

Zarrab had built an extensive network in Turkey and possessed detailed knowledge of the financial and trading mechanisms Iran used to bypass sanctions.

Cases such as his gave US authorities valuable insight into how Iranian sanctions evasion networks operate, allowing Washington to target them more effectively. Zarrab later cooperated with US investigators and was released from custody. According to reports, he now lives in the United States under a new identity.

"People like Zarrab or Zanjani are cultivated within the system and maintain connections to different centers of power," France-based economist Jamshid Assadi told DW.

Can the US 'asphyxiate' Iran without taking on China? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

According to reports, Zanjani's rise began some 30 years ago during his military service, when he worked as a driver for the governor of Iran's central bank. The position is said to have opened doors to influential circles and provided him with key business contacts. How many billions of dollars flowed through his network and companies, and how much he personally earned from those activities, remains unclear.

In February 2024, Iranian media reported that assets linked to Zanjani had been repatriated from abroad. His wealth, they said, had grown beyond the value of his outstanding liabilities. In 2025, he was released from prison and quickly returned to the business world. Through one of his companies, he signed a multibillion-dollar contract with Iran's state railway operator.

At the same time, Zanjani has sought to reinvent himself. In an open letter to US business magnate Elon Musk, he offered his company as a bridge for economic cooperation between Iran and the United States. He now presents himself as an entrepreneur, mediator and advocate of dialogue.

After the United States placed Zanjani back on its sanctions list in January 2026, Washington expanded its measures in July to target a broader network of companies and business associates linked to him.

Just one day before the new sanctions were announced, Zanjani opened a cafe and pastry shop in western Tehran and attended a celebratory launch event. The business was shut down by authorities the following day.

Allies to adversaries: US-Iran relations over the decades To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Can the US cripple Iran's shadow networks?

The key question, however, is whether the latest US measures can truly reach the networks underpinning Iran's shadow economy.

According to Assadi, many of the traditional sanctions evasion routes are now well known and increasingly difficult for Tehran to use. The United States has warned numerous countries that their companies, banks and private-sector actors could face penalties if they help Iran bypass restrictions.

At the same time, Iran has spent decades adapting to economic pressure and finding new ways around it. Whether Washington's latest sanctions will significantly weaken those networks remains uncertain. But the return of Babak Zanjani suggests Tehran is once again turning to the businessmen who helped it weather previous periods of economic isolation.

This article was originally written in German.

Edited by: Srinivas Mazumdaru

World.title: Sánchez: “Si existieran pruebas contra Marruecos actuaríamos, pero no hay evidencias sólidas”
World.content:
Pedro Sánchez ha dado un giro a su discurso sobre Marruecos en el debate en el Congreso sobre la crisis de Ceuta. El presidente ha admitido que entiende que muchos ciudadanos piensen que Rabat está detrás de la entrada masiva de migrantes, y no lo ha descartado completamente, pero asegura que de momento no tiene pruebas porque ningún servicio le ha planteado algo definitivo en este sentido, y por eso de momento está a la espera de que avancen las investigaciones. Sánchez ha recordado que una decisión de choque con Marruecos tendría graves consecuencias “sin marcha atrás”, y por eso para tomarla tiene que estar muy seguro.

“Si existieran pruebas [de la participación de Rabat], actuaríamos en consecuencia. Este Gobierno no tiene miedo a enfrentarse a otros poderes extranjeros. Pero vamos a trabajar cargados de hechos probados. Otros nos llevaron a una guerra con pruebas falsas”, ha dicho en referencia a José María Aznar y la guerra de Irak. El presidente ha criticado expresamente a Aznar por recordar el episodio de Perejil con orgullo, cuando, según el presidente, fue una demostración de lo que no hay que hacer. La idea de Sánchez era clara: esto podría llevar a un conflicto incluso armado con Marruecos, algo frecuente en la historia de las dos naciones, y por eso no se puede tratar a la ligera. Pero ha dejado la puerta abierta a un cambio si algún informe de inteligencia concluye que fue Marruecos. “Esto a día de hoy es descartado por nuestros servicios de inteligencia, digo de momento”, ha insistido. “Dejemos trabajar a los servicios”, ha dicho también en la réplica ante la posibilidad de que aparezcan esos datos definitivos y haya que tomar decisiones. Sánchez ha terminado el debate dejando claro que él no va a iniciar un conflicto con Marruecos solo por presión política. “Hoy, en esta Cámara, hemos escuchado a muchos que quieren reventar nuestras relaciones de vecindad. Esa es su propuesta: escalar sin reservas un conflicto. Yo no puedo hacerlo, no debo hacerlo. No lo voy a hacer”, ha insistido.

El presidente del PP, Alberto Núñez Feijóo, da la réplica al discurso del presidente Sánchez este jueves en el Congreso. Claudio Álvarez

Por el contrario, el líder de la oposición, Alberto Núñez Feijóo, y el de Vox, Santiago Abascal, han dejado claro que no tienen ninguna duda de que fue Marruecos y han exigido una represalia contundente. “La operación salió de Marruecos, fue consentida por Marruecos y hay indicios de que Marruecos la coordinó y que el Gobierno lo sabía porque fue advertido de ello. Dimita por incompetente o por cómplice. Usted pagará ante la justicia”, ha lanzado Feijóo, que ha sostenido que Sánchez tiene miedo a Rabat porque le encontraron algo inconfesable en su teléfono cuando le espiaron con el sistema Pegasus, una cuestión que circula mucho en redes sociales sin evidencia alguna. “¿Qué documento o conversación había en su teléfono para que se comporte de esta manera? ¿Qué sabe Marruecos de usted? ¿Por qué le tiene tanto miedo?“, le ha lanzado Feijóo.

Abascal ha ido directo a la acusación de traición. ”Sánchez es un traidor a España. Incluso a su propio partido. Hoy también traidor a los policías, a los que ha querido señalar como responsables por no avisar. Le vemos muy valiente con el rey de España y muy sumiso con el de Marruecos. No fue una crisis migratoria, fue una invasión”, ha insistido. “No nos hable de niños, usted tiene la empatía de un asesino en serie”, ha lanzado en la réplica.

El líder de Vox, Santiago Abascal, da la réplica al presidente del Gobierno, este jueves en el Congreso. Claudio Álvarez

En la réplica, Sánchez les ha contestado con una pregunta. “¿Qué habrían hecho? ¿Habrían ordenado a la policía disparar a la población civil? ¿Habría preferido matar a cientos o miles de jóvenes para evita tener que gestionar una crisis al otro lado de la frontera? Un gobierno del PP con Vox descolgando el teléfono para ordenar eso no lo quiero para mi país ni para ninguno. ¿Y ahora? ¿Expulsaría a todos los inmigrantes sin tramitar la ley de asilo? Eso es ilegal. ¿Recurriría a los gorilas de desokupa? Usted no sabe nada de gestión migratoria. Solo intenta sacar tajada", le ha esperado a Feijóo. “Si la solución pasa porque nos van a enchironar a todos, ¡menudo respeto a la independencia del poder judicial!“, ha rematado. “Ceuta no necesita discursos matonistas de patio de colegio, sino sentido común, templanza y un gobierno valiente, un gobierno que plante cara a los poderosos y que proteja y sirva a la gente”, ha insistido.

Feijóo respondió luego que él no está a favor de disparar a nadie y que la guardia civil no lo ha hecho nunca, al contrario que Marruecos. “Vamos a tener una buena relación con marruecos, sí. Basada en la lealtad”, aseguró el líder del PP. “¿Qué habría hecho yo? No irme de vacaciones. Cesar al ministro del interior por incompetente. Acompañar al rey a Ceuta y no reprocharle que no vaya. Y no broncearme en ninguna playa", ha rematado el líder de la oposición, que ha vuelto a tocar el delicado terreno de la familia del presidente: “¿Usted recomendaría a sus hijas pisar por la noche la playa de El Trampolín [donde duermen los inmigrantes en Ceuta]. Pues ya está“. Aina Vidal, de Comunes, le contestó después con otra pregunta: “¿Y usted, señor Feijóo, llevaría a su madre a la residencia pública de Madrid Santa Sofía, donde hay ratas y sarna? ¡Ya está bien!”

Sánchez ha endurecido en este debate su discurso con Marruecos, ha criticado abiertamente a los ministros marroquíes que reivindicaron la soberanía de Ceuta y Melilla, ha insistido en que su Gobierno garantizará siempre la españolidad de estas dos ciudades, e incluso ha desvelado un movimiento que hasta ahora se había mantenido en secreto, esto es, que el 21 de agosto Exteriores convocó a la embajadora de Marruecos en España para protestar por estas declaraciones de dos miembros de su Gobierno.

Ante la polémica desatada porque en esas fechas la embajadora no estaba en Madrid, Exteriores aclara a EL PAÍS que la convocatoria fue a ella, y se habló telefónicamente con ella para trasladar el malestar por las declaraciones de los ministros, pero como no estaba en Madrid, el que acudió al ministerio fue el encargado de negocios, algo habitual en los usos diplomáticos.

El presidente, Pedro Sánchez, contesta a los grupos parlamentarios, este jueves en el Congreso. Claudio Álvarez

El presidente incluso ha hablado de un replanteamiento de la colaboración con Marruecos, una frase a la que se ha aferrado Sumar para hablar de “rectificación”, como ha dicho el ministro de Derechos Sociales, Pablo Bustinduy, “Tenemos que seguir colaborando con Marruecos. Pero después de lo ocurrido esta cooperación tiene que ser diferente”, ha dicho Sánchez. El presidente parece dispuesto a ir más allá si se demuestra que Rabat estaba detrás, pero ha insistido en que para eso necesita pruebas.

“Nadie ha aportado pruebas que puedan concluir que esta entrada masiva fuera diseñada o ejecutada por las autoridades marroquíes”, ha insistido el presidente. “Sabemos que el 30 de julio la gendarmería permitió el cruce de la frontera. Y que después lo controló. ¿A qué se debió la falta de control? ¿Hubo incapacidad o inacción? Nuestros servicios de inteligencia darán con todas las claves. Vamos a hacer públicos todos los informes. De momento, ninguna de estas instituciones ha entregado evidencias sólidas de que Marruecos planificara o ejecutara este episodio", ha insistido. El Gobierno aclara que muchos de esos informes tienen que ser desclasificados por el Consejo de Ministros, así que de momento no hay fecha para publicarlos pero la idea es hacerlo con casi una decena en breve. Margarita Robles, ministra de Defensa y máxima responsable del CNI, se ha mostrado incómoda con el anuncio y ha sido la única de los ministros socialistas que no lo ha aplaudido.

La ministra de Defensa, Margarita Robles, no aplaude la intervención del presidente del Gobierno este jueves en el Congreso. Claudio Álvarez

Sin embargo, la soledad del presidente en el Congreso ha sido muy evidente. No solo PP y Vox han apostado por la autoría de Marruecos. También sus aliados en la izquierda. Enrique Santiago, secretario general del PCE y un peso pesado en el mundo a la izquierda del PSOE, ex secretario de Estado en el Gobierno de Sánchez, ha sido muy directo. “Marruecos ha organizado esto con Israel. Convoque a la embajadora de Marruecos de forma oficial. Que Felipe VI llame a Mohamed VI. Presidente, se ha actuado tarde, sin dimensionar la crisis humanitaria. Se ha tardado un mes en convocar el Consejo de Seguridad, IU lo pidió el 8 de agosto”, le ha lanzado. Y además ha pedido traer a la península a todos los inmigrantes que quedan en Ceuta y tratarlos con humanidad: “No son rubios ni todos son cristianos, pero tienen derechos humanos que debemos proteger”. Aina Vidal, de los Comunes, ha ido en la misma línea: “La política de apaciguamiento con Marruecos ha fracasado”.

Gabriel Rufían, de ERC, ha sido muy directo: “Yo acuso a Marruecos de enviar a 80.000 personas para cargarse al Gobierno de España con el apoyo de Washington y Tel Aviv y con la colaboración de la derecha y ultraderecha española. Mohamed VI es un asesino, y ustedes unos pusilánimes”, le ha lanzado al PP y Vox.

El portavoz de ERC en el Congreso, Gabriel Rufián, este jueves en el Congreso de los Diputados. Claudio Alvarez

En su discurso, Sánchez ha hecho más anuncios de protección de Ceuta y Melilla, como ampliaciones del control fronterizo, una estructura fija en el mar para evitar los cruces a nado, una revisión de la colaboración con Marruecos para reforzar el control, y decisiones políticas como intentar incluir a Ceuta y Melilla en la unión aduanera europea o darles una silla permanente en el Comité de las Regiones, algo que, según ha recordado, nunca hizo el PP en todos sus años de Gobierno, además de organizar un viaje del Rey “en las próximas semanas”, de nuevo un movimiento que, según ha insistido, el PP nunca se animó a hacer.

Sánchez ha explicado con detalle que ningún organismo avisó de que podía haber un cruce tan masivo como el que hubo. Y ahí también ha revelado varios informes de diferentes instituciones que apuntaban a un aumento de entradas a nado, pero ni de lejos auguraron el paso de 72.000 personas. Y ha insistido en que no hay que olvidar el aspecto humanitario y el respeto a las personas que intentan migrar huyendo de la pobreza y la guerra.

“No se puede coger a un ser humano del brazo y arrojarlo al otro lado de la frontera como si fuera un saco de tierra”, ha recordado para explicar que las devoluciones tienen sus trámites legales que son lentos. Sánchez ha insistido en que la diferencia de renta per cápita entre Ceuta y Marruecos es de ocho veces, y eso impulsa la inmigración irregular. “Podemos hacer un muro de 100 metros, pero siempre habrá gente dispuesta a echarse al mar para cruzar. Tenemos que reforzar nuestra frontera física, pero también tenemos que dar una alternativa legal y real a quienes quieren venir a trabajar a nuestro país y que además necesitamos, porque tenemos un reto demográfico”, ha dicho también, recuperando un discurso proinmigración que prácticamente enarbola en soledad en Europa.

“A base de cerrar agencias de cooperación, recortando esas políticas como hacen el PP y Vox, no reducimos la inmigración. Por cada euro menos que gastemos en cooperación, habrá que gastar 10 más en fronteras. Nuestro modelo no es el del miedo, es el de la humanidad y la solidaridad. Puede que no sea muy popular hoy, pero es el que funciona. Hemos reducido un 40% las entradas irregulares en las fronteras”, ha rematado Sánchez, que ha terminado con un agradecimiento directo y en primera persona a los ciudadanos de Ceuta por haber cuidado y ayudado a los inmigrantes.

El presidente Sánchez y el vicepresidente Cuerpo, al inicio de la sesión plenaria. Claudio Álvarez

“Ceuta saldrá reforzada de este embate”, les ha lanzado para concluir, prometiéndoles que en dos semanas más sacarán a otros 1.500 inmigrantes de las calles y les darán un lugar digno donde dormir mientras se procede a su devolución. “No vamos a parar hasta que se recupere vuestra normalidad. No nos vamos a olvidar. Este Gobierno no renunciará jamás a la soberanía de Ceuta y Melilla”, les ha asegurado.

World.title: Que nadie se quede fuera
World.content:
La voluntaria Pepi Solana durante una clase de refuerzo a niños en en la asociación Juniors en el barrio de la Viña (Cádiz), en uno de los programas de acción social de CaixaBank.

Personas mayores activas, emprendimiento local, población que vive en el entorno rural... La sociedad cambia y los servicios financieros se adaptan a colectivos con las mismas necesidades que el resto. El compromiso social de CaixaBank pone el foco en la atención al cliente esté donde esté y la integración de personas en situación de vulnerabilidad

“Son cuestiones básicas que pueden cambiar la vida de una persona”. Así resume Pepi Solano (San Fernando, Cádiz, 58 años) lo que supone aprender conceptos y poder adoptar costumbres de economía básica entre los más jóvenes. Solano, a través de Voluntariado CaixaBank, participa desde 2015 en distintos programas sociales en Cádiz, desde apoyo escolar hasta acompañamiento a personas mayores, y este tipo de consejos los imparte a alumnos de 4º de la ESO. Por ejemplo, que el ahorro comienza si guardan dos de los cinco euros de su paga, o que “las tarjetas no se prestan a nadie”. “Alguno se queda con cara de: ‘¿Cómo?’. Otros directamente se justifican: ‘Bueno, es que es mi amigo...’. Y rápidamente les tienes que decir que eso no se hace”, describe.

La visión del voluntariado que da Solano es uno de los espejos del propósito social de CaixaBank: conseguir que cada uno transforme su realidad con algo de ayuda. El banco, desde sus inicios en 1904 como Caja de Pensiones para la Vejez y de Ahorros de Cataluña y Baleares, se creó con el objetivo de que la población pudiera ahorrar, y hoy mantiene actualizado su compromiso social. Entre sus principales acciones están las de adaptarse a las necesidades de las personas en situación de vulnerabilidad (canaliza ayudas a más de 5.000 entidades sociales en todo el país a través de la colaboración con la Fundación “la Caixa”), facilitar a las personas mayores la gestión de su dinero, llegar a aquellas zonas rurales más aisladas o ayudar en el impulso a los emprendedores que lo necesitan. Como la propia entidad afirma, sus productos financieros se conciben para ofrecer oportunidades, favorecer la integración y fortalecer el bienestar colectivo.

Los ejes de CaixaBank que modelan una banca más humana Accesibilidad, también en zonas rurales Sus 4.200 oficinas dan cobertura en más de 3.700 municipios de toda España, con una presencia en el 99% de localidades con más de 5.000 habitantes, según datos de CaixaBank. La entidad también está presente en las zonas rurales: Es el único banco en 460 pueblos, y sus oficinas móviles llevan servicios financieros a más de 1.420 localidades sin sucursal bancaria o con acceso limitado en las que residen más de 630.000 personas.



Fotos: CaixaBank Acompañamiento personalizado a personas mayores CaixaBank ha desarrollado un protocolo de atención especial para las personas mayores, que incluye la formación de más de 30.000 empleados en atención preferente, más de 11.000 cajeros de uso fácil, horario de caja sin restricciones, adelanto del pago de pensiones al día 24 y asistencia personal por teléfono y WhatsApp con más de 600 agentes. La oferta la completa su programa Generación+, con servicios como la planificación del ahorro, el acompañamiento para la jubilación o la gestión de la prestación de dependencia. Inclusión social para grupos vulnerables La entidad financiera ofrece servicios personalizados para colectivos en situación de vulnerabilidad. Unos 400.00 clientes tienen cuentas de pago básicas y la entidad tiene oficinas, cajeros y plataformas digitales accesibles y fomenta el lenguaje económico claro. Para las personas con discapacidad auditiva, ha desplegado en toda su red el servicio de videointerpretación en lengua de signos SVisual, que permite a este colectivo acceder a la información bancaria de manera autónoma. Un sostén para los emprendedores El banco social del Grupo CaixaBank, MicroBank, cerró 2025 con cerca de 280.000 operaciones por más de 2.400 millones de euros. Sus funciones han favorecido el emprendimiento, la creación de empleo y la igualdad de oportunidades. Esta propuesta se suma a otras iniciativas, como los Premios EmprendeXXI para startups de alto potencial; la imaginPlanet Challenge de imagin para jóvenes con proyectos de sostenibilidad; o el programa Tierra de Oportunidades, que fija población y crea empleo en el entorno rural para hacer frente al reto demográfico.

Esta idea tan amplia de inclusión real se traduce directamente a pie de calle en medidas concretas, como que la mayor parte de las oficinas de CaixaBank estén diseñadas para ser accesibles físicamente, con rampas, puertas automáticas y mostradores adaptados para personas con movilidad reducida. Sus cajeros también están adaptados a personas con discapacidad, con opciones como un teclado en braille y navegación guiada por voz para personas como problemas visuales, menús fáciles de entender y pantallas con alto contraste. Con estas medidas, CaixaBank trata de establecer un equilibrio entre el negocio y diferenciarse con la dimensión social.

Su consejero delegado, Gonzalo Gortázar, sostiene que “CaixaBank es una entidad con valores profundos, capaz de tener éxito en el negocio y, al mismo tiempo, aportar una dimensión social fundamental”. Y añade: “Tenemos una manera de hacer banca diferente, centrada en la inclusión financiera, tanto por nuestra presencia territorial, con una red extendida por toda España, como por nuestro compromiso en no dejar a nadie atrás”, explica el CEO del banco.

Una nueva visión de las personas sénior

A veces, son las oficinas las que llegan a los usuarios, y no al revés. El servicio de las 32 oficinas móviles de CaixaBank permite realizar las operaciones bancarias más habituales (sean o no clientes de la entidad) a casi 630.000 personas que viven en más de 1.420 pequeñas poblaciones sin oficina bancaria o con restricciones que limitan el acceso a los servicios financieros. Casi 270 de estas localidades tienen menos de 100 habitantes. Estas oficinas sobre ruedas suponen un importante impulso a la inclusión financiera, recorriendo cada mes más de 75.000 kilómetros en 17 provincias de siete comunidades autónomas.

Hay un colectivo que se ve más beneficiado con el servicio de oficinas móviles: el 70% de usuarios de oficinas móviles son personas de más de 65 años. Cuatro de cada 10 clientes de este segmento en España confían en CaixaBank, según datos de la entidad. Y es probable que la cifra aumente, si se tiene en cuenta que dentro de 50 años el 30,9% de las personas residentes en España tendrán 65 años o más, según el Instituto Nacional de Estadística (INE).

Para adaptarse a esta evolución demográfica, CaixaBank ha rediseñado su propuesta de valor. La entidad trata de fortalecer a este grupo de edad que, más o menos activo, no solo necesita que se le pongan las cosas fáciles ―por ejemplo, a través del protocolo de atención especial―, sino también productos adaptados a la mayor longevidad.

A través de programas como Generación+, CaixaBank proporciona asesoramiento patrimonial, apoyo en la dependencia y soluciones financieras adaptadas a las necesidades de cada etapa vital. Ramiro Elena

A través de programas como Generación+, CaixaBank ofrece asesoramiento integral del patrimonio, ayuda en la tramitación de la dependencia, rentas vitalicias para complementar la pensión sin renunciar a la herencia o se encargan de elaborar testamentos y garantizar que se respeten las voluntades. Su enfoque se basa en la diversificación y en moldear las soluciones al ciclo vital de cada cliente, de manera que la planificación financiera evolucione con sus necesidades (y con sus circunstancias). El objetivo, señalan desde la compañía, es combinar eficiencia fiscal, liquidez, rentabilidad y protección.

La apuesta por considerar a este grupo demográfico como personas activas también se respalda en el emprendimiento sénior, y los microcréditos pueden servir de incentivo. Durante 2025, MicroBank, el banco social de CaixaBank (como ellos lo denominan), financió 2.303 proyectos de emprendimiento liderados por personas de 55 años o más, por un valor total de 36,5 millones de euros. Su importe medio se ha situado en cerca de 15.900 euros: la mayoría (el 77%) solicitó financiación para ampliar su negocio, mientras que el 23% lo ha hizo para abrir nuevas iniciativas empresariales.

Emprendedores rurales, al frente

Esos microcréditos del banco social llegan, además, a otras generaciones, y el año pasado destinaron financiación principalmente a cinco sectores: restauración, transporte por carretera, belleza, albañilería y reformas y talleres mecánicos. La estrella fue el primero, la restauración, que implicó más de la mitad de los 4.477 nuevos negocios que se alcanzaron gracias a la entidad en España en ese periodo de tiempo.

Enfocada en emprendedores rurales con proyectos activos, la entidad bancaria impulsa además el programa Tierra de Oportunidades, que busca fijar población y empleo en la España rural, a través de ayuda económica, formación y acompañamiento. Una de las iniciativas beneficiadas en la última edición fue la empresa Gurevet, en Mezkiritz (Navarra), que presta atención de servicios veterinarios de animales de compañía a domicilio en toda la Comunidad Foral. Al principio, en 2021, Teresa Etxarri (32 años, Mezkiritz, Navarra) empezó sola en su furgoneta adaptada (cuenta un quirófano para hacer cirugías urgentes o sencillas). Con el tiempo, se incorporó su hermana como auxiliar y gerente y, desde hace un año, cuentan también con otra veterinaria porque abrieron una clínica.

Mi hermana y yo somos de un pueblo muy pequeño, del Pirineo navarro. Los servicios llegan en furgoneta: el panadero, el carnicero, el pescadero... y dijimos: ¿por qué no también la veterinaria? Es una forma de poder ayudar a diferentes zonas. Teresa Etxarri, veterinaria y empresaria de Gurevet (Mezkiritz, Navarra)

Pero la cualidad de sus servicios reside en que Etxarri se desplaza hasta los hogares para vacunar, realizar consultas o chequeos o aplicar cuidados paliativos, entre otras cosas, sobre todo a perros y gatos. “Hay cosas que empiezan siendo algo leve que, si no tuviésemos este servicio, se quedarían sin atender y acabarían siendo cosas graves; la gente es más consciente de tener las vacunas al día o de esterilizar a sus animales”, detalla. La relación con el cliente es más cercana, se basa en la confianza, y ellos responden. “Queremos dar a las zonas rurales el mismo servicio que tendrían en una ciudad”, incide.

Gracias a la aportación de CaixaBank, la emprendedora consiguió un apoyo no solo económico, sino también visibilidad: “Por ejemplo, nos ayudaron a hacer vídeo en condiciones para redes sociales. La verdad, es que nos han ayudado a coger confianza con determinados clientes”. En definitiva, Tierra de Oportunidades les sirvió de “acompañamiento y de difusión”.

La veterinaria Teresa Etxarri (derecha), atiende a un perro dentro de su furgoneta. Cedida por CaixaBank

La “inquietud de ayudar”

La vocación de ayudar es una especie de “inquietud” que se lleva dentro siempre, califica Pepi Solano. “Sabes que quieres hacer algo, pero no sabes cómo ni dónde”, describe. Esta andaluza ha podido desplegar esa energía de la mano de Voluntariado CaixaBank. “Por mediación de su voluntariado, ellos enseguida te localizan y te dicen: ‘Pepi, mira, nos están pidiendo ayuda en tal sitio’. Y yo respondo: ‘Ahí estamos”.

Mi marido, que trabajaba en CaixaBank, sabía que yo tenía la inquietud de probar un voluntariado y me enseñó las oportunidades que daba el banco. Nos metimos juntos a ayudar y, desde hace más de 10 años, colaboro con distintas entidades sociales. Pepi Solano, colaboradora en proyectos de Voluntariado CaixaBank en Cádiz

Desde hace más de una década ha participado en talleres de cocina online para jóvenes migrantes, actividades para niños con discapacidad, visitas a las residencias de mayores o apoyo escolar a chicos de un barrio vulnerable de Cádiz. “Algunos de los que ayudé de pequeños ya son mayores de edad y seguimos en contacto. A veces, vamos a tomar un café o me llaman, me van contando su vida”, describe, con cariño. La han acompañado (se han contagiado de su entusiasmo) su marido, sus dos hijas y algunos amigos. Todos han tenido la misma sensación: “Siempre sales de allí feliz y piensas: esto hay que repetirlo”.

Como ellos, un total de 24.000 personas participaron en actividades de voluntariado en 2025, más de 19.000 eran empleados ―el 45% de la plantilla―. Además, entre mayo y junio de este año se ha celebrado la cuarta edición del Mes Social que, gracias a la colaboración de unas 1.400 entidades sociales locales, ha beneficiado a más de 155.000 personas en situación de vulnerabilidad y ha permitido impulsar más de 4.600 actividades solidarias en todas las comunidades autónomas. Solano afirma que las personas a las que ayuda responden con rotundidad: “Siempre te dan mucho más de lo que tú das”, asegura.

World.title: Calpe, renovarse a la sombra del Peñón
World.content:
Además de por su paquidérmica y famosa formación rocosa, la ciudad alicantina merece una visita por las Salinas, el conjunto arqueológico Baños de la Reina y una gastronomía en la que destaca la gamba blanca

Siempre que vuelvo a Calpe (cosa que pasa menos veces de las que querría) me sorprende y me exalta la colosalidad irredenta del peñón de Ifach. Esta paquidérmica protuberancia, ocasionalmente envuelta de nubes como la aureola de un santo, parece siempre a punto de saltar sobre el mar, que le es refugio y no abismo. Y, en efecto, ese tosco poliedro es una prolongación de la cordillera Bética, que se sumerge audazmente bajo las olas para dirigirse a Mallorca. Un tótem prodigioso, una ofrenda desmesurada y, quizás, en su priapismo cósmico, un tabú.

El parecido de esta gran roca con la de Gibraltar ha propiciado teorías diversas, normalmente descabelladas pero siempre amenas. Que Gibraltar e Ifach estuvieron unidos físicamente antes de abrirse el Estrecho es una de esas leyendas. Sí que es cierto que, en la antigüedad, el nombre Calpe designaba al peñón de Gibraltar. En un tiempo tan dado a las supercherías y otros golpes en el pecho de la ignorancia suprema me extraña que nadie haya propuesto que este titánico pedrusco pueda ser una ofrenda a algún dios. O quizás un monumento obra de los extraterrestres, como algunos partidarios desaforados del delirium tremens dicen que son las pirámides de El Cairo. Ajeno a todas nuestras elucubraciones, el Peñón sigue aquí, como el dinosaurio de Monterroso: una erección ciclópea, una insurgencia calcárea insolente y retadora, un desorbitado capricho morfológico.

Con este atractivo paisajístico, la ciudad alicantina necesita poco más para atraer visitantes. Y, sin embargo, las calidades de su oferta no dejan de aumentar. Ya se sabe que desde hace décadas recibe un elevado número de turistas extranjeros (muchos, hoy, residentes permanentes), principalmente procedentes del Reino Unido, Alemania, Bélgica y los Países Bajos. Este carácter cosmopolita no le ha hecho perder personalidad. Su casco antiguo con restos de los muros medievales resulta muy evocador, con sus calles estrechas, sus plazas tradicionales y edificios históricos como la iglesia Antigua (del siglo XV) y el Torreó de la Peça (baluarte defensivo de la antigua muralla). A esto une una variada oferta de restauración y comercio, amén de las actividades náuticas de su puerto deportivo o el senderismo que puede practicarse en el Peñón.

Torreó de la Peça, baluarte defensivo de la antigua muralla, en Calpe. TONO BALAGUER (GETTY IMAGES )

Entre sus atractivos naturales están las Salinas y el conjunto arqueológico Baños de la Reina. Las Salinas son parte de una antigua bahía cerrada por una barrera de dunas que unía el Peñón con el continente. La explotación de sal se cerró en 1988, así que, clausurada la industria, ha florecido la biodiversidad: allí viven 173 especies diferentes de aves. En cuanto a Baños de la Reina, es un yacimiento arqueológico, anexo a las Salinas, donde debió vivir un noble romano. Además de su lujosa villa, incluye una piscifactoría (donde se llevaba a cabo la salazón del pescado), unas termas, una noria y cuatro aljibes.

Esta antigua actividad pesquera ha llegado hasta la actualidad. A diferencia de otros destinos muy orientados exclusivamente al turismo, Calpe ha mantenido una flota de arrastre significativa. Su puerto alberga una de las lonjas más importantes de la zona, donde se realiza la ancestral e imprescindible subasta del pescado y el marisco locales.

Vista de Las Salinas, parte de una antigua bahía cerrada por una barrera de dunas que unía el Peñón con el continente. Jacek Krysciak ( GETTY IMAGES )

Su gran tesoro marino es la gamba blanca. Aunque la gamba roja de su vecina Dénia tiene una fama más consolidada, las propiedades de la blanca (su dulzura natural, su carne firme y sedosa, el suave aroma a yodo acabada de pescar) no son precisamente despreciables. Desde 2025, este fruto del mar goza de marca de calidad propia. Según el Portal Agrari de la Generalitat, ese año se capturaron y comercializaron más de 1.600 toneladas de gamba blanca en la Comunidad Valenciana (casi toda en la costa de Alicante). Es la tercera especie local en número de capturas (después del boquerón y de la sardina): genera 13,5 millones de euros, superando a la gamba roja y al boquerón, que hace años lideraban el ránking marino. Y ahora ese tesoro, que era cuantitativo, ha empezado a volverse cualitativo.

Parte de los Baños de la Reina, un yacimiento arqueológico anexo a Las Salinas. Teo Moreno ( Alamy / CORDON PRESS )

Es precisamente en la gastronomía donde Calpe ha afinado más su renovación en los últimos tiempos. La versatilidad culinaria de ese prodigioso crustáceo ha llamado la atención de los chefs más reputados de la zona. Dos ejemplos: los restaurantes Onami y Beat.

Marisco fresco expuesto en el puerto pesquero de Calpe, Alicante. Manoli Perez ( Alamy / CORDON PRESS )

Onami abrió este pasado mes de junio en el hotel A.R. Diamante Beach. Este imponente establecimiento ya disponía de otros dos locales de restauración, el Audrey’s (el primer local con estrella Michelin de Calpe) y el Amas. Onami comparte chef con Amas: Diego Laso. La diferencia entre los dos —inspirados ambos en la cocina japonesa— es que en Onami no hay carta y se come en la barra. El servicio está concebido como un menú degustación al estilo kaiseki-ryori: la forma más refinada y tradicional de la alta gastronomía japonesa. Onami es un juego de palabras entre ona (ola, en valenciano/catalán) y umami. Esto da la medida de su filosofía: ofrecer un diálogo entre la cocina valenciana y la nipona. De aquí la receta de gamba blanca en Amas (curada con sake y servida con crema inglesa y algas de Galicia), o el nigiri de este mismo crustáceo en Onami, simplemente pelado y servido sobre arroz.

Segundo ejemplo: el restaurante Beat (una estrella Michelin), ubicado en The Cookbook. Este hotel acaba de renovarse en profundidad. En Beat reina desde hace diez años José Manuel Miguel, el único cocinero valenciano que ha obtenido estrellas Michelin en Francia y en España. Si en Onami dialogaban la cocina local con la nipona, aquí la fusión está protagonizada por lo valenciano y lo francés. El gran referente de José Manuel Miguel es Paul Bocuse, emblema de la nouvelle cuisine gala. El bogavante lo cocina a la manera de la Salade de homard à la française de Bocuse, pero la gamba blanca no requiere mayor transformación: su hechizo radica en la ausencia de cocción.

Con todo esto ya se puede volver a visitar Calpe y saborear algo más que la siempre imponente vista de su Peñón. Tradición y modernidad, lo llaman.

World.title: National water shortage officially over but troubles continue
World.content:
The Netherlands is officially out of a water shortage, but the drought that left houseboats stranded and cargo barges part-loaded throughout the summer will be felt for months to come, the infrastructure ministry has said.

Weeks of rain and falling demand have allowed the ministry to move the country from level two to level one on its three-stage scale of water shortages – from an actual shortage back to an impending one. Crops are being harvested, farmers are irrigating less and cooler weather means less water is evaporating.

The government team that met weekly through the summer to tackle the shortage will now disband, though the national water distribution committee, which warned of serious water shortages in July, will keep meeting, and the weekly drought monitor continues.

Recovery will take months

The downgrade does not mean the drought is over. The Rhine is still carrying only about half its normal volume for early September and river levels could stay low until the end of the year. Groundwater will also take even longer to get back to normal levels.

For the houseboat owners stranded on stretches of the Rhine that dried up months ago, there will be little immediate relief. Their homes will not refloat until levels rise. Shipping also faces reduced services and delays at locks.

Water abstraction restrictions still apply across the higher sandy soils of the east and south, and salinisation of the IJsselmeer remains a concern for drinking water suppliers, though some water boards have begun rolling back restrictions. Drinking water supplies remain secure.

World.title: Inspectors allow only Dutch online abortion service to continue
World.content:
The Dutch’ healthcare inspectorate has found that the country’s only online abortion service fell short on its duties for care, but will let it keep operating after the site agreed to change its practices.

Thuisabortus.nl, which launched in March, was the first service in the Netherlands to let women get the abortion pill prescribed without an in-person visit to a GP or clinic.

The inspectorate, the IGJ, said the main problem was that women who ordered the pill through the website usually had no personal contact with a doctor before it was prescribed but it also found no serious risk to patients and so no reason to shut it down.

As a remedial measure, the site has since telephoned every woman who applies, discussing the stage of the pregnancy, possible complications, aftercare through her own GP and alternatives to abortion.

Concerns raised at launch

When the site was launched, the family doctors organisation KNMG and the GP organisation LHV questioned whether issuing the pill without a consultation met the legal duty of care.

Health minister Sophie Hermans told MPs on Wednesday that the government regretted the shortcomings, and described the conversation between a woman and her doctor as an “essential part” of careful abortion care.

The site’s founder, GP Peter Leusink, said he would comply but disagreed, arguing that a phone consultation is not needed for safe care and pointing to home use of the pill in the US, the UK and Sweden. “We have to comply with that outdated law,” he told NRC.

Doctors remain divided

The abortion doctors’ association NGvA said the report confirmed its concern that the platform had started in a hurry and overlooked parts of proper care, and that it was now exploring a digital service of its own. The GPs’ professional body NHG has backed online abortion care as a useful addition and called for GPs and the site to work together.

The LHV said it still had concerns about who handles complications at night and at weekends. The orthodox Protestant SGP and the ChristenUnie went further, with SGP MP Diederik van Dijk saying the service should have been taken offline.

GPs have been able to prescribe the abortion pill since the start of 2025, after completing extra training. Thuisabortus.nl says it has prescribed around 1,680 pills since April, about a quarter of all abortion pills issued in the Netherlands. The inspectorate has given the site until mid-November to complete the remaining changes.

World.title: Illegal casinos hijack thousands of Dutch websites
World.content:
At least 1,000 legitimate Dutch and European websites, many belonging to companies, charities and freelancers, have been quietly turned into shopfronts for illegal online casinos, an investigation by radio station BNR has found. The real figure might be over 8,000.

The sites have nothing to do with gambling, and their owners are usually unaware. Criminals either hack poorly secured websites and add casino pages, or buy up an organisation’s expired domain name and fill it with gambling content.

Because search engines already trust those addresses, the casino pages rank highly. Someone searching for an online casino may land on a seemingly reputable site before being redirected to an illegal operator.

BNR found gambling pages on an old domain once used by broadcaster and writer Wilfried de Jong, on sites formerly run by the liberal VVD party in Zeeland and Brabant, and on the website of a business lawyer, where at least 50 casino pages had been added.

The national gambling authority called it “a very big problem” and is working with SIDN, the body that manages Dutch internet domains, to shut down redirect pages, but the process is slow because there is no legal power to block the sites, which SIDN says it wants.

It can also do little about .com or .eu addresses, which fall outside SIDN’s remit, so it is hoping Google will step in. The search engine removes adverts for illegal casinos but leaves the sites and redirect pages in place.

The cabinet said in June it was drawing up new tools with the authority to tackle illegal gambling, including the power to block websites. Regulators have struggled to keep up, with more now being spent on illegal sites in the Netherlands than on legal ones.

World.title: Minister given permission to axe far-right TV broadcaster
World.content:
The Netherlands’ media minister, Rianne Letschert, has obtained the legal authority to strip the far-right broadcaster Ongehoord Nederland (ON) of its licence, meaning it could be taken off air from public broadcasting and lose its public funding.

The Dutch media authority set out a case in a letter to Letschert, weeks after ON presenters spoke of their approval and agreements with certain Adolf Hitler remarks in a July broadcast.

It called the show a turning point and said it no longer trusted ON to run its operations properly.

Letschert has said a licence can only be withdrawn once two formal sanctions are in place, both of which have now been fulfilled. The first was a fine imposed last September for conflict-of-interest breaches and for ignoring editorial rules, and a separate penalty order for withholding records of how it spent public money.

ON director Peter Vlemmix told the ANP news agency the broadcaster would continue its “fight for survival” and accused the authority of overlooking improvements made over the past year.

Letschert has promised to tell MPs her decision on ON’s future before a parliamentary debate on September 24.

World.content:

A court in The Hague ruled on Thursday that the public prosecution service (OM) must hand over the names the 14 prominent doctors who signed a letter urging an investigation into the case of Milou, a 17-year-old died by euthanasia in 2023.

Her parents, who were subjected to death threats after the letter was leaked, sued to obtain the names of the medical professionals who penned the later.

The OM had refused to provide the names, six of which are already known, citing privacy concerns.

Judges in The Hague said that it was “unreasonable to refuse to provide the letter containing names to the parents” who have a “compelling interest” in the information.

The parents could choose to pursue disciplinary or civil legal action against the doctors.

Milou had suffered from mental health problems from the age of 11 following sexual abuse. She was again sexually abused in an institution by another patient.

After years of treatment and various suicide attempts, she chose euthanasia at the age of 17 on the grounds of unbearable mental suffering.

The psychiatrist who approved her decision acted in accordance with the guidelines, the regional euthanasia review committee RTE found.

The committee reviews all euthanasia procedures to make sure the correct procedures have been followed and reports back to the OM, which now has five days to hand over the names.

World.title: Student room shortage stays above 20,000 despite new builds
World.content:

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

More students in the Netherlands are staying in their parents’ home or giving up the search for a place of their own, as the shortage of student housing remains high despite thousands of new rooms being built each year.

The country is short of more than 20,200 student rooms, barely down from 21,000 a year earlier, according to the annual student housing monitor from knowledge centre Kences, published this week.

Social housing providers have built nearly 5,000 units a year since 2022, meeting the targets they were set.

Kences had expected the shortage to climb, because private landlords have been selling up in response to new rent rules and higher taxes. Some 32,300 fewer students have rented from private landlords since 2024.

That did not translate into a sharp rise, largely because student numbers have also dropped, including among international students. The share of students living away from home has fallen from 50% to 43% over eight years.

Fewer rooms, riskier ads

The rooms still on the private market are increasingly hard to rent safely. Many are advertised above the legal limit.

Scammers, meanwhile, have flooded TikTok with fake listings that pocket deposits for rooms that do not exist.

Internationals are especially exposed to housing fraud, as they rarely have a family home to fall back on and often do not know their rights.

Kences wants the profit tax paid by housing associations scrapped, which it says would fund 15,000 to 25,000 more student homes over ten years. “Every euro we hand to the tax office, we would rather put into housing,” director Reijnder Jan Spits told broadcaster NOS.

Even if every current building plan goes ahead, the centre warned, the shortage could still stand at between 10,000 and 35,000 rooms in eight years.

World.title: Cybercrime and online fraud hit 2.5 million people in 2025
World.content:
An estimated 2.5 million people in the Netherlands fell victim to cybercrime or an online form of fraud, deception or intimidation last year, according to a new report by prosecutors and police that warns the threat is becoming harder to contain.

The Cybercrimebeeld Nederland, published every two years by the public prosecution department (OM) and the Dutch police, says offenders are increasingly working across borders and paying for whatever expertise they lack.

Technical skill is now widely for sale, the report says: ready-made tools, stolen data and services allow novice hackers to create complex attacks.

“Criminals combine data from earlier hacks with newly stolen data,” said Christa de Pagter, the national public prosecutor for cybercrime. Offenders use it to make more targetted attacks on victims, she said, often posing as a bank or crypto platform to pressure them into acting.

State actors blur the line

The report also revealed the growing role of state actors, which it says are increasingly entangled with criminal groups through hybrid warfare, eroding the line between cybercrime and national security. States can use criminals as proxies, directing them or supplying money and infrastructure.

In May, Dutch investigators arrested two men over servers used for Russian-linked cyberattacks; the report also cites two 17-year-olds detained last year for mapping wifi networks around government buildings in The Hague.

Lured through online games

Prosecutors and police also describe a new generation of young, Western cybercriminals, driven by money and status rather than ideology, who meet in loose online networks and specialise in data and cryptocurrency theft. They range in age from 11 to 25, police cybercrime lead Stan Duijf told broadcaster NOS.

Children are often lured in through online games such as Roblox, Fortnite and Minecraft, where they can be groomed in chat rooms. “It’s just like the schoolyard: they start with mischief,” Duijf said – but some go on to become cybercriminals.

The report highlights this year’s hack on Odido, which police believe a Dutch gang using the name ShinyHunters carried out, exposing the data of 6.2 million customers and prompting a €1 million ransom demand the firm refused.

AI is described as a “catalyst”: the report says it does not fundamentally change cybercrime but increases its speed and scale, and makes scam emails harder to spot.

World.title: Rabbit farms face prosecution over abuse footage
World.content:
Sixteen Dutch rabbit farms could face criminal prosecution after undercover footage showed bunnies being lifted by the ears and thrown into crates, and sick animals beaten to death, junior agriculture minister Silvio Erkens has said.

The images, filmed by campaign group Animal Rights, were shot at 16 companies that export live rabbits to slaughterhouses in Belgium. They show the animals being picked up by the ears, fur, legs or head and thrown in large numbers into transport crates and shopping trolleys, where they can be crushed.

“What can be seen in the footage is terrible,” Erkens said in answer to parliamentary questions from D66 and the animal rights party PvdD, calling the treatment unacceptable. Some people, he added, appeared to feel free to handle animals this way when no inspector was nearby.

The food safety board NVWA has received a large amount of recent footage and is checking it for authenticity. If abuse is found companies are prosecuted. In 2024 a slaughterhouse was fined for cruelty after activists released undercover video.

Footage seen so far points to structural and serious failings in how the animals are handled, Erkens said. He has also set up new checks on how rabbits are caught and loaded – a stage of animal transport that inspections had largely overlooked, and will update parliament by the end of the year.

President Karol Nawrocki has launched a programme allowing Polish companies looking to expand into international markets to apply to join his foreign visits. “Seats on the presidential plane will soon be available to Polish businesses,” Nawrocki, who is aligned with the opposition, announced in a video published on X. “I want Polish companies, including small and medium-sized ones, to be able to establish new contacts, develop existing business relationships and successfully conquer foreign markets alongside the president.” Już niedługo miejsca w prezydenckim samolocie będą dostępne także dla polskiego biznesu. Chcę, żeby polskie firmy, również te małe i średnie, mogły u boku prezydenta nawiązywać nowe kontakty, rozwijać już istniejące relacje biznesowe i z sukcesem podbijać zagraniczne rynki.… pic.twitter.com/kO6L1t1m4D — Kancelaria Prezydenta RP (@prezydentpl) September 3, 2026 To launch the programme, Nawrocki’s office is already accepting applications from business representatives interested in joining the president on his trip to New York later this month to attend the United Nations General Assembly. A one-day Polish-American Economic Summit is also planned during the visit, linked to Poland’s participation in this year’s G20 summit, which is being hosted by the United States. When deciding which businesses to invite on the trip, the presidential chancellery says it would seek “well-established companies with the potential to grow in the US market and seeking new partners and opportunities for collaboration” Those selected will be invited to travel on the presidential flight from Warsaw to New York and back, and will also receive local transportation. However, other costs, such as accommodation, meals and any necessary visas, will have to be paid by the businesses themselves. Nawrocki’s office says that the new programme was launched in response to long-standing calls from businesses for presidential foreign visits to be used to promote the international expansion of Polish companies. Opportunities to join presidential visits will be offered regularly, with details of new application rounds published on the prezydent.pl website. In recent years, a growing number of Polish companies have expanded abroad, helped by the country’s strong economic growth over the past three decades. Poland has summoned Russia’s ambassador in response to recent hostile actions against Germany. “[We] expressed our strong condemnation of state terrorism perpetrated by Russia – because what is a problem for one ally is a problem for the entire alliance,” said Polish foreign minister Radosław Sikorski. “Putin’s Russia remains one of the most serious security threats – not just for Europe, but for the entire world order,” he added. “Its goal is to permanently destroy the European security architecture.” 💬 Nie ma zgody na podpalenia, ataki na kolej, morderstwa i inne prowokacje. Polska też wezwała ambasadora Rosji po to, aby wyrazić nasze stanowcze potępienie dla terroryzmu państwowego autorstwa Federacji Rosyjskiej. | wicepremier, minister spraw zagranicznych @sikorskiradek… pic.twitter.com/LChAjwsX8H — Ministerstwo Spraw Zagranicznych RP 🇵🇱 (@MSZ_RP) September 3, 2026 On Tuesday, the German government announced that it held Russia responsible for an attempted drone attack on Leipzig airport last month. While they are still being investigated, on Wednesday, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk suggested that they may also be part of “Russia’s escalatory actions throughout the region”. On Thursday, the spokesman for Poland’s foreign ministry, Maciej Wewiór, confirmed to the Polish Press Agency (PAP) that Russia’s ambassador to Warsaw, Georgy Mikhno, had been summoned to the ministry. Wewiór said that Poland wanted to convey “our firm opposition to the escalation of Russia’s aggressive actions” as well as to show solidarity with Germany. A number of other European leaders have also this week expressed solidarity with Germany, including European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte. Poland has itself been a major target for Russia. Earlier this year, a report by the International Centre for Counter-Terrorism found that Poland was the “primary focus” of Russian sabotage. It has also suffered cyberattacks, disinformation campaigns, and “weaponised migration” on its eastern border. In response, Poland has successively closed down all of Russia’s consulates in the country, with Moscow responding by doing the same with Polish consulates operating on its territory. This week, after a fire broke out at a drone factory in Poland, Tusk said that there is “no doubt” it was caused deliberately and suggested it was also likely carried out on behalf of Russia. World.title: Poland moves to allow local communities to ban short-term rentals
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland’s government has approved legislation that would allow local communities to ban short-term rentals – the type of privately owned accommodation offered through services such as Airbnb and Booking.com. Such services have boomed in Poland in recent years, like in other parts of the world. But that has prompted a backlash from many communities, which argue that short-term rentals can cause disruption, reduce the availability of housing, and drive up prices. However, the proposed measures have already caused divisions within the ruling coalition and must still be approved by parliament, where the government has a majority, and by President Karol Nawrocki, who is aligned with the right-wing opposition and has vetoed a record number of bills. ❗ Rada Ministrów przyjęła autopoprawkę do projektu ustawy dotyczącego najmu krótkoterminowego. Nowe rozwiązania dadzą mieszkańcom i samorządom konkretne narzędzia do reagowania tam, gdzie najem krótkoterminowy powoduje problemy z bezpieczeństwem i porządkiem publicznym. ➡️… pic.twitter.com/7KvW2O4AKW — Ministerstwo Sportu i Turystyki (@SPORT_GOV_PL) September 2, 2026 Speaking ahead of a cabinet meeting on Wednesday, Prime Minister Donald Tusk confirmed that, following a “difficult process” of discussion, his coalition, which ranges from left to centre right, had agreed on the measures. They would grant “greater rights for residents, communities, housing cooperatives and local authorities regarding the situation in the short-term rental market”, said Tusk. “Wherever order, safety and basic comfort of life are threatened, decisions can be made to exclude these types of businesses.” The new rules would allow homeowner associations (wspólnoty mieszkaniowe) and housing cooperatives (spółdzielnie mieszkaniowe) to prohibit short-term rentals. If a majority of members voted to adopt such a ban, operators of short-term rental properties would have six months to end operations. Municipal councils (rady gmin), at the request of the mayor, would also be given the power to designate specific areas within their territory in which short-term rentals would be banned or restricted (for example, to a certain number of days a year). There would also be greater powers for residents and housing groups to initiate official inspections of properties if they believe there are violations of public safety and order rules. If a property violated such regulations three times within six months, it would be banned from operating for a year. Tusk noted that, if the bill becomes law, it would not fully go into force until 2028, in order to give enough time for businesses and communities to adapt to the new rules. If Poland does introduce the new measures, its cities could follow the example of many of their European counterparts, such as Barcelona, Paris and London, which have introduced various restrictions on short-term rentals. The European Union has also moved to more tightly regulate the sector. EU to help tourism hotspots crack down on Airbnb-style holiday rentals https://t.co/0Y5nzfZZYF — Financial Times (@FT) August 30, 2026 The measures have been subject to intense debate within the ruling coalition. When the legislation was first submitted to parliament in July, some parts that had previously been included, such as provisions allowing municipalities to ban short-term rentals in certain areas, were removed. That prompted a backlash from two junior coalition partners in particular, The Left (Lewica) and the centrist Poland 2050 (Polska 2050), prompting further discussions over the summer, resulting in the bill now being toughened again. The Left celebrated the government’s decision to restore tougher elements of the bill, saying it would help avoid “situations where short-term rentals turn into a nightmare, stripping residents of their peace”. The leader of Poland 2050, Katarzyna Pełczyńska-Nałęcz, declared that they had “scored another goal against the lobbyists” by toughening the legislation. World.title: NfP podcast: How small towns became a testing ground for Poland’s far right
World.content: In our new podcast, Notes from Poland’s editor-in-chief Daniel Tilles speaks with deputy editor-in-chief Alicja Ptak about her research into how four contentious issues – migration, women’s rights, Jewish heritage and LGBT+ rights – have played out in 19 smaller towns and cities in Poland. They discuss how national far-right talking points are being imported into smaller towns, how these issues are covered and contested at the local level, and what this all means ahead of next year’s parliamentary elections. This conversation was based on a report produced as part of Notes from Poland’s new bespoke service offering our expertise to clients.
