Iranians meanwhile expressed dismay over the return to hostilities.

The war erupted on February 28 with US-Israeli attacks on Iran that killed its supreme leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei.

A fragile ceasefire collapsed in July after attacks on commercial ships in the Strait of Hormuz, through which one-fifth of world oil supplies previously flowed.

Israel’s defence minister meanwhile said his country was prepared to respond “with great force” if attacked by Iran over the Jewish high holiday season, which begins in mid-September.

“For now, they are striking throughout the region except us,” Israel Katz said.

World.title: US extends Middle East deployments into 2027 as Iran conflict drags on
World.content:
WASHINGTON: The United States is extending the deployment of thousands of American troops and military assets across the Middle East into 2027, signalling Washington is preparing for a prolonged conflict with Iran.

The deployment extensions, ordered by Secretary of War Pete Hegseth, will affect US Army units, air-defence forces, fighter squadrons and Navy personnel operating in and around the Middle East, according to The Wall Street Journal.

The US military currently has roughly 50,000 troops in the region.

Quoting from a letter sent by military leaders to soldiers’ families, The Journal reported that elements of the Army’s 82nd Airborne Division, one of the US military’s principal rapid-response forces, could remain in the region well into 2027.

“We do not share that lightly, and we understand that a longer tour weighs heavily on every household, including our own,” the letter said.

The extensions represent a significant shift from expectations at the beginning of the US campaign against Iran. Hegseth had presented the operation as a swift and decisive military action. Six months into the conflict, however, the Pentagon is preparing for deployments lasting a year or longer.

Army air-defence units responsible for intercepting Iranian missiles and drones have also had their normal deployment periods extended. Their standard nine-month tours have in some cases been stretched to a full year, while some units originally scheduled for assignments in Europe or the Pacific have spent more than a year in the Middle East.

The prolonged deployments are raising concerns about the effect on military readiness.

“The operational tempo for air defence units before this war was already among the highest of the joint force,” Tom Karako, director of the Missile Defence Project at the Centre for Strategic and International Studies, told The Journal.

Extended deployments, he warned, could wear down troops, delay equipment maintenance and hamper longer-term military modernisation.

The strain is also being felt by Navy personnel. Fighting in the region has disrupted the Navy’s normal ability to resupply forces, forcing greater reliance on the remote US base at Diego Garcia in the Indian Ocean.

Sailors aboard some warships have consequently faced reduced opportunities for mail, care packages and time away from their vessels.

The US Navy currently has about 19 warships operating in connection with the regional military posture, while additional aircraft and air-defence systems remain deployed to protect American forces and bases.

The Pentagon’s open-ended deployment framework is intended to preserve the president’s military options as the conflict develops. It does not necessarily mean that all of the forces now in the region will remain there continuously until 2027, but it gives commanders and the White House a baseline force from which operations can continue or be expanded.

The uncertainty is particularly striking because Trump has privately discussed with advisers whether to declare the conflict with Iran over, even as American and Iranian forces continue to exchange direct strikes.

The longer the conflict continues, military commanders face a difficult balance: maintaining sufficient forces to defend American personnel and preserve the president’s options while preventing repeated and extended deployments from exhausting troops, disrupting family life and leaving less time to maintain and modernise the wider US military.

World.title: Hawala networks increasingly use virtual assets, fintech to conceal illicit wealth: FATF, OECD
World.content:
ISLAMABAD: Traditional underground financial networks, including hawala and other similar service providers (HOSSPs), have become increasingly professionalised and are making greater use of virtual assets and fintech platforms to conceal billions of dollars in illicit wealth, according to a new joint report by the Financial Action Task Force (FATF) and the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD).

The report was jointly prepared by the two Paris-based organisations, which specialise in financial and economic matters.

Based on feedback from around 45 jurisdictions and organisations, including India and Pakistan, the report highlighted cases involving illicit money transfers through such HOSSPs. In both India and Pakistan, it noted the growing role of underground banking and financial networks in facilitating illicit finance.

The report highlighted the vulnerability of these systems to money laundering and terrorist financing, with some cases involving more than €500 million being laundered through underground banking and hawala-based schemes within just a few months.

It found that the criminal misuse of underground banking and HOSSPs was a widespread global phenomenon, with more than 80pc of reporting jurisdictions identifying these systems as among the principal channels or techniques used for professional money laundering.

Referring to an episode involving a hawala network that used social media and mobile money transfers to facilitate transactions with Pakistan, the report said the Central Bank of Oman (CBO) received intelligence through its whistleblower channel about individuals suspected of operating an unlicensed cross-border remittance business to Pakistan.

The reporting entity detected the activity after observing a sudden reduction in customer remittances through specific corridors, the report said.

The CBO conducted further enquiries, including engaging with customers, joining the relevant WhatsApp group and collecting supporting evidence before reporting the case. Its follow-up enquiries, including social media monitoring and off-site analysis, identified a WhatsApp group named “XX Money Exchange”, which was operated by foreign nationals to advertise foreign exchange and remittance services to expatriate communities in Oman.

The hawaladars offered rates below the formal market rate, with minimal or no fees, and encouraged customers to share the group with others seeking to remit funds. Customers transferred money to the suspected hawaladars either in cash or through mobile-linked transfers. The hawaladars then sent screenshots showing proof of payment through an e-wallet to a corresponding e-wallet maintained with a payment service provider in the destination jurisdiction.

“The scheme exploited lower-cost remittance channels in destination countries, including fee-free transfers to Pakistan through channels such as Raast, as well as exchange rate differentials offered by some digital wallet or payment providers,” the report said.

This allowed the hawaladars to generate margins while offering cheaper remittance services. Omani authorities identified six suspected individuals believed to form a connected network of hawaladars, with transaction flows of approximately $72,293 recorded over a one-year period.

Likewise, illegal online gambling proceeds were being laundered through HOSSP-based networks in India. The report said Indian authorities had identified a professional money laundering (PML) scheme linked to an illegal online gambling platform that generated proceeds from sports betting, card games and other forms of online wagering.

The platform relied on a decentralised network of “panel operators” to manage customer deposits and withdrawals. These operators used UPI, online banking, digital wallets, mule accounts and accounts opened using stolen identities to receive and transfer funds.

The structure enabled the organisers to separate the gambling platform from the financial flows supporting it. A portion of the proceeds was converted into cash and moved abroad through hawala and other underground banking channels. The funds were then reintroduced into India as purported foreign investment from the UAE, disguising their criminal origin, the report said.

The report was prepared with input from experts from 32 jurisdictions, including Pakistan, as well as 22 FATF members and three observers — Europol, Interpol and UNODC.

It said that while HOSSPs could serve legitimate purposes, the provision of underground banking or unregistered HOSSP services was generally a criminal offence in most countries and contravened FATF standards. The standards recommend that countries require such entities to be licensed or registered to provide these services.

The report emphasised how underground banking and hawala networks had evolved into increasingly organised, business-like structures. It said these networks had become highly sophisticated, scalable and commercially operated, contributing to the emergence of “money laundering as a service” — the systematic outsourcing of money laundering functions to specialists — and professional money laundering as a commercialised business model.

Such networks offer lower commission rates and can move large volumes of value rapidly across borders, making them attractive to organised crime groups, the report said.

The FATF also warned of the increasing involvement of lawyers, accountants, auditors, notaries, corporate formation agents, financial consultants, real estate agents, casinos and junket operators in facilitating such schemes.

It also highlighted the growing integration of these networks with the formal financial sector, saying professional money launderers were increasingly using bank accounts, fintech platforms, payment service providers, virtual IBANs, prepaid cards and virtual asset wallets as entry and exit points in money laundering cycles, exploiting regulatory blind spots.

Discussing the rise of “digital hawala”, the report said nearly 70pc of respondents had identified the integration of new technologies and a growing shift towards digital hawala. These included operators using encrypted messaging applications such as WhatsApp, Telegram and Signal, as well as digital tools to coordinate transactions; customers initiating transfers through bank accounts, mobile wallets, fintech applications or instant payment systems; and operators using virtual assets, including stablecoins, to settle balances among themselves.

The report also identified the use of AI-based tools and the development of purpose-built “hawala apps”.

These developments can improve the efficiency of PML services, make illicit funds easier to conceal, and expand the geographic reach and resilience of underground banking- and HOSSP-based professional money laundering schemes.

The report’s findings demonstrated that the criminal use of these systems was no longer limited to cash-based crimes such as drug trafficking or smuggling. “Today, criminals are using these systems to launder proceeds from a broader spectrum of criminal economies including fraud, cyber-enabled crime, terrorist financing, illegal gaming and gambling and transnational organised crime,” it noted.

Through a series of operational case studies, the report shows how professional money laundering networks increasingly rely on underground banking systems, for example, to move proceeds from large-scale cross-border drug trafficking, or use digital hawala networks to finance members of terrorist organisations.

Drawing on evidence from more than 50 jurisdictions across the FATF Global Network and partner organisations, the report provides a global picture of how these systems operate and identifies good practices to help jurisdictions and the private sector strengthen their ability to detect, investigate, prosecute and disrupt the professional money laundering infrastructure that enables serious and organised crime, corruption, fraud and terrorist financing.

The findings highlight the importance of combining targeted prevention and enforcement measures with proportionate financial inclusion efforts, supported by legal clarity, enhanced detection capabilities, public-private feedback loops, domestic co-ordination and international co-operation.

World.title: 'A daughter of the nation': PM Shehbaz lauds courage of Pims nurse Razia Noreen during hospital fire
World.content:
Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif on Thursday praised the courage of a nurse who saved an infant from a deadly fire at the Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences (Pims) that killed 14 babies last week.

The fire early last Wednesday drew shock and horror across the country with lawmakers in both houses of parliament demanding accountability.

Footage from the incident showed that a nurse, Razia Noreen, entered the nursery at around 6:39am and emerged seconds later carrying a baby, rescuing the child. She then attempted to re-enter the nursery shortly afterwards.

The prime minister met with Noreen personally at the PM House in Islamabad, where the nurse recounted how she discovered the fire and her efforts to save the children in the maternity ward.

In a conversation at the PM House, the premier lauded the nurse, saying that the whole nation was not only praising her courage and bravery but was proud of her.

“You are truly a daughter of the nation,” he told her, adding that her actions would be recorded in history.

The nurse recounted that while preparing medication, she shut the medicine cabinet to suddenly catch sight of the fire.

“I threw the cabinet door shut and rushed inside,” she said, adding, “I didn’t even think about it.”

Noreen said that she had also told another nurse to “save the kids”, who had conducted rescue efforts outside the ward where there were more babies and their mothers.

“Post-natal mothers have undergone operations,” she said. “She immediately tried to rescue them … she knew that I was inside and would do something.”

Noting that the fire was very strong, she rescued one of the smaller babies and brought him outside to leave “in safe hands” with someone she knew.

“When Dr Abdul Rehman came out, I handed [the baby] over and rushed back inside,” she said, but added that as she was rescuing the second baby, a sudden blast caused a blackout.

PM Shehbaz reiterated that the whole nation was paying tribute to the nurse’s actions and added, “The mother of the child you saved will bless you.”

Noreen stressed that it was her “responsibility” to act, as nurses were given the responsibility of taking care of others’ children. She also expressed that she wished she could have saved the remaining children.

The premier noted that on March 23, the nurse would be given the Sitara-i-Khidmat and Rs10 million for her service. Noreen thanked PM Shehbaz and expressed her gratitude for bestowing such an honour on her.

PM Shehbaz had earlier approved the award and a cash reward for the nurse, who had “saved a child without regard for her own life”, according to the PMO.

“Razia Noreen has demonstrated an exceptional sense of responsibility and humanity. The entire nation, including myself, is proud of Nurse Razia Noreen for risking her own life to save the child. Such dutiful individuals cannot be praised enough,” he was quoted as saying.

World.title: Act for Nutrition conference: Experts call for food, nutritional security to be recognised as fundamental rights amid malnutrition crisis
World.content:
Day 2 of the conference concludes; World Bank official calls for understanding WASH-related drivers of malnutrition.

Listen to article 1x 1.2x 1.5x

A two-day international conference, ‘Act For Nutrition: The Emergency We Can No Longer Ignore’, held at Islamabad’s Serena Hotel, concluded on Thursday, with experts calling for food and nutritional security to be recognised as fundamental rights.

The conference aimed to address Pakistan’s persistent nutrition and stunting crisis.

As the conference came to a close, Dawn CEO Nazafreen Saigol-Lakhani, in a statement, said, “Pakistan’s nutrition crisis demands a coordinated response across health, agriculture, water, education, social protection and economic policy, tailored to local realities”.

On the first day, experts at the conference warned that more than four in 10 children under five were stunted and malnutrition was costing Pakistan close to $17 billion annually.

They also said that malnutrition was produced by a combination of poor diets, inadequate healthcare, weak water and sanitation services, poverty and other factors, making a multisectoral response essential.

The two-day conference brought together policymakers, international development leaders, health professionals and nutrition experts to confront the burgeoning crisis and build momentum for urgent, coordinated action.

View the full agenda here.

4:55pm - Conference concludes

4:40pm - Malnutrition ‘greatest barrier’ to development: WHO official

Representative of the World Health Organisation (WHO) in Pakistan Dr Dapeng Luo, in his closing remarks, stressed that malnutrition remained the “greatest barrier” to health, development, and opportunities.

He noted that nutrition was “much more than access to food” and further stated that “predictable and solid regulation” was needed as a way forward.

4:30pm - BNP showed nutrition can be integrated into social protection, says WFP official

WFP’s Country Director for Pakistan Anita Hirsch also noted the progress of the Benazir Nashonuma Programme (BNP), which she said had shown that nutrition can be integrated into national social protection.

“As we look ahead, one priority is to sustain those gains, continue to scale up and integrate services for millions of Pakistani women and children,” Hirsch said.

4:22pm - WFP official shares her key takeaways

World Food Programme’s Country Director for Pakistan Anita Hirsch shared her key takeaways from the two-day conference.

“Pakistan continues to face a high level of malnutrition. More than 40pc of children under five are stunted. This means children whose growth and cognitive development are compromised,” Hirsch said.

She continued: “Second takeaway was that timing matters; the first 1,000 days represent a critical window that will have lifelong implications for the potential for children and potential for Pakistan, and that adolescence also matters.”

Hirsch also noted the economic cost of malnutrition, remarking that it remained a barrier to national growth and prosperity. “17bn dollars are lost every year to malnutrition and stunting,” she said.

“My last takeaway was that addressing malnutrition is not just about food alone; it is about health, education, women’s empowerment, behaviour change.

“It takes a village; it is our collective responsibility, and it is also a national emergency and one that we must collectively address.”

4:15pm- Expert calls on govt to recognise food and nutritional security as a fundamental right

Chairperson SUN Movement Dr Irshad Danish also recommended that the government should recognise food and nutritional security as a fundamental right in the Constitution.

“There are some provisions, but nutrition and food security are not fundamental rights,” he said.

He also recommended that nutrition should be institutionalised as a sector and stressed the need for multisectoral coordination.

4:10pm - Pakistan’s nutritional burden must be treated as a national emergency, says expert

Dr Irshad Danish, who is the chairperson of the Scaling Up Nutrition movement, summarising the two-day conference, said that in the discussions held, it was recognised that “scale and severity of Pakistan’s malnutrition burden must be treated as a national emergency and put forward some recommendations”.

Outlining one of the recommendations made, Dr Danish said, “First, we propose and recommend that the government should appoint dedicated nutrition coordinators and focal persons at national and international level”.

4:07pm - Closing session titled ‘Stronger Together — The Pakistan Nutrition Pact’ begins

The final session of the day has begun.

3:45pm - Addressing malnutrition collective responsibility: Sarwat Gillani

Actress Sarwat Gillani said that addressing malnutrition was a collective responsibility.

“It should be portrayed as everyone’s responsibility because only then can it be resolved because it is in every province,” Gillani said.

“So we have to work on this problem collectively,” she added.

3:40pm - Sarwat Gillani stresses use of ‘intelligent marketing’

Actress Sarwat Gilani emphasised the use of “intelligent marketing” in addressing societal issues, including malnutrition.

“Intelligent marketing is the answer to so many of our problems. In this day and age where everything is on a credit card or a mobile phone [..] if we have all the right creative minds along with experts, we can all sit down and come up with a strategic marketing campaign,” she said.

3:30pm - Film mogul highlights importance of radio, PTV in reaching the masses

Satish Anand, the chairman of EverReady Pictures, highlighted the importance of radio and PTV for reaching the masses.

He said that radio was widely listened to by people living in rural areas. He added that PTV could also be effectively used to communicate social issues.

Satish Anand, the chairman of EverReady Pictures speaks at the conference. — White Star/ Tanveer Shahzad

3:20pm - Sarwat Gilani says malnutrition caused by host of factors

Actress Sarwat Gilani, who is also an ambassador for Special Olympics Pakistan and the Indus Hospital and Health Network, said that there had been a lot of “repetition” during the conference as people cited data and statistics.

“If this repetition, can be disseminated on an every day level, it would have a more lasting result,” she said. She said that malnutrition was not a “disease” and was caused by a host of factors.

She also called for focusing on the solution rather than the problem.

Actress Sarwat Gillani speaks at the conference. — White Star/ Tanveer Shahzad

3:17pm - Journalist notes lack of focus on nutrition in media

Journalist Zarrar Khuhro termed malnutrition a “silent crisis” and went on to say that there was limited conversation about the issue in the media.

“You will see a press release perhaps [..] but that does not cause a conversation at the household level and [..] if you can’t do that, then you have no hope of societal change”.

“That is what we need, not just top-down change but critical mass at the family level, personal individual level, identifying this issue and seeking solutions and creating what we call a public buy-in,” he said.

Journalist Zarrar Khuhro speaks at the conference, — White Star/ Tanveer Shahzad

3:12pm - Panel discussion on communicating for change begins

A panel discussion on communicating for societal change has now begun.

3:10pm - Official says 1 in 4 children in Punjab suffering from stunted growth

Dr Usman Ali Khan, the programme director of the Punjab Family Planning Programme, said that comparing the surveys from 2018 and 2024 showed progress.

However, despite this improvement, there were 5.5m malnourished children in the province, he said. He said that one in four children in the province suffered from stunted growth.

He said that the province was actively screening women and children that could be suffering from malnutrition and stunting.

3:05pm - Nutritional financing a provincial budgetary question, says Punjab govt official

Punjab government’s special secretary, Aurangzaib Haider Khan, presented three priorities to the forum.

“First, a common nutritional indicator so that provincial data can be compared, rather than merely collected,” Khan said.

Secondly, he called for an “honest recognition of the fiscal architecture [under] the 18th Amendment” and added that nutritional financing was predominantly a provincial budgetary question.

Third, Khan said was that “birth spacing also belongs inside the nutritional agenda, rather than besides it”.

Punjab government’s special secretary, Aurangzaib Haider Khan, addresses the Act for Nutrition conference. — White Star/ Tanveer Shahzad

2:57pm - Govt official says Punjab carries majority of nutritional burden

Punjab government’s special secretary, Aurangzaib Haider Khan, delivering his address, said that Punjab shouldered the majority of the country’s nutritional burden due to the size of its population

“Let me be direct on what has moved in this scenario: Stunting among children under five has fallen from 36pc in 2018 to 27pc now.”

However, the government official held that the progress made was insufficient, as “more than one in four children“ remain stunted, leading up to around 5.5m children across the province.

2:52pm - Minister says fathers must recognise a child’s nutrition as their responsibility

Information Minister Attaullah Tarar said that public service messaging on nutrition must address the whole family, not just the mother.

“Too often, we place the entire burden of a child’s nutrition on women, while decisions about food purchases, healthcare and women’s workloads may be taken by other members of the family. A mother cannot carry this responsibility alone,” he said.

“Fathers must understand that nutrition is also their responsibility,” he said.

2:50pm - Minister calls for improving public service messaging

Information Minister Attaullah Tarar highlighted the need for the right kind of messaging to tackle malnutrition. He said that communication could nutrition outcomes if it was done differently.

“Public service messaging must move beyond telling people that malnutrition is a serious problem. Every message must give families practical steps they can take. Every message should have a result-oriented approach,” he said.

He said that awareness programmes often focused on the problem rather than the solution.

2:44pm - Info minister says malnutrition not simply a health issues

Information Minister Attaullah Tarar said that malnutrition was not simply a health issue.

“It is a moral challenge, an economic imperative and a national emergency,” he said. The minister went on to say that malnutrition was shaped by maternal health, feeding practices, unsafe water, inadequate healthcare, climate vulnerabilities and unequal access to essential services.

He further said that the Act for Nutrition conference should not be a one-off event, saying it should be an “action plan which we can implement throughout the year”.

Information Minister Attaullah Tarar addresses the Act for Nutrition conference. — White Star/Tanveer Shahzad

2:40pm - Info minister stresses need for communication, awareness to tackle malnutrition

Information Minister Attaullah Tarar, in his address, said that communication and awareness were essential for tackling malnutrition. He hailed DawnMedia group for raising awareness of the issue.

He said that more than 40pc of children in Pakistan were stunted, while maternal mortality rate was 155 deaths per 100,000 live births.

“Malnutrition costs Pakistan more than $17bn annually. If the right kind of strategy can be deployed across the country, the impact it would have on our gross domestic growth would benefit the common man,” he said.

“Behind every stunted child is potential that may never be fully realised. Behind every malnourished mother is a family at greater risk. And behind every year of inaction is another generation beginning life at a disadvantage,” he said.

2:00pm - Lunch break

1:40pm - UK expert stresses need for safely managed water and sanitation

Oliver Cumming, the environmental health lead at the London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine, said: “The prospect of safely managed water and sanitation in Pakistan is not something which can be achieved tomorrow, and it is not as simple as shifting gears that you go from basic to safely managed.”

However, he suggested that recognition towards the goal could lead to universal access to safely managed WASH services sooner rather than later.

“We have to be realistic that it will not happen tomorrow, but putting in place the investment, the political arguments […] universal access to safely managed services can become possible within a decade,” he added.

“This is where we need to get if we really want to solve the problem of chronic malnutrition.”

1:25pm - Expert says water quality a ‘big issue’ for Pakistan

Dr Saima Khan — a water, sanitation and hygiene policy specialist — called for targeting the 36 districts in the country contributing to stunting in children. She said that WASH infrastructure investments should be done in these districts.

She also said that water quality was a “big issue” for Pakistan. She said that the country’s northern areas, Azad Jammu and Kashmir and Gilgit-Baltistan had no infrastructure for sanitation or sewerage. She said that this was deteriorating the quality of drinking water in these areas.

1:05pm - WB official calls for understanding WASH-related drivers of malnutrition

Senior water specialist at the World Bank, Basharat Saeed, underscored the significance of gaining a “sophisticated understanding” of WASH-related drivers behind child malnutrition.

“You need to look at what are the processes at a given location that are leading to the accumulation of faecal waste, accumulation in a way that it is exposing sensitive ecosystem and exposing people to faecal pathogens,” Saeed said.

He added that it should also be made possible to track the common pathways for oral transmission for faecal material.

“If you can map that out at the start of a programme design, then you know what sort of WASH investment is needed,” he said, stressing the need for a sophisticated understanding of WASH-related drivers of malnutrition.

He added that as a result of adopting such an approach, the “proposed solution will also become slightly more comprehensive”.

Senior water specialist at the World Bank, Basharat Saeed, addresses the Act for Nutrition conference. — White Star/Muhammad Asim

12:49pm - UK expert says water and sanitation alone cannot end stunting

Oliver Cumming, the environmental health lead at the London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine, said that water and sanitation alone cannot end stunting, but it was essential part of the comprehensive strategies needed to address it.

He said that for the water and sanitation sector, nutrition was often peripheral, adding that this needed to change.

He said that 20pc of children in South Asia were stunted at birth, highlighting the need for prevention and an integrated approach to the issue.

12:45pm - WaterAid official calls for moving towards delivering multisectoral approach

Country director at WaterAid, Mian Muhammad Junaid, stressed that the conversation on a multisectoral approach needed to move beyond talking and towards financing and delivering results.

“We are working in silos; we still tend to organise ourselves in sectors, where nutrition sits in one policy sector, health in another, water and sanitation somewhere else, climate separately, social protection is another,” Junaid said.

He went on to note that a child did not experience these boundaries; rather, it was a lived reality for them.

“This is where I think Pakistan needs to move from talking about a multisectoral approach to actually financing and delivering one,” he added.

12:41pm - WaterAid official says child’s environment important for addressing malnutrition

In his keynote speech, Mian Muhammad Junaid, the country director for WaterAid, raised alarm at the impact of lack of water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH) services on a child’s development and nutrition.

“A child cannot be well nourished if the environment in which the child grows is making them sick,” he said. He said WASH services were often an “important but missed” aspect of addressing malnutrition.

“WASH is a part of nutrition,“ Junaid said.

“A child may receive the right food, nutritional counselling, cash transfer and access to health facilities, but if the child is repeatedly exposed to contaminated drinking water, faecal contamination, poor sanitation and an unhealthy environment, we are asking that child to grow and develop against very difficult odds,” he said.

Mian Muhammad Junaid, the country director for WaterAid, addresses the Act for Nutrition conference. — White Star/Muhammad Asim

12:40pm - Panel discussion on contribution of dirty water, poor sanitation to stunting begins

A panel discussion on how dirty water and poor sanitation contribute to stunting has now begun.

12:38pm - BISP official says policies, legislation remain ‘only on paper’

Tehmina Gulzar, the deputy director of nutrition at the Benazir Income Support Programme, said that hygiene, agricultural, sanitation sectors had to come together to respond to malnutrition.

She said that BISP had trained doctors, paramedical staff and teachers on adolescent nutrition to bring knowledge to communities.

She also said that while policies and legislation were drafted, they were “only on paper”.

“We need to bring them into practice. All sectors are working on [nutrition], but they are fragmented efforts,” she said, highlighting the need for the digital integration of all sectors.

12:31pm - Expert says malnutrition not ‘poverty-related’

Dr Farhana Memon, the programme director of Reproductive, Maternal, Neonatal and Child Health, dispelled the perception that malnutrition was tied to poverty.

“It is said that malnutrition is just poverty-related; I don’t think so. I have been in the field for 27 years, and whenever I ask a woman what she has eaten for breakfast, she will tell me she had tea and rusk,” Dr Memon said.

“We have failed to convince her that she can get an egg for the same cost,” she said.

“Let’s take an example of two issues in public health — breastfeeding and micronutrient deficiencies — these are not poverty-related; it’s knowledge-related,” she said.

12:15pm - BISP official says social protection programmes can play ‘significant role’ in improving nutrition outcomes

Tehmina Gulzar, the deputy director of nutrition at the Benazir Income Support Programme, said that social protection programmes can play a “significant role” in improving nutrition outcomes.

She added that BISP was a very good example of how social protection programmes could contribute toward human capital development.

She also said that BISP had a huge collection of data that could be used by different sectors involved in addressing nutrition.

Tehmina Gulzar, the deputy director of nutrition at the Benazir Income Support Programme, addresses the Act for Nutrition conference. — White Star/Muhammad Asim

12:01pm - Expert says nutrition cannot be viewed in isolation

CEO of the Pakistan Alliance on Early Childhood Development Khadija Khan warned against viewing nutrition in isolation.

“Because for holistic development, you need a complete package and that package is described in the nurturing care framework, which is talking about good health, adequate nutrition, responsive caregiving, safety, security and early learning opportunity.”

She held that until and unless these inputs were met, it was not possible to achieve holistic child development.

“We do talk about a multisectoral approach and an integrated approach, but still the families are knocking on different doors for different services. In reality, we do not really give integrated services to our children,” Khan added.

11:49am - Non-profit head says people do not ‘believe in the system’

Shahid Lone, the chairman of the Allah Walay Foundation, said that if policymakers and those responsible for implementation did not put their “soul” into what they were doing, then what they were aiming for “would never work”.

He acknowledged that his take was more “philosophical”. He highlighted that government officials say one thing on stage and another when they are behind the scenes.

“We have policies, we have departments, but we have people who do not believe in the system,” he said. He questioned how those who did not have vision or believed in their work could implement policies.

Shahid Lone, the chairman of the Allah Walay Foundation, addresses the Act for Nutrition conference. — White Star/Muhammad Asim

11:37am - ‘Behaviour of healthcare providers pathetic’

Dr Farhana Memon, the programme director of Reproductive, Maternal, Neonatal and Child Health, also criticised the behaviour of healthcare workers.

“The behaviour of healthcare providers is pathetic,” Dr Memon said, noting that most healthcare workers did not counsel patients on family planning, nutrition, or vaccination.

“We have been trying to change the behaviour of the community for the past decade, but now it is time to change the behaviour of healthcare providers.”

“If a person or a woman comes into contact with you, please don’t waste the opportunity,” she urged.

11:34am - Expert decries lack of dedicated funding for nutrition

Programme director of Reproductive, Maternal, Neonatal, and Child Health Dr Farhana Memon decried the lack of funds to address malnutrition.

“If you want to [translate] policies into action, you should have some cost,” she said, adding that donors largely funded efforts to end malnutrition.

“This is not the solution,” Memon remarked, adding that nutrition should be treated as a separate entity.

She further urged that the government must utilise every access point as an opportunity to counsel families about nutrition.

Programme director of Reproductive, Maternal, Neonatal, and Child Health Dr Farhana Memon speaks at the Act for Nutrition conference. — White Star/Muhammad Asim

11:25am - Session on multisectoral approach to nutrition begins

A session on the multisectoral approach to nutrition has now begun.

11:20am - KP CM says govt working on addressing malnutrition

Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Chief Minister Sohail Afridi, in a video message, said that facilitation centres were being established to address malnutrition among pregnant women and young children.

He said that the provincial government, under PTI founder Imran Khan’s vision, was working on this issue and others.

He ended by thanking DawnMedia for highlighting malnutrition and other social issues.

Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Chief Minister Sohail Afridi’s video message at the Act for Nutrition conference. — White Star/Tanveer Shahzad

11:10am - Govt official calls for cohesive national narrative on malnutrition

Dr Shabana Haider, member (population) in the Planning Commission of Pakistan, stressed the need for a cohesive national narrative in addressing malnutrition.

“Do not go switching your national narrative; sometimes it is said that two kids are enough, sometimes it is one, and sometimes you ask women to time their pregnancies. Please develop a narrative that you can lead on and that everybody — from development partners to private sector — can converge on,” she said.

11:00am - Govt official says nutritional challenges cannot be addressed without acknowledging population dynamics

Dr Shabana Haider, member (population) in the Planning Commission of Pakistan, said that nutritional challenges could not be addressed without acknowledging population dynamics and demographic dividends could not be reaped without investing in nutrition.

She said that while Pakistan had done a lot on the policy side, the documents themselves were not enough.

“We are very good at framing policies … sorry, excuse me, this has to change … let’s all recognise that our priority has not been population,” she said, adding that population had been neglected as a subject.

10:50am - KP govt official says malnutrition, family planning interlinked

Dr Fazal Majeed, the director of nutrition at the Directorate General Health Services for Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, said that Pakistan had a stunting growth rate of 40pc, adding that it was 48pc in KP’s merged districts.

He also said that almost 40pc of women of reproductive age were also anaemic, calling the figures “alarming”.

“Malnutrition, family planning … are interlinked,” he said. He said some of the barriers in KP were fragmented delivery points, geographical and security-related.

Dr Fazal Majeed, the director of nutrition at the Directorate General Health Services for Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, addresses the Act for Nutrition conference, — White Star/Tanveer Shahzad

10:35am - Public health professional says history of Pakistan’s health programmes ‘one of isolation’

Dr Talib Lashari, a public health professional with the Sindh government’s health department, said that the nexus between nutrition and family planning was “well established but poorly practised in Pakistan”.

“The history of Pakistan’s public health programmes and initiatives is one of isolation. All the programmes have been well-designed and, to some extent, properly funded, but they were implemented in isolation,” he said.

10:24am - Govt adviser says nutrition needs to be reclassified as a capital expenditure

Adnan Pasha Siddiqui, the adviser to the minister of finance, said that nutrition needed to be reclassified as a capital expenditure rather than as an expense.

“So this single accounting decision suppresses the investment narrative permanently … these are fundamental flaws we need to correct,” he said.

Adnan Pasha Siddiqui, the adviser to the minister of finance, addresses the Act for Nutrition conference. — White Star/Tanveer Shahzad

10:17am - Govt adviser says lack of investment in nutrition hurts Pakistan’s GDP

Adnan Pasha Siddiqui, the adviser to the minister of finance, said that burgeoning population and lack of resources were a “collective failure of capital investment”.

“We are reflecting everything nutrition-related as a health expenditure … every rupee that is withheld from a pregnant women’s diet is a deduction from the country’s gross domestic product in the future,” he said. He said that in the country, nutrition was divided across several sectors.

Siddiqui said that the annual loss from malnutrition was $17bn. He said that in South Asia, labour productivity was suppressed because of nutrition.

“And it is a structural liability to our sovereign credit profile,” he said.

10:08am - World Bank official says nutrition is viewed through ‘a human capital lens’

Sara Shahzad, the senior health specialist from the World Bank, said that the group had 10-year country partnership framework with the government of Pakistan focused on six priority areas, one of which was stunting reduction.

“So the way the World Bank looks at population stabilisation and nutrition, specifically the stunting agenda, is through a human capital lens,” she said.

Talking about stunting, she said that 30-40pc of it occurred before a child was born.

“So, the first 1,000 days are absolutely critical but also the adolescence period,” she said.

Sara Shahzad, the senior health specialist from the World Bank, speaks at the Act for Nutrition conference. — White Star/Tanveer Shahzad

9:58am - Expert highlights ‘experimentation’ in Pakistan’s population planning

Dr Ali Mir, the country director for the Population Council, said that there was always a tendency in Pakistan of “making the same mistakes again and again”. Talking about Pakistan’s previous population reforms, he highlighted wavering political commitment and policy inconsistency.

“We never explicitly had a population policy till 2002. It was always couched in development planning,” he said.

He said that due to this, Pakistan was constantly “experimenting”. Dr Mir said that now things were moving in the right direction, with the establishment of the Population Council.

Dr Ali Mir, the country director for the Population Council, speaks at the Act for Nutrition conference. — White Star/Tanveer Shahzad

9:55am - Doctor says nutrition is ‘not an isolated event’

Dr Saima Hamid, the programme and research lead at the Population Council, said that Pakistan’s population growth rate is at 2.55pc. She said that in 28 years, the country’s population would double, putting a huge burden on resources.

“This clearly is a challenge of not just the quantity but also the quality of diet. We need to ensure that diverse nutrition reaches those most vulnerable,” she said.

She also said that Pakistan’s domestic food security was on the decline, adding that “nutrition is not just an isolated event”.

“One sector isn’t really responsible … there is a clear intersection of nutrition, food security, health, purchasing power,” she said.

9:52am - Session on population and resources has begun

A session on how a nation cannot feed, educate or employ what it cannot count on sustaining has now begun.

9:50am - 2nd day of conference begins

The second day of the conference begins with a short film titled Leaky Guts from the Aga Khan University.

World.title: Abhinandan, shot down by PAF in 2019, retires from IAF: report
World.content:
Indian Air Force (IAF) pilot Abhinandan Varthaman, who was held captive for three days after Pakistan shot down his MiG-21 fighter during Operation Swift Retort in February 2019, has retired from the force and joined a private airline as a commercial pilot, Indian broadcaster NDTV reported.

According to the broadcaster, Abhinandan joined a Goa-based regional carrier FLY91, which began operations in March 2024 and currently operates a fleet of six ATR 72-600 aircraft.

“The former group captain and Vir Chakra awardee, who served in the Air Force for 22 years, has joined Goa-based regional airline FLY91 as a pilot,” NDTV reports citing The Press Trust of India, which quoted sources.

The Press Trust of India report claimed that Abhinandan joined the private airline in August.

“So far, Varthaman has not issued any statement on the matter. A FLY91 spokesperson also refused to release any personal information about employees, saying it is a private matter,” NDTV adds.

In February 2019, after an attack in India-occupied Kashmir’s Pulwama area claimed the lives of 44 Indian paramilitary personnel, Indian forces launched air strikes on Balakot in Azad Jammu and Kashmir, claiming to have hit a camp operated by a banned organisation.

The Indian air strikes caused “no casualties and no damage on the ground due to the bombs being dropped”, according to the region’s police chief.

The following day, Islamabad carried out strikes from Pakistani airspace targeting military installations across the Line of Control (LoC).

In an ensuing air battle, two Indian aircraft were shot down, with Pakistan capturing Indian pilot Abhinandan and holding him in custody for three days.

A video statement then emerged of Abhinandan, lauding the Pakistani military for the treatment meted out to him after his arrest.

“I would like to put this on recordl, and I will not change my statement if I go back to my country also,” he said. “The officers of the Pakistani Army have looked after me very well. They are thorough gentlemen, starting from the captain who rescued me from the mob.”

Abhinandan was also holding a cup of tea in the video, which he said was “fantastic”.

On March 2, 2019, Abhinandan was released and crossed over the Wagah Border to return to India, in a move aimed at de-escalating tensions between Islamabad and New Delhi.

Two years later, Abhinandan was conferred the Vir Chakra — India’s third-highest military honour — for his actions during the 2019 air battle and for reportedly shooting down a Pakistani F-16 — a claim that has been debunked by Pakistan and foreign media outlets.

Abhinandan, however, has never publicly claimed the kill.

Then Director General of Inter-Services Public Relations Major General Asif Ghafoor said all four “missile seeker heads” were recovered intact from the wreckage of the Indian pilot’s MiG-21 fighter jet, implying that they were never fired.

Foreign Policy magazine interviewed two US defence officials with “knowledge of the count” of Pakistan’s F-16 jets and both confirmed that all the F-16s were “present and accounted for”.

World.title: Nepal must rebuild thousands of homes, no letup in search for missing
World.content:
Nepal will have to rebuild around 20,000 houses in flood-ravaged areas, authorities said on Thursday, as rescuers continued to search for workers trapped in tunnels linked to hydropower projects and thousands remain missing after last week’s catastrophe.

A glacier collapse on August 26 sent a deluge of ice, rock and mud sweeping through the impoverished nation’s border region with China, wiping out settlements and villages and leaving few houses standing and undamaged.

“Our preliminary estimates are that 7,500 houses have been completely destroyed, either washed away or buried under debris and mud,” Dharma Raj Upreti, chief of the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority, told Reuters.

Even houses still standing were not habitable, Upreti said, with authorities estimating that around 20,000 would have to be rebuilt in different, safer locations.

“We anticipate that the resources required for rebuilding will be substantial,” Foreign Minister Shisir Khanal told foreign ambassadors in Kathmandu.

At least 1,252 people were killed in Nepal last week as houses, streets and schools in towns and villages near the border with China’s Tibet were swept away. More than 4,200 people are still missing and thousands more displaced.

China has put the death toll in Tibet at 21, with 541 others listed as missing.

Prime Minister Balendra Shah’s cabinet set September 7, the 13th day after the disaster, as a day of national mourning in Nepal, the cabinet spokesperson said. In Hindu tradition, the 13th day traditionally marks the end of the formal mourning period.

Search for missing continues

More than 9,300 Nepali army troops were on the ground in the affected areas of Timure in Rasuwa, Nuwakot, Dhading, Chitwan and Nawalparasi East, coordinating search and rescue of the injured and helping with management of bodies, clearing blocked roads, and providing emergency medical treatment, an army statement said.

An Australian medical student whose partner went missing near the Nepal-China border urged tech companies to do more to help find him and others caught up in the disaster by sharing tracking data that could narrow the search areas for rescue teams.

At least 583 foreign nationals were missing in the floods, Nepal said on Thursday, many of them pilgrims and trekkers.

An army officer, who spoke on condition of anonymity as he is not authorised to speak to the media, said the search was continuing with experts from India, South Korea and China for at least 900 survivors believed to be trapped in the tunnels related to hydropower projects.

Army spokesperson Raja Ram Basnet said two bodies had been recovered from the tunnel of Langtang Khola hydropower plant.

Australia pledged additional support and said it would also share telecommunications data with Nepali authorities.

China has sent a third batch of aid to Nepal, including tents, blankets, medical protective suits and satellite communication equipment, the foreign ministry said, adding that the weather offices of the two countries were in contact with each other.

Reports on the rescue efforts in Tibet, largely provided by Chinese state media, have slowed a day after the G216 national highway leading to the site was reopened.

Both China and Nepal have said the floods were a result of climate change, with foreign minister Khanal telling ambassadors that the disaster had a “deeper significance” beyond the immediate emergency.

“Nepal contributes a negligible share of global emissions, yet our people bear a disproportionate burden of the impacts of a warming Himalayas,” he said.

Getting children back to school

Authorities were working to restore regular routines as much as possible, with a focus on getting children into makeshift schools.

More than a week after the flood, at least 22,000 children urgently need safe drinking water, sanitation and hygiene support, UNICEF said in a statement.

“Our priority is to restore normal life. We are considering if children can be taught in the holding centres,” said Phanindra Paudel, an official at Nepal’s National Emergency Operation Centre.

Finding safe buildings in which to hold classes was a challenge, teachers said.

“We are looking for safe, empty buildings or other schools where we can resume classes. The school building was completely washed away, so we will have to build a new one in a safer location,” said Rajendra Dawadi, headmaster of a school, who helped save about 900 students by evacuating them in time.

Shanti Sunar, 45, escaped the disaster with her husband but lost her house and a small shop she ran.

“I have been visiting the site almost every day. I can recognise where our house stood, but there is no trace of it now. We cannot rebuild at the same location because it is not safe. I expect the government to relocate us to a safer place.”

PM Shehbaz assures Nepal ambassador of continued relief assistance

Meanwhile, Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif assured Nepal’s Ambassador to Pakistan Rita Dhital of Pakistan’s continued support in a visit to the Nepalese Embassy in Islamabad, the Prime Minister’s Office (PMO) said.

“In his message, the Prime Minister conveyed Pakistan’s deepest sympathies to the government and people of Nepal, and to the bereaved families who lost their loved ones in the tragedy,” the PMO said.

PMO added that the premier told the ambassador that Pakistan would be dispatching emergency relief assistance to Nepal later in the week.

“He offered continued support to Nepal and hoped that the resilient people of Nepal would emerge stronger from this tragedy,” the statement added.

World.title: Ramisa rape and murder: Sohel Rana mentions new name as charges framed
World.content:
A new name has surfaced in the Ramisa rape and murder case, with prime accused Sohel Rana telling reporters today that a man called "Dollar" was responsible for the rape and murder of the eight-year-old girl.

However, no further details about the person were immediately available.

Sohel made the claim while being escorted to the courtroom of the Dhaka Metropolitan Children Violence Suppression Tribunal.

"I am at fault, and Dollar is also at fault. I am not the only culprit," he told reporters.

Standing in the courtroom's dock, he shouted at the lawyers present in the courtroom after the hearing, and said, “I did not commit the rape; I only dismembered the body. A man named Dollar committed the rape. I have sinned, so punish me for that sin.”

At that time, Sohel further claimed that Dollar had promised to pay him Tk 2 lakh if he could bring the girl to him.

However, police officers present immediately stopped him from speaking further.

Sohel also claimed that his wife, Swapna Khatun, was innocent.

Earlier in the day, Sohel and Swapna were brought to the lock-up of the Metropolitan Sessions Judge's Court in Dhaka.

Later, Judge Masrur Salekin of the tribunal framed charges against the couple in the case over the rape and murder of Ramisa in Dhaka's Pallabi area.

Both accused pleaded not guilty after the charges were read out, said Bench Assistant Pankoj Peter Gomes.

The judge also fixed tomorrow for the start of the trial, with the victim's father, Abdul Hannan Mollah, scheduled to testify first, he added.

On May 24, Sub-Inspector Ohiduzzaman of Pallabi Police Station submitted the charge sheet before the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate's Court in Dhaka, accusing Sohel of rape, murder and destruction of evidence, and Swapna of destruction of evidence and providing false information.

Several hours later, the CMM Court transferred the case to the Children Violence Suppression Tribunal for trial.

Ramisa, a second-grade student of Popular Model High School, was found beheaded on May 19 in the house of her neighbour, Sohel.

The following day, Ramisa's father filed a case with Pallabi Police Station, accusing the couple and an unidentified person.

According to the case statement, Sohel lured Ramisa into his room and raped her. Investigators said he later slit her throat and attempted to dismember the body to conceal the crime.

On May 20, police produced Sohel and Swapna before a Dhaka court, and court sources said Sohel agreed to give a confessional statement before a magistrate. The third and unidentified accused was on the run. Dhaka Metropolitan Magistrate Aminul Islam Junaid recorded Sohel's confessional statement after police brought him to the magistrate’s chamber, said a court staff member.

Sub-Inspector Ohiduzzaman of Pallabi Police Station told The Daily Star that day, the prime accused had already admitted to the crime during primary interrogation.

On May 22, the Dhaka Bar Association decided not to provide legal assistance to the accused following an emergency virtual meeting of its executive committee, citing the gravity of the allegations.

The next day, the government appointed Supreme Court lawyer Musa Kalimullah as a state defence counsel to represent the accused to ensure a fair trial.

This report has been corrected at 4:43pm. In the earlier version, Sohel Rana’s comment was misreported. We regret the error.

World.title: Why Bangladesh must pivot to renewable energy now
World.content:
There are moments in a nation’s history when a crisis does more than create hardship. It reveals the weakness of an old system and opens the door to a better one. Bangladesh is now standing at such a moment.

The country is facing an energy crisis that no longer centres on power cuts. It is affecting factories, farms, schools, offices, exports, foreign currency reserves, and the daily life of ordinary people. What we are seeing today is not just a temporary shortage of gas or fuel. It is a signal that our energy system has become too dependent on imported fossil fuels.

More than 60 percent of Bangladesh’s energy demand is met through imports. LNG, coal, oil, and other fossil fuels have kept the country running for years, but this dependence has become risky and expensive. Global fuel markets are unstable because of geopolitical tension, supply chain disruption, and price volatility. For a country like Bangladesh, this creates double pressure: fuel supply becomes uncertain while fuel costs keep rising.

The government is now spending more than BDT 200 crore per day in energy subsidies. Annual energy import expenditure remains around USD 12 billion, putting serious pressure on foreign currency reserves. Nearly 70 percent of Bangladesh’s LNG imports come from Qatar. If supply is disrupted, Bangladesh can quickly face a severe shortage. In the power sector, daily gas demand exceeds 2,500 mmcfd, but supply sometimes falls to 850–900 mmcfd. This can create a power generation shortfall of 1,500–1,800 MW. Overall, the daily gas shortage exceeds 1,100 mmcfd, and peak-time electricity shortages may reach nearly 2,000 MW.

Bangladesh also has a weak Strategic Petroleum Reserve. The current reserve capacity is sufficient for only about 35–40 days, well below that of countries such as China and Japan. This makes the national energy system even more vulnerable.

Visual: Teeni and Tuni

The impact is already visible. In the readymade garments sector, gas shortages and load shedding are reducing productivity by 25–30 percent in many cases. This threatens export earnings, foreign currency reserves, and economic stability. The crisis has also reached ordinary households. Although Bangladesh declared 100 percent electrification in 2022, many rural areas still experience 10 to 20 hours of load shedding every day during summer. This affects education, small businesses, agriculture, and people’s dignity.

We have also seen long lines at fuel stations, schools moving online, and offices shortening working hours because of fuel shortages. These are not isolated events. They show how deeply energy insecurity can disturb national life.

Over the last 15 years, electricity tariffs in Bangladesh have been increased on many occasions, including more than 10 rounds of increases at both bulk and retail levels. This path is not sustainable. Fossil-fuel-based electricity depends on imported fuel, global prices, the availability of the dollar, subsidies, and repeated tariff adjustments. Solar power offers a different path. With a one-time investment, solar can provide stable energy for 15–20 years. Once installed, its fuel cost is almost zero.

The economic comparison is clear. A 1 MW HFO-based power plant produces electricity per year at a cost of nearly BDT 190 crore, with much of the cost paid in foreign currency. In contrast, a 5 MW solar project requires a one-time investment of around BDT 25 crore, after which fuel costs are practically zero. Each 1 MW of solar power can save around USD 325,000 per year in foreign currency.

This is why renewable energy should not be discussed solely in technical terms like decarbonisation, emissions, and sustainability. For Bangladesh, renewable energy means jobs, fuel independence, savings in foreign currency, industrial competitiveness, agricultural protection, and economic strength. Policymakers and stakeholders can lead this transformation, inspiring confidence in a sustainable future.

Despite Bangladesh’s potential, renewable energy contributes less than 5 percent to power generation, far below the global 30 percent target by 2030. Clear, measurable goals and timelines are essential for effective policy planning and investment decisions.

Renewable energy equipment imports face around 50–60 percent in duties and taxes, hindering local manufacturing growth. Policy reforms that reduce import duties and support local industry can accelerate renewable deployment and reduce dependency on imports.

For Bangladesh, renewable energy means jobs, fuel independence, savings in foreign currency, industrial competitiveness, agricultural protection, and economic strength. Policymakers and stakeholders can lead this transformation, inspiring confidence in a sustainable future.

Import duty is usually imposed to protect the local industry. But where local production is not yet significant, a high duty only increases project costs, reduces investment returns, and slows renewable energy expansion. Policy reforms can unlock this potential, making stakeholders feel their efforts directly contribute to progress.

India, Pakistan, Vietnam, and China have expanded solar and wind power by offering low or zero import duties, tax exemptions, and low-interest financing. Many countries have also reduced duties on lithium-ion batteries and energy storage systems. Bangladesh should learn from these examples.

The barriers are clear: high duties and VAT, high financing costs of 10–12 percent or more, limited access to easy loans, slow approval processes, net metering delays, high LC margin, weak Merchant Power Policy, lack of clear policies for rooftop solar, utility-scale solar, floating solar, agrivoltaics, solar irrigation, and hybrid solar-storage, weak local manufacturing, and insufficient grid digitalisation. Addressing these collectively can accelerate Bangladesh's renewable journey, uniting stakeholders in a common goal.

One urgent reform is customs assessment. The current weight-based assessment system does not reflect the actual value of solar equipment. It can create artificial overvaluation and raise duties by three to four times. Bangladesh should shift to transaction-value-based assessment using pro forma or commercial invoice values, in line with international practice and WTO customs valuation principles.

The second urgent reform is the elimination of customs duty on renewable energy equipment. This should apply to Solar PV Module, Photovoltaic Cell, Solar Inverter, DC Cable, Data Logger, Aluminium Mounting Structure, Battery Pack, Battery Cell, BMS Circuit Board, PV DG Controller, Hybrid Controller, Solar Plant Safety Aluminium Walkway Mesh, Safety Accessories, and related components.

Current TTI rates are high. Solar PV Module carries 26.90 percent, Photovoltaic Cell 25.75 percent, Solar Inverter 28.73 percent, DC Cable 58.40 percent, Data Logger 37.25 percent, Aluminium Mounting Structure 58.40 percent, Battery Pack and Battery Cell 58.40 percent, BMS Circuit Board 31.50 percent, pack materials 37.25 percent, PV DG Controller or Hybrid Controller 89.08 percent, and Solar Plant Safety Aluminum Walkway Mesh 37.25 percent. These should be reduced to zero percent for renewable energy expansion.

The third reform is a tax holiday. Rooftop solar power producers and project companies should receive benefits comparable to those of utility-scale renewable energy producers. A practical structure could be a 100 percent tax holiday for the first 10 years, 50 percent for the next 3 years, and 25 percent for the next 2 years. This should apply to CAPEX, OPEX, IPP, and MPP models. A broader 10–20 year tax holiday for renewable energy projects should also be considered.

Bangladesh has a remarkable solar opportunity already waiting on its rooftops. About 7 percent of the country’s land is covered with concrete or other built structures. This means more than 10,000 square kilometres, or about 10 billion square meters of built surface. If only 30 percent is usable, that would give around 3 billion square meters. At 10 square meters per kW, this can create nearly 300 GW of solar potential. Bangladesh’s peak demand is only around 16–18 GW. The opportunity already exists on rooftops, factories, warehouses, schools, hospitals, government buildings, and commercial establishments.

Rooftop solar should therefore be relaunched nationwide with a clear business model. Utility-scale solar also needs support through unused khas land, transparent tendering, and grid readiness. Floating solar, river-based solar, agrivoltaics, solar irrigation, and hybrid solar-storage should receive separate policy attention.

The suspended solar projects must also be revisited. A total of 31 solar power projects, with a combined capacity of more than 3,000 MW, were previously suspended or cancelled. Many were being developed by foreign investors, with more than USD 200 million reportedly already invested. If implemented, these projects could save around BDT 10,800 crore annually in energy import costs. They should be reassessed and revived quickly.

Energy storage is another missing pillar. Solar and wind need storage support to become more reliable. Duties on lithium-ion batteries, BESS, and other storage systems should be reduced to zero. This will help stabilise renewable power and support future grid flexibility.

Electric vehicles can also become part of the solution. In China, Japan, and the United States, EVs are increasingly seen as mobile energy storage systems. A typical EV battery has a capacity of 40–70 kWh, enough to power an average household for 1–2 days. If Bangladesh had 1 million EVs, the country would have 40–70 GWh of distributed storage. This is several times higher than the daily peak demand gap. Solar-powered EV charging, vehicle-to-home, and vehicle-to-grid systems should be included in future energy planning.

If Bangladesh had 30–40 percent of the grid powered by solar, along with solar-powered EVs, the country would be far less exposed to global fuel market shocks. Long fuel lines, online schooling, shorter office hours, and industrial disruption could be reduced. Solar, storage, and EVs should now be planned together.

Finance will decide how fast this transition happens. Renewable energy projects cannot grow at interest rates below 10–12 percent. Long-term financing should be available at an interest rate of 3.5–4.5 percent. A 10–15-year financing facility at a maximum interest rate of 5 percent should be introduced. Bangladesh Bank’s green refinancing fund should be expanded. Rooftop and residential solar customers should be eligible for collateral-free loans. The LC margin for renewable equipment should be limited to 5%.

Net metering must be simplified. Approval should be completed within 15–30 days through a one-stop service. Approval, interconnection, inspection, billing adjustment, and utility coordination should all be simple and time-bound. Wheeling charges for renewable energy should also be kept reasonable and low. The Merchant Power Policy should be clear, simple, and investment-friendly so that industries and commercial consumers can directly procure renewable electricity.

Agriculture should also be included in the solar transition. Bangladesh can set a target to convert 1.5 million diesel irrigation pumps into solar pumps. This will reduce diesel imports, lower farmers’ production costs, and protect the environment. The program should include duty-free facilities, low-cost loans, investment support, and local service networks.

Waste-to-energy should also receive policy support. City corporations need clear rules, easy financing, and private-sector participation to enable urban waste management and distributed power generation to work together.

Bangladesh now needs a phased national roadmap for renewable energy.

In the short term, within 0–6 months, customs duty, VAT, and taxes on renewable energy equipment should be reduced to zero. Duties on lithium-ion batteries, BESS, and energy storage should be withdrawn. Approval for net metering should be obtained within 15–30 days. Industrial and commercial solar installations should be eligible for special incentives. The 31 suspended solar projects should be reassessed. Wheeling charges should be rationalised. Solar, storage, and EV charging should receive urgent policy support. Collateral-free lines of credit should be introduced for rooftop solar. NBR should quickly implement assessment reform and a 0 percent duty.

In the medium term, within 1–3 years, renewable energy financing should be available at a maximum interest rate of 5 percent for 10–15 years. The LC margin should be limited to 5 percent. Land banks and grid infrastructure should be developed for utility-scale solar. Merchant Power Policy and MPPA should be simplified. Rooftop solar, utility-scale solar, and hybrid solar-storage projects should receive a 10–15-year tax holiday. A national program should convert 1.5 million diesel pumps into solar pumps. Rooftop solar should be made mandatory or incentive-based for government buildings, industrial zones, EPZs, economic zones, and large commercial buildings. EV solar charging and distributed storage policies should be developed. Renewable energy skill development and employment programs should also be launched.

In the long term, within 3–10 years, Bangladesh should aim to reach more than 10,000 MW of solar power by 2030. Offshore and onshore wind should be developed. Floating solar, river-based solar, and agrivoltaics should be implemented. A National Energy Storage Strategy should be prepared. Smart grid and power sector digitalisation should be accelerated. Local assembly and manufacturing of solar panels, inverters, mounting structures, battery packs, BMS, and EV charging equipment should be encouraged. Regional power trade should be expanded. The Renewable Purchase Obligation should be introduced. Fossil fuel subsidies should be gradually redirected to a renewable energy transition fund.

Image Visual: Anwar Sohel

The benefits can be large. Energy import costs will fall. Pressure on foreign currency reserves will decline. Industrial production costs will reduce. Export competitiveness will improve. The subsidy burden will decrease. New investment will grow. Renewable energy can create 20–25 jobs per MW through rooftop solar, utility-scale solar, solar pumps, EV charging, battery storage, smart grids, manufacturing, installation, operation, and maintenance.

The government may worry about revenue loss from tax and duty exemptions. But this should be seen as an investment. In the short term, there may be a limited impact on revenue. In the long term, Bangladesh can save far more by reducing fuel imports, lowering subsidies, saving foreign currency, strengthening industries, and attracting new investment.

Bangladesh’s energy crisis is a major challenge but also a historic opportunity. The crisis is not only a supply problem. It is a policy framework problem. Renewable energy, especially solar power, storage, and EV integration, can be among the most practical solutions for the country.

The question is no longer whether Bangladesh should adopt renewable energy. The real question is how quickly, how systematically, and how boldly the country can complete this transition.



Mohammad Ataur Rahman Sarker is a renewable energy entrepreneur and the secretary of the Bangladesh Sustainable and Renewable Energy Association.

Md. Tanvir Siraj is a renewable energy researcher.

World.title: The forgotten art of Bengali advertising
World.content:
I have never seen someone at a rustic village market, anklets jingling, shouting slogans for "Khol Company’s Ringworm Ointment." No smooth-talker has ever leaned in, fanning out thin booklets like a deck of cards, whispering rhythmically, "Here are the mysteries of Gopal Bhar, and here—the secret love letters."

I never hid colourful s of a reclining Gauhar Jaan, cigarette in hand, between the folds of shirts in my drawer. I did indeed rummage through my grandfather’s pockets to collect old tram tickets, but none of them bore that curious notice for "Ashtavakra Toothpowder." Perhaps the elders of the house witnessed a tram tearing through the heart of a half-awake city, bearing the Khadi Pratisthan’s pledge for cow protection—but there was no question of me witnessing such a sight.

An iconic early 20th-century  for Bukhsh Ellahie & Co., featuring classical maestro Gauhar Jaan holding a cigarette to promote their brand

Someone’s great-grandfather might have known which drummers came beating the kara and nakara to announce, "Tonight at seven, the Chaitanya-lila folk play commences." I never heard the name of a young "lad" like Dhiren Bal, who reportedly painted the  for "Himkalyan Hair Oil" at a three-way junction in Dinajpur.

While searching the Panjika (almanac) for the auspicious moment of a wedding, I never had the chance to chuckle at the suggestive illustrations for "Libido-Enhancing Tablets." On a morning shortly after Mahatma Gandhi’s assassination, I didn't sit with a newspaper wondering which artist, known only as "Munshi," had used swirling brushstrokes to sketch a portrait as a final tribute on behalf of some bankrupt cotton mill.

I saw none of this because I hadn't been born yet. Most of those who witnessed it are now gone forever. Yet, even without being born in that era, I have managed to 'see' it all. The old, withered newspapers and digital archives acted like Alibaba’s cave, revealing to me a lost jewelry box. To me, those vintage s were not just pages of history; they were the precious Sita-har, the Jhumko, and the Nak-chabi themselves. I saw those 'ornaments'—the lost illustrations—and through them, I glimpsed a world that has otherwise vanished.

Actually, on a sudden whim, I spent a long time digging through ancient newspapers and periodicals. My eyes kept getting stuck on the bizarre s still surviving on the faded, brownish-yellow newsprint of yore. I was looking, most of all, at the illustrations.

As I tasted this history, I remembered a book I read long ago: The Lost Tribes of Israel by Tudor Parfitt. Many believe that since the foreign invasions of Israel in the 8th century BC, at least twelve tribes went missing. Mr. Parfitt scoured the planet in search of them—a search that reportedly continues today. Some even believe the signs of those lost people are visible in the Afghans.

Looking at the drawings for old s, I felt I found a resemblance between those legendary lost tribes and these forgotten illustrators. That is why the book came to mind. It also felt as though there was no such mismatch that could prevent us from linking these unknown artists’ ghosts to their successors, even without a DNA test!

The connection might be clear, but can we not grant them even a small corner in the history of Bengal's illustrative arts?

Renowned figures like the artist Raghunath Goswami continue to say—no, those  drawings or ideas are not even worth considering. They claim it is a "mindless and indiscriminate simplification of art objects." They say the expression has neither grace nor form. Artistic value? Far from it!

For some reason, despite respecting the scholars' verdict, I grew stubborn. As I weighed the pros and cons, even the "ugly" artworks of those who drew s for ringworm cures or hair-growth tonics began to pull at my eyes. I saw in them plenty of humour, and plenty of heartache too. Nevertheless, I began looking for a way to have a long conversation with those early advertising artists.

A representative of a "vanishing species" like O.C. Ganguly (Arun Kumar Gangopadhyay) introduced me to a certain "madman." He had a crow's nest of hair. His lower garment was draped over his chest like a shawl. He wore a striped vest. His hands were shackled in massive iron rings.

It is precisely these kinds of s that art critics have referred to as brainless and ugly art. The  regarding the cure for insanity, however, dates back to 1952. Yet, long before that, a group of young artists from agencies had completely transformed the face of Bengali ads.

Apparently, such a madman would no longer need to be restrained. Why? Because the illness would be cured simply by administering "ABD Pills" and "Dutta Oil." Such was the claim of the "Bengali Asylum" of Dutta Nagar, Dum Dum, whose head office was at 29-A Vivekananda Road (Phone: Jorasanko 5220).

Seeing the address "Jorasanko" in that illustrated ad, I was immediately reminded of the Tagore family—specifically, their members who struggled with mental health. One was Birendranath Tagore, the fourth son of Maharshi Debendranath. He was brilliant at mathematics but suddenly fell victim to "wind-disease" (mental instability). The other was Somendranath, another brother of Rabindranath.

The Nobel laureate poet knew well which medicines helped the "insane." I learned of another —not for the ABD Pills of Dum Dum, but a special notice from "S.C. Roy & Co." at 167/3 Cornwallis Street. They advertised Dr. Umesh Chandra Roy’s world-famous "Great Cure for the Mad," priced at five rupees per bottle. The ad claimed that for over 70 years, this medicine had cured "millions of violent madmen and all kinds of nervous patients." This  would appear with a quote from the poet himself, saying: "...I have been aware of its efficacy for a long time." Was the "Great Cure for the Mad" then used on Birendranath or Somendranath? I know bringing up Rabindranath's name is somewhat irrelevant, but seeing these old drawings makes my mind wander in a thousand directions!

The illustrated  I mentioned was published in 1952—the day I saw the picture of the shackled madman in the paper. That drawing was made several years after legendary artists had already begun to dominate Bengali advertising. By then, Bengalis had seen hundreds of fantastic drawings for various products. A legend like O.C. Ganguly was earning forty rupees a month at Calcutta’s "Stronach Advertising" as early as 1937. An agency named "Paradise Advertising" existed in Calcutta in 1928.
