World.title: Eating Less Reduced Breast Tumors in Mice, Chinese Study Finds
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018965/Eating Less Reduced Breast Tumors in Mice, Chinese Study Finds
World.content:
Chinese researchers have found that caloric restriction may inhibit tumor growth by affecting how tumors send signals.

The findings, which could enhance existing cancer treatments, were published last month in the journal Cancer Research in a joint study by researchers at Sun Yat-sen University Cancer Center, Guangdong Provincial People’s Hospital, the Cancer Hospital of Shantou University Medical College, and St. John’s University in New York City.

Observing how caloric restriction impacts tumor size and number in mice with breast tumors, the researchers found that caloric restriction disrupts the signals tumors use to recruit and reprogram the body’s wound-healing cells — known as cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs) — for their own use. This helps to convert the tumor’s immunosuppressive environment into one more favorable to cancer-fighting cells.

Yang Lu, the study’s corresponding author and a doctor at Guangdong Provincial People’s Hospital, told Sixth Tone that the idea for the study arose from questions about diet that she and the other researchers frequently receive from patients.

“Patients are always asking us, ‘What should I eat? How should I eat?’” Yang said. “To be honest, I didn’t know how to answer that before. But I really wanted to find a clear answer to that question.”

The study used a dietary program on the mice known as a “fasting-mimicking diet,” or FMD, in which calorie intake is sharply reduced, triggering a series of stress responses and cellular repair functions.

Research in recent years has shown that an FMD may enhance anti-cancer immunity in several instances, including altering gut microbiota to suppress colorectal cancer and enhancing breast cancer endocrine therapy. However, exactly how the method works and how it might inform cancer treatment remains unclear.

Previous research has predominantly focused on how FMDs alter tumor cells, tumor-attacking T cells, and the environment of cells, molecules, and blood vessels in the presence of tumors. This latest study instead examined the diet’s effects on CAFs.

The researchers randomly divided the mice into two groups: mice with unrestricted access to food and mice that underwent FMD — a cycle of one day of 50% calorie restriction, three days of 90% calorie restriction, and three days of unrestricted feeding. The experiment lasted three weeks.

The results showed that tumors in mice on a calorie-restricted diet were significantly reduced in volume and weight. The number of spontaneously occurring tumors in the diet group also significantly decreased.

Through RNA sequencing and cell-cell communication analysis, the researchers found less glucose availability and tumor-cell breakdown in the dieting mice. This in turn lowered secretion of the signaling molecule PDGFC, a CAF-binding protein released by tumor cells to suppress the host’s immune system.

This also reduced the proportion of immunosuppressive, inflammatory CAFs (iCAFs), while increasing the proportion of tumor cells with signs of programmed cell death. As a result, the tumor’s immunosuppressive environment was weakened, allowing more immune system cells to enter and fight the tumor.

The team also found that combining caloric restriction with a PDGFR inhibitor, a drug used to block tumor blood vessel formation, further weakened the tumor’s immunosuppressive environment. The results suggest that such a diet could work alongside existing cancer therapies to enhance anti-tumor activity.

However, the researchers noted several limitations. Among them, the study did not examine in detail how iCAFs affect the behavior and function of immune cells within tumors. It also remains unclear how the study’s mechanisms may impact different tumor types.

The authors wrote that while fasting “holds promise” as a way to enhance or work alongside cancer treatment, “large-scale clinical trials are needed to validate its efficacy, safety, and feasibility in cancer patients, alongside biomarker studies to optimize … combination therapy and long-term outcomes.”

Yang, the corresponding author, said the team has already begun incorporating FMD-based dietary recommendations into clinical trials involving cancer patients. Patients may be advised to reduce their calorie intake for several days before and after a treatment cycle, although specific dietary plans may vary.

In the future, the team hopes to develop better drugs and dietary interventions and eventually extend the approach to other cancer types.

“People’s lifestyles and individual differences are very diverse,” Yang said. “As the research becomes clearer, we hope to eventually develop personalized nutrition plans for different patients.”

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: Science Photo library/VCG)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018961/Behind China’s Unlikely Box-Office Hit, Indie Filmmakers Struggle to Be Seen
World.title: Behind China’s Unlikely Box-Office Hit, Indie Filmmakers Struggle to Be Seen
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018961/Behind China’s Unlikely Box-Office Hit, Indie Filmmakers Struggle to Be Seen
World.content:
Watching “Niu Lai” was an experience like no other. The theater was surprisingly busy for a late Sunday-night screening, with a crowd eager to watch China’s most notorious cartoon calf and his mother. For the first half hour, I was surrounded by laughter, fueled by the characters’ crude 3D modeling, wooden movements and facial expressions, and baffling, sometimes uncanny dialogue that was already trending on social media. Yet as the story took a sadder, more unsettling turn, the room grew quieter, and I began to wonder: Perhaps the creators, a mother-and-son duo with no industry experience, really did have something serious to say.

After grossing just 5,500 yuan ($815) in its first week, the animated film, reportedly made by 34-year-old amateur filmmaker Xin Yumeng using secondhand equipment, experienced an extraordinary box-office turnaround, taking in 50 million yuan ($7.44 million) by Aug. 26. It has since been dubbed China’s answer to “The Room,” Tommy Wiseau’s 2003 drama that began as a box-office bomb before achieving cult status for its notoriously crude production.

On review sites and social media, many viewers have wondered how such a production managed to secure screens alongside blockbusters like Christopher Nolan’s “The Odyssey” and Wen Muye’s “Once Upon a Time in the Middle East.” But the question can also be framed another way: What does it take for a domestically made, independent, low-budget film to actually reach Chinese audiences?

Producing a film in China involves a multilayered procedure. First, a filmmaker must own or work with a licensed production company to file the project with the National Film Administration (NFA), generally through its provincial bureaus. Once production is complete, the finished film undergoes a content review as well as a technical review covering elements such as visuals, audio, and subtitles. Films that pass the process receive a public screening permit from the NFA.

Such a procedure requires expertise and effort in paperwork, yet 764 films were produced in China in 2025 alone, although that was down from a pre-pandemic high of 1,037 in 2019. “Even doctoral students of the Beijing Film Academy may make a film with a public screening permit as their thesis project,” Kong Degang, a lecturer who studies theater arts at Nanjing Normal University, said. “The real question is: Do you distribute your film in theaters, or sell it to television or streaming services?”

Indeed, most films approved by regulators either never make it to theaters or disappear from them within days. To secure theatrical screenings, filmmakers generally need to work with distribution companies and share revenue. Distributors’ decisions are driven by a film’s commercial prospects, often judged by factors such as star power, high-end visual effects, or sophisticated marketing campaigns, advantages that independent productions rarely possess. Teams with strong connections to theater chains also have a better chance of securing screens. “China has an unforgiving film market. Without sufficient industry resources, a high box office is unlikely,” Kong said. On one day in August, more than a dozen films screening in China grossed less than 10,000 yuan ($1,487).

This dynamic creates a Matthew effect, in which films that perform strongly from the outset receive more screenings and therefore have a better chance of further success. That forces filmmakers to maximize their initial impact through costly promotional campaigns or exhausting roadshows. Luka Yuanyuan Yang, director of the 2024 documentary “Chinatown Cha-Cha,” told me that while commercial productions can spend as much on distribution and marketing as they do on production, independent filmmakers rarely have that luxury. Instead, her team held advance screenings city by city, and she once rushed to host events in two cities on the same day.

“You are racing against time,” Yang said. “You must seize the 10 days before and after your premiere. If you lose those 10 days, you lose everything.”

Global funding cuts, the pandemic’s impact, and competition for audiences from short-form videos have further squeezed independent filmmakers at every stage of production and distribution. Ma Guyuan, an independent director and playwright who left Beijing for a break in southwestern China’s Yunnan province, said tighter oversight of film companies’ finances since the late 2010s has contributed to a more cautious investment climate. Even with support from film festivals, which can provide funding to selected projects, she has often had to subsidize her work with personal savings. Young filmmakers from less affluent backgrounds frequently finance their projects by taking jobs in advertising or online television. Some have left the industry altogether.

“Life is short,” Ma said. “It makes a huge difference whether you spend 10 years in a declining industry or a rising one.”

In 2016, the government-backed Nationwide Alliance of Arthouse Cinemas was established to partner with theaters across China and help distribute low-budget and arthouse films, including Yang’s “Chinatown Cha-Cha.” Participating theaters reserve a minimum of three screenings a day for films distributed through the alliance. But this safety net has its limits, particularly as many theaters struggle financially. In 2025, the alliance cut ties with 516 of its more than 2,000 partner theaters for failing to meet their screening commitments.

Asked whether “Niu Lai”’s success could be replicated, my interviewees were skeptical. “We have seen a Yang Yu,” Ma said, referring to the pharmacy student-turned-animator whose 2025 “Ne Zha 2” became China’s highest-grossing film. “But there are 9,999 other Yang Yus who are never seen by the public.”

For Kong, a more open and vibrant film culture is essential if a wider range of work is to thrive. Yet rising ticket prices and increasingly fragmented leisure time encourage both audiences and the industry to play it safe, favoring directors, actors, and franchises with proven track records.

Nevertheless, “Niu Lai”’s unexpected surge has jolted a market hungry for something different. “Commercial productions have kept people stuck in habitual ways of thinking about what a film should be,” said Yang, who expressed “respect” for “Niu Lai”’s “handcrafted” approach.

Perhaps that is the significance of “Niu Lai.” Its success does not offer a formula that other independent filmmakers can simply reproduce. But its unlikely journey from a 5,500-yuan opening week to packed screenings is a reminder that audiences can still make room for films that fall far outside the industry’s conventional ideas of what is commercially viable, or even what a film is supposed to look like.

(Header image: Visuals from VCG, reedited by Sixth Tone)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018960/Chinese County Takes Aim at Soaring Bride Prices
World.title: Chinese County Takes Aim at Soaring Bride Prices
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018960/Chinese County Takes Aim at Soaring Bride Prices
World.content:
A rural Chinese county is working to end the practice of grooms and their families spending exorbitant amounts to ask for their brides’ hands in marriage — a custom known as “bride price.”

Authorities in Shicheng County in the eastern Jiangxi province have worked to drastically reduce bride prices in its community over the last four years. The share of families who pay under 50,000 yuan ($7,400) rose from 16% in 2022 to over 27% in 2025, according to a national rural customs meeting to review the county’s progress on Aug. 26 in the nearby city of Ganzhou, state news agency Xinhua reported Thursday.

Bride price, or cai li, first emerged as a custom during the Western Zhou dynasty (1046–771 BC). At the time, suitors asked their potential bride’s family for consent to marry her by presenting them with gifts such as deer hides and silk. Gifts also compensated the family for the labor deficit incurred when their daughter left the home and symbolized the man’s ability to provide for his future family. It therefore followed that the more generous the gift, the more desirable the man.

But the custom has evolved to reflect social status and power, with brides’ families asking for increasingly vast sums. In part because of a nationwide gender imbalance, average rural bride prices surged from 10,000 to 20,000 yuan in the early 2000s to roughly 140,000 yuan in 2021, according to research conducted by Wuhan University, in the central Hubei province. Today, some pay up to 2 million yuan.

For years, the central government has attempted to rein in the practice. This year’s national annual rural policy document, released in February, also called for continued crackdowns on high bride prices and the promotion of “simple” and “civilized” wedding traditions.

In line with the new policy, government departments in Shicheng County are working together to use pilot programs and public matchmaking services to decrease or eliminate family spending on bride prices.

At the national meeting in Ganzhou, officials discussed new data that revealed a shift: almost a third of the 361 couples who married in Shicheng County in the first half of this year reportedly paid no bride price — in contrast to years past, when bride price was expected.

In some Shicheng County villages, the rejection of high bride prices has been enshrined in local rules and customs, reportedly cutting total wedding costs to about one-fifth of what they used to be. “Red and white” councils, or hongbai lishihui — named for the colors that represent weddings and funerals — have been established to “step in” to correct excessive spending on bride prices.

Changxi village in the county has also promoted lower costs for weddings in general, ensuring that wedding banquets are kept under 680 yuan per table.

The villagers have also developed a consensus that bride prices should be kept at either 3,600 or 6,900 yuan — considered lucky in Chinese culture as “six,” or liu, is a homophone of “smooth,” and “nine,” or jiu, is a homophone of “a long time,” symbolizing a long marriage.

Shicheng also offers rewards to couples and their parents who do not spend vast sums on bride prices. Such families can apply for a card granting them access to discounts on wedding banquets, discounted business loans, free entrance to local attractions, and free pregnancy checks. Over 1,000 cards are said to have been issued this year.

“The card is not just about money; it’s an honor,” Lai Hua, deputy director of Shicheng Civil Affairs Bureau, told domestic media. “We want people who support the new customs to feel recognized, rewarded, and proud.”

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: Wrapped bundles of cash given as bride prices in Sinan County, Guizhou province, Feb. 22, 2026. VCG)

World.title: ‘Supersized’ El Niño may become strongest ever recorded, UN says
World.content:
EL NIÑO. A ship transits the Panama Canal near the Gamboa hydrometeorological monitoring station as a lack of rainfall linked to El Nino affects the water levels, in Gamboa, Panama, on August 27, 2026.

'El Niño is being supersized before our eyes. The science leaves no room for doubt: The planet is in uncharted waters, and those waters are heating up,' says United Nations chief Antonio Guterres

GENEVA, Switzerland – The El Niño weather phenomenon is set to intensify further into 2027 and could be the strongest ever, raising risks of extreme weather into next year, the World Meteorological Organization said on Thursday, September 3.

The UN weather agency said its forecasts showed a near 100% likelihood that El Niño would persist through February 2027, fueled by exceptionally warm Pacific Ocean temperatures. This is the first time it has expressed such a degree of certainty, the WMO said.

“If this trajectory continues, it may be stronger than anything since our monitoring began. So literally off the charts,” WMO Secretary-General Celeste Saulo told a Geneva press conference.

El Niño is a periodic warming of sea surface temperatures in the eastern Pacific caused by weakening trade winds. It occurs every two to seven years and tends to last up to 12 months, causing intense rains and droughts across Latin America.

A very strong El Niño can significantly shift rainfall and temperature patterns worldwide, and fuel extreme weather, such as droughts and typhoons.

Warming ocean

While it is a naturally occurring phenomenon and not directly linked to fossil fuel-driven climate change, it can be intensified by warmer ocean temperatures, which are.

“El Niño is being supersized before our eyes. The science leaves no room for doubt: The planet is in uncharted waters, and those waters are heating up,” said UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres.

Sample Pacific Ocean temperatures in this year’s El Niño — one of just four categorized in the top “very strong” bracket in records dating back to 1950 — are already more than 2 degrees Celsius (3.6 degrees Fahrenheit) above normal, the WMO said.

The event has already had an impact on soft commodities in tropical areas, causing a severe food crisis across Central America’s Dry Corridor.

‘Pulse’ in global temperatures

It is set to peak towards the end of this year, the WMO said in a statement. But its effects will continue into 2027 and are set to leave higher global temperatures next year in its wake, WMO officials said.

“Normally after an El Niño event we tend to see a pulse in the global temperatures — a temporary one,” Wilfran Moufouma Okia, the WMO’s chief of climate prediction services, told reporters, referring to 2024, which was the hottest year so far. “2027 has the potential to be the warmest on record.”

The WMO said it was stepping up preparedness and early warning efforts in preparation to allow states to take early action, such as switching to drought-resistant crops in some places.

“WMO is committed to working closely with partners across the United Nations and humanitarian system to provide the climate intelligence and insights needed to support disaster management and climate-sensitive sectors like agriculture, health, energy and water resources,” Saulo said. – Rappler.com

World.title: Feminist activist Gloria Steinem dies at age 92
World.content:
WOMEN'S RIGHTS. Gloria Steinem protests against the opening of the first United States branch of De Beers jewelry store in New York, on June 22, 2005.

The co-founder and consulting editor of Ms. Magazine championed the feminist movement from the late 1960s onwards and inspired generations of women

Gloria Steinem, the American writer, lecturer, activist, and organizer who fought for gender equality and women’s civil and reproductive rights for more than five decades, has died, her foundation said. She was 92 years old.

The co-founder and consulting editor of Ms. Magazine championed the feminist movement from the late 1960s onwards and inspired generations of women.

She died on Wednesday, September 2, her foundation said in an Instagram post on Thursday, September 3.

“From reluctant spokesperson to a beacon of positive change, hers is a singular journey — an American leader who can speak to us all,” film and theater director Julie Taymor said of Steinem in a 2017 New York Times interview.

Taymor directed the 2020 film “The Glorias,” depicting Steinem’s life across the years and based on her 2015 best-selling autobiography “My Life on the Road.” She was also the subject of a 2018 play, “Gloria: A Life,” and a 2011 HBO documentary, “Gloria: In Her Own Words.”

Steinem said she considered herself “an entrepreneur of social change.”

“I want to do justice to the women I meet, to tell their stories,” she told the New Yorker magazine in 2015. “It’s making connections, and using myself to listen, because we can’t empower women without listening to their stories.”

Steinem founded the National Women’s Political Caucus in 1971 with former US Representatives Bella Abzug and Shirley Chisholm and writer Betty Friedan, whose 1963 book “The Feminine Mystique” ushered in the second wave of feminism.

Among other groups, she also created the Coalition of Labor Union Women, the Women’s Media Center, Voters for Choice, and the Ms. Foundation for Women.

In 2013, then-president Barack Obama awarded her the Presidential Medal of Freedom, the highest US civilian honor.

With her signature long, blonde-streaked, center-parted hair and aviator glasses, Steinem was the glamorous, hip symbol of the feminist movement, which she emphasized should embrace women of every race.

“If you’ve suffered discrimination, you’re sensitive to it on every level. I learned feminism largely from Black women. Women of color basically invented feminism,” she told the New Yorker.

‘A bunny’s tale’

Steinem was born on March 25, 1934, in Toledo, Ohio, the younger of two daughters. Her father was a traveling antique dealer. Because the family moved frequently she did not attend school regularly until about seventh grade.

Her parents separated when she was 11, following which Steinem lived with and took care of her mother, who had a mental breakdown and suffered from depression.

The experience impacted Steinem’s views on social injustice and marriage, which she believed robbed women of choices and many of their civil rights.

“I’d already been the very small parent of a very big child, my mother. I didn’t want to end up taking care of someone else,” she was quoted as saying.

After graduating from Smith College, Steinem began freelancing as a journalist.

In 1963, she worked as a Playboy bunny for 11 days for a story for Show magazine. Her two-part groundbreaking expose, “A Bunny’s Tale,” detailed the poor pay and sexist treatment Playboy bunnies — originally waitstaff — endured. The story was made into a 1985 TV movie starring Kirstie Alley.

In 1968, Steinem helped found New York magazine, where her essay titled “After Black Power, Women’s Liberation” established her as a feminist leader at a time of roiling social change.

But it wasn’t until she attended an abortion speak-out in a New York church the following year that Steinem — who had had a then-illegal abortion in London when she was 22 — said her life as a feminist activist really began.

Ms. Magazine, which she co-founded in 1971, tackled abortion and other issues such as sexism, equal pay, and domestic violence — a far cry from the diet of beauty, cookery and supporting-your-husband topics that were the staple of magazines aimed at women.

An early issue included the names of 52 women, including Steinem, who had had abortions, and called for the procedure to be legalized ahead of the landmark 1973 Roe v. Wade ruling that recognized women’s constitutional right to abortion in the US for nearly half a century.

‘Quintessence of female revolution’

Steinem was often critical of the limitations of marriage. “Women are not going to be equal outside the home until men are equal in it,” she said.

She had no children of her own, and it was not until she turned 66 that she decided to wed — to South African businessman and environmentalist David Bale, the father of actor Christian Bale.

“I hope this proves what feminists have always said — that feminism is about the ability to choose what’s right at each time of our lives,” she said in a statement about the marriage. David Bale died of brain cancer in 2003.

Steinem continued working into her 80s. She wrote numerous books, including 1986’s “Marilyn: Norma Jean” about Marilyn Monroe, “Revolution from Within: A Book of Self-Esteem” about personal development, and books of essays.

She narrated and conceived the idea for an Emmy Award-winning documentary about child abuse, “Multiple Personalities: The Search for Deadly Memories,” for HBO in 1993 and produced the Lifetime film “Better Off Dead.” She also hosted “Woman,” a documentary series about violence against women, for the Viceland TV channel.

Author Carolyn Heilbrun — who penned 1995 biography “Education of a Woman: The Life of Gloria Steinem” — described her as “the epitome of female beauty and the quintessence of female revolution.” – Rappler.com

World.title: Sandiganbayan orders Manuel Bonoan’s release after junking of 5th Division cases
World.content:
BONOAN. Former public works secretary Manuel Bonoan arrives at the anti-graft court Sandiganbayan in Quezon City on June 2, 2026, for the arraignment of his graft case.

The former Department of Public Works and Highways chief is on bail for the 2nd Division case, while the 5th Division recently dropped the cases against Bonoan following a request from the Office of the Ombudsman

MANILA, Philippines – The anti-graft court Sandiganbayan ordered the release of former Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) secretary Manuel Bonoan following the dismissal of his plunder and graft cases before the 5th Division.

“Accordingly, the oral motion of Atty. [Steffanie] Ong is hereby granted. The Commitment Orders (Pending Trial) issued by this court against Manuel Manligas Bonoan in Crim. Case No. E-SB26CRM0005 and Crim. Case No. E-SB26CRM0006, dated June 19, 2026, are hereby recalled,” said a portion of the resolution dated Thursday, September 3.

“Police Brigadier General Portia B. Manalad of the Philippine National Police (PNP) Health Service General Hospital is hereby ordered to release from custody Manuel Manligas Bonoan, unless he is being detained for other lawful reason,” it added.

Bonoan is facing two sets of cases before the Sandiganbayan, where Senator Jinggoy Estrada is also accused: one count of graft at the 2nd Division, and a count of plunder and graft at the 5th Division.

The former DPWH chief is on bail for the 2nd Division case, while the 5th Division recently dropped the cases against Bonoan following a request from the Office of the Ombudsman. This paved the way for Bonoan’s temporary freedom.

The Ombudsman sought the junking of cases against Bonoan because he is the latest prospect to be a state witness in the multibillion flood control scandal. This bid, however, is still uncertain because while he is on bail at the 2nd Division, the said division rejected the motion that sought the dismissal of the graft case.

In June, the Ombudsman announced its intention to put the former DPWH chief on the list of state witnesses.

It believes that Bonoan’s testimony can pin former speaker Martin Romualdez and shed light on how lawmakers allegedly inserted allocations in the national budget through the DPWH. – Rappler.com

World.title: DOJ: Minor faces multiple murder charges over Tacloban school shooting
World.content:
TRAGEDY. San Jose National High School after a shooting incident that left three students dead and 11 others injured, on June 22, 2026.

Three counts of murder and two counts of attempted murder are filed against the 15-year-old student

MANILA, Philippines – The Department of Justice (DOJ) filed multiple murder charges against the 15-year-old student tagged in the June 22 school shooting at San Jose National High School in Tacloban City which killed three students and injured 20 others.

Following the inquest proceedings on July 13, Tacloban City prosecutors filed three counts of murder and two counts of attempted murder against the 15-year-old boy before the Family Court of Tacloban City Regional Trial Court on July 13, the DOJ announced on Thursday, September 3.

The agency said that the minor allegedly conspired with a 14-year-old boy who was found to be not criminally liable.

“The murder case is pending in court,” it said.

In the press briefing, Justice Undersecretary Ian Norman Dato disclosed that Tacloban prosecutors ordered the filing of additional charges against the 15-year-old student:

Four counts of frustrated murder, with recommended bail of P72,000 for each count

Six counts of attempted murder, with recommended bail of P36,000 for each count

According to Dato, Tacloban prosecutors found that the 15 year old “acted with discernment” and in “conspiracy with a second minor.”

“If the CICL (child in conflict with the law) has shown his ability to distinguish between right and wrong and still proceeded to commit the wrong, his acts prior, during, and after the incident would form the context within which to determine discernment,” Dato explained without mentioning specifics of the case.

He said that while the local social welfare and development official initially determines discernment of the CICL, it is not binding on the prosecutors.

“The prosecutors have looked into the entirety of the documentary evidence. I believe some psychological reports have been looked into,” the DOJ official added.

Although the 14-year-old student is exempt from criminal liability, the Department of the Interior and Local Government previously said he would undergo an intervention program.

On August 18, another fatal school shooting incident occurred, this time in Zamboanga City. Two students were killed at Ateneo de Zamboanga University’s junior high school campus, including the perpetrator.

The incidents have sparked discussions of responsible gun ownership, strengthening school safety, and addressing mental health issues among the youth. – Rappler.com

World.title: Rappler Live Jam: The cast of ‘Muli: An OPM Musical’
World.content:
LIVE

Set across the '90s and early 2000s, the musical 'Muli' moves through different eras and sounds of OPM

MANILA, Philippines – Muli: An OPM Musical brings its original music to Rappler Live Jam on Thursday, September 3, giving audiences a preview of the songs behind its story of missed chances, old dreams, and the prospect of starting anew.

The musical follows Anita, a 42-year-old housewife who finds herself looking back on the past two decades and reflecting on the possibilities of the different paths she might have taken. Her daughter Kath encourages her to look beyond the life she has built around motherhood and rediscover the dreams she once had for herself.

Set across the ’90s and early 2000s, the musical moves through different eras and sounds of OPM, with 11 original songs written and produced by singer-songwriter Nica del Rosario and musical director and composer Matthew Chang alongside talents from FlipMusic, the team behind BINI favorites “Pantropiko,” “Salamin, Salamin,” and “Karera,” as well as the Sarah Geronimo hit “Tala.”

The musical stars Gawad Urian award-winning actress Kakki Teodoro as Anita and OPM artist Janine Teñoso as her daughter Kath, with ensemble cast members Vien King, Marvin Ong, Justine Peña, Marynor Mademesila, and Baus Rufo.

Muli also marks Janine’s theater stage debut after establishing herself through OPM and Filipino OST hits.

Showdates run from September 11-27 at the Globe Auditorium, Maybank Performing Arts Theater at the BGC Arts Center in Taguig City.

Catch the cast of Muli: An OPM Musical on Rappler Live Jam on Thursday, September 3, at 8 pm, by bookmarking this page or heading to Rappler’s YouTube! – Belle Calica/Rappler.com

World.title: Sandiganbayan again denies Jinggoy Estrada’s bid for bail
World.content:
BJMP. Senator Jinggoy Estrada arrives at the Sandiganbayan graft court in Quezon City on June 2, 2026, for the arraignment of his graft case.

MANILA, Philippines – The anti-graft court Sandiganbayan upheld its resolution to deny Senator Jinggoy Estrada’s request for bail in his flood control-related case.

In a resolution dated Thursday, September 3, the court’s 5th Division junked Estrada’s motion for reconsideration, which appealed the court’s earlier resolution to deny the bail request.

“Accordingly, the court finds no cogent reason to disturb its earlier ruling. Until a hearing determines that the evidence of guilt is not strong, the court has no basis to set a bail amount. Consequently, the motion is denied,” the resolution penned by Associate Justice Gener Gito read.

“Wherefore, premises considered, accused Jose ‘Jinggoy’ Pimentel Ejercito Estrada’s Motion for Reconsideration dated August 3, 2026 is denied for lack of merit,” it added.

Associate Justices Zaldy Trespeses and Maryann Corpus-Mañalac concurred.

Estrada was charged with plunder and graft cases in May due to his alleged involvement in the flood control corruption.

The Sandiganbayan junked Estrada’s request in July because it had no legal basis and was filed prematurely. This denial, however, does not preclude Estrada from filing an actual bail petition before the Sandiganbayan, where the prosecution will try to establish that the evidence of his guilt is strong.

In its recent resolution, the Sandiganbayan did not give weight to Estrada’s claim that he is not a flight risk, explaining that “such circumstance does not authorize the court to dispense with the requisite bail proceedings and immediately fix bail.”

Estrada also used the Enrile doctrine, where the court granted former senator Juan Ponce Enrile’s request for bail due to humanitarian concerns.

“The [Enrile] ruling cannot reasonably be understood as establishing a general rule that an accused charged with an offense punishable by reclusion perpetua may obtain bail without the requisite determination of whether the evidence of guilt is strong merely upon showing that he is not a flight risk, possesses substantial social or political ties, or has previously complied with travel conditions imposed by this court,” it explained.

“The considerations concerning his alleged lack of flight risk do not dispense with the antecedent determination of whether the evidence of guilt is strong. Neither does Enrile, considering the exceptional factual circumstances underlying that ruling, authorize the court to circumvent the procedure regarding discretionary bail under the circumstances of this case,” it added. – Rappler.com

World.title: New name, old problems? Bulacan water woes continue despite PrimeWater rebrand
World.content:
TAWID-UHAW. Weak water supply comes out of a Tawid-Uhaw PrimeWater station in San Jose Del Monte, Bulacan.

Residents of San Jose del Monte, Bulacan cry for help amid continued water service problems despite PrimeWater's acquisition by Crystal Bridges Holding Corp. in December 2025

A new name did not erase PrimeWater Infrastructure Corporation’s longstanding problems.

Despite its rebranding as Hiraya Water Corp., persistent water woes and unfulfilled obligations continued to hound the private concessionaire, with consumers bearing the brunt.

In San Jose del Monte City, Bulacan, Senator Raffy Tulfo — chairperson of the Senate Public Services committee — said over 47,000 households remained reeling from frequent service interruptions, as well as discolored water supply even months after Lucio Co’s Crystal Bridges Holding Corp. acquired PrimeWater in late 2025.

“Nung pumasok ang PrimeWater, ‘yung ganda ng serbisyo ng water district…nawala,” Irene del Rosario, resident and former San Jose del Monte city councilor, told the Senate Public Services Committee during a hearing on the joint venture agreements (JVAs) of water districts and private entities on Thursday, September 3.

(When PrimeWater entered into the picture, the good services of the water district vanished.)

Del Rosario recalled the water district entered into a JVA with PrimeWater in 2018 following an “unsolicited” proposal from the private concessionaire. This was allegedly approved by then newly-appointed members of the board of directors.

“Walang public consultation. Hindi alam ng taumbayan na ang tubig namin ay iliipat na sa isang private concessionaire…[Ngayon], ganun pa rin, as expected,” she said.

(There was no public consultation. We did not know that our water service would be transferred to a private concessionaire. Now, our situation remains the same, as expected.)

Residents of San Jose del Monte have repeatedly called for intervention amid continued poor water service in the area. In March, the city government assumed control of the water service previously managed by PrimeWater. It tapped Metro Pacific Water (MPW) to take over the service as an interim operator two months later.

MPW head of legal Roberto Rey Rodrigo said the company had started rehabilitating the city’s water service assets but admitted that San Jose del Monte had a deficit of about 70 million liters to fulfill its daily water requirement.

“Unfortunately, to take on such a monumental task would require a long-term concessionaire,” Rodrigo added.

On August 23, a crowd consisting of many local residents chanted “Tubig! Tubig! Tubig!” (Water!) in a sports event after learning that Mayor Rita Robes, and her husband, Congressman Arthur Robes, were at the venue.

“Sumigaw sila ng ‘Tubig!’ Kasi wala talaga kaming tubig,” Akbayan Councilor Ronalyn Pordan previously told Rappler. (They shouted “Water!” because we really have no water.)

Senator Raffy Tulfo, chairperson of the Senate panel, flagged Hiraya Water for the persistent water issues in its areas of operation. He also questioned the concessionaire over its corporate records, citing a Securities and Exchange Commission record showing it previously listed “restaurants, parlors, beer houses and snack bars” as its nature of business.

“Nagbago na ang owner ng PrimeWater, pero patuloy pa rin ang reklamo,” said Tulfo. (The ownership of PrimeWater changed but the complaints over their service have not stopped.)

“To be fair, Crystal Bridges did not create PrimeWater’s problems. Pero kapag bumili ka ng kumpanya, hindi lang assets at revenue ang kasama. You inherit the existing contracts, debts and obligations, pending cases, unfinished commitments and consumers na galit na, uhaw pa,” the lawmaker added.

(To be fair, Crystal Bridges did not create PrimeWater’s problems but when you buy out a company, you acquire not only their assets and revenue, but also their existing contracts, debts and obligations, pending cases, unfinished commitments and consumers who are not only angry but also thirsty.)

PrimeWater

PrimeWater is a Villar-owned water and wastewater services provider that previously partnered with over 77 water districts in the country. Following the acquisition, Hiraya Water took over the existing JVAs.

Senator Risa Hontiveros, during the legislative inquiry, said she received information that eight water districts are signifying intention to exit the JVA amid the persistent service issues.

Hontiveros asked Hiraya Water whether it intended to file cases or impose penalties on water districts should they pursue the unilateral termination of their contracts.

“Mayroon pong procedure set in place and signed by both parties and was cleared by regulatory bodies. Sana sundin ‘yun,” Hiraya Water president Jose Paulino Santamarina said.

(There’s a procedure set in place and signed by both parties. It was also cleared by regulatory bodies. We’re hoping it will be followed.)

The Public-Private Partnership (PPP) center said Hiraya Water failed to secure the consent of any of the 77 water districts during the acquisition. Sans written consent, the Office of the Government Corporate Counsel (OGCC) said the water districts can move to terminate the JVAs as they were not formally informed of the ownership change.

Apart from the water districts, some private subdivisions including La Poblacion in San Jose del Monte also appealed to Hiraya Water to allow them to exit the water service agreement.

“I-turnover ‘nyo na kami sa water district, ‘yun lang ang solution dun,” said La Poblacion resident Charlie Marciano. (We’re appealing for Hiraya Water to turn over our water service to the city water district. That’s the only solution to our problem.)

Is anyone listening? – Rappler.com

World.title: Kazakhstan Wins 18 Medals At World Nomad Games In Kyrgyz Republic
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan’s national team has won 18 medals at the sixth World Nomad Games currently underway in the Kyrgyz Republic, including six gold, one silver and 11 bronze medals, reported the Ministry of Tourism and Sports.

Kazakh athletes have reached the podium across several traditional sports, including horse-based competitions, traditional wrestling, strength disciplines and hunting with birds of prey.

Audaryspak – four gold, one silver

Kazakhstan claimed four gold medals and one silver in audaryspak, a traditional horseback wrestling competition in which riders attempt to unseat their opponents from horseback.

Nurtalap Kerim won the gold medal in the up-to-60-kilogram category after defeating a Kyrgyz athlete in the final. Sailau Mukhammedzhan also defeated a Kyrgyz opponent, winning the final 2-1 in the up-to-70-kilogram category.

Daryn Otkelbay became the champion in the 90-kilogram category, while Syrym Izbasarov won gold in the 100-kilogram category. Rasul Kuraiysh, competing in the up-to-80-kilogram category, took silver after losing to a Kyrgyz athlete in the final.

Zhamba atu – one gold

Abzal Tulybekov won gold in zhamby atu, a Kyrgyz-style traditional horseback archery discipline in which riders shoot at targets while riding at speed.

Tug-of-war – two gold

Kazakhstan won two gold medals in tug-of-war, a team strength competition in which two teams pull on opposite ends of a rope.

The national team took first place in both the 8×8 and 4×4 events.

Alysh – three bronze

Kazakhstan won three bronze medals in alysh, a traditional form of belt wrestling in which competitors use a belt and grips to throw their opponents to the ground.

Turmukhanbet Kalmukhan finished third in the up-to-60-kilogram category in the classical style.

Zhandos Abubakir also took bronze in the up-to-60-kilogram freestyle event. In the over-100-kilogram category, Nursultan Kozhageldy finished third after five bouts.

Mas-wrestling – one bronze

Nursultan Yesimbay won bronze in mas-wrestling, a traditional strength competition in which two athletes sit opposite each other and pull a wooden stick toward themselves.

He finished third in the up-to-90-kilogram category.

Spine-bone breaking – one bronze

Kazakhstan also secured a bronze medal in spine-bone breaking, a traditional strength event involving the breaking of an animal’s spinal bone.

The discipline is among the newer events included in the World Nomad Games program.

Sambo – one gold, two bronze

Kazakh athletes also competed in sambo, a martial art and combat sport that combines wrestling and throwing techniques with grappling elements.

Sapar Bolat, competing in the over-98-kilogram category, won the gold medal. Yerkebulan Nygmetov (up to 79 kilograms) and Zhandos Beisenbayev (up to 64 kilograms) claimed bronze.

Qusbegilik – one silver, one bronze

Kazakhstan also won two medals in qusbegilik, the traditional art of hunting with trained birds of prey. Bagdaulet Babazhan finished second in itelgi salu, a discipline involving hunting with a saker falcon, while Yerlan Kenzhetayev took bronze in the itelgi event featuring the same bird.

World.title: Kazakhstan, Laos Seek New Routes for Trade and Cooperation
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan and Laos are seeking to expand trade, investment and transport cooperation as the two countries look to deepen bilateral ties, Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev said during talks with Lao President Thongloun Sisoulith in Astana on Sept. 3, reported Akorda.

Tokayev described Sisoulith’s visit as historic, as it marks the first official visit by a Lao president to Kazakhstan. He also noted that 2027 will mark the 30th anniversary of diplomatic relations between the two countries.

“Relations between our states are friendly. We cooperate closely on the international stage, primarily within the United Nations. I would also like to express my sincere appreciation for Laos’ support for our initiatives within the Conference on Interaction and Confidence-Building Measures in Asia (CICA),” Tokayev said.

He said the visit would give new impetus to bilateral relations and that the two governments would begin implementing the agreements reached during the talks. Tokayev described Laos as an important and reliable partner for Kazakhstan in Southeast Asia, noting its steady economic growth and progress in energy, agriculture, industry and tourism.

“We support expanding trade and economic cooperation with Laos, viewing it as an important foundation for strengthening bilateral ties. We see significant potential for increasing Kazakh exports, particularly in metallurgy, food, petrochemicals, agriculture, chemicals, machinery and pharmaceuticals,” Tokayev said.

According to the TradeReport Telegram channel, Laos’ economy grew by around 4.8% in 2025. Kazakhstan imported $428,000 worth of goods from Laos in January-June 2026, while annual imports have never exceeded $1.4 million.

Logistics emerge as a key area of cooperation

Transport and logistics could offer another avenue to expand bilateral economic ties, with Tokayev highlighting Laos’ transformation from a landlocked country into a potential regional transit link.

“Kazakhstan has the largest transport network in Central Asia and is actively developing the Trans-Caspian International Transport Route, which connects China and Europe. Our country handles around 85% of continental freight traffic between China and Europe,” Tokayev said.

He noted that Kazakh terminals operate at the ports of Batumi in Georgia and Lianyungang in China, while Kazakhstan has also launched a logistics hub in Xi’an, China, whose platform could be used by Lao freight carriers.

“We see an opportunity to use our transport corridors to facilitate access for Lao products to Central Asian and European markets. Kazakhstan is interested in expanding its exports to Southeast Asian markets through Laos,” he said.

Tokayev also highlighted the role of the Laos-China railway in strengthening Laos’ transit potential and creating new opportunities to connect ASEAN with China and Europe.

“I propose that our governments work toward concluding relevant intergovernmental and interagency agreements in transport and logistics,” he said.

The Laos-China railway, which began full operations in 2021, has strengthened Laos’ position along regional trade routes and could create opportunities for Kazakhstan to use the country as a gateway to Southeast Asian markets.

Tokayev also invited Lao companies to make greater use of the opportunities offered by the Astana International Financial Centre (AIFC).

“The AIFC has become an international platform for doing business and attracting investment. It brings together more than 6,300 registered companies from more than 90 countries, creating a dynamic business environment. Through the AIFC platform, $27 billion in investment has been attracted to Kazakhstan,” Tokayev said.

“For Lao companies, the AIFC can serve as an effective tool for entering the Kazakh market and expanding their presence across Central Asia,” he said.

Longstanding ties

Sisoulith said he had seen firsthand Kazakhstan’s development and the scale of the transformations taking place under Tokayev’s leadership.

“It is a great honor for me to make this official visit to Kazakhstan as president and to meet with you today. I sincerely believe that my visit will make a significant contribution to strengthening bilateral relations. I am confident that during our talks we will be able to discuss a wide range of issues and identify promising areas for cooperation and further joint work,” Sisoulith said.

He highlighted that Kazakhstan has consistently maintained good and stable relations with Laos and has supported the country since its national liberation struggle.

“Regardless of how circumstances have changed, relations between Kazakhstan and Laos, as well as our fraternal ties and mutual goodwill, have remained unchanged. I believe that this visit will contribute to further strengthening and expanding friendly relations between our two countries,” Sisoulith said.

He also emphasized Kazakhstan’s contribution to training specialists for Laos.

“Hundreds of Lao citizens have received their education and graduated from educational institutions in Kazakhstan. Today, many of them work in public service, run businesses or hold senior positions at the national and local levels. They all remember Kazakhstan warmly for the support and assistance they received during their studies,” Sisoulith said.

Tokayev and Sisoulith also discussed cooperation in culture, humanitarian affairs and tourism, as well as opportunities to strengthen ties between higher education institutions.

The two countries also exchanged several intergovernmental documents in the presence of the two heads of state, covering political consultations, law enforcement, digital development and cooperation between their capitals.

World.title: Kazakhstan Signs Contract For Construction Of First Nuclear Power Plant
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan has signed a contract to design, supply and build its first nuclear power plant, moving the long-planned project into a new practical phase as the country seeks to strengthen energy security and prepare for growing electricity demand.

The contract was signed between Kazakhstan Nuclear Power Plants and Atomstroyexport, a subsidiary of Russia’s Rosatom state nuclear corporation, on the sidelines of the 11th Eastern Economic Forum in Vladivostok.

The signing was attended by Chairman of Kazakhstan’s Atomic Energy Agency Almasadam Satkaliyev and Rosatom Director General Alexei Likhachev.

The agreement marks a significant step in Kazakhstan’s plans to introduce nuclear generation into its energy mix. However, the project has not yet reached the final implementation stage. Under the intergovernmental agreement signed on May 28, 2026, the parties will continue the required procedures, including the necessary approval by the Kazakh government.

From political decision to construction project

The contract moves the first nuclear power plant project beyond early site selection and political decision-making toward detailed implementation. Kazakhstan approved the construction of a nuclear power plant through a national referendum in October 2024. The project is planned for the Zhambyl district of the Almaty Region, with construction expected to take about eight years.

Rosatom was selected from a shortlist that also included China National Nuclear Corporation, France’s EDF and Korea Hydro & Nuclear Power.

Rising electricity demand puts energy security at the center

The government sees nuclear power as a response to a structural increase in electricity demand. Kazakhstan’s economy, industrial production and infrastructure are expanding, while digitalization and the development of artificial intelligence are creating additional demand for stable electricity supplies. Unlike intermittent renewable sources, nuclear power is designed to provide continuous baseload generation.

Globally, nuclear energy supplies nearly 10% of electricity generation and around 20% in advanced economies, according to the International Energy Agency. With global nuclear capacity approaching 413 gigawatts across 32 countries, nuclear power remains a major source of low-carbon electricity.

The IEA estimates that nuclear power currently prevents around 1.5 gigatonnes of carbon dioxide emissions and 180 billion cubic meters of gas demand each year. For Kazakhstan, the attraction of nuclear generation is therefore twofold: it could provide additional stable capacity while supporting the country’s longer-term efforts to reduce the carbon intensity of its power sector.

At the same time, nuclear power is not a substitute for renewable energy. The IEA has emphasized that nuclear and renewable generation can complement each other as countries seek to decarbonize their electricity systems. For Kazakhstan, which has significant wind and solar potential, the final energy model will likely depend on how nuclear generation is integrated with existing thermal plants and the expanding renewable sector.

The bigger opportunity may be industrial

The economic significance of the project could extend beyond electricity generation. The Atomic Energy Agency has emphasized localization as a priority, aiming to involve Kazakh companies, specialists, goods, works and services as extensively as possible in the construction process.

This is particularly important because a nuclear power plant is a highly complex industrial project. Its supply chain requires specialized equipment, engineering expertise, safety systems and technical standards. Building those capabilities domestically could give Kazakhstan an industrial base for future nuclear projects and related activities. The government has said the first plant should help create national competencies and a personnel reserve for the further development of the nuclear sector.

Uranium producer seeks a larger role in nuclear energy

Kazakhstan enters the nuclear era from an unusual position: it is the world’s leading uranium producer but does not currently generate electricity from nuclear power. That creates an opportunity to connect the country’s existing position in the global uranium industry with a domestic nuclear energy value chain.

The first power plant could become the foundation for a broader nuclear-energy cluster, particularly if Kazakhstan proceeds with its stated plans to build three nuclear power plants.

The government has described the project as part of Kazakhstan’s efforts to strengthen energy independence and technological sovereignty. Those goals will ultimately be measured not only by the plant’s completion but by what Kazakhstan can build around it.

A successful project could provide reliable baseload electricity, support industrial growth, create specialized jobs and help establish domestic nuclear competencies. It could also give Kazakhstan greater flexibility as it balances rising electricity demand with decarbonization goals.

For a country already in a leading position in the global uranium industry, the first nuclear power plant could mark a shift from primarily supplying nuclear raw materials to producing nuclear energy.

World.title: Kazakhstan Forms New Government With Majority Of Ministers Retaining Posts
World.content:
ALMATY – Kazakhstan has formed a new government, with most ministers retaining their positions while several key ministries received new heads, according to presidential decrees and orders.

Mukhtar Tileuberdi was appointed Minister of Foreign Affairs, returning to the position he held from 2019 to 2023. Before the appointment, he served as Kazakhstan’s Ambassador to Austria and Permanent Representative of Kazakhstan to International Organizations in Vienna. He replaced Yermek Kosherbayev, who had headed the Foreign Ministry since September 2025.

Several ministries have received new leadership

Murat Mukhanov was appointed Minister of Emergency Situations, replacing Chingiz Arinov. Mukhanov previously headed the Mangystau Region Department of Emergency Situations and later served as chief of staff of the Ministry of Emergency Situations.

Alibek Kuantyrov was appointed Minister of Ecology and Natural Resources, replacing Yerlan Nyssanbayev. Since 2024, Kuantyrov had served as Deputy Minister of Foreign Affairs. He previously headed the Ministry of National Economy.

Arman Kyrykbayev was appointed Minister of Culture and Information, replacing Aida Balayeva.

Several members of the government retained their positions

Dauren Kosanov was reappointed Minister of Defense, while Yerzhan Sadenov was reappointed Minister of Internal Affairs. Madi Takiyev will continue as Minister of Finance, Nurlan Sauranbayev as Minister of Transport, Yerlan Akkenzhenov as Minister of Energy, and Yersaiyn Nagaspayev as Minister of Industry and Construction.

Arman Shakkaliyev was reappointed Minister of Trade and Integration, while Yerlan Sarsembayev will continue to head the Ministry of Justice. Zhuldyz Suleimenova retained the post of Minister of Education, Akmaral Alnazarova will continue as Minister of Health, and Nurzhan Nurzhigitov will remain Minister of Water Resources and Irrigation.

Askarbek Yertayev was reappointed Minister of Labor and Social Protection of the Population, Aydarbek Saparov will continue as Minister of Agriculture, Yerbol Myrzabosynov as Minister of Tourism and Sports, and Sayasat Nurbek as Minister of Science and Higher Education.

Galymzhan Koishybayev was appointed Deputy Prime Minister and Chief of Staff of the government. Serik Zhumangarin was appointed Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of National Economy, while Zhaslan Madiyev was appointed Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Artificial Intelligence and Digital Development. Nurlybek Naliyev was reappointed First Deputy Prime Minister, while Kanat Bozumbayev was appointed Deputy Prime Minister.

Tokayev also made several appointments outside the ministerial posts. Yermek Abdramanov was appointed Deputy Head of the Presidential Administration. Murat Kaiyrbek was appointed Head of the Presidential Representative Office in the Kurultai of Kazakhstan.

World.title: Experts: Productivity, Not GDP Rankings, Will Define Kazakhstan as GDP Nears $469 Billion
World.content:
ALMATY – Kazakhstan’s nominal gross domestic product could reach $468.8 billion by 2030, potentially placing the country among the world’s 45 largest economies. But economists say the more important question is whether the expansion reflects stronger productivity, diversification and investment rather than simply larger nominal output.

The projection, based on International Monetary Fund (IMF) data, puts Kazakhstan’s economy within reach of a new group of economies approaching or exceeding $500 billion in annual output.

Economist Ruslan Sultanov, author of the Tengenomika Telegram channel, said that the ranking itself should not be treated as the main measure of economic success.

“The main indicator of success should be the quality of this growth. Productivity, real incomes and well-being are more important than a place in the ranking: economic scale acquires meaning when the standard of living rises alongside it,” Sultanov wrote.

A separate long-term projection by Goldman Sachs places Kazakhstan among the world’s 30 largest economies by 2075, with a projected GDP of about $2.1 trillion. Almas Issayev, an oil and gas industry professional with more than a decade of project management experience at Tengizchevroil, said in his LinkedIn post that a $2–3 trillion economy by 2075 could be within Kazakhstan’s reach, supported by population growth, continued energy revenues, reinvestment, innovation and the country’s position as a Eurasian transport hub.

Kazakhstan enters a new economic bracket

The IMF-based projection estimates Kazakhstan’s nominal GDP at $468.8 billion in 2030, roughly $100 billion more than its current level. At that size, Kazakhstan would rank around 45th globally and would be close to economies approaching the $500 billion threshold.

Nigeria is projected at $464.8 billion, while Portugal is estimated at $444.9 billion, Peru at $437.1 billion and Finland at $388.6 billion. The next group is already close to the half-trillion mark. Chile is projected at $496.8 billion, while the Czech Republic could reach $506.8 billion.

The comparison illustrates Kazakhstan’s potential movement into a larger economic category. But the country would not be moving into a static ranking: other emerging markets are also expected to expand significantly over the same period.

A larger world economy raises the bar

The global economy is projected to exceed $150 trillion in nominal GDP by 2030. The United States is expected to remain the world’s largest economy, with GDP of about $37.7 trillion, equivalent to around 25.1% of global output. China is projected at $26 trillion, while Germany and India are expected to be almost equal at approximately $6.18 trillion and $6.17 trillion, respectively.

The United Kingdom is projected at $5.14 trillion, Japan at $5 trillion, France at $4 trillion, Brazil at $3.2 trillion, Italy at $3.04 trillion, and Canada at $3 trillion.

At the same time, several emerging economies are expected to gain weight. Indonesia could surpass $2 trillion, while Türkiye is projected to approach that level. The Philippines, Bangladesh, Malaysia and Vietnam are also expected to enter the group of the world’s 35 largest economies.

For Kazakhstan, this means that growing in absolute terms will not necessarily translate into gaining economic influence relative to other countries. The country will have to boost productivity and competitiveness while competing with economies undergoing their own rapid expansion.

The bigger question is the quality of growth

A larger nominal GDP can expand the domestic market, increase investment capacity and strengthen a country’s economic weight. But GDP rankings say relatively little about how the benefits of growth are distributed or whether living standards are improving. Sultanov therefore places greater emphasis on the composition of future growth.

For Kazakhstan, the critical indicators will include productivity, the development of domestic production, the emergence of more sophisticated industries and the growth of private investment. Another consideration is how much additional domestic demand the domestic economy captures.

“Pursuing growth solely through quantitative measures can increase nominal GDP, but it will have a significantly smaller impact on the economy if the additional demand is directed towards imports, prices, or investments with low returns,” Sultanov wrote.

This makes the transition from resource-driven growth to productivity-driven growth particularly important.

The 2075 question

Goldman Sachs’ The Path to 2075 projection places Kazakhstan among the world’s top 30 economies by 2075, with GDP of about $2.1 trillion. Reaching that level would require a much longer time horizon than the expansion projected for 2030.

Issayev notes that several structural factors could support such growth, beginning with demographics. According to him, Kazakhstan’s energy sector could bridge the resource-based economy of today and a more diversified economy in the future.

For Kazakhstan, the central challenge will be to use its resource revenues, demographic potential and geographic position to build productive capacity that remains competitive as the global economy changes.

“Economic scale acquires meaning when the standard of living rises alongside it,” Sultanov wrote.

In this sense, reaching half a trillion dollars would be a significant milestone, but not an endpoint. The more consequential question is whether each additional dollar of GDP represents greater domestic value creation, higher productivity, stronger private investment and rising real incomes.

World.title: Kazakhstan Set to Join Digital Cooperation Organization as Membership Expands to 24 Countries
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan is set to join the Digital Cooperation Organization (DCO) as a new Member State, opening opportunities for greater cooperation in digital technologies, AI, innovation and digital trade.

The DCO, the world’s first standalone international organization dedicated to accelerating the inclusive and sustainable growth of the digital economy, announced on Aug. 28 that its Council had approved Kazakhstan’s candidature alongside seven other countries.

The move could expand the DCO’s membership from 16 to 24 countries, representing approximately 980 million people, or around 12% of the global population, according to the DCO.

Alongside Kazakhstan, the approved candidate countries are Albania, Azerbaijan, Kenya, Lebanon, Palestine, Syria and Zambia. Tajikistan will join the organization as an Associate Member.

Kazakhstan’s prospective accession would mark the DCO’s first expansion into Central Asia and create a new regional axis for digital cooperation. The organization said the move reflects growing international interest in cooperation on digital policy, artificial intelligence, cross-border data flows, digital public infrastructure and digital skills.

“The rules of the digital economy on data, artificial intelligence, and cross-border trade are being written now, and rules written without you are rules you inherit rather than shape,” said DCO Secretary-General Deemah AlYahya.

The approval of candidature begins the formal accession process. Kazakhstan’s membership will take effect after it completes its internal accession procedures and deposits its instrument of accession in line with the DCO’s founding documents.

The DCO was established in 2020 and currently brings together 16 countries, representing more than 800 million people. Its agenda focuses on promoting digital inclusion, innovation, entrepreneurship and cooperation in the digital economy.

World.title: Kazakhstan Expands Mineral Exploration, But Experts Say Discovery – Only First Step
World.content:
ALMATY – Kazakhstan is expanding geological exploration, increasing geological knowledge and identifying new mineral resources, but experts say the key challenge is no longer simply discovering what lies beneath the country’s vast territory. It is turning geological potential into economically viable projects, investment, production and higher-value exports.

The government is increasing the detail of geological surveys, digitizing decades of accumulated geological information and introducing Big Data and artificial intelligence tools. But geological discovery is only the first step in a much longer process.

“An identified resource is primarily confirmation of the presence of certain mineralization. But this is not enough for an investor,” said Qanat Qudaibergen, chairman of the board of GWM Capital, in a conversation with the Astana Times.

From geological discovery to an investment decision

Kazakhstan is increasing the scale and detail of geological studies as part of efforts to strengthen the country’s mineral-resource base. Geological and geophysical exploration at a scale of 1:200,000 currently covers about 2.04 million square kilometers. The government plans to increase this figure to 2.2 million square kilometers in 2026.

At the same time, the country has begun 20 projects involving more detailed geological mapping at a scale of 1:50,000. The projects will cover 100,000 square kilometers and focus on areas considered prospective for gold, copper, polymetals, rare and rare-earth metals, lithium, tungsten and molybdenum.

Qudaibergen said that a significant amount of work remains between identifying a resource and making an investment decision. Infrastructure is another critical factor, he said, including electricity, water, roads, railway logistics and access to qualified personnel.

“Only after passing all these stages is it possible to speak about a full-fledged investment decision, financing and construction,” Qudaibergen said, highlighting that this distinction is important when assessing the results of geological exploration.

Askar Ismailov, an oil and gas industry expert, made a similar distinction, noting that geological exploration can produce several different levels of information.

“It is very important not to confuse three completely different things: a geological anomaly, a resource and an economically recoverable reserve,” he said.

According to him, a report that geologists have identified a prospective area or estimated forecast resources in millions of tons does not mean that Kazakhstan has automatically obtained a deposit worth billions of dollars.

New resources expand the base, but do not automatically create new production

Kazakhstan has also recorded an increase in its mineral-resource base following geological exploration. The 54 newly registered deposits over the two years were accompanied by growth in resources and reserves across several commodities.

Kazakhstan currently has around 10,000 deposits of various mineral resources on the state register. Yet the scale of the resource base does not necessarily translate into an equivalent number of new mines or industrial projects.

Qudaibergen said that a more meaningful measure of exploration success would be how many newly identified objects eventually progress from geological discovery to internationally recognized resources and reserves, financing, construction and commercial production.

Critical minerals create a window of opportunity

The growing global demand for critical minerals gives Kazakhstan an additional opportunity to turn its geological potential into a broader industrial role. The country is exploring for lithium, tungsten, molybdenum, rare and rare-earth metals, and other strategic resources. Research has already been completed at 11 sites included in the geological exploration program.

The Kuiraktykol site in the Karagandy Region has been identified as particularly promising, with high forecast concentrations of lanthanum, cerium, neodymium and yttrium. Total forecast resources across the sites amount to 935,400 tons. At the Irgiz area, C2-category reserves have additionally been estimated at 795,800 tons.

Developing these resources could be important for Kazakhstan’s industrial diversification, but Qudaibergen cautioned against equating the presence of critical minerals with a strong position in global value chains.

“Competition today is no longer so much for ore as for control over the entire chain: deposit-beneficiation-metallurgy-chemical processing-materials-components-final products,” he said.

For Kazakhstan, this raises a strategic question: where along these chains can the country create competitive advantages rather than simply export concentrates?

“At the same time, I am not a proponent of the approach that requires us to produce a final product from every mined mineral within Kazakhstan. This is not always economically justified,” he said.

The untapped potential above ground

Qudaibergen also pointed to a less conventional component of Kazakhstan’s mineral potential: resources already accumulated on the surface. These include beneficiation tailings, metallurgical slag, cakes and sludges, ash and slag from power generation and other industrial waste.

Many of these materials accumulated decades ago, when extraction technologies were less efficient, and some rare and rare-earth metals were not considered target products.

“What was historically considered waste can today, with new technologies, prices and the changing structure of global demand, in some cases be regarded as secondary mineral raw material,” he said.

This could create an additional avenue for developing critical-mineral production without opening new mines while also addressing accumulated environmental liabilities.

Oil exploration faces a different question

The challenge of converting geological potential into production is particularly important for oil, where Kazakhstan is simultaneously planning a major expansion of domestic refining capacity. The country is targeting a total oil-processing capacity of about 40 million tons per year through the expansion of the Pavlodar, Shymkent and Atyrau refineries and the construction of another refinery with capacity of around 10 million tons, according to Ismailov.

That creates a different set of requirements for geological exploration: the country needs to understand not only how much oil may exist underground, but how much production can realistically be made available to domestic refineries over the long term.

“Today a significant part of crude oil is exported. With 40 million tons of annual refining, a large guaranteed domestic market for crude emerges, which is currently not fully secured by the resource base,” Ismailov said.

One possible option would be to negotiate additional supplies from large oil projects such as Tengiz and Kashagan. Ismailov, however, considers this approach less promising and argues that greater attention should be given to exploration and the development of new reserves.

For geological exploration, this means linking long-term resource planning with the expected production profile of existing fields and future domestic demand.

Digital geology seeks to connect data with investment

Digitalization is becoming another key part of the transformation. The Unified Subsoil Management Platform now contains a map of Kazakhstan’s subsoil use, with 66,100 first volumes of geological reports linked to 109,500 study contours.

More than 4.8 million units of primary geological information have also been digitized, including about 4.3 million paper sheets, 355,000 graphic attachments, 97,000 magnetic tapes and 62,000 cartridges.

One important step in connecting data with investment is Kazakhstan’s transition toward international standards for reporting mineral resources and reserves. According to Qudaibergen, the KAZRC system is aligned with the CRIRSCO family of international reporting standards. This makes geological information more comparable with projects in major mining jurisdictions and can help investors, banks and mining companies assess the quality and economic potential of Kazakh projects.

“Essentially, we are beginning to speak to the global investment community in one professional language,” Qudaibergen said.

The next test is conversion, not discovery

Kazakhstan is entering a new phase of geological development in which the quantity of information is growing alongside the sophistication of the tools used to analyze it. The country is mapping larger areas, conducting more detailed surveys, expanding its mineral-resource base, digitizing geological archives and exploring the potential of critical minerals and technogenic resources.

For Qudaibergen, Kazakhstan has a strong starting position because of its large territory, established geological expertise and significant underexplored potential. Modern geophysics, remote sensing, large-scale data processing and AI can allow previously studied territories to be examined in new ways.

“If this opportunity is used correctly, Kazakhstan has the potential to become not just a major supplier of mineral resources, but one of the key centers for critical minerals and materials for global industry,” he said.

World.title: Kazakhstan Marks First Kazakh Tazy Day
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan is celebrating Kazakh Tazy Day for the first time on Sept. 3, commemorating the anniversary of the breed’s preliminary recognition by the Fédération Cynologique Internationale (FCI) in 2024, reported the Ministry of Ecology and Natural Resources.

The FCI made the decision in Amsterdam on Sept. 3, 2024, granting preliminary recognition to the Kazakh tazy and officially recognizing Kazakhstan as the breed’s country of origin.

The tazy has lived alongside people in the Great Steppe for centuries, serving as a hunting companion and becoming an important part of Kazakh culture and daily life. Its place in Kazakh tradition is also reflected in the FCI breed standard, which refers to the tazy as one of the Zheti Kazyna (Seven Treasures) of the Kazakh people.

From national heritage to international recognition

Efforts to preserve and promote the breed gained momentum in recent years. In 2022, President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev instructed the government to take measures to preserve the national breed and promote it internationally.

A major step came Aug. 22, 2023, when the Union of Cynologists of Kazakhstan became a full member of the FCI at the federation’s General Assembly in Geneva. The membership enabled the country to formally submit the tazy for international recognition. In March 2024, Kazakhstan submitted documentation on the breed to the FCI.

The same year, Astana hosted a specialized breed exhibition where international experts examined 100 Kazakh tazy of various ages, colors, origins and types. The dogs were evaluated for their physical structure, movement and compliance with the breed standard.

In an interview with The Astana Times, FCI President Tamás Jakkel praised Kazakhstan’s progress and said a long-term program is now underway to achieve full recognition.

“We have outlined a program for the next several years to reach final recognition. I offered my support and partnership, and we agreed to continue cooperation,” he said.

Jakkel noted that the issue has broad public relevance given the large number of households that own dogs.

Preserving the breed through science

Preliminary recognition is only one stage of the process. The tazy must undergo a lengthy observation period during which the stability of the breed is assessed across several generations. This includes monitoring pedigree records, health, genetic diversity, breed characteristics and natural and working abilities.

Kazakhstan has also established its first DNA bank for the tazy and tobet, another national dog breed. The initiative follows several years of nationwide genetic research aimed at preserving the breeds’ genetic heritage and preventing genetic loss.

According to Anastasia Perfilyeva, a biology researcher at the Institute of Genetics and Physiology, genetic analysis confirmed that the tazy is an ancient, independent breed.

Researchers also found that the tobet developed at the intersection of Arctic and East Asian dog lineages and is genetically distinct from more than 140 dog breeds worldwide, including other guardian breeds.

Today, nearly 4,000 tazy are registered in the Union of Cynologists of Kazakhstan’s unified pedigree book. The actual population is believed to be higher because many dogs in rural and remote areas have yet to be included in centralized records.

Specialists continue working across the regions to conduct breeding assessments, document pedigrees and monitor the breed’s genetic diversity.

In 2025, The tazy received a patent from National Institute of Intellectual Property Qazpatent.

Tazy gains global visibility

Alongside scientific and breeding work, Kazakhstan has stepped up efforts to promote the tazy internationally.

The breed made its official debut at the World Dog Show in Helsinki in 2025.

In June 2026, Kazakhstan presented 12 tazy at the World Dog Show in Bologna. The breed was also showcased to international judges during the FCI World Judges Congress. A national pavilion introduced visitors to the tazy and Kazakhstan’s traditions and culture.
