The breed has also featured in high-profile diplomatic and cultural exchanges. Tokayev has previously gifted Kazakh tazy dogs to French President Emmanuel Macron and renowned Kazakh singer Dimash Qudaibergen, drawing further attention to the breed as a symbol of the country’s national heritage.

The Kazakh tazy was also included for the first time in “Dogs of the World,” a book by U.S. illustrator Lili Chin featuring more than 600 dog breeds.

“I remember seeing a video from Kazakhstan of tazy dogs hunting a wolf. They were incredibly fast and worked as a team. I love that tazy are valued not only as hunters but also as beloved companions and family dogs,” Chin told The Astana Times.

Kazakhstan is also expanding infrastructure for the preservation and development of its national dog breeds. A National Center for Kazakh Dog Breeds is under construction in the Zhetysu Region. The facility will support breeding programs, maintain the national pedigree registry, train cynology specialists and host exhibitions, trials and competitions.

The next stage will be particularly important for the tazy. Full FCI recognition will depend on demonstrating the breed’s stability over several generations while preserving its distinctive characteristics, genetic diversity and working qualities.

World.title: Social assistance is shrinking in Azerbaijan: Is poverty falling, or are low-income people losing support?
World.content:
Targeted social assistance in Azerbaijan

In Azerbaijan, the authorities have raised the income threshold for classifying families as low-income. It would be logical to expect this to increase both the number of people receiving assistance and the amount of support they receive. However, official statistics show the opposite trend: both the number of families receiving targeted state social assistance and the amount paid per person are falling.

According to the State Statistics Committee, as of 1 July, 349,300 people from 78,900 families received targeted social assistance. A year earlier, the system covered 353,300 people from 80,300 families. This means that over the year, the number of families receiving assistance fell by 1,400, while the number of recipients fell by 4,000.

The decline becomes even more striking over the longer term. In mid-2017, 498,400 people received this type of assistance. Over nine years, that figure fell by 149,100, or about 30%. Meanwhile, the country’s population increased during the same period.

These figures raise an important question: have the incomes of low-income families increased enough for them to no longer need social assistance, or has the system stopped reaching some people who still need support?

The income threshold has risen, but social assistance has fallen

Targeted social assistance is not a fixed payment. The authorities calculate it as the difference between the needs-based threshold for all family members and the family’s average monthly income. The calculation takes into account income from the previous 12 months.

In 2025, the needs-based threshold stood at 285 manats (approx. $167.65) per person. In 2026, the authorities raised it to 300 manats (approx. $176.50), an increase of 5.3%. Despite this, the average payment per person fell from 100.37 to 97.94 manats (approx. $59 to $57.70). In nominal terms, the payment fell by 2.43 manats (approx. $1.43), or 2.4%.

Applying the current formula to the average figures suggests that the system calculated recipients’ average monthly income per person at 184.63 manats (approx. $108.60) in 2025 and 202.06 manats (approx. $118.90) in 2026. This represents a nominal increase of 9.4%. Mathematically, the lower payments reflect the fact that, according to the system’s calculations, family incomes grew faster than the needs-based threshold.

However, these figures do not prove that the financial situation of all low-income families has improved. The average for families that remained in the system in mid-2026 is being compared with the average for families that received assistance a year earlier. Families whose payments stopped or whose applications were rejected no longer form part of the new average.

Our calculations, based on official data, show that total monthly payments to recipients fell from about 35.46 million (approx. $20.86 million) to 34.21 million manats (approx. $20.12 million). The government therefore reduced its monthly spending on this group by about 1.25 million manats (approx. $735,300), or 3.5%, in nominal terms.

The assistance has lost even more purchasing power

According to July 2026 data, annual inflation stood at 5.8%, while food inflation reached 7.3%. After taking price rises into account, the purchasing power of the 97.94-manat payment fell by about 7.8% compared with the 100.37-manat payment a year earlier. If we consider only food price increases, the decline approaches 9%.

After receiving assistance, the system brings a family’s calculated income per person up to the needs-based threshold of 300 manats. However, this represents only a 5.3% increase from last year’s level of 285 manats. That increase falls short of overall inflation and especially of food price growth. As a result, even the minimum income of families that remain in the social assistance system has not increased in real terms.

The number of people receiving assistance is not the number of people living in poverty

The State Statistics Committee’s final data for 2025 put the poverty line at 286 manats (approx. $168.20) and the poverty rate at 5.2%. With a population of 10.26 million, this amounts to roughly 534,000 people.

At the end of the same year, 336,000 people received targeted social assistance, or about 3.3% of the population. The authorities use different methodologies and reporting dates to calculate these figures, so we cannot directly compare them. Nevertheless, the gap of about 198,000 people clearly shows that the number of assistance recipients cannot serve as a measure of poverty in the country.

Moreover, earning less than 300 manats does not in itself qualify a person for assistance. Under the rules, a family must show that factors beyond its control have caused its low income. The official criteria allow authorities to reject an application if the family owns or uses a car, has two properties of the same type at different addresses, or has carried out purchase or sale transactions worth more than 12 times the subsistence minimum over the previous 12 months. Authorities can also reject an application if an able-bodied family member has turned down two suitable job offers.

Based on the 2026 subsistence minimum, the threshold for purchase and sale transactions stands at 3,600 manats (approx. $2,118). Authorities can also reject assistance if a family spends 45 manats (approx. $26.50) or more per person each month on utilities and communications. For a family of four, that amounts to 180 manats (approx. $106) in total. The authorities also count money and gifts from relatives, as well as estimated income from a household farm or garden, when calculating family income.

These criteria may help identify hidden income and assets. However, the same rules can exclude a family with a low cash income if it owns an old car, faces high utility bills or mainly survives on financial support from relatives.

The number of pensioners is falling, while more people receive age-related benefits

Another question arises when we examine other social security figures. On 1 July 2025, Azerbaijan had 1,103,300 pensioners. A year later, the figure had fallen to 1.1 million. At the same time, the average pension rose by 10.5% to 594.4 manats (approx. $350). However, the number of pensioners fell by 3,300.

Meanwhile, the number of people who do not qualify for a labour pension but receive a 220-manat age-related benefit (approx. $130) rose from 166,200 to 177,500. We cannot say that the changes in these two groups involve the same people. However, the fall in the number of pensioners as the elderly population grows, alongside the rise in recipients of a lower benefit, requires a separate explanation in terms of access to labour pensions.

What data the government should disclose

To treat a decline in the number of assistance recipients as evidence of falling poverty, we need more than one headline figure. The Ministry of Labour and Social Protection of the Population should report how many families entered the system over the past year, how many stopped receiving assistance, how many applicants faced rejection and why authorities rejected their applications.

The government should also report how many families failed to qualify under each criterion, including car ownership, purchase and sale transactions, utility costs, discrepancies in income data and refusal to accept an offered job. It should also disclose how many decisions authorities reviewed following complaints and what share of assistance recipients are children.

Without this data, we cannot conclude that poverty has fallen. So far, the official statistics show only this: the number of people covered by targeted social assistance has fallen, the average payment has declined in nominal terms, and its purchasing power has fallen even further.

Targeted social assistance in Azerbaijan

World.title: Beslan school siege 22 years on: Where does investigation stand and what did victims achieve?
World.content:
Beslan school siege anniversary

Twenty-two years have passed since the Beslan school siege, one of the most tragic events in the modern history of North Ossetia.

Commemorative events are being held across the republic, but there is still no complete clarity over what exactly happened during the attack.

“Three days in hell”: Timeline of the attack

On 1 September 2004, militants took pupils and teachers at School No 1 in Beslan hostage, including children starting their first year at school, their parents and babies who were with them.

In the first hours of the siege, the militants shot dead the adult male hostages. They held the others in the school’s gymnasium for three days, denying them water and making political demands, including the withdrawal of Russian troops from Chechnya.

The militants also demanded the presence of the then president of North Ossetia, Alexander Dzasokhov, Ingush President Murat Zyazikov, and CIS Executive Secretary and former Russian Security Council Secretary Vladimir Rushailo. None of them complied with the demand.

The North Ossetian authorities attempted to negotiate the release of the hostages, but without success. On 2 September, former Ingush President Ruslan Aushev managed to negotiate with the Ingush members of the militant group. He was allowed into the gymnasium and secured the release of around 20 women with babies.

At noon on the third day, two explosions were heard in the gymnasium.

According to some of the hostages and the official account, one of the explosive devices that the militants had placed along the walls detonated. A fire broke out in the gymnasium and the militants began shooting at the hostages.

An unofficial account, however, maintains that the explosion and subsequent fire were caused by an external strike on the school building using a Shmel rocket launcher.

This account remains disputed, with the North Ossetian and wider Russian authorities rejecting it as unfounded. FSB special forces, who were rehearsing an assault plan in a nearby village when the explosions occurred, were then urgently deployed to Beslan. Fighting with the militants ensued, during which most of the hostages were freed.

However, the death toll was still extremely high. A total of 334 people were killed in the attack, including 314 hostages and 20 members of the FSB special forces, Interior Ministry and Emergencies Ministry. Another 783 hostages were injured.

According to the official account, there were 32 militants. All were killed except Nur-Pashi Kulayev, who was detained and later sentenced to life imprisonment.

However, the criminal investigation launched immediately after the attack has still not been concluded. Relatives of the victims disputed the authorities’ official account and demanded an “objective and fair investigation”. According to some former hostages, there were more than 32 militants and some may have escaped.

There were also claims that the attackers had hidden weapons inside the school in advance and that some of the militants had previously gained access to the building by posing as workers carrying out repairs.

Commemoration ceremony in the gymnasium where the hostages were held

22 года спустя

On 1 September 2026, the Mothers of Beslan public organisation held its annual press conference.

The organisation’s leader, Susanna Dudiyeva, reported some progress in the criminal investigation, which she said had been made possible following a meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin two years ago, when he visited Beslan ahead of the 20th anniversary of the attack. According to Dudiyeva, Putin subsequently issued instructions to the head of Russia’s Investigative Committee, Alexander Bastrykin.

Dudiyeva told the press conference that investigators had established that there were in fact more than 32 militants and that the criminal case remained open because not all of those killed had been identified. In particular, investigators have been unable to identify one of them, a Saudi national, as the Saudi authorities have not been cooperating with Russian investigators.

The health of former hostages was one of the main issues discussed at the press conference. The Mothers of Beslan committee has successfully campaigned for victims of the attack and their relatives to receive regular social and medical assistance. A comprehensive rehabilitation programme for those affected by the attack has been extended until 2030, while funding for their medical treatment has been increased.

“I would say that rehabilitation at health resorts is going well. There are some problems and some issues, but they can all be resolved. It is particularly encouraging that the children of former hostages who were born after the attack are now also receiving rehabilitation. Almost no other victims of terrorist attacks in Russia have access to this kind of rehabilitation,” Susanna Dudiyeva said.

The question of granting victims an official legal status remains a pressing issue. The adoption of relevant legislation would open up significant new opportunities to provide support to survivors and even their children.

Elvira Tuayeva, a member of the Mothers of Beslan organisation, said the group would continue campaigning for a law establishing the legal status of victims of terrorist attacks, not only those affected by the Beslan siege but by all terrorist attacks that have taken place in Russia.

World.title: Georgian businessman, animal rights activist Tamaz Elizbarashvili begins prison hunger strike
World.content:
Activist Elizbarashvili on hunger strike

Georgian businessman, animal rights activist and outspoken critic of the Georgian Dream government Tamaz Elizbarashvili, who was detained earlier, has gone on hunger strike.

Tamaz Elizbarashvili was detained at his home after law enforcement officers searched his car and flat. The Interior Ministry said the search of Elizbarashvili’s car was carried out as part of an investigation into alleged threats and the illegal acquisition and possession of weapons.

According to his lawyer, Elizbarashvili is currently being held in administrative detention.

What is known so far?

According to Elizbarashvili’s lawyer, Iako Siranashvili, her client was detained by law enforcement officers as he was attempting to jump from a balcony and take his own life.

Siranashvili said Elizbarashvili attempted to take his own life after seeing law enforcement officers use force against his lawyer and witnessing his children in distress.

“Tamaz Elizbarashvili was going to take his own life when he saw me being pushed into the building and beaten. When he saw his children crying and in distress, he tried to jump from the balcony. Tamaz was detained over this and charged with disobeying police orders,” Siranashvili said.

According to the lawyer, law enforcement officers tried to take her phone away when she began filming the search. She alleges that around 20 officers then used physical force against her.

“They tried to take my phone away to stop me filming the search. Anyone is allowed to film, especially a lawyer. They probably wanted to plant a weapon or some other prohibited item, but I prevented them from doing so because I was filming. Around 20 people then attacked me: they grabbed me and snatched the phone from my hands. When I resisted their attempts to take it, they twisted my arms, threw me to the ground and began kicking me,” Siranashvili said.

The lawyer said she had sustained injuries to various parts of her body and was having difficulty walking. Siranashvili said she had left the clinic of her own accord.

“My injuries are such that I can barely walk. I have difficulty moving around. My left arm is in severe pain. My hearing has also deteriorated and I have swelling around my facial bone. I left the clinic of my own accord because I did not think it was necessary to remain there,” she said.

According to Siranashvili, an investigation has been launched under Article 333 of Georgia’s Criminal Code, which covers abuse of official powers. She said, however, that investigators should also examine whether offences had been committed under Articles 364 and 365, which concern obstruction of a lawyer’s professional activities.

“What angers me most is not the fact that I was beaten, but that I was prevented from carrying out my professional duties. That is what makes me most angry, as does the fact that violence was used against a lawyer. Other articles must also be applied; the investigation cannot be limited to Article 333 alone,” the lawyer said.

She said her health had so far prevented her from attending the investigative authorities for a medical examination.

“I feel very unwell and have not yet been physically able to get to the relevant authorities. Investigators have ordered a medical examination, and I hope it will be carried out,” Siranashvili said.

World.title: Former head of Armenia’s State Revenue Committee arrested after appearing in court on stretcher
World.content:
Former Armenian revenue chief in court on stretcher

In Armenia, the arrest of former State Revenue Committee chairman Gagik Khachatryan has sparked widespread debate. He faces charges of accepting a particularly large bribe and money laundering. The Anti-Corruption Court is also considering cases seeking to confiscate allegedly illicitly acquired property from Khachatryan and people linked to him, including his sons.

However, the video that his lawyers shared on social media, rather than the charges against Khachatryan, has caused the biggest public outcry. The footage shows National Security Service officers carrying the 71-year-old Khachatryan, who is groaning in pain, from a bed onto a stretcher during his arrest. His lawyers said they consider the law enforcement officers’ actions equivalent to torture.

Human rights defenders and civil society representatives have also condemned the actions. They said authorities handled the transport of a person with serious health problems “improperly”, causing him physical suffering.

“No legal procedure or procedural necessity can justify violating human dignity,” experts from the NGO Disability Rights Agenda said.

What is Khachatryan accused of: all known details

The Investigative Committee said the previous day that investigators had carried out searches at the homes of the former head of the State Revenue Committee and his son as part of a case involving particularly large-scale bribery and money laundering. They also searched the offices and branches of more than 20 companies linked to them. Shortly afterwards, reports emerged that authorities had arrested Gagik Khachatryan for two months.

According to the case file, Khachatryan faces charges of:

accepting a particularly large bribe from the directors of Progress Armenia and Local Developers,

misappropriating 174 million 581 thousand drams ($482,000) in state funds during the reconstruction of the Dilijan training centre,

illegally transferring property belonging to a local university, worth 208 million 908 thousand drams ($577,000),

and laundering particularly large sums of money. The charge concerns concealing 151 million 126 thousand drams ($417,000) of illegally obtained funds.

Meanwhile, the Anti-Corruption Court is hearing a case seeking the confiscation of allegedly illicitly acquired property. The Prosecutor General’s Office is seeking to confiscate from Khachatryan and people linked to him:

193 properties, including properties in Yerevan’s most expensive central district,

89 properties in Kotayk Province,

stakes in 29 legal entities,

14 movable assets,

bonds worth $1,451,074,

a bank deposit of $147,210,

claims arising from loans worth approximately $23.1 million, 409.8 million drams (more than $1 million) and €9,800, and

7 billion 761 million drams ($49 million).

Defence lawyers and prosecutors disagree over the defendant’s health

The Prosecutor General’s Office says it conducted a forensic medical examination.

“Khachatryan has no health problems that could prevent him from taking part in any procedural actions as part of the criminal proceedings,” the experts concluded.

However, his defence team takes the opposite view.

Lawyer Yerevan Sargsyan told reporters that in June, authorities also took Khachatryan to the investigative body and then to court on a stretcher. At the time, however, the court found that his detention could pose health risks.

“They waited so long until they got the [forensic medical] conclusion they wanted. How they did it is known to them. And now they have organised the arrest in the same way again,” Sargsyan stressed.

Ombudsman’s office examines the case

On 2 September, a day after the lawyers published the video, the Human Rights Defender’s Office issued a statement. It said that the ombudsman had initiated an urgent examination of the case. A team of experts has already gone to the penitentiary to speak with Khachatryan and monitor respect for his rights.

The ombudsman’s office has also asked the relevant authorities for explanations to establish all the circumstances. After it completes the investigation and reviews its findings, the Human Rights Defender will present its position.

Comments

Human rights defender Zaruhi Hovhannisyan believes that the published photograph of the defendant on a stretcher in the courtroom is “not simply a sad scene”. In her view, the situation raises questions about the state’s attitude towards human rights:

“The photograph shows a 71-year-old man with serious health problems lying on a stretcher, completely covered, in the middle of a courtroom. People involved in the proceedings, tables, microphones and documents surround him. On one side stands the entire institutional machinery of criminal justice, organised by the state. On the other stands a person whom the system completely ignores.

The issue is not to make people feel sorry for the man lying on that stretcher, or to discuss why he ended up in court, what case he faces or how many charges he faces. The issue is that this is an extremely dangerous picture. When the state becomes accustomed to subordinating human dignity to a judicial process, it puts not only one person’s rights at risk but also the boundary that should prevent the state from gaining unlimited power over an individual. Human dignity and the prohibition of torture limit the state’s power over a person.”

Former head of Armenia’s State Revenue Committee in court on a stretcher

The NGO Disability Rights Agenda also issued a statement about the videos that Gagik Khachatryan’s lawyers circulated:

“According to the defence, doctors diagnosed Gagik Khachatryan with spinal stenosis in 2015 and implanted special devices in his cervical spine. The footage also shows him in a semi-conscious state while people were moving him.”

The organisation’s experts believe the authorities should structure the court proceedings in a way that prevents harm to a person’s health or humiliating conditions. Appropriate specialists should accompany people with limited mobility at all times. Medical professionals should supervise their movement and authorities should provide the necessary technical equipment.

“Regardless of the nature of the charges or his former position, humanitarian principles and safeguards for physical integrity must remain unchanged,” the statement says.

The organisation called on law enforcement agencies to take the following steps during further procedural actions:

rely only on impartial professional assessments,

provide the necessary medical care,

prevent any actions that cause a person unnecessary physical pain.

Former Armenian revenue chief in court on stretcher

World.title: Amnesty International: Georgia must not deport Denis Kulanin to Russia
World.content:
Denis Kulanin’s case

Amnesty International is calling on the Georgian authorities to prevent the deportation of Russian citizen Denis Kulanin to Russia, where the organisation says he faces a real risk of imprisonment and torture.

The organisation says Georgia should protect Kulanin from being forcibly returned to Russia because he has publicly opposed Russia’s war in Ukraine and expressed support for opposition leader Alexei Navalny. According to Amnesty International, both positions could lead to criminal prosecution in Russia.

“Denis Kulanin has publicly opposed Russia’s war in Ukraine and expressed support for Alexei Navalny — both actions constitute criminal offences in Russia and can lead to imprisonment. The Georgian authorities must ensure that he is not deported to Russia. Amid the harsh repression of people who oppose the war, he faces a real risk of arbitrary criminal prosecution, imprisonment, torture or other ill-treatment,” said Denis Krivosheev, Amnesty International’s deputy director for Eastern Europe and Central Asia.

He said Georgia must uphold the principle of non-refoulement, which prohibits returning a person to a country where they face a real risk of serious human rights violations.

“The Georgian authorities must also ensure that Denis Kulanin has an effective opportunity to seek international protection, including by allowing him to leave voluntarily for a safe third country,” Krivosheev added.

Who is Denis Kulanin?

Denis Kulanin is a Russian citizen who lived in Georgia and took part in pro-European protests. Police arrested him on 28 March 2025 during a demonstration outside parliament. The authorities accused him of smashing a police car window and sentenced him to two years in prison.

On the Orthodox Christian feast of the Dormition of the Mother of God, President Mikheil Kavelashvili pardoned Kulanin. However, because Kulanin is not a Georgian citizen, the authorities did not release him. Instead, they transferred him to the migration department.

According to his lawyer, deporting Kulanin to Russia would be both unacceptable and dangerous. While in detention, Kulanin sent a letter in which he wished Ukraine glory and peace. His lawyer says that in Russia, authorities can interpret almost any statement about the war in a way that could lead to criminal charges.

Denis Kulanin. Photo: Publica

On 30 August 2026, the Tbilisi City Court ordered Denis Kulanin to be held at the temporary detention centre run by the Georgian Interior Ministry’s Migration Department. He will remain at the centre until the grounds for his detention cease to apply or the authorities enforce the decision to deport him from Georgia, but for no longer than three months.

On 31 August, Kulanin’s lawyer was told that he would not be allowed to leave Georgia voluntarily until the Tbilisi City Court considers his deportation case.

On 1 September, Kulanin’s lawyer said the Migration Department had asked the Tbilisi City Court to deport him to his country of citizenship, the Russian Federation.

Denis Kulanin’s case

World.title: Opinion: ‘An attempt to make Abkhazia’s residents feel part of single political space with Russia’
World.content:
Abkhazia is actively preparing for Russia’s State Duma elections, which will take place on 20 September 2026. Most Abkhazia residents hold dual Abkhaz-Russian citizenship, which gives them the right to vote in the elections.

Russia will open 319 polling stations in 152 countries for citizens voting abroad. 35 of them — more than 10% — will open in Abkhazia.

Many people think this is excessive for a small republic with a population of 250,000.

One of those who objects is Akhra Bzhania, a prominent Abkhaz blogger and public figure. He believes that the “excessive” number of polling stations and the active election campaign aim to create a sense among Abkhazia’s residents that they somehow “belong” to Russia.

Akhra Bzhania: “There is a standard procedure for people with dual citizenship who vote abroad.

Usually, two or three polling stations open, plus a polling station at the consulate or embassy. That’s it.

Abkhazia cannot use its budget to cover the costs of holding a constitutional event of a foreign state. That makes no sense.

If someone argues that the Russian side is paying for the campaign, that is even worse!

Let me explain why. Fifty or 60,000 votes from Abkhazia will have no impact on the overall balance of parties in the State Duma.

This means the election campaign here must serve a different, ideological purpose — to create a sense among Abkhazia’s citizens that they share a single political and administrative space with Russia. And from there, a common state is not far away.”

I have no doubt that some Abkhaz citizens with dual citizenship care deeply about the differences between the programmes of Russian political parties. For them, State Duma elections are therefore not only a civic but also a political act.

But in that case, they can plan ahead and vote in Sochi, Krasnodar or Moscow, as Russians living in Armenia, Kyrgyzstan and elsewhere do.

Yet our entire republic is covered with banners urging people to vote for a government body of another country! We plan to open 35 polling stations, just as we do for our own presidential elections!

It seems strange to me — and not only to me — and out of line with the status of our state and the level of Abkhaz-Russian relations.”

The terminology, place names and views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial position of this website.

Abkhazia prepares for Russia’s State Duma elections

World.title: What Pashinyan and Putin agreed in Bishkek amid peak tensions in relations
World.content:
Pashinyan-Putin meeting in Bishkek

Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan and Russian President Vladimir Putin met in Bishkek, where an SCO+ meeting was held as part of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation summit. Their talks took place late in the evening.

There was no shortage of issues to discuss as bilateral relations have recently become increasingly strained. The previous meeting between Pashinyan and Putin took place on 1 April. Since then, Armenia held parliamentary elections in June, in which Pashinyan’s party won a majority and formed a government. However, the Russian president has yet to congratulate Pashinyan on his victory.

Judging by statements from Moscow, the main issue concerning the Russian authorities is Armenia’s ambition to join the European Union.

In the opening minutes of the Bishkek meeting, Putin said Armenia’s aspiration to join the EU was the country’s legitimate right. However, he said this “creates difficulties” for Armenia’s membership of the Russian-led Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU).

“The sooner Armenia decides on the issue of joining the EU, the better. Moscow needs to understand how to develop relations further. The adoption of a law launching the process of Armenia joining another organisation amounts to a declaration of withdrawal from ours,” Putin said.

Pashinyan responded by reiterating that Armenia had no intention of leaving the EAEU.

The Armenian prime minister also recalled that, under the EAEU’s charter, there was no procedure for expelling a member state unless the country itself decided to leave.

“We greatly value our relations with the Russian Federation. We hope these relations are important to Russia as well. I think that Armenia and Russia, and we personally, should treat these relations with great care. I want to confirm that I personally and our government treat them with great care. I am sure that you also treat these relations with great care, and I want to thank you for that,” Pashinyan said.

He stressed that the issue of EU membership had not yet reached the stage at which a referendum could be held. He explained that Armenia did not currently have the alternative of actual EU membership to put before the public. In other words, the issue would be decided once the Armenian authorities had a concrete alternative to offer voters.

Putin, however, stood his ground: “The people should indeed always have a choice. So give them one, and we will close the matter. That’s all. The simplest thing is to ask people: what do you want — this or that?”

After the meeting, the Armenian prime minister posted a video on social media summarising the outcome of the talks.

Pashinyan described the meeting as “very good” and said he and Putin had agreed to continue their “sincere and constructive dialogue” during his visit to Moscow, which is apparently expected to take place in the near future.

“It should be noted that bilateral relations between Armenia and Russia are extremely important for both countries. […]However, it should also be noted that, in the new environment and under the new circumstances, there is a need to rethink these relations. I am convinced that, as a result of this reassessment, relations will become better, more constructive, more mutually beneficial and warmer,” he said.

Context: other issues on agenda

In Armenia, the meeting had been expected to involve difficult discussions on several critical issues. Armenian analysts had also warned that the meeting was unlikely to produce any positive developments on any of them.

In Armenia, there were expectations that the two leaders would discuss holding a referendum on whether the country should remain in the EAEU or pursue EU membership.

Russia and other EAEU member states have recently been pressing for such a referendum. The Armenian authorities have responded that there is little point in holding one at this stage, as the country has not yet formally applied for EU membership.

The EAEU comprises Russia, Belarus, Armenia, Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan.

Meanwhile, there has already been talk within the EAEU of discussing Armenia’s status in the bloc. However, under the union’s charter, only Armenia itself can decide to withdraw. As Pashinyan has repeatedly pointed out, there is no other procedure for ending its membership.

At the same time, on 24 August, the Armenian prime minister raised the possibility of submitting a formal application for EU membership. This prompted a fresh wave of criticism and an even sharper reaction in Russia. Commentators there said that “EU membership is a marathon lasting decades”, while Yerevan would feel “the costs of breaking with Russia and the EAEU here and now”.

Russian experts even predicted a “fatal outcome” for Armenia. According to them, the country faces a choice between “Turkification” and a “Ukrainian scenario”.

The two leaders had also been expected to discuss Russian restrictions on imports of Armenian food and other goods, which were introduced in May and remain in place.

Russia has traditionally been a key export market for Armenia. However, since the restrictions were introduced — which Russia has attributed to concerns over product quality — Armenian goods have increasingly been exported to EU countries, where higher standards apply.

Armenian analysts had also expected the two leaders to discuss Armenia’s membership of the Russian-led CSTO military alliance.

The Collective Security Treaty Organisation comprises Russia, Belarus, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan and Armenia.

Armenia has effectively frozen its participation in the organisation for the past two years in response to what Yerevan sees as inaction by its allies.

When Azerbaijani forces entered Armenia’s sovereign territory in 2021-22, its CSTO allies neither intervened nor condemned Baku’s actions. They argued that the Armenian-Azerbaijani border had not been delimited. Pashinyan responded:

“To say that there is no border between Armenia and Azerbaijan is to say that the CSTO has no defined area of responsibility. And if there is no area of responsibility, then there is no organisation.”

While Pashinyan had previously said he was not concerned about the possibility of Armenia being expelled from the military bloc, just a week before his meeting with Putin he went further, saying he would welcome such a move:

“At least it would relieve us of the dilemma of whether or not to leave [the CSTO].”

In addition, ahead of the leaders’ meeting, Russian presidential aide Yuri Ushakov said the talks would take place at a time “when opposition leaders are being arrested en masse in Armenia”.

He was referring, among others, to the arrest of former Armenian President Robert Kocharyan. Kocharyan is accused of abuse of office, accepting a particularly large bribe and money laundering. A court ordered him to be held for two months. It is the former president’s fourth arrest.

In Armenia, there was speculation that Putin, who has close ties with Kocharyan, might once again ask for his release.

During his previous meeting with Pashinyan in April, Putin expressed hope that Russia’s “friends” and pro-Russian political forces would be able to take part in Armenia’s elections.

He was believed to have been referring to the party of Russian businessman Samvel Karapetyan, who is currently under house arrest on charges of making calls to seize power, as well as a bloc led by former President Robert Kocharyan. Both contested the elections but failed to secure a parliamentary majority.

Representatives of Armenia’s ruling party believe that these pro-Russian forces are encouraging the Russian authorities to take steps that could fuel public discontent. Pashinyan’s team believes the opposition hopes to use such discontent as a means of coming to power.

World.title: Ex Georgian PM Gharibashvili: Unanswered questions over deaths under current leadership
World.content:
Ex-Georgian PM Gharibashvili accuses authorities

Former Georgian Prime Minister Irakli Gharibashvili has published another letter from prison, calling on the authorities to answer questions about the circumstances surrounding the death of Lazare Jorbenadze, a human rights defender who had criticised current Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze.

Gharibashvili writes that Jorbenadze died by suicide shortly after journalist Dito Chubinidze published an article for which Jorbenadze had given an interview.

The newspaper Asaval-Dasavali, which published the interview, questioned the theory that Jorbenadze died by suicide. Gharibashvili stresses that the public should receive an answer about the real cause of Jorbenadze’s death.

The former prime minister says he decided to speak publicly on the issue after comparing the contents of a letter he received from government representatives in February this year with other circumstances surrounding the case.

According to Garibashvili, on February 12, he was sent, on the instructions of Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze and Deputy Prime Minister Mamuka Mdinaradze, an article published in Asaval-Dasavali on February 2, 2026.

The article featured an interview by journalist Dito Chubinidze with Lazare Jorbenadze. Gharibashvili says the article focused mainly on criticism of Kobakhidze and serious allegations against him.

The former prime minister says the message he received expressed suspicion that he himself was behind the article.

“I was sent a message expressing the suspicion — based on a completely false assumption — that I was behind the article,” Gharibashvili writes.

Gharibashvili says he categorically rejected the allegations and told the government representatives that publishing “commissioned articles” was not something he did.

In his letter, Gharibashvili also mentions journalist Dito Chubinidze and former Alliance of Patriots leader Irma Inashvili, stressing that he had no involvement in their political or journalistic activities.

The former prime minister believes these events shed more light on one of the points in the letter he received, which referred to “supporters” such as Dito Chubinidze and Irma Inashvili.

“Now the picture is clear to me, and I have received answers to all my questions: why did the first point of the letter say that ‘such supporters as Dito Chubinidze and Irma Inashvili’ raise serious doubts and cause significant damage to the interests of the Kobakhidze-Mdinaradze team” Gharibashvili writes.

In another part of the letter, the former prime minister criticises Mamuka Mdinaradze, saying that his mistakes led not only to his removal from office but also to his departure from politics.

Gharibashvili stresses, however, that in his view, Mdinaradze’s departure from politics will not make up for the damage he believes Mdinaradze and Irakli Kobakhidze caused to the country, its people and the ruling Georgian Dream party.

Gharibashvili also writes that questions remain in society about the deaths of other people during the period when Irakli Kobakhidze and Mamuka Mdinaradze were leading the country.

Context

The first corruption charge against former Georgian Prime Minister Irakli Gharibashvili was brought in October 2025. Investigators accused him of legalising illicit income on a particularly large scale. A second charge – accepting a bribe on a particularly large scale – was brought on August 24, 2026.

Gharibashvili made his first statement from prison on August 17. In a Facebook post, he wrote that a letter had been sent to him on the orders of Bidzina Ivanishvili [oligarch, founder and honorary chairman of the ruling Georgian Dream party] and that it “left him no choice” but to confront the “evil that insults his dignity”.

Gharibashvili published his second letter from prison on August 19. In it, the former prime minister claimed that the aim of his arrest was his political destruction and said he had initially decided against legal action to avoid confrontation with the authorities.

According to Gharibashvili, he was forced to fight back.

Gharibashvili also said he received a letter from Mamuka Mdinaradze in July. He said that on the same day he explained his position to Mdinaradze and again confirmed that he had no intention of returning to politics.

News from Georgia

World.title: Azerbaijan plans $10.13 million power substation in Nakhchivan
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 3. A new 110/35/10 kV substation and control center will be built in Nakhchivan city to replace the existing Koroglu substation.

According to information posted on Azerbaijan's Unified Internet Portal for Public Procurement, the project will be carried out by Azerishiq Open Joint Stock Company.

The new substation will have a capacity of 2x40 MVA. The project will also include construction of a control center for the substation.

Harmony Industrial Construction and Engineering Group is expected to carry out the construction work.

According to the information, the project will cost 17.223 million Azerbaijani manats, or approximately $10.13 million.

The new substation is expected to help modernize Nakhchivan city's electricity transmission and distribution infrastructure.

Azerbaijan is implementing large-scale projects aimed at increasing electricity generation and diversifying its energy system. The development of renewable energy sources is a key priority of the country's energy strategy. Major investment projects to build solar and wind power plants are currently being implemented in Azerbaijan with BP, Masdar, ACWA Power, China Gezhouba Group Overseas Investment, SOCAR Green and other partners.

As a result of these projects, thousands of megawatts of new generation capacity are expected to be added to Azerbaijan's energy mix in the coming years. This is expected to reduce domestic demand for natural gas and allow more gas to be exported.

According to Energy Minister Parviz Shahbazov, the share of renewable energy sources in Azerbaijan's energy mix is expected to reach about 43% by 2035 as a result of these projects.

The minister said Azerbaijan is implementing strategic projects to establish a new energy and investment platform between Central Asia and neighboring regions. One of the key initiatives, he said, is the Central Asia-Azerbaijan Green Energy Corridor project.

"The creation of a Trans-Caspian energy corridor that will connect the electricity systems of Azerbaijan, Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan is part of our countries' strategic vision," Shahbazov said. "This project also creates broad opportunities for developing the Middle Corridor, which will serve as a green energy bridge between Europe, Asia and China via the Caspian Sea."

According to the minister, the Green Corridor Alliance joint venture, based in Baku, is already operating and coordinating feasibility studies financed by the Asian Development Bank and the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development.

Meanwhile, intensive work is continuing on the Caspian-Black Sea-Europe Green Energy Corridor, as well as the Azerbaijan-Türkiye-Europe and Azerbaijan-Georgia-Türkiye-Bulgaria energy interconnectors.

Shahbazov said green energy corridors are "shaping the geoeconomic map of the future" and that the initiatives will not only promote energy exports but also stimulate the development of digital connectivity, fiber-optic infrastructure and regional economic cooperation.

World.title: Tokayev tasks new FM with strengthening Kazakhstan's foreign policy
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 3. President of Kazakhstan Kassym-Jomart Tokayev instructed newly appointed Foreign Minister Mukhtar Tleuberdi to strengthen the country's balanced foreign policy, according to the presidential press service.

During the meeting, Tokayev outlined key priorities for the Foreign Ministry, including the strengthening of Kazakhstan's balanced foreign policy and the development of economic diplomacy.

"Particular attention was paid to intensifying multilateral cooperation and improving the effectiveness of efforts to protect the rights and interests of Kazakh citizens abroad," the presidential press service said.

Tokayev and the newly appointed foreign minister also reviewed the schedule of upcoming international events involving the president.

Yesterday, Mukhtar Tileuberdi was appointed Kazakhstan’s Minister of Foreign Affairs by presidential decree. He had previously headed the ministry; in September 2019, he was appointed Minister of Foreign Affairs. Since 2023, he had served as Ambassador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary of Kazakhstan to Austria and Permanent Representative of Kazakhstan to international organizations in Vienna.

On August 28, the Government of Kazakhstan resigned before the newly elected unicameral parliament - the Kurultai. Following this, President of Kazakhstan Kassym-Jomart Tokayev formed a new government and made a number of appointments to state bodies.
