World.title: Labor shuts down course linked to student visa misuse
World.content:
A graduate diploma used as a vehicle for international students to remain in Australia will be effectively shut down under the federal government's first use of new cancellation powers.

Transfers into the Graduate Diploma of Management (Learning) have surged in recent years, with the government concerned students are using it to maintain their visa status rather than for genuine study.

The VET course crackdown is part of a broader effort to improve the quality of the international education sector and comes as the government is looking to slow migration arrivals.

Assistant Minister for International Education Julian Hill said Labor was acting to ensure Australia remained a "trusted global education destination" to protect students and "prevent misuse of the visa system".

"Australia continues to welcome genuine international students seeking a premium education and must maintain a ruthless focus on quality, integrity and a great student experience," he said.

Julian Hill says Labor is acting to ensure Australia remains a trusted global education destination for students. (ABC: Matt Roberts)

Mr Hill accused the previous Coalition government of leaving a "shocking mess" with unsustainably high growth in the "least reputable" parts of the international education sector.

Earlier this year, Mr Hill imposed a 12-month freeze on private colleges and training organisations applying to offer new courses to international students, which he said would give the national regulator more time to investigate concerns about poor quality providers.

High transfer rate sparked concern about diploma

The cancellation of the management diploma was sparked by concerns around the large volume of international students who were already in Australia switching into the course.

Transfers jumped from 510 people in 2020 to 4,000 in 2025, with 77 per cent of the students switching to the diploma coming from elsewhere in higher education.

It meant students could switch into the course without necessarily needing a new student visa application.

Australia suspends new private college bids to enrol international students Australia suspends private colleges from applying to offer new courses to international students as part of a crackdown on abuse in the student visa system.

Almost half of the people approved to enrol in the diploma did not commence in 2025, while completion rates were significantly below other VET courses.

There are 452 VET providers registered to deliver the course to international students with 41,033 active confirmed enrolments, including 15,772 students recorded as currently studying.

Students who have already started will be able to complete their studies; however, VET providers and education agents are prohibited from recruiting more international students.

Labor using visa regulation to slow migration intake

The government has been increasingly turning to regulatory and administrative levers to slow visas and new arrivals as it tries to bring net overseas migration (NOM) down.

NOM is running at about 300,000 a year, but Labor wants to get it back toward its forecast of 225,000 by 2028.

Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke has changed visa processing priorities to favour skilled migrants already in Australia, effectively slowing applications from offshore workers.

Backpacker visas have also been slowed for applicants from 24 countries.

The prime minister has vowed not to make British backpackers work in regional areas as part of a looming migration overhaul. (AAP: Dan Peled/ file photo)

Mr Burke appeared to leave the door open to changing working holiday visa arrangements for British backpackers, before Prime Minister Anthony Albanese ruled them out.

Mr Albanese said the government would "continue to honour" the existing arrangements outlined in the Australia-UK free trade agreement.

The ABC has also previously reported the federal cabinet was considering stripping work rights from people whose protection claims had been rejected.

The number of people on bridging visas has risen from 130,450 in 2017 to 413,000 in 2026.

There was also a short-lived possibility Labor would cut Australia's humanitarian intake from 20,000 back toward the previous baseline of 13,750, but Mr Albanese has since guaranteed this would not occur.

World.title: UN warns El Niño could be strongest in decades
World.content:
El Niño could be the strongest since records began four decades ago, the United Nations' climate agency has warned, with the UN chief warning the world is in the "danger zone of extreme weather".

The naturally occurring weather phenomenon is set to become "very strong" in the months ahead and is near certain to persist through to February, the World Meteorological Organization (WMO) said Thursday.

El Niño warms surface temperatures in the central and eastern equatorial Pacific Ocean, bringing worldwide changes in winds, pressure and rainfall patterns.

A view of cracked ground at a dam in Zimbabwe during an El Niño-induced drought, 2024. (Reuters: Philimon Bulawayo)

"If this trajectory continues, it may be stronger than anything since our monitoring began — so literally off the charts we have used for the past four decades," WMO chief Celeste Saulo told reporters in Geneva.

El Niño will peak towards the end of this year — though its knock-on impacts for the climate will continue well into 2027, said the WMO.

Heat in the oceans releases more slowly into the atmosphere, pushing up global temperatures the following year.

The powerful 2023-24 El Niño contributed to 2024 being the warmest year on record, and "we should not be surprised if this record is broken", Ms Saulo added.

"El Niño is firmly established and will intensify into a very strong event in the coming months, with big impacts on rainfall and temperature patterns and associated risks of floods, drought and extreme heat," the WMO said.

El Niño is a natural climate phenomenon and is not caused by climate change.

Record rainfall linked to El Niño caused flooding in Rio Grande do Sul state, Brazil, 2024. (Reuters: Amanda Perobelli)

But scientists expect it will exacerbate the heat of a planet already warming from burning fossil fuels, while amping up weather extremes.

"El Niño is being supersized before our eyes," said UN chief Antonio Guterres.

"The science leaves no room for doubt: the planet is in uncharted waters, and those waters are heating up. Sea surface temperatures are rising, temperatures keep climbing, and the world is in the danger zone of extreme weather," he said.

'Massive blow' to economies

"This exceptional El Niño … has the potential to deliver a massive blow to communities and economies across the world", said Ms Saulo.

" We are already seeing disruption and devastation from droughts and floods, and we expect these impacts to increase as El Niño intensifies. "

She put disaster management authorities and climate-sensitive sectors like agriculture, health, energy and water on notice, saying there was "no time to lose" in getting ready.

El Niño typically takes place every two to seven years and lasts about nine to 12 months.

Ocean temperatures hit record high The world's oceans have reached their hottest temperatures on record and are likely to warm even more in the next few months, data shows.

Conditions oscillate between El Niño and its opposite La Niña, with neutral conditions in between.

"Fuelled by exceptionally warm ocean conditions across the tropical Pacific, El Niño is expected to strengthen further during the coming months to a very strong intensity," the WMO said.

The UN agency classifies El Niño events as weak, moderate, strong or very strong, meaning it is set to reach the highest level out of four.

The WMO said there was an "exceptionally high likelihood of nearly 100 per cent" that El Niño will continue through to February.

Pacific Ocean heating up

El Niño can reshape weather and climate patterns thousands of kilometres away from the tropical Pacific.

Every El Niño is different, but major events often follow familiar patterns.

This includes drought across parts of the Amazon, Indonesia and Australia, disrupted monsoons in India, and shifting rainfall throughout the tropics.

El Niño is often associated with drought across Australia due to its influence on winter and spring rainfall. (ABC News: Jess Davis)

For September-November, WMO forecasts indicate an increased likelihood of above-normal temperatures "across almost all land areas", alongside rainfall patterns showing a "pronounced and classic atmospheric response to the strong Pacific El Niño", the UN's weather and climate agency said.

The index, which measures sea surface temperature anomalies in the central eastern equatorial Pacific, has strengthened from an average 1.5C above normal between May and July.

Weekly values between late July and mid-August ranged from around 2.2C to 2.6C above average, indicating continued El Niño intensification.

In some areas, subsurface ocean temperatures were more than 8C above average during July and early August.

AFP

World.title: Iconoclast feminist Gloria Steinem dies aged 92
World.content:
Gloria Steinem, the author and activist who became one of the most visible voices of the US women's movement and a fierce feminist, has died aged 92.

With her trademark streaked hair parted down the middle and large aviator glasses, Steinem, a co-founder of Ms. Magazine, was a hugely recognisable presence wherever she went.

And she went everywhere; much of her life as an advocate was spent on the road, speaking at college campuses and community centres, at rallies and marches.

She died Wednesday, local time, at her home in New York City, according to her and her foundation's social media pages.

Gloria Steinem rose up as a feminist figure amid the days of Roe v. Wade. (Getty Images: Barbara Alper)

She began her career as a journalist, notably one who reported, in 1963, on degrading conditions in Hugh Hefner's Playboy empire, an undercover assignment she came to regret.

In 1968, Steinem helped found New York magazine, where her essay titled "After Black Power, Women's Liberation" established her as a feminist leader at a time of roiling social change.

But it was not until she attended an abortion speak-out in a New York church the following year that Steinem — who had a then-illegal abortion in London when she was 22 — said her life as a feminist activist really began.

"That speak-out was the beginning of activism for me," Steinem told The AP in an email in 2022, reflecting on the reversal of Roe v Wade.

" Either our control over our own bodies is equal, regardless of sex or race, or we're not living in a democracy. "

Ms. Magazine, which she co-founded in 1971, tackled abortion and other issues such as sexism, equal pay, and domestic violence.

The magazine was a far cry from the diet of beauty, cookery and supporting-your-husband topics that were the staple of magazines aimed at women.

An early issue included the names of 52 women, including Steinem, who had had abortions, and called for the procedure to be legalised ahead of the landmark Roe v Wade ruling.

Steinem also founded the National Women's Political Caucus in 1971 with former US representatives Bella Abzug and Shirley Chisholm and writer Betty Friedan, whose 1963 book The Feminine Mystique ushered in the second wave of feminism.

Among other groups, she created the Coalition of Labor Union Women, the Women's Media Center, Voters for Choice, and the Ms. Foundation for Women.

From writer to resounding voice

Writer and political activist Gloria Steinem during a women's march on Washington in 2017. (AP: Jose Luis Magana)

Though she soon became a well-known activist, those who watched Steinem denounce discrimination for years likely never suspected that she first had to overcome a deep fear of public speaking.

She would have stuck to writing, she said, if only editors at the time had been willing to let her write about the women's movement.

But they were not interested, she told the AP in 2015.

"So I ended up going out and speaking, which was my nightmare," she said.

"I mean, I was terrified. But I'm grateful, even though I still get scared even now."

Time hardly slowed Steinem down; well into her 80s, she was travelling the globe and speaking out on issues of importance to her.

These included everything from genital mutilation to Korean reconciliation, but it was equality for women that took precedence.

"Being a feminist means that you see the world as whole instead of half," she once said.

"It shouldn't need a name, and one day it won't."

Broadway star, film subject and children's book author

As the years went on, Steinem's visibility endured.

At 83, she sat in the front row of her first fashion show, a guest of designer Prabal Gurung.

Gloria Steinem stands in front of an issue of Ms. Magazine, featuring a smiling and very pregnant Carter. (Getty Images: Bettmann)

A few days after her 85th birthday, she was leading a women's "talking circle" at an off-Broadway play celebrating her life, where one by one, women in the audience — many fighting tears — rose to thank her and tell their own stories of discrimination.

In 2020, her life was the subject of a feature film, The Glorias, based on her 2015 memoir My Life on the Road, and starring Julianne Moore.

And at 91, she collaborated on a picture book with Liberian peace activist and Nobel laureate Leymah Gbowee, aimed at inspiring young people to change the world, published earlier this year.

'Rot in hell': Coping with the critics

The constant visibility came with a price; even in her later years, Steinem expressed frustration that despite her accomplishments, she was often described as beautiful or glamorous (a 1992 Vanity Fair profile even noted her "spectacular racehorse legs").

It was a label she said unfairly detracted from her message.

"Nobody ever called me beautiful until I was publicly a feminist, and that was in my mid-30s," she told AP in a 2011 interview.

"It was clear that label was being assigned to me.

"The most hurtful part is that you work very hard, and people say it's because of your looks."

Gloria Steinem has died, aged 92. (Annie Leibovitz)

Of course, Steinem also had to deal with hostility. Sometimes it came from surprising places.

Appearing on Larry King's talk show on CNN in 1990, she was visibly stunned when a female caller greeted her cheerfully, then told her to "rot in hell" because she had ruined "the beautiful American family."

But by then, she noted, at least people were taking feminists seriously.

That was not the case in 1971 when she co-founded Ms. Magazine and many commentators — especially male — dismissed it as ridiculous, predicting an early demise. The magazine continues to this day, published by the Feminist Majority Foundation.

Among Steinem's detractors was US president Richard Nixon, who was caught on an Oval Office tape ridiculing both her and the "Ms." title.

The ridicule was mutual: in a 1972 National Press Club speech, Steinem called Mr Nixon "the most sexually insecure chief of state since Napoleon."

It was just one example of Steinem's trademark wit.

Before she married at 66, she often explained her single-hood by saying "I can't mate in captivity."

Laughter, she wrote, was "the only free emotion — the only one that can't be compelled."

Wires

World.title: V/Line CEO jailed and facing deportation over secret commissions
World.content:
A former V/Line chief executive has been jailed and is facing deportation, after admitting to misconduct in public office and receiving secret commissions.

Four other people were also sentenced on Thursday after pleading guilty to their part in the corruption scandal involving the awarding of major contracts within V/Line and Metro to cleaning company Transclean.

An IBAC investigation, which used video surveillance, telephone intercepts and hidden cameras, uncovered that valuable cleaning contracts were awarded and extended.

The value of the cleaning contracts, and the variations to them, was in the order of $40 million initially, with variations to the end of March 2019 to more than $54 million.

James Pinder was sacked by V/Line after giving evidence at the IBAC hearing. (Supplied: Andrew McPherson)

James Pinder, 58, was sacked as V/Line CEO after his appearance before a public inquiry into the matter and charged with misconduct in public office.

The court heard he had established an undeclared relationship with Transclean boss George Haritos and corruptly received $330,000 dollars influencing him to favour Transclean.

The court heard James Pinder used the secret commissions to buy a house in Williamstown. (Supplied: IBAC)

The bulk of those funds were used to purchase a home in Williamstown after he was refused a bank loan.

He was sentenced to two years and eight months imprisonment, and must serve one year and nine months before becoming eligible for parole.

Pinder, who was born in West London, is now facing deportation.

"As of today you are uncertain as to whether you will be of liberty in the Australian community again," Judge Todd said.

George Haritos was captured on surveillance videos played to the IBAC hearing. (News Video)

Haritos, 71, pleaded guilty to a charge of conspiracy to give a secret commission and two charges of giving a secret commission.

Judge Todd described him as the "common denominator" in almost every event.

His family wept as he was sentenced to two years and three months in prison.

He will be eligible for parole in a year and five months.

Transclean employee Steven Kyritsis received a community corrections order.

Haritos' brother in-law and Transclean director Alex Kyritsis, 69, and his nephew Steven Kyritsis, 42, who was a Transclean employee, were each given community correction orders for their part — pleading guilty to a charge of conspiracy to give a secret commission and giving a secret commission respectively

Maria Tsakopoulos, 45, who had been in a relationship with Haritos until early this year, was also given a community corrections order for conspiracy to destroy evidence and giving a secret commission.

She was accused of creating and planning to destroy a sham document, created for the purpose of attempting to explain the cash flow of $320,000 into Mr Pinder's bank account.

Steven Collin, a solicitor, earlier pleaded guilty in the Magistrates' Court to a charge of conspiracy to destroy a document.

He was convicted and was earlier sentenced to a one-year community corrections order.

Former Metro trains manager Peter Bollas was sentenced in 2024 to a community corrections order for three years and six months.

World.title: Hawks complete stunning upset over Freo to clinch prelim berth
World.content:
James Sicily (right) had a huge night in the Hawks' backline as his team took care of the Dockers in the west (Getty Images)

The Hawks kicked six goals to one in a dominant first half in Thursday night's clash to set up the 10.12 (72) to 5.10 (40) win and secure a home preliminary final.

Fremantle, who had been a perfect 12-0 at Perth Stadium this season, will now confront either Carlton or Geelong in a cut-throat semi-final in Perth next week.

The Dockers were a dominant force during the home-and-away season, stringing together a 14-game winning streak at one stage on the way to a league-best 19-4 record.

But the minor premiers looked overawed in the finals cauldron on Thursday night in front of 59,446 fans — Fremantle's largest ever home crowd.

Fremantle's first-half return of 1.4 (10) was their lowest such score in a final, even worse than the 1.6 (12) they kicked across the opening two quarters of their 2013 grand final loss to the Hawks.

The Dockers will now have to win their semi-final and then an away preliminary final in order to make their first grand final since 2013.

Sicily, Tom Barrass and Josh Battle were rocks in defence, keeping Jye Amiss, Josh Treacy and Patrick Voss to two goals and 19 disposals between the three of them.

Treacy's first kick of the game — a set-shot goal — only arrived with five minutes remaining in the match.

Hawks veteran Jack Gunston kicked two clutch goals in the first-half onslaught, while Dylan Moore chipped in with two majors.

Watson was a human highlights reel at times on the way to two goals from 19 disposals.

"The belief in the group's outstanding," Watson told Fox Sports after the match.

"We knew it was going to be hot. It was hot early, but the boys stood up well."

Fremantle ruckman Luke Jackson kicked the opening goal of the match, but the rest of the first half belonged to Hawthorn as their slick ball movement and fierce tackling left the Dockers looking second-rate at times.

Watson's soccered goal from nearly 20m out sparked a run of four consecutive goals as the Hawks took a surprise 28-9 lead into quarter-time.

Hawthorn's pressure continued to be off the charts in the second term.

And even when Fremantle hit back — like when Karl Worner won a holding-the-ball free kick for his chasing tackle on Max Beattie — the Hawks didn't give up.

When Worner played on and took a bounce from that free kick, Beattie ran hard to put pressure on the kick.

It resulted in a turnover and a running goal to Moore as Hawthorn's lead expanded to 33 points by half-time.

There wasn't anything obvious in the half-time stats to suggest what was going wrong for Fremantle.

But the naked eye could decipher their problem — an inability to handle Hawthorn's intense pressure.

Jordan Clark's high-flying mark on top of Jack Ginnivan was a rare highlight for Fremantle in the first half.

Hawthorn forward Mitch Lewis suffered a huge scare when he hurt his shoulder in a heavy landing, but he was able to return for the start of the second half.

Fremantle broke Hawthorn's run of six goals when Jye Amiss kicked truly one minute into the third quarter.

But luck wasn't on Fremantle's side, with Watson kicking his second to restore the 33-point margin at the final change after his direct opponent Brandon Walker had rolled his ankle in the previous play.

Watson put the icing on the cake early in the final quarter when he gathered the ball at full pace on the wing, handballed to himself while under pressure from Luke Ryan, before regathering to kick it to Harry Morrison for the sealing goal.

AAP

World.title: Broncos send Haas out a winner with top score of 2026 against Dogs
World.content:
The Broncos have won a final-round contest against the Bulldogs 34-20, in a game that doubled as superstar prop Payne Haas's farewell from Brisbane.

Haas scored the opening try as the Broncos notched up their equal highest score of a disappointing 2026 season, tied with their tally from a 34-30 win over the Raiders four weeks earlier.

Halfback Ben Hunt said the team had extra motivation to send Haas out a winner before he heads to South Sydney from 2027.

"Payne means a hell of a lot to this club, he really does," Hunt told ABC Sport.

"It's been a very disappointing year, but to come out here tonight, the boys really carried themselves in a great way and really showed up for Payne.

"He deserved the win tonight."

The teams were tied 10-10 at half-time, but the Broncos, sparked by Hunt and hooker Billy Walters, exploded after the break with four tries in 15 minutes to jump out to a 24-point lead.

Canterbury hit back with tries to Viliame Kikau and Lachlan Galvin, but they could not get close enough to truly challenge the Broncos, who will finish 14th or 15th in their failed premiership defence.

Look back all the action in our live blog below, and check out all the stats in the full ScoreCentre.

World.title: They had no place in Sydney's gang war. They died anyway
World.content:
A tradie standing in a front yard with kids. A university student asleep in his bed.

Neither had links to organised crime. Both ended up dead.

Their murders are the latest loss of life in Sydney's sprawling gang war, where innocent people are increasingly being targeted, mistaken for someone else, or murdered because of who they are related to.

Police blame inept teenagers being contracted by overseas criminals, who are willing to murder for a few thousand dollars.

Authorities say eight people have been killed in cases of mistaken identity since 2021.

Count those allegedly targeted because they are family members of gang members, or were innocent bystanders, and that figure climbs to 14.

Here are the stories of the innocent victims caught in the crossfire.

Joshua Macdonald, September 2026

Joshua Macdonald with his aunt Darlene. ( )

It was mid-afternoon and Joshua Macdonald had parked his work van in the driveway of a Merrylands West home.

He, another man and two children were in the front yard.

The Central Coast tradie, who co-owns an electrical business, celebrated his 40th birthday last week.

"He was a very beautiful man with his whole life ahead of him and that has been taken away," his Aunt Darlene told the ABC.

" He was so loved and I am very proud of what he achieved in his very short life. "

Police believe the intended target, who allegedly had links to the notorious Alameddine crime network, was associated with the property but did not live there.

The ABC has obtained CCTV which captures the sound of the gunshots and the car speeding down the street.

Marco Tapia, September 2026

Shooting victim Marco Tapia. ( )

Biomedical engineering student Marco Tapia was asleep in his bed when masked intruders broke in and shot him dead.

His parents were also at the Glen Alpine family home when the balaclava-clad gunmen entered.

The 23-year-old was in his third year of a degree at the University of Technology Sydney, was a volunteer youth leader and trained in martial arts.

After the shooting, 'Coconut Cartel' gang figure Iziah Utai shared a social media post saying the offenders had "popped the wrong person didn't even get the right house".

Police believe a feud between the self-proclaimed Coconut Cartel, which takes its name from a historic slur against Pasifika people, and rival Alameddines is fuelling the violence.

Iziah Utai is hiding overseas after attempts on his life, and that of his innocent father ex-NRL player Matt Utai, who narrowly survived a drive-by shooting in February.

Chris Baghsarian, February 2026

Chris Baghsarian. ( )

Eighty-five-year-old grandfather Chris Baghsarian was kidnapped from his North Ryde home in February and taken to a Dural "stronghold" according to police.

After an 11-day search, his remains were found near a golf course in Pitt Town in Sydney's north-west.

Police believe a relative of Sydney businessman Dimitri Stepanyan was the intended target, and Mr Baghsarian was taken by mistake.

A dozen people have been charged over his death, including a 19-year-old.

Gilbert Shino, August 2025

Gilbert Shino. ( )

39-year-old Gilbert Shino was walking with a friend, who allegedly had links to an Assyrian crime gang, when he was gunned down outside a busy Sydney pub in front of patrons.

The two men were heading back to their car after watching an Ultimate Fighting Championship event at the inner west pub when the hitmen opened fire from a Ford Mustang.

Mr Shino died. His friend, Maradona Yalda, survived. Police believed Mr Yalda was the intended target.

A female pub worker said she heard a bullet "whiz" past her, and patrons told the ABC the saw a "little flash" from the gun and threw themselves on the floor.

Luke Manassa, June 2025

Luke Manassa. ( )

Luke Manassa, a 21-year-old university student, was stabbed while visiting the home of someone "well known" to authorities.

Police say he was attacked by men wielding machetes, in a horrific case of mistaken identity.

Police allege the two masked men 'lay in wait' ahead of the attack, which was described as "very, very amateurish".

Three teenagers, a 16-year-old and two 17-year-olds, have been charged over the attack.

Police allege the contract was for someone else, and Mr Manassa was targeted by mistake.

Mr Manassa was well-loved figure in the local Christian-Lebanese community, studying at university and working in his family's construction business.

John Versace, May 2025

John Versace. ( )

John Versace, a 23-year-old tradie, was killed in front of his parents in the driveway of their Condell Park home in 2025. The hitmen had targeted the wrong home.

Mr Versace pulled up in his ute before being fired at 10 times, in what police described as a "brutal and execution-style killing".

In video taken in the aftermath of the shooting, Mr Versace's family could be heard pleading: "Who would do this?"

"There is nothing to suggest Mr Versace was anything but a hardworking young man who was living at home with his family and trying to set himself up for the rest of his life," Superintendent Jason Box said following the shooting.

Mr Versace's death was one of several that led to the formation of Taskforce Falcon, a new police unit set up to investigate a string of shootings in Sydney, being run by Superintendent Box.

Three men have been charged over the murder, one aged 19.

Thi Kim Tran, April 2025

Thi Kim Tran. ( )

Police alleged Ms Tran's husband had fallen foul of a Victorian-based Vietnamese drug syndicate who accused him of stealing drugs.

A "contracted kill crew" had attempted to lure the husband out by sending him photo of his kidnapped wife, but when he could not be contacted, they killed her, Homicide Squad Commander Superintendent Joseph Doueihi alleged at the time.

An eight-year-old boy in the home was hit with a baseball bat during the kidnapping and had to be treated in hospital.

Nine people have been charged and are before the courts, the youngest aged 20.

Kim Duncan, April 2025

Kim Duncan died from a leg wound after multiple shots were fired at the Ambarvale home.

Kim Duncan, 65, was visiting her son at his Ambarvale home in Sydney's south-west when she was shot in the leg during a drive-by shooting.

The passionate Penrith Panthers supporter had recently moved from Tamworth to Sydney to be closer to family.

Police said the grandmother had been caught in the crossfire of a "beef" with a person who lived at the home.

Ms Duncan's daughter Cassandra Dowd told the ABC said she will "never get over" the loss of her mother.

"She was our mum. She was happy, she was loving, she was definitely an innocent in all of this," Ms Dowd said.

Three people have been charged over Ms Duncan's death, including a 19-year-old.

Bol Deng, February 2024

Bol Deng ( )

Twenty-year-old Bol Deng was killed during a peak hour drive-by shooting in Fairfield Heights. Mr Deng was simply standing outside his home; his family nearby.

The hit was targeted, but not because of his criminal connections.

Police alleged the hit on Deng was an act of retribution, after his brother was named as the alleged gunman in the assassination of underworld kingpin Alen Moradian in a Bondi carpark in 2023.

A 25-year-old has been charged over his alleged role in the contract killing.

Ahmad Al-Azzam, July 2023

Ahmad Al-Azzam ( )

25-year-old Ahmad Al-Azzam died in hospital after being shot while sitting alone in his car in Greenacre.

Police alleged the hitmen mistook Mr Al-Azzam for a member of a rival network, thought to be the Comanchero bikie gang.

The men in the stolen vehicle also shot a 22-year-old man and 19-year-old woman who were sitting in a nearby car. Police allege the innocent members of the public had caught the attention of the shooter when their brake lights lit up. They survived.

"It's one of the most callous crimes that I've seen in my 28 years in regard to investigating organised crime," Detective Chief Superintendent Jason Weinstein said following the attack.

Eight people have been charged; the youngest alleged offender aged 21.

Taha Sabbagh, March 2023

Taha Sabbagh. ( )

Forty-year-old Taha Sabbagh was driving his young son to a boxing lesson at Elite Fight Force gym in Sefton when a masked man shot him multiple times through his windscreen and car door.

"It's horrendous to think a 12-year-old had to witness his father being shot dead in this manner," Homicide Squad Detective Superintendent Danny Doherty said at the time.

Court documents stated Taha was "seated in the driver's seat of his car and the child watched helplessly from the carpark, screaming".

A 26-year-old man was later sentenced to a non-parole period of 12 years over the murder.

Court documents reveal police prosecutors thought the intended target was probably the gym owner, who drove a similar car to Mr Sabbagh, as they could find "no known motivation" for the Sydney father's murder.

"His brother gave evidence of his devoted and quiet family life, prosocial connections and stable employment," court documents read.

Amy al-Hazouri, August 2022

Amy Hazzouri. ( )

Hairdresser Amy al-Hazouri was sitting in the backseat of a car in Panania with a client when at least a dozen bullets were fired into their vehicle.

Both the 39-year-old and her client Lametta Fadlallah were killed in what police believe was a targeted shooting of Ms Fadlallah who was a former partner of an underworld figure.

Ms al-Hazouri had recently become engaged, and her family had been planning to travel to Australia from Lebanon to celebrate.

NSW Police homicide squad boss Danny Doherty described the shooting as "unprecedented" and said it broke an unwritten rule of not targeting women and family.

Toufik Hamze, October 2021

Toufik Hamze ( )

Toufik Hamze, 64, was gunned down while getting into a red ute outside his Guildford home. His son, the likely target given his criminal connections, was also killed.

Their deaths came at the height of tit-for-tat shootings between the rival Hamzy and Alameddine clans over the city's drug trade.

A 16-year-old boy was among those charged. The teenager later pleaded guilty to being an accessory after the fact and was handed a two-year intensive corrections order.

Mustapha Naaman, January 2021

Mustafa Naaman. ( )

Police said 29-year-old Mustapha Naaman had simply been in the wrong place at the wrong time.

He and his 23-year-old friend were driving a car identical to the intended target — a white Mercedes.

Police said the hit had been intended for two members of the Hamze crime family, who had left a boxing event in Hurstville moments earlier.

Instead, the gunmen killed Mr Naaman and seriously injured his friend.

World.title: Realtor raided after allegations agent sold client's home to himself
World.content:
Authorities in Western Australia have searched the offices of a Perth property firm amid allegations its owners used a shell company to buy their own client's home without telling him.

Ideal Realty, based in the southern suburb of Willetton, was initially issued a warning by the state's consumer protection department for an alleged breach of laws relating to conflicts of interest around the sale of a Kenwick home in 2024.

Home owner blindsided by agents who allegedly secretly bought his home A Perth real estate agency has been issued a warning for allegedly breaching conflict of interest laws after its agents bought a home that they were hired to sell.

The department today sent officers to execute a warrant at the company and the ABC understands the raid was aimed at scrutinising documents related to that deal.

Disclosure failings

The ABC has previously reported that two years ago, Ideal Realty was hired to sell the home of Perth man Chao "Jack" Wu.

After six days on the market Mr Wu said he received three offers, the highest of which was from a company called "Generation Two".

Mr Wu alleged that it was only after he accepted a final offer from this company that he learned that it was owned by two licensees of Ideal Realty — Roy Li and Lynn Ting, whose legal names are Liang Li and Lin Ding.

Roy Li of Ideal Realty conducted the sale. (ABC News: Gian De Poloni)

He said he proceeded with the sale because he feared that, as he had already signed the sale contract, he would be liable for damages.

Mr Li has denied misleading his client, and said he told Mr Wu before making the offer that he and his partner were the true buyers.

However, Mr Li has conceded that he failed to ensure Mr Wu signed a legally required written disclosure form acknowledging his interest in the transaction.

Roy Li is one of the owners of Ideal Realty, based in Perth's southern suburbs. (ABC News: Mitchell Edgar)

He also conceded that at least one home open at the property was cancelled at the last minute, with potential buyers only able to view the outside of the property, due to the rental tenant refusing to grant access at the last minute.

Do you know more about this story? Contact Rebecca Trigger.

New evidence sparks raid

Consumer Protection Commissioner Trish Blake said new evidence allowed the case to be reopened.

She said investigators would examine documents related to the transaction with Mr Wu to determine whether a breach had occurred.

Consumer Protection authorities raided the office on Thursday. (ABC News: Mitchell Edgar)

Ms Blake said it was not an offence for a real estate agent to buy the property that they're selling, but there must be full disclosure in advance.

"That's really critical because the vendor has to be able to make a fully informed decision about whether they accept that offer or whether they maybe want to wait for a different offer to come in," the commissioner said.

If a breach of this kind is established, companies can face fines of $25,000 while individuals can be fined $5,000.

Trish Blake said this marked an important stage in the investigation. (ABC News: Samantha Goerling)

The commissioner said such a finding could also lead to a question as to whether a person is fit and proper to hold a real estate license.

"For any real estate agent, to be fit and proper, we're looking all the time at things like honesty, accountability, and respect for the law," Ms Blake said.

"That would be a question that we might take to the State Administrative Tribunal."

Ms Blake said it was important the public could have trust in agents and the industry more broadly.

Inflated sales figures

Last week, Mr Li was also referred to the Real Estate Institute of WA's professional standards tribunal over discrepancies in the sales prices he listed with the agency.

Analysis by the ABC found discrepancies in around a third of the listed sale prices when compared to official prices recorded on the state land register.

Real estate agent's sales data under scrutiny after awards disqualification A top-ranked WA real estate agent is disqualified from this year's industry awards after discrepancies emerge in his reported sales data.

Mr Li told the ABC the inaccuracies were introduced when he inadvertently listed the asking price instead of the actual sale price for some properties.

He also listed around $10 million in sales of properties he or his fellow licensee, Ms Ding, owned, which were later removed from the site.

He said this occurred because they were initially listed but then withdrawn from the market.

Mr Li, who last year won a prestigious award given to the top one per cent of real estate agents by sales values and volume, has been banned from participating in the institute's annual awards this year.

World.title: ‘You have to hope for a time like this’: The full story behind Will Day’s tears
World.content:
SportAFLAFL 2026 ‘You have to hope for a time like this’: The full story behind Will Day’s tears Peter Ryan September 4, 2026 — 1:11am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Loading

Perth: Will Day’s emotions were not the same as his teammates after the Hawks claimed the first sport in this year’s preliminary finals with their brilliant win over Fremantle. He was in tears in a post-match interview, and then hugged his mum, Monique, and dad, Julian, in the Optus Stadium rooms with as much vigour as any of the 57 fierce tackles the Hawks had laid during the pressure-packed win, 5.10 (40) to 10.12 (72). After missing the past two finals series through injury, he had finally made it to the line for his first final. Will Day is arguably the Hawks’ most important player. AFL Photos Sam Mitchell knew how big a moment it was for the 25-year-old, saying post-game he could only imagine how he must have felt when he woke up on Thursday morning with the match just hours away.



Day decided there was only one way for him to attack what was ahead of him. “I just stripped back all the pressure, [and] took off all the expectation,” Day said. “I knew just by being out there I was going to help the team, so I did not want to try to do too much.” View post on X As he spoke, the emotion welled in his eyes again as familiar faces in the rooms loomed in his vision. “I just keep locking eyes with a lot of people that have helped me so much ... they are happy tears,” he said.



Happy tears were everywhere for Hawks fans who have ridden Day’s journey, ruing his absence through injury in their past two finals series when they seemed a midfielder short. After missing out on securing Essendon skipper Zach Merrett through the trade period, they then had their summer ruined by the sight of Day leaving the track with a shoulder injury in early January. James Sicily, who was brilliant in the qualifying final, celebrates the win with co-captain Jai Newcombe. AFL Photos The optimism most Hawks fans carry as though it’s a birth right suddenly slipped. To make matters worse, Day, himself, was quite reasonably wondering how his shoulder had become as pear-shaped as his career.



“[I was] pretty defeated. The last two finals series, especially last year losing the preliminary final, you feel so helpless, you just want to be out there and help,” Day said. Related Article AFL 2026 Dockers v Hawks player ratings: From a skipper’s career night, to the gun forwards who disappeared “It was tough early [this year], but you just have to switch to a positive outlook. It was very tough and very much easier said than done, but you just have to hope for a time like this, and it has been so worth it.” Against the Dockers, he was more than just out there helping. With James Sicily putting on a masterclass down back with a best-on-ground performance alongside his defensive allies Josh Battle, Blake Hardwick and Tom Barrass (who all dominated their opponents), the scene was set for Day to break open the game.



When the Dockers threatened to charge with minutes remaining in the third quarter, Day won two critical possessions that helped Nick Watson to deliver the settler. Editor's pick Exclusive

AFL 2026 Sydney Swan Nick Blakey tells associates he wants to be traded Watson, Dylan Moore and Jack Ginnivan rattled the Dockers’ defence with their pressure from the start, while the Hawks surprised the Dockers by pushing Jack Gunston high and leaving Mabior Chol deep. There was nothing Hollywood about the Hawks this time around. Instead, they produced a low-budget, no frills classic. Day finished the match with 24 disposals and eight centre clearances to show why he was so missed in September.



Mitchell hugged him post-match. He knew what his midfield star had overcome to be there with his mates, one match away from being in a grand final. View post on X “He showed it a lot more than I did, but I felt exactly how he looked after the game,” Mitchell said. The contrast with Justin Longmuir could not have been more stark as the Dockers coach attempted to rally his demoralised team after their first loss at home for the season. Day (centre) sings the Hawks’ famous song alongside Nick Watson, Mabior Chol, coach Sam Mitchell, and Dylan Moore. AFL Photos



“It’s not the way we wanted it to go [tonight], but we are not dead and buried,” he said. The Dockers could do worse than look to the way Day responded to his January jolt for inspiration. Because, to adapt a line from Mike Brady’s One Day in September, the resilient Hawks midfielder is finally seeing “the joy that hard work brings”. Keep up to date with the best AFL coverage in the country.

World.title: AFL Finals 2026: ‘It’s in our hands’: Ginnivan, Hawks look straight to an MCG prelim final
World.content:
Dockers coach Justin Longmuir spoke to the media post-game.

On the difference between the sides:

“There was a lot of different aspects. The contests were pretty even, but their contest method was better than ours.

“They were a little more decisive in getting it to the outside.

Dockers coach Justin Longmuir. AFL Photos

World.title: Dockers v Hawks player ratings: From a skipper’s career night, to the gun forwards who disappeared
World.content:
Loading

It loomed as a good, old-fashioned “danger game” for the Dockers, who finished clear on top of the ladder, but no one could have predicted just how thoroughly they’d be outplayed by Sam Mitchell’s men in their qualifying final at Optus Stadium. Our experts, AFLW star Libby Birch (Dockers) and Scott Spits (Hawks) rate every player’s performance from a stunning night out west. Justin Longmuir’s Dockers were thoroughly outplayed from the outset. AFL Photos



Fremantle (3) Caleb Serong: He worked his way into the contest after a quiet start, but never exerted his usual influence around stoppage. Didn’t help the midfield play to the conditions. 4/10 (5) Heath Chapman: Provided important drive from an under-siege defence, although he was beaten in the air in some costly moments. 6/10 (6) Jordan Clark: Fremantle’s standout, defending desperately and repeatedly driving them forward with bold run and excellent ball use in his milestone match. Fremantle’s best player for the night. 8/10 Two-time All-Australian Jordan Clark could hold his head high for the Dockers. AFL Photos



(8) Andrew Brayshaw: He started slowly and his early possessions lacked impact, but lifted after half-time to inject urgency and kick a much-needed goal. 6/10 (9) Luke Jackson: Kicked the opener, competed strongly around the ground and was Fremantle’s second most influential player through the first half. 7/10 (10) Shai Bolton: He was barely sighted early on a night that should have suited him, before providing flashes of energy through give-and-go football after half-time. 4/10 (13) Luke Ryan: Valiant and unrelenting under sustained pressure, he read the play well and producing several important spoils. 7/10 (16) Murphy Reid: The youngest player on the field looked composed around stoppage and was clean when opportunities came, but he struggled to impact in the second half. 5/10



(18) Mason Cox: Struggled to impact early as Jackson’s ruck support, but improved as the game wore on and took important defensive marks. 4/10 (20) Patrick Voss: Could not win enough contests ahead of the ball and was repeatedly worked underneath it by James Sicily. 2/10 Patrick “Prancing Pony” Voss had a night to forget. AFL Photos (21) Oscar McDonald: Conceded an early high free kick to Jack Gunston and lost another crucial contest in the goal square on a difficult night. 4/10 (23) Karl Worner: Produced a huge chase-down tackle and a goal-saving smother, but an errant kick that gifted Hawthorn a goal proved costly. He gave it a crack. 6/10



(24) Jye Amiss: He was frustrated and largely unsighted in the first half, but gave Fremantle an immediate lift with the opening goal after the half-time break. 3/10 (25) Alex Pearce: Battled hard against Mitch Lewis and offered a strong presence in a defence that was repeatedly placed under pressure. 7/10 Alex Pearce (second from left) will set his men to bounce back and go again next week. AFL Photos (26) Hayden Young: His early ball use was uncharacteristically poor and he struggled to generate his usual damage through the midfield. 4/10 (28) Neil Erasmus: One of Fremantle’s better early contributors, using the ball with purpose and looking through the corridor when others played safe. 6/10



(30) Nathan O’Driscoll: Needed to be stronger aerially early, but lifted his intensity and produced a fierce third-quarter tackle on Newcombe. 3/10 (31) Brandon Walker: A surprise inclusion for just his second game of the year, he competed bravely on Watson before an ankle roll contributed to another Hawks goal and his night done. 5/10 (32) Michael Frederick: Was unable to find space or use his speed, remaining largely unsighted. 2/10 Josh Treacy and his teammates had a horror night against a rampaging Hawks side. AFL Photos (35) Josh Treacy: He fought a difficult battle against Hawthorn’s organised defence but had little impact and went without a single kick deep into the third term. 2/10



(39) Sam Switkowski: He had a brilliant third quarter and kicked a huge goal to give Fremantle a (slight) sniff – the first finals major of his career. 6/10 (43) Isaiah Dudley: Missed an early opportunity but grew into the contest, improving his defensive pressure and contributing to Fremantle’s second-half ball movement. 4/10 (44) Matthew Johnson: One of Fremantle’s better midfielders in the first half, competing strongly and providing some composure amid Hawthorn’s pressure. 5/10 Sam Mitchell embraces Nick Watson after a finals win for the ages. AFL Photos



Hawthorn (1) Harry Morrison: Showed a few flashy moments midway through the third term. He can point to kicking the first goal of the final term, giving Hawthorn a match-high 38-point lead, for his golden moment. 5.5/10 (2) Mitch Lewis: A player of influence. He overcame a shoulder injury scare just before half-time. Look back to the early minutes of the game, when the action was hot, and Lewis pulled off a great run-down tackle and earned a free kick. 7/10 (3) Jai Newcombe: Not Hawthorn’s most important or valuable player, but that was a good sign for the brown and gold. Led Hawthorn’s tackle count at the main break, however. 6/10 (4) Jarman Impey: Reliable deep in defence in his All-Australian season. It was hard to find fault with his game as Hawthorn’s defence shone brightly all the way. 6/10



(5) Nick Watson: A top game. Lively and dangerous from start to finish, he kicked a goal out of nowhere – Hawthorn’s first – after just six minutes. It was emblematic of Hawthorn’s smash and grab approach. For Hawthorn’s most “Hollywood” player, it was instead a blue-collar night. 8/10 View post on X (6) James Sicily: A sterling game and one easily worthy of best on ground honours. A pillar in Hawthorn’s brutal defensive unit all match, he completely nullified Voss’ danger and influence, especially in the first half when the win was set up. Composed and reliable, this was a true leader’s match. 9/10 (8) Dylan Moore: He kicked Hawthorn’s second goal – again when the match was up for grabs – but it was his work-rate that stood out. “That workrate is as good as it gets,” reflected Kane Cornes on Seven, noting Moore’s ability to run hard back at goal. “Their tackling in the forward half has been unbelievable.” 6.5/10 (9) Connor Macdonald: Got better and better as the match wore on, and had some influence in the third term when Hawthorn had to keep the threatening Fremantle at bay. 6/10



(10) Karl Amon: Another solid contributor. By early in the final quarter he only had kicks – not handballs – on the tally board, showing just how much the Hawks rely on his foot skills. 5.5/10 (12) Will Day: One of Hawthorn’s best, who effectively became “the Clearance King”. Like others, Day got better and better as the game wore on and never stopped running. He went one-on-one with Brayshaw at stages and won the battle. 7.5/10 View post on X (15) Blake Hardwick: Went to the dangerous Reid early on. Hawthorn basically didn’t have a passenger in their 23, and Hardwick deserves recognition too. 5.5/10 (16) Massimo D’Ambrosio: Had a fantastic game and was influential (especially in the first quarter) when the game was being won. While he missed two shots at goal in the opening stanza, he dragged in nine touches as he regularly found space with his hard-running. 8/10



(17) Lloyd Meek: Probably won’t get enough plaudits for an impressive game. Won the opening tap-out against Luke Jackson but, yes, was done for holding the ball moments later. Got some eye-catching clearances, a trait normally reserved for his immediate foe Jackson. 7.5/10 Editor's pick Opinion

AFL 2026 In an AFL world of corporate-style spin, we shouldn’t slam North’s leaders for speaking their ‘Clarko’ truth Jake Niall Chief football writer, The Age (18) Mabior Chol: Did his bit and with style. As Hawthorn ran with Jack Gunston a bit further from goal than normal, Chol became the focal point in the forward line. Importantly, he got physical in countless marking contests, bringing the ball to ground at the very least. 7/10 (19) Jack Gunston: He gave Freo’s Oscar McDonald a bath. He regularly beat his man in the first half as Hawthorn stamped their authority on the game. By early in the second term, the veteran already had his two goals. He only touched the ball five times, but that didn’t matter. 7.5/10 (23) Josh Weddle: Another player vying to be Hawthorn’s best (behind Sicily) on a memorable night for the brown and gold. He was especially influential in the second quarter as Hawthorn looked to consolidate their great start. 8/10



Josh Weddle and the Hawks were all over Sam Switkowski and the Dockers. AFL Photos (24) Josh Battle: He played an outstanding game and was a crucial member of Hawthorn’s brilliant defensive unit. He went to Treacy and won that battle in a horrid game for Freo’s forwards. Dragged in 16 disposals in a top game. 8/10 (25) Josh Ward: Another top contributor, he worked hard across the game. In one first-quarter moment, he pulled off an excellent pass to D’Ambrosio up forward, but his teammate was off-line with the kick. Raised his arms in celebration after a defensive spoil by a teammate at one point. 6/10 (28) Cam Mackenzie: Another player who had a growing influence across the game. Had 11 touches by half-time and finished with 20. 6.5/10 (33) Jack Ginnivan: Had an unsung, low-key role early for the Hawks after returning to the team, but the 2023 Collingwood premiership player had a huge moment in the second half by taking a composed mark, and going back and kicking a goal that, again, kept Freo at bay. 6.5/10



Tom Barrass and the Hawks didn’t give the Dockers an inch of space all night. Getty Images (37) Tom Barrass: He played a brilliant defensive game. He manned Jye Amiss for most of the game and, like others in the brown and gold, won his night. Look back at the moment when Barrass applied an excellent punch deep in defence just before half-time. That was telling. Then in the third term he took a few key intercept marks. 8/10 (40) Max Beattie: An inexperienced player who looked comfortable out there in what could have been a tough environment. He did have one bad turnover in the second term when he really shouldn’t have been run down. Only had about 60 per cent game time. 4.5/10 (42) Bailey Macdonald: Also had limited game time and picked up eight touches. There were no Hawthorn passengers, remember. 5/10 Keep up to date with the best AFL coverage in the country.

World.title: Sydney scientist behind ‘moon landing’ cancer vaccine wins top science prize
World.content:
NationalCancer Sydney scientist behind ‘moon landing’ cancer vaccine wins top science prize Angus Dalton September 3, 2026 — 10:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The scientist who transformed advanced melanoma into a treatable cancer and led a recent large-scale trial into a world-first personalised mRNA cancer vaccine has won the research prize at Australia’s premier science awards. Professor Georgina Long was cautious to discuss the melanoma vaccine trial given that full results won’t be released until October, but described it as an “absolute landmark, fork-in-the-road for cancer” ahead of being awarded the Eureka Prize for Scientific Research at the Australian Museum on Thursday night. Professor Georgina Long has won the Eureka Prize for Scientific Research. Tim Bauer “It represents a huge body of work and team effort, and it’s an honour, really, to represent all the people that I lead,” the former Australian of the Year said of the award. “We’re a small but mighty country. We’ve got to keep the investments in Australia. We’ve got to take greater risks.”



Long is on a sabbatical in Lisbon, Portugal, away from her duties as medical director of the Melanoma Institute Australia at the University of Sydney to think and plan the next stages of her research. The new vaccine, developed by Moderna and Merck, aims to prevent recurrence of melanoma after a tumour is removed. Long was the principal investigator of the phase 3 trial and said it provided “the first real data that demonstrates mRNA technology can absolutely change the face of cancer”. Without yet providing details, the companies said on August 20 that the late-stage trial produced clinically and statistically significant improvements in high-risk melanoma patients. Moderna’s market value leapt by $62 billion in a day. “We are not even a speck of dust in this universe. And there’s only one point: to make a difference as much as you can, and do it well.” Professor Georgina Long For the trial, 1137 high-risk melanoma patients were given the cancer drug Keytruda. Half also received the experimental vaccine.



Researchers sequenced patients’ tumours after surgery and identified mutations, unique to each person’s cancer, that code for abnormal proteins on the surface of cancer cells called neoantigens. A custom mRNA vaccine was crafted for each patient based on the specific neoantigens in their tumour, teaching the immune system exactly what to look for. Normal cells have proteins which stop the immune system attacking healthy tissue. Melanomas hijack these cellular signals, masquerading as normal cells and growing unchecked. Keytruda stops this from happening, ripping off melanoma’s invisibility cloak. Results presented from a much smaller phase 2 trial in June showed combining Keytruda and the vaccine led to a 49 per cent reduction in the risk of recurrence or death, compared to just the cancer drug.



As the president of Merck put it, the mRNA vaccine, called intismeran autogene, gives the immune system the scent of the enemy. Then Keytruda releases “the dogs of war”. “It is a moon-landing moment,” Long said. Others are investigating whether the same approach could work in lung and pancreatic cancer. Britain’s King Charles is briefed by co-medical director Georgina Long as he visits the Melanoma Institute of Australia in Sydney in 2024. AFP The award on Thursday was in recognition of more than a decade of research. When Long started working in melanoma, faces in her waiting room would change within six to nine months. “It was the orphan cancer up until about 15 years ago. You think of the worst cancers now, and I can name them – pancreatic cancer [and] glioblastoma – melanoma was worse than those two. Nothing worked ... chemotherapy did nothing.



“The waiting room would be completely different because people died, and the majority of people died within 12 months.” Long and her collaborators have turned that story around. A trial Long led in 2018 found combining two immunotherapy drugs – nivolumab and ipilimumab – had a 46 per cent response rate in patients with melanoma that had metastasised to the brain, compared with 20 per cent when just one drug was used. The finding changed clinical practice “overnight”. Seven-year follow-up data reported in The Lancet Oncology last year found 51 per cent of patients given the combination immunotherapy as a first-line treatment had survived, compared with 29 per cent on the single drug. That’s just some of Long’s work, which is credited with ushering the survival rate of advanced melanoma from 5 to 50 per cent. She and colleague Professor Richard Scolyer were named Australians of the Year in 2024 for their research on cancer.



Crucially, tactics pioneered in melanoma treatment have gone on to have a “massive impact” in cancers of the lung, kidney, head, neck and bladder and some lymphomas, Long said. Professor Georgina Long and Professor Richard Scolyer at a ceremony in Canberra where they were named joint Australians of the Year in 2024. Alex Ellinghausen “Every single drug developed in melanoma first … has gone on to impact an extraordinary number of patients with other cancers,” Long said. Long’s focus is on the patients resistant to treatment: the difficult territory between what we know and don’t know where “courageous medicine happens”, such as the testing of drugs never trialled in people. She calls it the “third space”. “We’ve cured 50 per cent, [but] we’ve still got 50 per cent who die, and they die quickly like the old days. They are our third space,” she said.



“We’re all on this planet for a tiny, tiny, tiny time. We are not even a speck of dust in this universe. And there’s only one point: to make a difference as much as you can, and do it well.” Examine, a free newsletter covering science, is sent every Tuesday.

World.title: Albanese and Pacific leaders to rebuke China after missile test. All except one
World.content:
PoliticsFederalPacific diplomacy Albanese and Pacific leaders to rebuke China after missile test. All except one Matthew Knott Updated September 3, 2026 — 10:00pm ,first published 1:34pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Koror City, Palau: Pacific leaders were preparing to call for at least a day’s notice of future ballistic weapons tests in a rebuke of China’s recent surprise firing of a long-range missile as they concluded a key regional gathering in Palau. The tiny island nation of Nauru was expected to be the only holdout as 17 of the 18 Pacific Island Forum members united to demand more transparency after being taken aback by Beijing’s test-firing an intercontinental long-range ballistic missile across the region in July. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and this year’s PIF chair earlier rejected any equivalence between American and Chinese missile testing, as Albanese declared China had shown “no respect” to the Pacific nations by firing a nuclear-capable weapon in their direction with minimal notice. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese speaking to reporters on the final day of the Pacific Islands Forum in Koror, Palau, on Thursday. AP Photo/Charlotte Graham-McLay Sources familiar with the draft leaders’ communiqué, scheduled to be released on Thursday evening, said the leaders were expected to register their concern about the recent test, noting the missile had flown over several member nations and without adequate notice.



Insisting they want the Pacific to be an “ocean of peace”, they were also expected to call for all states undertaking such tests to provide at least 24 hours’ notice in accordance with international protocols. Related Article Exclusive

Pacific diplomacy Key Pacific leader pushes for ‘united front’ against China’s missile tests China gave select countries only around two hours’ notice of its most recent test, the first time it had test-fired a ballistic missile from a nuclear-powered submarine into international waters. Some Pacific countries were not notified at all. In a win for Albanese and Palau’s President Surangel Whipps Jr, the draft statement being readied for release on Thursday afternoon went further than that issued by Pacific foreign ministers in August, which called only for “transparency and reassurance” on missile testing in the region. But it was not as severe as an earlier draft statement that called out China by name and said the Pacific “will not be defined by the strategic interests of others”.



Nauru was expected to register its opposition to this section of the communiqué in a footnote, reflecting its deepening ties with Beijing. Nauru and Kiribati had both earlier been singled out as blocking a powerful joint condemnation of China’s missile test. As he prepared to host Pacific leaders at his family home for a private retreat, Whipps Jr said he believed it was “important that we have a unified position” about China’s missile testing. Echoing his remarks in a recent interview with this masthead, Whipps said: “A unified Pacific voice is critical in getting Beijing to respect sovereignty, to respect transparency, and to be a responsible partner. I think that’s the message that we should send to Beijing.” The fact that the US regularly test-fires its own missiles into the region, mostly from California towards a testing range in the Marshall Islands, had hampered efforts to convince leaders to agree to a powerful joint statement.



Kiribati’s President Taneti Maamau told his nation’s parliament in August that while he was “not happy” with China over its test, he could not turn a blind eye to missile testing by the US and other countries. Albanese told reporters on Thursday that “the situations are very different”, arguing: “The US gives proper notice, has an agreement with the Marshall Islands. What we saw with the Chinese test was a firing of a missile with very little notice.” Related Article Analysis

Pacific diplomacy China’s Pacific missile launch is a diplomatic misfire He also noted China had fired its missile from a nuclear-powered submarine towards Nauru and Tuvalu “with no respect for those nations, and that is why it brought such a strong response from the Pacific, including from Australia”. Standing in front of a solar power plant co-funded by Australia, Whipps backed Albanese, saying: “The United States has an agreement with the Marshall Islands. They notify and they say it’s going there. What about the rest of us in the Pacific? Don’t we deserve the same? As I have said, there’s a there’s a lot of space between Japan and Guam. Why don’t you send it there?”



Whipps has strongly defended Taiwan’s right to participate in the Pacific Islands Forum as a development partner despite strong protestations from China. The early days of the summit were overshadowed by a warning from China’s Pacific envoy that there would be “consequences” for Taiwan’s strong representation at this year’s event. Whipps said maintaining the longstanding principle that both China and Taiwan can attend the forum as partners was “keeping the Pacific together because we respect each other’s sovereignty, we respect each other’s partnerships and we should maintain that because we are one family”. Palau, a former US territory, is one of the few nations left in the world that continues to formally recognise Taiwan rather than Beijing. World.title: ‘You have to hope for a time like this’: The full story behind Will Day’s tears
World.content:
SportAFLAFL 2026 ‘You have to hope for a time like this’: The full story behind Will Day’s tears Peter Ryan September 4, 2026 — 1:11am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Loading

Perth: Will Day’s emotions were not the same as his teammates after the Hawks claimed the first sport in this year’s preliminary finals with their brilliant win over Fremantle. He was in tears in a post-match interview, and then hugged his mum, Monique, and dad, Julian, in the Optus Stadium rooms with as much vigour as any of the 57 fierce tackles the Hawks had laid during the pressure-packed win, 5.10 (40) to 10.12 (72). After missing the past two finals series through injury, he had finally made it to the line for his first final. Will Day is arguably the Hawks’ most important player. AFL Photos Sam Mitchell knew how big a moment it was for the 25-year-old, saying post-game he could only imagine how he must have felt when he woke up on Thursday morning with the match just hours away.



Day decided there was only one way for him to attack what was ahead of him. “I just stripped back all the pressure, [and] took off all the expectation,” Day said. “I knew just by being out there I was going to help the team, so I did not want to try to do too much.” View post on X As he spoke, the emotion welled in his eyes again as familiar faces in the rooms loomed in his vision. “I just keep locking eyes with a lot of people that have helped me so much ... they are happy tears,” he said.



Happy tears were everywhere for Hawks fans who have ridden Day’s journey, ruing his absence through injury in their past two finals series when they seemed a midfielder short. After missing out on securing Essendon skipper Zach Merrett through the trade period, they then had their summer ruined by the sight of Day leaving the track with a shoulder injury in early January. James Sicily, who was brilliant in the qualifying final, celebrates the win with co-captain Jai Newcombe. AFL Photos The optimism most Hawks fans carry as though it’s a birth right suddenly slipped. To make matters worse, Day, himself, was quite reasonably wondering how his shoulder had become as pear-shaped as his career.



“[I was] pretty defeated. The last two finals series, especially last year losing the preliminary final, you feel so helpless, you just want to be out there and help,” Day said. Related Article AFL 2026 Dockers v Hawks player ratings: From a skipper’s career night, to the gun forwards who disappeared “It was tough early [this year], but you just have to switch to a positive outlook. It was very tough and very much easier said than done, but you just have to hope for a time like this, and it has been so worth it.” Against the Dockers, he was more than just out there helping. With James Sicily putting on a masterclass down back with a best-on-ground performance alongside his defensive allies Josh Battle, Blake Hardwick and Tom Barrass (who all dominated their opponents), the scene was set for Day to break open the game.



When the Dockers threatened to charge with minutes remaining in the third quarter, Day won two critical possessions that helped Nick Watson to deliver the settler. Editor's pick Exclusive

AFL 2026 Sydney Swan Nick Blakey tells associates he wants to be traded Watson, Dylan Moore and Jack Ginnivan rattled the Dockers’ defence with their pressure from the start, while the Hawks surprised the Dockers by pushing Jack Gunston high and leaving Mabior Chol deep. There was nothing Hollywood about the Hawks this time around. Instead, they produced a low-budget, no frills classic. Day finished the match with 24 disposals and eight centre clearances to show why he was so missed in September.



Mitchell hugged him post-match. He knew what his midfield star had overcome to be there with his mates, one match away from being in a grand final. View post on X “He showed it a lot more than I did, but I felt exactly how he looked after the game,” Mitchell said. The contrast with Justin Longmuir could not have been more stark as the Dockers coach attempted to rally his demoralised team after their first loss at home for the season. Day (centre) sings the Hawks’ famous song alongside Nick Watson, Mabior Chol, coach Sam Mitchell, and Dylan Moore. AFL Photos



“It’s not the way we wanted it to go [tonight], but we are not dead and buried,” he said. The Dockers could do worse than look to the way Day responded to his January jolt for inspiration. Because, to adapt a line from Mike Brady’s One Day in September, the resilient Hawks midfielder is finally seeing “the joy that hard work brings”.
