AFL Photos (26) Hayden Young: His early ball use was uncharacteristically poor and he struggled to generate his usual damage through the midfield. 4/10 (28) Neil Erasmus: One of Fremantle’s better early contributors, using the ball with purpose and looking through the corridor when others played safe. 6/10



(30) Nathan O’Driscoll: Needed to be stronger aerially early, but lifted his intensity and produced a fierce third-quarter tackle on Newcombe. 3/10 (31) Brandon Walker: A surprise inclusion for just his second game of the year, he competed bravely on Watson before an ankle roll contributed to another Hawks goal and his night done. 5/10 (32) Michael Frederick: Was unable to find space or use his speed, remaining largely unsighted. 2/10 Josh Treacy and his teammates had a horror night against a rampaging Hawks side. AFL Photos (35) Josh Treacy: He fought a difficult battle against Hawthorn’s organised defence but had little impact and went without a single kick deep into the third term. 2/10



(39) Sam Switkowski: He had a brilliant third quarter and kicked a huge goal to give Fremantle a (slight) sniff – the first finals major of his career. 6/10 (43) Isaiah Dudley: Missed an early opportunity but grew into the contest, improving his defensive pressure and contributing to Fremantle’s second-half ball movement. 4/10 (44) Matthew Johnson: One of Fremantle’s better midfielders in the first half, competing strongly and providing some composure amid Hawthorn’s pressure. 5/10 Sam Mitchell embraces Nick Watson after a finals win for the ages. AFL Photos



Hawthorn (1) Harry Morrison: Showed a few flashy moments midway through the third term. He can point to kicking the first goal of the final term, giving Hawthorn a match-high 38-point lead, for his golden moment. 5.5/10 (2) Mitch Lewis: A player of influence. He overcame a shoulder injury scare just before half-time. Look back to the early minutes of the game, when the action was hot, and Lewis pulled off a great run-down tackle and earned a free kick. 7/10 (3) Jai Newcombe: Not Hawthorn’s most important or valuable player, but that was a good sign for the brown and gold. Led Hawthorn’s tackle count at the main break, however. 6/10 (4) Jarman Impey: Reliable deep in defence in his All-Australian season. It was hard to find fault with his game as Hawthorn’s defence shone brightly all the way. 6/10



(5) Nick Watson: A top game. Lively and dangerous from start to finish, he kicked a goal out of nowhere – Hawthorn’s first – after just six minutes. It was emblematic of Hawthorn’s smash and grab approach. For Hawthorn’s most “Hollywood” player, it was instead a blue-collar night. 8/10 View post on X (6) James Sicily: A sterling game and one easily worthy of best on ground honours. A pillar in Hawthorn’s brutal defensive unit all match, he completely nullified Voss’ danger and influence, especially in the first half when the win was set up. Composed and reliable, this was a true leader’s match. 9/10 (8) Dylan Moore: He kicked Hawthorn’s second goal – again when the match was up for grabs – but it was his work-rate that stood out. “That workrate is as good as it gets,” reflected Kane Cornes on Seven, noting Moore’s ability to run hard back at goal. “Their tackling in the forward half has been unbelievable.” 6.5/10 (9) Connor Macdonald: Got better and better as the match wore on, and had some influence in the third term when Hawthorn had to keep the threatening Fremantle at bay. 6/10



(10) Karl Amon: Another solid contributor. By early in the final quarter he only had kicks – not handballs – on the tally board, showing just how much the Hawks rely on his foot skills. 5.5/10 (12) Will Day: One of Hawthorn’s best, who effectively became “the Clearance King”. Like others, Day got better and better as the game wore on and never stopped running. He went one-on-one with Brayshaw at stages and won the battle. 7.5/10 View post on X (15) Blake Hardwick: Went to the dangerous Reid early on. Hawthorn basically didn’t have a passenger in their 23, and Hardwick deserves recognition too. 5.5/10 (16) Massimo D’Ambrosio: Had a fantastic game and was influential (especially in the first quarter) when the game was being won. While he missed two shots at goal in the opening stanza, he dragged in nine touches as he regularly found space with his hard-running. 8/10



(17) Lloyd Meek: Probably won’t get enough plaudits for an impressive game. Won the opening tap-out against Luke Jackson but, yes, was done for holding the ball moments later. Got some eye-catching clearances, a trait normally reserved for his immediate foe Jackson. 7.5/10 Editor's pick Opinion

AFL 2026 In an AFL world of corporate-style spin, we shouldn’t slam North’s leaders for speaking their ‘Clarko’ truth Jake Niall Chief football writer, The Age (18) Mabior Chol: Did his bit and with style. As Hawthorn ran with Jack Gunston a bit further from goal than normal, Chol became the focal point in the forward line. Importantly, he got physical in countless marking contests, bringing the ball to ground at the very least. 7/10 (19) Jack Gunston: He gave Freo’s Oscar McDonald a bath. He regularly beat his man in the first half as Hawthorn stamped their authority on the game. By early in the second term, the veteran already had his two goals. He only touched the ball five times, but that didn’t matter. 7.5/10 (23) Josh Weddle: Another player vying to be Hawthorn’s best (behind Sicily) on a memorable night for the brown and gold. He was especially influential in the second quarter as Hawthorn looked to consolidate their great start. 8/10



Josh Weddle and the Hawks were all over Sam Switkowski and the Dockers. AFL Photos (24) Josh Battle: He played an outstanding game and was a crucial member of Hawthorn’s brilliant defensive unit. He went to Treacy and won that battle in a horrid game for Freo’s forwards. Dragged in 16 disposals in a top game. 8/10 (25) Josh Ward: Another top contributor, he worked hard across the game. In one first-quarter moment, he pulled off an excellent pass to D’Ambrosio up forward, but his teammate was off-line with the kick. Raised his arms in celebration after a defensive spoil by a teammate at one point. 6/10 (28) Cam Mackenzie: Another player who had a growing influence across the game. Had 11 touches by half-time and finished with 20. 6.5/10 (33) Jack Ginnivan: Had an unsung, low-key role early for the Hawks after returning to the team, but the 2023 Collingwood premiership player had a huge moment in the second half by taking a composed mark, and going back and kicking a goal that, again, kept Freo at bay. 6.5/10



Tom Barrass and the Hawks didn’t give the Dockers an inch of space all night. Getty Images (37) Tom Barrass: He played a brilliant defensive game. He manned Jye Amiss for most of the game and, like others in the brown and gold, won his night. Look back at the moment when Barrass applied an excellent punch deep in defence just before half-time. That was telling. Then in the third term he took a few key intercept marks. 8/10 (40) Max Beattie: An inexperienced player who looked comfortable out there in what could have been a tough environment. He did have one bad turnover in the second term when he really shouldn’t have been run down. Only had about 60 per cent game time. 4.5/10 (42) Bailey Macdonald: Also had limited game time and picked up eight touches. There were no Hawthorn passengers, remember. 5/10 Keep up to date with the best AFL coverage in the country.

World.title: Sydney scientist behind ‘moon landing’ cancer vaccine wins top science prize
World.content:
NationalCancer Sydney scientist behind ‘moon landing’ cancer vaccine wins top science prize Angus Dalton September 3, 2026 — 10:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The scientist who transformed advanced melanoma into a treatable cancer and led a recent large-scale trial into a world-first personalised mRNA cancer vaccine has won the research prize at Australia’s premier science awards. Professor Georgina Long was cautious to discuss the melanoma vaccine trial given that full results won’t be released until October, but described it as an “absolute landmark, fork-in-the-road for cancer” ahead of being awarded the Eureka Prize for Scientific Research at the Australian Museum on Thursday night. Professor Georgina Long has won the Eureka Prize for Scientific Research. Tim Bauer “It represents a huge body of work and team effort, and it’s an honour, really, to represent all the people that I lead,” the former Australian of the Year said of the award. “We’re a small but mighty country. We’ve got to keep the investments in Australia. We’ve got to take greater risks.”



Long is on a sabbatical in Lisbon, Portugal, away from her duties as medical director of the Melanoma Institute Australia at the University of Sydney to think and plan the next stages of her research. The new vaccine, developed by Moderna and Merck, aims to prevent recurrence of melanoma after a tumour is removed. Long was the principal investigator of the phase 3 trial and said it provided “the first real data that demonstrates mRNA technology can absolutely change the face of cancer”. Without yet providing details, the companies said on August 20 that the late-stage trial produced clinically and statistically significant improvements in high-risk melanoma patients. Moderna’s market value leapt by $62 billion in a day. “We are not even a speck of dust in this universe. And there’s only one point: to make a difference as much as you can, and do it well.” Professor Georgina Long For the trial, 1137 high-risk melanoma patients were given the cancer drug Keytruda. Half also received the experimental vaccine.



Researchers sequenced patients’ tumours after surgery and identified mutations, unique to each person’s cancer, that code for abnormal proteins on the surface of cancer cells called neoantigens. A custom mRNA vaccine was crafted for each patient based on the specific neoantigens in their tumour, teaching the immune system exactly what to look for. Normal cells have proteins which stop the immune system attacking healthy tissue. Melanomas hijack these cellular signals, masquerading as normal cells and growing unchecked. Keytruda stops this from happening, ripping off melanoma’s invisibility cloak. Results presented from a much smaller phase 2 trial in June showed combining Keytruda and the vaccine led to a 49 per cent reduction in the risk of recurrence or death, compared to just the cancer drug.



As the president of Merck put it, the mRNA vaccine, called intismeran autogene, gives the immune system the scent of the enemy. Then Keytruda releases “the dogs of war”. “It is a moon-landing moment,” Long said. Others are investigating whether the same approach could work in lung and pancreatic cancer. Britain’s King Charles is briefed by co-medical director Georgina Long as he visits the Melanoma Institute of Australia in Sydney in 2024. AFP The award on Thursday was in recognition of more than a decade of research. When Long started working in melanoma, faces in her waiting room would change within six to nine months. “It was the orphan cancer up until about 15 years ago. You think of the worst cancers now, and I can name them – pancreatic cancer [and] glioblastoma – melanoma was worse than those two. Nothing worked ... chemotherapy did nothing.



“The waiting room would be completely different because people died, and the majority of people died within 12 months.” Long and her collaborators have turned that story around. A trial Long led in 2018 found combining two immunotherapy drugs – nivolumab and ipilimumab – had a 46 per cent response rate in patients with melanoma that had metastasised to the brain, compared with 20 per cent when just one drug was used. The finding changed clinical practice “overnight”. Seven-year follow-up data reported in The Lancet Oncology last year found 51 per cent of patients given the combination immunotherapy as a first-line treatment had survived, compared with 29 per cent on the single drug. That’s just some of Long’s work, which is credited with ushering the survival rate of advanced melanoma from 5 to 50 per cent. She and colleague Professor Richard Scolyer were named Australians of the Year in 2024 for their research on cancer.



Crucially, tactics pioneered in melanoma treatment have gone on to have a “massive impact” in cancers of the lung, kidney, head, neck and bladder and some lymphomas, Long said. Professor Georgina Long and Professor Richard Scolyer at a ceremony in Canberra where they were named joint Australians of the Year in 2024. Alex Ellinghausen “Every single drug developed in melanoma first … has gone on to impact an extraordinary number of patients with other cancers,” Long said. Long’s focus is on the patients resistant to treatment: the difficult territory between what we know and don’t know where “courageous medicine happens”, such as the testing of drugs never trialled in people. She calls it the “third space”. “We’ve cured 50 per cent, [but] we’ve still got 50 per cent who die, and they die quickly like the old days. They are our third space,” she said.



“We’re all on this planet for a tiny, tiny, tiny time. We are not even a speck of dust in this universe. And there’s only one point: to make a difference as much as you can, and do it well.” Examine, a free newsletter covering science, is sent every Tuesday.

World.title: Albanese and Pacific leaders to rebuke China after missile test. All except one
World.content:
PoliticsFederalPacific diplomacy Albanese and Pacific leaders to rebuke China after missile test. All except one Matthew Knott Updated September 3, 2026 — 10:00pm ,first published 1:34pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Koror City, Palau: Pacific leaders were preparing to call for at least a day’s notice of future ballistic weapons tests in a rebuke of China’s recent surprise firing of a long-range missile as they concluded a key regional gathering in Palau. The tiny island nation of Nauru was expected to be the only holdout as 17 of the 18 Pacific Island Forum members united to demand more transparency after being taken aback by Beijing’s test-firing an intercontinental long-range ballistic missile across the region in July. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and this year’s PIF chair earlier rejected any equivalence between American and Chinese missile testing, as Albanese declared China had shown “no respect” to the Pacific nations by firing a nuclear-capable weapon in their direction with minimal notice. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese speaking to reporters on the final day of the Pacific Islands Forum in Koror, Palau, on Thursday. AP Photo/Charlotte Graham-McLay Sources familiar with the draft leaders’ communiqué, scheduled to be released on Thursday evening, said the leaders were expected to register their concern about the recent test, noting the missile had flown over several member nations and without adequate notice.



Insisting they want the Pacific to be an “ocean of peace”, they were also expected to call for all states undertaking such tests to provide at least 24 hours’ notice in accordance with international protocols. Related Article Exclusive

Pacific diplomacy Key Pacific leader pushes for ‘united front’ against China’s missile tests China gave select countries only around two hours’ notice of its most recent test, the first time it had test-fired a ballistic missile from a nuclear-powered submarine into international waters. Some Pacific countries were not notified at all. In a win for Albanese and Palau’s President Surangel Whipps Jr, the draft statement being readied for release on Thursday afternoon went further than that issued by Pacific foreign ministers in August, which called only for “transparency and reassurance” on missile testing in the region. But it was not as severe as an earlier draft statement that called out China by name and said the Pacific “will not be defined by the strategic interests of others”.



Nauru was expected to register its opposition to this section of the communiqué in a footnote, reflecting its deepening ties with Beijing. Nauru and Kiribati had both earlier been singled out as blocking a powerful joint condemnation of China’s missile test. As he prepared to host Pacific leaders at his family home for a private retreat, Whipps Jr said he believed it was “important that we have a unified position” about China’s missile testing. Echoing his remarks in a recent interview with this masthead, Whipps said: “A unified Pacific voice is critical in getting Beijing to respect sovereignty, to respect transparency, and to be a responsible partner. I think that’s the message that we should send to Beijing.” The fact that the US regularly test-fires its own missiles into the region, mostly from California towards a testing range in the Marshall Islands, had hampered efforts to convince leaders to agree to a powerful joint statement.



Kiribati’s President Taneti Maamau told his nation’s parliament in August that while he was “not happy” with China over its test, he could not turn a blind eye to missile testing by the US and other countries. Albanese told reporters on Thursday that “the situations are very different”, arguing: “The US gives proper notice, has an agreement with the Marshall Islands. What we saw with the Chinese test was a firing of a missile with very little notice.” Related Article Analysis

Pacific diplomacy China’s Pacific missile launch is a diplomatic misfire He also noted China had fired its missile from a nuclear-powered submarine towards Nauru and Tuvalu “with no respect for those nations, and that is why it brought such a strong response from the Pacific, including from Australia”. Standing in front of a solar power plant co-funded by Australia, Whipps backed Albanese, saying: “The United States has an agreement with the Marshall Islands. They notify and they say it’s going there. What about the rest of us in the Pacific? Don’t we deserve the same? As I have said, there’s a there’s a lot of space between Japan and Guam. Why don’t you send it there?”



Whipps has strongly defended Taiwan’s right to participate in the Pacific Islands Forum as a development partner despite strong protestations from China. The early days of the summit were overshadowed by a warning from China’s Pacific envoy that there would be “consequences” for Taiwan’s strong representation at this year’s event. Whipps said maintaining the longstanding principle that both China and Taiwan can attend the forum as partners was “keeping the Pacific together because we respect each other’s sovereignty, we respect each other’s partnerships and we should maintain that because we are one family”. Palau, a former US territory, is one of the few nations left in the world that continues to formally recognise Taiwan rather than Beijing. World.title: Gloriavale Christian School registration cancelled following special ERO review
World.content:
Gloriavale Christian School's registration cancelled Checkpoint Download MP3 6m

The secretary for education has confirmed Gloriavale Christian School's registration as a private school will be cancelled, after considering the findings of a special Education Review Office review.

Secretary Ellen MacGregor-Reid told the school's leaders in December that she was cancelling its registration because of serious concerns the school was not a physically and emotionally safe place for students.

The school remains open as a result of a High Court challenge by the board, with a judicial review hearing set down for three days in October.

On Thursday, Education Services deputy secretary Geoff Short said the ministry had applied to the court to lift orders preventing the school's closure.

"The secretary for education has decided to cancel Gloriavale Christian School's registration as a private school after considering findings from a special review by the Education Review Office," he said.

"The school currently has around 80 students enrolled and the ministry will work with the school community to determine the most practical timing for the school's closure, with students' best interests guiding those discussions.

"The ministry has applied to the court to lift interim orders relating to the secretary for education's December 2025 decision to cancel the school's registration as a private school to enable this latest decision to be implemented.

"Further information is being provided directly to affected families."

Education Minister Erica Stanford said she trusted that the secretary's decision-making process was robust.

"The secretary for education clearly has concerns, as do the Education Review Office, into the quality of the education that's being provided and the situation those children are in.

Erica Stanford. RNZ / Nick Monro

"I have absolute and utter confidence in Ellen MacGregor-Reid as the secretary for education to have made the right decision."

The special review considered whether Gloriavale met the private school registration criteria and the extent to which it had addressed previous Education Review Office (ERO) concerns identified in a November 2024 visit and July 2025 special review.

ERO's special review report published on Thursday said the school was not meeting one of eight registration criteria, to provide a physically and emotionally safe place for students.

"Inconsistencies between the school and community child protection policies limit assurance that governance oversight is effective and that the school is consistently a physically and emotionally safe place for students," the report said.

"Information was withheld from ERO in relation to provision, monitoring and reporting requirements for health and safety to and by the premises owners.

"ERO is not confident that systems are operating effectively to identify, manage and monitor risk over time or that reasonable steps have been taken."

The report noted that the Teaching Council was investigating two allegations of staff misconduct. The school had provided ERO with the letter of suspension for one staff member.

"Staff members subject to role restrictions have continued to operate in restricted areas. Evidence gathered onsite indicates that one staff member continued to participate in board meetings, despite a requirement that they not do so," the report said.

ERO said Gloriavale's school met the criteria relating to suitable premises, provision of tuition, suitable staffing, suitable equipment, curriculum, managers assessed as fit and proper and suitable tuition standards.

"Overall, some improvement is evident. However, these improvements are partial and, in key areas, not yet sustained," ERO said.

"ERO is not yet confident that the school's systems are sufficiently embedded, consistent and reliable to ensure ongoing compliance with the requirements for registration over time."

The report said the school was providing education for students in Years 1 to 8, with a roll of 84 students.

Gloriavale Leavers Support Trust manager Liz Gregory told Checkpoint she believed the school would always struggle to meet safety criteria.

"Just with the history of Gloriavale, just the way it has operated and the coercive controlling nature. Basically I think the past has caught up with their present," she said.

Gregory said student enrolment at a mainstream school would be a "last resort" for Gloriavale.

"They will keep fighting. Every other option would be preferable to them. It does look like a school closure will go ahead, what the final schooling options look like for the students there, that's yet to be seen."

In a statement, the Gloriavale Christian School board said it was considering its options.

"The school strongly disagrees with the ministry's decision and is currently considering its options to challenge it. Given that the matter is ongoing, we will not be making any further comment at this time," the board said.

Ministry letters to Gloriavale obtained by RNZ under the Official Information Act in May detailed concerns from community members, specialists and agencies about the private school, as the secretary moved to cancel its registration.

The letters noted concerns about most teenagers being prevented from progressing beyond Year 11, a lack of support for young victims and abusers and students not being able to use school toilets without fear.

Separately, an Education Review Office special review of homeschooling by Gloriavale families concluded that they were not meeting the legal requirements.

The agency said homeschooling families were living and learning in overcrowded hostels that could be unsafe and some of the children were struggling to write.

In June the ministry said two surplus classrooms were relocated to Awahono School in Ahaura to support roll fluctuations and could also cater for Gloriavale students if families choose to enrol their children there in future.

In a statement in December, Gloriavale's school board said it was "deeply disappointed" by the ministry's decision to cancel its registration.

World.title: Middlemore Hospital swamped in 'appalling' late-night surge of patients
World.content:
An emergency department (ED) doctor at Auckland's Middlemore Hospital says there were more than 100 people waiting to be seen late on Wednesday night.

They told RNZ it was an "appalling" situation for all involved.

They said Middlemore hit 103 patients waiting in queue at 11.15pm, with seven doctors rostered overnight.

They said these patients were in addition to those already under treatment and waiting for beds.

Last year's record was 109 patients, they said.

The nurses union says nurses described the past 24 hours as hectic, staff swamped with patients with medical issues stemming from the flu.

Health New Zealand group director of operations for Counties Manukau, Vanessa Thornton, said in a statement there were 457 presentations to Middlemore's ED in the 24-hour period from midnight on Wednesday, following consecutive days of high demand for care.

Earlier on one of the days in August, Middlemore's ED saw 494 presentations - the highest number of patients over a 24-hour period for this year.

Thornton said the demand reflected increased seasonal illness in the community.

"Additional staffing and operation support is being brought on at Middlemore, and we are reviewing elective services.

"Where appropriate, patients are being moved from Middlemore to Manukau Health Park to improve hospital flow, and we are looking to maximise the use of Hospital in the Home and work regionally with other hospitals to improve patient flow and free up capacity."

"Hospital in Home" allows eligible patients to receive hospital-level care in their own home rather than staying in hospital, a Health NZ communications staffer explained.

RNZ has approached HNZ for comment on whether patients from Middlemore ED have been transferred to other regional hospitals on Wednesday.

New Zealand Nurses Organisation (NZNO) president Anne Daniels, who's also an ED nurse at a tertiary hospital, questions how HNZ will find the resourcing to help with the situation at Middlemore Hospital.

"On the face of it they're actually doing something, I'm pleased that they got a plan in place, "but the fact is that all those strategies require resourcing and there aren't enough nurses, we know that for a fact - we know there's a total recruitment freeze, even though there's 1400 vacancies on Te Whatu Ora's job list for nurses," she said.

Daniels said hospital transfers for sick patients require nurses, and she wonders whether the people HNZ are assigning those jobs are competent to do the transfers.

She pointed to a report by NZNO that found New Zealand public hospitals were short of 587 nurses for every shift in 2024.

Daniels said while "Hospital in Home" is a good strategy, district nursing staffing is already overstretched.

"All of these things are a sign of desperation," she added.

Hospitals already weren't coping before the flu came, and now the influx of flu patients has made existing problems in the health system more visible, said Daniels.

She said EDs across the country were struggling.

Daniels said she took a neighbour into ED three times these past few weeks and was "flabbergasted" at what she saw.

World.title: Conservation bill clause puts economic growth ahead of conservation, critics say
World.content:
The government has kept a controversial clause in its Conservation Amendment Bill, which critics say undermines the purpose of conservation law.

The draft bill, released by the Environment Select Committee, retains clause 6(ea) which says the Department of Conservation (DOC) should recognise and enable "economic opportunities" on conservation land to "the greatest extent practicable".

Greenpeace spokesperson Gen Toop said the government was attacking the fundamental principle of conservation land.

"What we are talking about here is public conservation land - that is land that is supposed to be protected and preserved for nature to thrive and for the public and for future generations to enjoy.

"It is not land that has been set aside for economic exploitation, but that is what this government is trying to change the law so it will be able to happen on that land."

Conservation Minister Tama Potaka backed down from other proposed changes earlier this year which would have made 2.8 million hectares of conservation land eligible for sale.

The revised bill has removed those changes.

But Toop said the bill was still "rotten to its core".

"We expect that if they are able to pass this bill we will see more mines - more open cast mines - on public conservation land.

"It's our opinion that conservation land should be a place where the native wildlife of New Zealand can thrive, and it should be a place we protect, for future generations can enjoy."

She said a proposal to set up visitor amenity areas on conservation land, which included toilets, visitor centres, accommodation, car parks, restaurants and cafes, was also controversial.

Toop said there were very few safeguards from development in these areas - and one day could see conservation land locked away for private luxury resorts.

"We do not want to see ancient forests felled for car parks."

Toop said she expected thousands of people to march against the bill later this month.

Green Party MP Ricardo Menéndez March was also against the clause.

"Allowing economic development at any cost without the consideration or protection of the environment will simply see environmental degradation and profits put over people and the planet."

Conservation Minister Tama Potaka said submissions were ongoing and he expected further amendments to the bill before the final report due in November.

He said the redrafted version of the bill was a procedural step to remove the land exchange and disposal provisions from it.

World.title: All Blacks bring in fresh legs for third test against the Springboks
World.content:
All Blacks coach Dave Rennie has made three changes to his starting XV for Sunday morning's third test against the Springboks in Johannesburg.

Hooker Codie Taylor, who started in the first and second tests, has been replaced in the run-on side by Asafo Aumua, who gets his first start in the test series after some impressive performances coming off the bench.

Taylor has been left out of the matchday 23, with Samisoni Taukei'aho coming into the reserves.

George Bower and Tyrel Lomax are retained as the starting props.

Sam Darry, who hasn't featured in either of the first two tests, starts at lock alongside Tupou Vaa'i, pushing Fabian Holland to the bench.

Peter Lakai, who was also impressive coming off the bench in Cape Town, will start at blindside flanker, with Simon Parker, who started at No. 6 last weekend, omitted from the matchday 23.

Peter Lakai will start at blindside in the third test against the Springboks. Photosport

Luke Jacobson remains at openside with captain Ardie Savea at No. 8.

Wallace Sititi will make his first test appearance in the series, coming into the 23 as loose forward impact.

The starting backline remains the same as last weekend with Cam Roigard and Ruben Love in the halves, Jordie Barrett and Quinn Tupaea in the midfield and Damian McKenzie, Will Jordan and Leroy Carter in the back three.

Prop Ethan de Groot and lock Josh Lord, who missed the second test with concussion, have cleared concussion protocols, but Rennie decided it would be best to give them another week to recover.

With the series tied 1-1 both sides are desperate to win the last test on South African soil before the fourth and final match in Baltimore in the US.

Sunday morning's (NZT) match is at the Soccer City stadium in Soweto, Johannesburg, which holds about 94,000 fans.

World.title: 'Under pressure' seed and grain seek green shoots in challenging market
World.content:
Market pressures are mounting on New Zealand's small but significant agricultural seed and grain sectors, considered vital to the $64 billion food and fibre industries.

High operating costs, wet weather, import competition and succession were some of the woes facing the country's legacy arable sector, raised at an industry event in Christchurch this week.

Seed and grain exports earned around $325 million each year in imports, largely driven by pasture and vegetable seeds, with just under half going to the European Union, followed by Australia, the United States, Japan and China.

But options for cropping farmers to sell their vegetable and pasture seeds or grains like malting or feeding barley locally were shrinking in Aotearoa.

In a blow after blow scenario just this year, major food companies McCain Foods and Heinz Wattie's confirmed they would close vegetable processing factories and cut vegetable product lines, and Malteurop will also shut its Rangitikei malthouse later this month.

The closures, affecting hundreds of farmers, would also have flow-on effects for rural service providers like seed processors and merchants, prompting conversations around industry resilience at the Seed and Grain New Zealand conference in Ōtautahi.

Wheat being harvested in Canterbury. SUPPLIED/Foundation for Arable Research

Chief executive Sarah Clark told attendees on Tuesday, domestic arable production should be strengthened.

"A resilient and sustainable arable sector is essential to New Zealand's food security, agricultural productivity, export performance, and to regional economies," she said.

"There are challenges including rising costs, climate-related disruption, regulatory burden and ongoing loss of productive land to dairy conversion."

In key cropping areas like Canterbury, some farmers were exiting arable or adding more livestock into their systems, with many chasing white gold in dairy.

High milk prices coupled with an end to the Canterbury Regional Council's ban on intensive dairy farm conversions were expected to see tens of thousands of more dairy cows added to the region's herd.

Harvests continue decline

It was a busy summer for cereal growers, though difficult harvest conditions were reported in most growing areas largely due to wet weather.

The 2026 harvest produced around 824,709 tonnes of wheat, barley and oats across more than 94,290 hectares, according to the Foundation for Arable Research (FAR)'s latest cereals survey of 110 farms as of 1 July.

Cereal production fell 3 percent on the year prior, by about 23,000 tonnes across six cereals, with harvested area down 4 percent.

Further declines were expected looking to the 2027 season with the harvest area forecast to drop 14 percent to around 81,400ha.

A field of clover that's gone to seed. David Birkett

Association president Edward Luisetti of Canterbury's Luisetti Seeds said it was a bad, wet arable harvest this year.

"The past 12 months have been challenging, while other sectors within agriculture have been experiencing record prices, seed and grain and the arable sector as a whole has been struggling," he said.

But he said the industry was collaborating with others across agriculture and with government officials to explore opportunities for recovery.

"There are green shoots, but let's hope they don't get frost heave or whipped out with Glyphosate."

Government officials on watch

The industry's challenges have caught the attention of new Associate Agriculture Minister and Wairarapa MP for National, Mike Butterick.

Speaking at the event, he said arable was integral to primary industries.

"There's no avoiding the fact that the sector is under pressure.

"Higher fuel, fertiliser, agrichemicals, machinery and labour costs that makes it difficult to protect margins even when productivity remains high.

"International competition remains intense and the impacts of bad weather can last for more than just a season as well.

"Those challenges have understandably raised concerns about confidence and future investment across the sector.

Butterick said the government was focussed on improving the planning and consenting regime and expanding market access for exporters, helped by free trade agreements.

He said officials had secured new market access for carrot seed into Mexico, and efforts were underway to try to get ryegrass seed into India, Peru, and radish seed into Ecuador.

"In many respects, the success of our wider agricultural story starts with arable sector.

"Seeds underpin agriculture and food security," he said.

Associate Agriculture Minister Mike Butterick with Seed and Grain New Zealand chief executive Sarah Clark at the industry conference in Christchurch on Wednesday. RNZ/Monique Steele

Also the Minister for Land Information, Butterick said the decisions by overseas-owned Heinz Wattie's and McCain Foods happened in the context of a lack of reliable water in Hawke's Bay and extremely volatile energy costs.

"Ultimately, it was a commercial decision that was made. But we do need to reflect as a country about some of the challenges, energy and water.

"A New Zealand company would've made the same decision, because those same underlying risks remain."

Butterick said New Zealand lacked access to capital and foreign investment was not a bad thing if it enabled New Zealand to grow.

Meanwhile, a forecast dry summer for the East Coast during El Niño was expected to drive up imports of palm kernel expeller (PKE) for dairy cows in particular, adding even more pressure on local maize growers competing with the usually cheaper feed supplement.

The Foundation for Arable Research (FAR) launched a landmark NZ Grown Grains certification last year to help consumers identify products made with local grain and promote local uptake among farmers.

It also released new research recently showing local feed grains had a lower carbon footprint than imported feeds, going off earlier assessments.

Freight and transport remained a top concern in the sector, like poor road conditions and ongoing challenges of getting grain between the North and South Islands via the Cook Strait.

Furthermore, back in July, Swire Shipping NZ cut its Pacifica domestic-flagged shipping service for containers and cargo between Tauranga, Auckland, Christchurch and Marsden Point.

World.title: String of earthquakes in Southern Alps not due to Alpine Fault - seismologist
World.content:
A string of earthquakes rumbling the Southern Alps north of Milford Sound are not due to the Alpine Fault, a seismologist says.

Dozens of aftershocks have been recorded in the lower South Island after a string of earthquakes that struck near Piopiotahi (Milford Sound) on Wednesday night.

A 5.5 magnitude earthquake struck about 6.15pm followed by a larger 5.6 shake shortly before 7pm.

Three further smaller quakes soon followed over the next hour.

The tremors have prompted calls for local authorities and central government to get around the table to nut out an emergency response plan.

Southland mayor warns of Milford Sound tsunami risk Morning Report Download MP3 6m

Southland's mayor Rob Scott was at his Lumsden home when an earthquake one-two punch struck the region.

According to GeoNet, almost 7000 people felt the quakes.

"Every earthquake seems to be different. The stronger one I felt was like a short sharp jolt," Scott said.

Both quakes were recorded at a depth of 5 kilometres.

Scott said the quakes served as a wake-up call around the area's emergency preparedness and how it will be funded.

"We've got a very small council and we're basically hosting a million people a year where there is a predominant risk lies," he said.

"For Milford, for something like that happening during the day, around 1pm during that peak time, when you've got 3500 people in the area. We need to be looking after them."

Earlier this week Scott suggested a possible limit on visitors to Milford Sound to lower the scale of a disaster - such as a tsunami or earthquake - following the devastating tragedy in Nepal.

Given Milford Sound's profile as the country's most renowned tourist attraction, central government should be involved, Scott said.

"It's a national crown jewel, it's a national treasure, it's something that we promote for people to come and see in New Zealand and it's in the national interest," he said.

"I think the drive and the funding for this work needs to come from a national level because it will be a national disaster if something did go wrong there. It's ensuring the right people in the right places because we can't just bury our heads in the sand and ignore it."

The aftershocks were expected to last for days with Earth Sciences NZ recording at least 81 known shakes since Wednesday night.

Earth Sciences NZ on-duty seismologist Sam Taylor-Offord said the quakes were not on the Alpine Fault.

"We're seeing a number of earthquakes that are about 15-20 kilometres southeast of the Alpine Fault and that is close. But there are many faults in this area."

The quakes were aligning with the Hollyford fault system, Taylor-Offord said.

Experts say the 600 kilometre Alpine Fault had a strong chance of rupturing in the next 50 years.

Taylor-Offord said determining what the future earthquake outlook looked like remained difficult.

"[There are] too many variables, but I can say this earthquake is close to the Alpine Fault which we know can host magnitude 7-8 earthquakes. We're expecting one in the next 50 years most likely.

World.title: Two people who were missing at Waikuku Beach brought to shore
World.content:
Two people who had gone missing at Waikuku Beach in Canterbury have been brought to the shore.

Emergency services have been searching for the pair since 6.30pm this evening, and police said they were found in the water by surf lifesavers.

St John ambulance said one person was in a serious condition and the other was in a moderate condition.

World.title: Greg O'Connor gives a bard's farewell to the House
World.content:
Outgoing Labour MP and former Deputy Speaker Greg O'Connor has something of a reputation around Parliament for his interest in poetry. It was fitting then that the MP for the disappearing North Wellington electorate of Ōhāriu, gave his entire valedictory speech in rhyming verse.

O'Connor has reportedly been known to spend some of his spare time tucked away in a corner of a Wellington suburban throwback, the Newlands Arms pub, putting pen to paper and composing stanzas on whatever subject takes his fancy.

His recent poetry-writing sessions, have likely featured preparing a farewell to Parliament. He took his colleagues, and a packed public gallery through his career, his background and his political convictions, while dishing out plenty of parting wisdom, and wry, sardonic comic relief along the way.

The Hansard record of Greg O'Connor's full valedictory statement is below.

A valedictory's a oncer, a privilege experienced by few, so I thought consigning it to verse would afford the moment its due.

There were other options, plenty of genres I could tap, I thought it might test the Speaker's patience, if I'd presented today in rap.

So, bow out I do before you, a humbling number have returned the RSVP. Not all MPs are afforded this privilege, many a parliamentary exit is involuntary.

I arrived nine years past, with Ōhāriu's blessing, though with a small-enough margin, that kept us till final count guessing.

To the good folk of my electorate, I'll always remain beholden, great local support, does the MP on their behalf embolden.

An electorate dominated by Mount Kaukau, the tower atop piercing the sky, which thanks to pest-free volunteers now has an increasingly native bird cry.

Being elected in to this House, and sitting up in the big Chair, has allowed use of the living and learning, that's gone into the making of this grey hair.

However, lessons and skills learnt before here, only get us in the door. The real honing of one's political craft, starts on this Chamber's floor.

VNP/Louis Collins

Most arrive as high achievers, and a desire to improve our world. With a determination to stand apart, when insults and vitriols hurled.

Such ideology seldom lasts, beyond the first derisory interjection. The aroha quickly melts away, with utu planned back in that direction.

But as I learnt as a young cop, no lesson comes without pain. Learning to hold one's own is how we best for our constituents gain.

There's those who abhor the division, believing it should all be done by consensus. Of course, removing robust debate would leave half the electorate defenceless.

In fact, there's plenty of times we largely agree; It's around philosophical differences we clash. Without an outlet for such digression of belief,

democracy will have done its dash.

I've had a privileged position in this place, arbitrating from the Speaker's Chair, in a world that's partisan and siloed, an ideal place to each argument hear.

You see much more while presiding; There's no place for members to hide. There are workhorses who carry a big load, the odd one happy to be along for the ride.

The MP demographic is pretty reflective, with personalities from quiet to loud. We look pretty much like the new New Zealand, though 'round one end of Myers-Briggs we crowd.

But for all that diversity, it's still down to numbers, however strongly the argument you mount, because to successfully prosecute your cause here, you need to learn how to count.

And as MMP matures and Kiwis become attuned to its power, mixes and matches of political persuasions are the reality of our politics now.

And while the theatre of question time is the public window to Parliament's soul, cross-party relationships are built outside here, even ignoring results of the latest poll.

Select committees and parliamentary trips, combined with sporting and cultural occasions, provide cross-party opportunities for dialogue, and in my case numerous abrasions.

I dragged this broken old body off to parliamentary rugby and cricket for the opportunity of cross-party mixing, though I did claim an ex-Black Caps' wicket. I should've invited Dion Nash here today.

So I reflect on my time in this place. Nine years has gone incredibly fast, proudly part of a mighty continuum which us all will long outlast.

I did manage a member's bill that passed through the House with ease, a law to curtail paedophiles' opportunities to offend against kids overseas.

Ultimately, Parliament's job is to pass laws, so I suppose in that regard I had some success, but it's the work we do for our constituents that rarely gets into the press.

Without a doubt, it's our staff members who are the heroes of answering the constituent's call. Leanne's been with me from the start. Actually, I found and recruited her in Johnsonville mall.

She'd run a pub in Johnsonville, so knew the local rogues, some here today. That's you, Kerry, Alan, Barry, Jono. She had kids at the local schools, so around the electorate knew her way.

She stayed with me all nine years, while Sophia taught her political nous. Knowing she always had my electorate back allowed me to concentrate on my work in this House.

We got her husband, John, voting for the first time ever. Honestly, I said, "Vote for whoever you like." But her real above and beyond was babysitting my disabled son, Mike.

Back to the topic of that mall, I met my office landlady in exactly the same spot. Within a month of being elected, I had secured staff and a location hot.

But while that mall proved a fertile recruiting ground, sadly, attempts to secure a rebuild have been frustrated. In any survey of what annoys my locals, "That bloody mall" is always top rated.

The powers of a local MP can't override land-banking calls. As Ronald Reagan would say to the Aussie owners, "Stride, bulldoze down those walls."

Now, sadly, I relinquish my Ōhāriu role, the electorate cruelly dissolved with the stroke of a pen. Normally when an MP says they lost their seat, some beggar has nicked it off of them.

In my case it's disappeared, gone to the graveyard of electorates past. I wonder, if it was held by a senior Minister, whether the axe would've come down as fast!

Ōhāriu's now divided in three, leaving locals to work out their new voting zone. Of course, it'll now take three MPs to do the job I used to do on my own.

I started my Police career up in Ōhāriu trying to keep northern streets free of crime, A slightly broader mandate as an MP, but people's needs don't seem to change with time.

The ethnic make-up is now way more diverse, and the housing's chomped up the farms, but if there's one place that's defied change, it's my mates in the Newlands Arms.

A true battlers' pub in a family suburb called Newlands, which looks very much like our new human fauna, there's an oasis of our past in its midst affectionately known as "Cobweb Corner".

Being comfortable in cafes and churches, with my wee red car announcing I'm around, meant I didn't need to hang around the office for citizens to know where I was to be found.

But most humbling of all, when I have my son Michael in tow, is that his sometimes intrusive and inquisitive nature could be challenging for those who didn't know.

But he was welcomed wherever we went, on sports fields and public meetings by all folk. I even once had the Chinese ambassador keeping him preoccupied while I spoke.

He proves people are inherently good, understanding there are those who will never survive on their own, from the generous Sir Mark and Dorothy, here today, to those putting up with him stealing their phone.

My vision was to build a role where Mike could participate too. It happened without ever being planned. He's now often expected to turn up too.

I spent 40 years in policing before plunging into this role. A new audience for all my war stories and police minister was my ultimate goal.

I'd policed pretty much everywhere possible, experienced Wairarapa's bombing and fires. I spent a year working undercover, where we got new names and survived as liars.

They were pretty formative years, where I met people smarter and cleverer than me, who, if they'd had the opportunities I've been afforded,

would have had lives likely crime free.

That's why I get frustrated when politicians with no idea yell, "More time!" Cleverer use of more shorter sentences can disrupt instead of displacing crime.

However, tough sentencing talk wins elections, so sheltered middle-class politicians talk tough. Making the crime and the punishment more proximate would mean our current cells are enough.

I do like the idea of the patch ban. Now they are hurriedly hidden when cops are around. That's a great message to impressionable youth, stopping gangsters from strutting around.

My undercover days taught me about gangs: That misogyny and stand-over rule. Forcing young ones to do their jail time is their most effective tool.

So that and detective work increased my understanding of policing's soul. This consolidation of my policing experiences set me up for my Police Association role.

It was from 20 years there as president, running a multimillion-dollar show, that I was exposed to the commercial world and understood the perils of poor cash-flow.

VNP/Louis Collins

So when I came to Parliament on the Jacinda wave, courtesy of Winston's then wise hand, I'd hoped a ministerial post might come my way eventually, once I'd learned the lie of the land.

However, a harsh lesson in politics was to follow: Media love you when you're providing a nice sound bite. But, as a politician, it's all about "Gotcha!" Any concessions become the highlight.

It resulted in a telling off from Jacinda herself, by phone, as it was done in a hurry. And while I was standing in an Indian takeaway deciding the spice level of my curry - and Sophia, here today, is my witness.

So it was backbench all the way, with a bird's eye view of the events that defined our time, during Christchurch terrorism and White Island, which dominated the party line.

And as a complete aside on the Christchurch shootings, the two cops who caught the offender once worked for me. They're types who lived close to the edge, but they're what we want tough cops to be.

Back now to the political career: By COVID, I was on the finance committee. The Reserve Bank Governor was a regular attendee, explaining his financial strategy.

As usual there's now a revision; Everyone's an expert in hindsight. It's so damned easy to forget those pictures of Italian doctors and nurses dying day and night.

Who can forget that first lockdown? We Wellington MPs got to play a special part. As the death toll around the world skyrocketed, here it never got off to that start.

We knew it was special times, that needed a response that was brave. A helluva lot of our elderly and sick would've been carted off to their grave.

Then came the aftermath. The term "anti-vaxxer" was born. A palpable anger and societal split came to a head out on Parliament's front lawn.

I personally came in every day, bringing my toothbrush when it looked like they'd Parliament surround. For those who condone or leverage mob rule, know civilisation quickly collapses when unbound.

If police had lost the battle that day, it would've been the country's eternal regret. I saw heroism in defence of New Zealand out there. I fear rewriting has minimised that threat.

And the House continued sitting, smelling of smoke permeating out on the green. I've witnessed plenty of violent behaviour, and this was as perilous as I've seen.

I'm often asked if I miss policing. That's one day I'd have gone back in the door. Those men and woman who battled out front dug deep to uphold the law.

Not long after that I was made Deputy Speaker, not a role I'd sought or understood. The bipartisan nature is certainly appealing, and you work out who at their job is any good.

I discouraged the reading of speeches and members for their oratory skills to try. It might be unfair to a few, screening that written out by that damned AI - this is not written by AI, but can you accuse -

SPEAKER: No, that's pretty clear.

GREG O'CONNOR: I was wondering if you can actually accuse yourself of hypocrisy, as far as reading speeches goes! Ah, for the days of "King Dick" Seddon, who could speak on his feet for many an hour. Times have moved on somewhat, but a good orator can still hold some power.

VNP/Louis Collins

Trouble is that the quality of the argument can be at odds with the manner in which it's put. Some of Parliament's best thinkers find it hard to with crap merchants' foot.

Being a backbencher in Government's frustrating, often restricted to 30-second spiels. That's why Opposition's the development opportunity, where you can pretty much say what you feel - if the Speaker's in a good mood!

So a parliamentary career should involve both. It takes time to develop the craft. You could do worse than study Winston for things you'll find in no Standing Orders draft.

Living on the edge of what's permitted, he keeps potential interjectors wary. Some wonder how he remains in the House; Others reckon he's got some photos of Gerry!

Traditions are important, to provide a context as we move with the times. Westminster provides the basis but not immovable bottom lines.

Dress standards and language are at the front line of that debate. Jeans and four-letter words are current ramparts. The no-go should always be language of hate.

Personal nastiness is incredibly unprofessional. It just lowers respect for the place. Those for whom it's their go-to should remember life's not a sprint but a stayer's race.

I leave here with faith in the institution that to an outsider can seem quaint and confusing. But it does the job it's meant to do, though the how can leave many musing.

We could do with slowing legislation's pace. Many bills are pushed through way too fast. Another layer of genuine debate might give more laws the chance to last.

We Speakers enforce the status quo, new rulings move things along, but removing big chunks of the process willy-nilly could create many an unintended wrong.

And I say to those of my age demographic who are quick to decry politics and all who take part that when our young folk hear nothing but criticism, in our democracy they'll inevitably lose heart.

Hell, I'm all West Coast Irish, where, whoever was Government, we were born agin 'em. However, several generations in, we learnt being inside best enables our opinion.

Another feature of being here is that MPs' ethnicities come to the fore. Though I'm fourth-generation New Zealand, I rode my Irish ancestors' shoulders to this floor.

And speaking of West Coast Irish, four of my siblings are here today. Growing up on a Buller dairy farm shaped the people we are today.

Privilege has little to do with money; It's books and stability and safety, being taught by those nuns at Granity Convent. Believe me not one was under 80!

Our parents, Eamon and Kath, gave us a great start, living down in the mighty Buller. Of course, these are the days I wish they were still here.

They couldn't have made our lives much fuller.

Thanks for making the trip here, family, especially my kids: Eve, Issac, and Mike. They've brought along grandson Freddy. Grandad says you can do what you like!

It was looking a bit unsure earlier, when Eve missed her flight from Sri Lanka. She navigated Isaac and Mike all her life, so no problem to get here without help from dad's banker.

Burgo and Vince are ex international colleagues. They've both worked many an Aussie police station. The way their politics are heading over there, I'm concerned they're here recruiting for One Nation!

I'd like to shout out to all who've made it, both from the Parsons and two sheds. There's a shearing and a boat one, from where there were a few hard-won votes for the reds.

It was from there and the KTC, the sporting clubs, cafes, and churches, I was privileged to receive votes, enabling me to resist right-wing lurches.

But, of course, it's always down to the local team, the ones who put up billboards and knock on doors, who deliver brochures by the thousands,

who got me into this place of making laws.

I must thank Margaret, Glen, and Judy, Keefe, Graham, Peter, and Lyra. With Alex, Kate, and Lucy, they formed the heart of the Ōhāriu fire.

To my campaign managers, Hamish and George, fortunately, both way smarter than me, you allowed me to follow my instincts, while your organisation skills were key.

They gave me the opportunity to be here, a privilege afforded few, a time dominated by the COVID pandemic, which threw all manifestos and strategies askew.

We tried to do a lot, and history will show most ideas were right. Our grandkids will study COVID's impact and know it was way more than a medical fight.

I think it's thrown the world off its axis, the way World War I last did, and it's a long way from a necessary correction, towards isolationism and despotism, we've slid.

The victims will always be the defenceless; Their survival is in political leaders' hands.

We only pass through this place once; We have to prioritise all in our fair lands.

The four-year term's a must. Meaningful change must be brave, giving the benefits time to accrue, before to the Treasury benches we wave.

My preference would've been to stay; I reckon I've got a few miles left on my clock. I'm not ready for the pipe and slippers, and there are more doors out there for me to knock.

But I leave one helluva lot wiser about the politics of our land. Best lessons are learnt by doing, and I've got a new respect for all those who stand.

It's the staff who keep this place ticking. The public servants would be most missed. It's they who are democracy's lube and yet daily in this place are dissed.

Let's not forget the real workers, like those who push the mail and cleaner's cart. Unlike we politicians, without the workers it would all fall apart.

I can't finish without mentioning my EA, Susan. She's managed to render me useless on my own, organised, loyal, and competent, forever available on the phone.

Both her and Leanne have their families present, and to thank them is only right. Nothing was ever too much trouble for those two,

including calls for help at night. -"Little Red" running out of petrol in *Ōhāriu Valley; there they were with the can of petrol - John and Leanne.

They both adopted dog Herbie, insisting he be in the gallery today. He's dreading my retirement. He'll miss the attention that in this place comes his way.

Having had EA support for 30 years, I've now got to get my own appointments right. The really scary day is coming when I have to book my own airline flight!

As members, we're well looked after, from the moment we walk in the door. Anyone who thinks it's about them should observe what happens when they're not an MP any more.

We have to own our wee slice of history despite the world around us looking vexed. We've won life's lottery to be Kiwis, so let's make it better for those who come next.

So thanks to all who have given me this opportunity. I'm ready for my next chapter 'cause next time I'm needing assistance, I'll say,

"Don't you know who I was?"

VNP/Louis Collins

My future's an unwritten chapter. It's great the family are all back in NZ. I'll make the most of every opportunity, because my next mention in this House will be when I'm dead.

You can watch Greg O'Connors full valedictory speech by clicking on the link.

World.title: Sabalenka fumes over reporter's 'parties' claim after US Open win
World.content:
Double defending champion Aryna Sabalenka has bristled at a reporter's suggestion the events and appearances surrounding the US Open had included "parties and fun" after she cruised past Polina Iatcenko 6-1, 6-1 on Thursday (AEST).

The Belarusian, who had faced a similar line of questioning after her first-round win, fired back that her off-court appearances had not come at the expense of her preparations for the grand slam.

"You guys are, like, a joke. Parties, fun … like, why would you even say that? Why would you even think about that? What kind of question is that?" the world number one said.

"Just because I posted, like, some activities with brands, and you think that I've been partying, not training?" she added, cutting the exchange short.

Turning to her performance against Iatcenko, the four-time grand slam winner said she was pleased with both her level and her focus after another dominant performance at Arthur Ashe Stadium.

"I've been working really hard, but I feel like I'm kind of moving away from trying to be perfect on court," Sabalenka said. "I know that you cannot be perfect, and I'm just trying to work with what I have right now."

Sabalenka will continue her search for a third straight title in New York and avoid ending the year without a major, as she tries to recover her best form after not winning a title since claiming the Miami Open in March.

"I think I struggled a little bit in the middle of the season. Once again, I'm not going to defend myself or explain why, what happened, but I'm happy with my level," the 28-year-old said.

"I can definitely say that mentally I'm way stronger than I was in the middle of the season, and physically I also feel stronger. I feel like I'm on my level of play, and I just want to bring the right focus on the match every time."

Reuters

World.title: Boyd 'extremely honoured' after signing two-year deal as Maroons coach
World.content:
Queensland great Darius Boyd has been unveiled as the next Maroons coach after Billy Slater's exit.

Boyd, who represented the Maroons 28 times in the State of Origin arena as a player, has signed a two-year deal. He is second on Queensland's all-time tryscorers list behind Greg Inglis.

Boyd, 39, said he is "extremely honoured" at receiving the chance to lead his state in the Origin arena.

"It's a privileged position, and I'm very grateful for the opportunity," he said.

Boyd (right) was a long-time Origin teammate of Slater (left) during his 28-game career for the Maroons. (Getty Images: Mark Metcalfe)

"I understand the responsibility that comes with the role as well. My job is to build on the legacy created by the many great Queensland players and coaches who have come before us."

Boyd's signing comes after Slater departed from the Maroons coaching role last month following a five-year stint at the helm.

Since his retirement as a player at the end of 2020, Boyd has coached Queensland's under-19 team to consecutive series wins over NSW.

Like Slater before him, Boyd joins Queensland with no prior NRL head coaching experience, although he has served as an assistant under Kevin Walters at the Broncos.

Slater ended his stint as Queensland's coach last month after three Origin series wins in five years. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor)

Queensland Rugby League (QRL) chair Brian Canavan said Boyd had "lived and breathed what it means to represent Queensland" as a player.

"His playing achievements speak for themselves, but what has impressed us just as much is the work he has done since retirement to develop as a coach and leader.

"He has built strong relationships throughout our pathways system, earned the respect of players and staff, and demonstrated a genuine commitment to helping young people reach their potential.

"Darius understands the responsibility that comes with the Maroons jersey. He knows our culture, our history and the standards required to succeed at the highest level."

World.title: Five Sydney Swans players to remain banned regardless of police investigation, coach says
World.content:
Sydney's five exiled players will remain stood down until the end of the AFL season, regardless of how an ongoing police investigation unfolds.

Victoria Police has interviewed four Sydney men as part of an investigation into sexual assault allegations during a post-AFL match party at East Melbourne's Pullman Hotel.

Swans players Isaac Heeney, Chad Warner, Nick Blakey, Riley Bice and James Jordon were suspended for the remainder of the season for "breaching club standards" and will not be at the SCG for the club's qualifying final against Brisbane on Saturday.

Police speak with four men over Sydney Swans scandal Victoria Police detectives confirm they have spoken with four Sydney men as part of their sexual assault investigation linked to the Sydney Swans.

Those suspensions are separate to the police investigation.

Swans coach Dean Cox reiterated those sanctions would remain unchanged despite police interviewing only four men.

Detectives confirmed they travelled to NSW this week to interview a 30-year-old Maroubra man, a 25-year-old Paddington man and two Randwick men aged 25 and 26.

No charges have been laid and the ABC is not suggesting any wrongdoing on the part of the five suspended players.

"All five will remain stood down from the football club," Cox said on Thursday.

"That's one thing that we spoke about at the start, the police investigation and then the behavioural nature of it.

The Swans kick off their finals campaign with a clash against reigning premiers Brisbane this weekend. (Getty Images: AFL Photos/Matt King)

"We're going to be separated, and that will still remain."

Police have flagged that an update to the investigation is not expected for at least eight weeks.

Cox, who has remained in contact with the five players over their wellbeing, said the timeframe was out of the club's control as it wrestled with making a call on the group's playing future.

The eight-week period takes in the free agency and trade period from October 2 to October 14.

"That's part of the investigation of the way they do it. I just focus on what we can control and what I can control," Cox said.

Andrew Pridham (right) said the suspensions would "torpedo" Sydney's premiership chances this year. (Getty Images: Mark Metcalfe)

Asked about potential impacts on the club's trade period, the Swans coach was short: "There are so many things that we need to talk about, so not for today."

While Sydney club chairman Andrew Pridham claimed the suspensions would "torpedo" the second-placed Swans' premiership hopes, Cox was adamant the playing group still had drive.

The Swans return to the SCG after a bye weekend following their emotional 53-point win over North Melbourne, where Cox and captain Callum Mills were in tears after the siren.

"There's still an expectation. You're hosting a qualifying final at home with a chance to go into a prelim, so there's still a hell of a lot at stake," Cox said.

"That's one thing that I want to make sure our players are aware of: the magnitude of this game for our football club and what we've spent so long trying to get to."

AAP

World.title: Season uncertainty 'challenging' for AFLW community
World.content:
The 2026 men's AFL season is still being contested and we already know when next year's grand final is set to be.

Compare that to the AFLW, where this season's decider was announced just before the start of round three, 13 weeks before the date.

Key dates for the men's season are announced well in advance, with possible season start dates, Gather Round weekend and the grand final for next year already known to fans.

This gives clubs and players heading on their off-season breaks clarity when planning for personnel to return to the club. One benefit of this is being able to time pre-season training in order to be in peak condition when the season begins in March.

Former AFLW player and senior coach Lauren Arnell says more certainty would allow clubs to plan their pre-season to get the best performance out of the playing group.

"It's challenging when you don't have absolute security on that because one week more or less in your preseason has a significant impact on all planning, not just high performance, but on what you can educate as a footy program as well," Arnell told ABC Sport.

More certainty around the fixture would allow teams to optimise their pre-season training. (Getty Images: Albert Perez)

The AFLW grand final will be played on November 27, after a 12-round home and away season.

The AFLW grand-final announcement came at half time of the men's Wildcard final between Collingwood and the Western Bulldogs, which the league said was a deliberate decision to get more coverage of the announcement.

Despite this, the broadcast on Foxtel/Kayo did not mention the announcement in the half-time break.

Men's players have 196 days from the key dates announcement to March 17, the earliest proposed date for the 2027 season to begin, and 395 days until next year's season decider. At the time of writing there are still 23 days until the 2026 grand final.

In a statement from the AFL accompanying the release, CEO Andrew Dillon highlighted the need for fans and clubs to be informed ahead of time.

"We're really pleased to be able to provide fans and clubs with this clarity well ahead of the 2027 season," Dillon said.

The AFL announced the women's fixture on May 21 of this year, giving clubs 80 days' notice, less than half the time their male counterparts have to prepare for the season.

Many AFLW players are still working full-time jobs outside their football careers and Arnell says more certainty would benefit them as well.

"There are still players in the competition working day jobs, and so those players letting their employers know has become more and more challenging," she said.

Rebecca Miller, who plays for the Richmond Tigers AFLW side, says an earlier fixture would also allow the league more time to promote the competition to fans.

"There's been times we've gone to community camps early in preseason or we've done appearances at a men's game early in the season and people are like, 'When are you playing?' And you're like, 'I don't know. I don't have a draw' so you just feel a bit silly in that regard," Miller told ABC Sport.

The last three AFLW grand finals have been sold out at Princes Park. (Getty: Josh Chadwick/AFL Photos)

Most AFL fans will know that the men's grand final is typically held in the last week of September and occasionally, like in 2027, in the first weekend of October. The AFLW grand final is yet to have that level of certainty, having been held in March, April, November and December across nine editions.

"It probably just goes back to that preparation; if we know the grand final, when and where it is before the season starts, again that marketing and promotion piece can really ramp up and make sure that our centrepiece is well attended and well watched and get the attendance they deserve," Miller said.

Conversely, the NRL announced its 2026 men's and women's fixtures on November 14, 2025, which gave NRLW clubs 230 days to prepare for their season to launch and allowed fans time to plan which games they want to attend the following season.

"They [the NRL] have the draw out for the men's and the women's team so at Christmas I can talk to my family about which games they're gonna go to and plan for it months in advance," Miller said, "to be able to go into the Christmas period and know your draw and be able to set yourself as a player but also as a fan and a member".

Richmond Tigers fans in Darwin celebrating a comeback win in their round three Dreamtime match against Essendon. (Getty: Celina Whan)

NRLW matches this year have had an average attendance of 4,915 after seven rounds. Round three of AFLW had an average crowd of 4,806 fans, which includes five double-headers with men's matches. If you count only standalone matches the average attendance is 2,293 for matches that provided a crowd number.

Miller believes that more notice would not just allow more time for promotion, it could also give players more motivation during a long preseason.

"It's so exciting and it just makes it all real. You circle a few games in particular from an individual point of view because you like playing that opposition or you have some beef against that opposition," she said.

"Your family and your friends can decide 'I want to come down to this game, come to that game' so it just makes it all real in your mind and you know why you're training, you know what you're training for".

Arnell believes the announcement of key dates is important but the next steps should come around fixturing.

"I think a priority for AFLW needs to be that all teams play each other once and then you start to land on where your season begins in a calendar and where your grand final sits," she said.

World.title: Fagan lashes Kangaroos over 'unfair' comments after Clarkson axing
World.content:
A shocked Chris Fagan has labelled North Melbourne's public explanation of coach Alastair Clarkson's axing "unfair" and hopes his old friend was given a chance to act on any feedback before the rug was pulled.

Clarkson, who coached Hawthorn to four premierships in an era-defining stint from 2005 to 2021, arrived at North as head coach amid great fanfare after being appointed in August 2022.

Yesterday, with a year to run on his contract, he was unceremoniously axed by football boss Todd Viney, a close friend, and club president Sonja Hood.

Clarkson sacked as Kangaroos hunt 'coach for the modern game' North Melbourne president Sonja Hood and football boss Todd Viney explain why the club is parting ways with Alastair Clarkson with a year to run on his deal.

Asked what type of coach the Kangaroos wanted, Hood, who declared Clarkson's appointment had not been an error, said: "This club needs a coach who can coach for the modern game.

"It'll be a coach who knows what they're doing, and it'll be a coach who's the best fit for this football club."

Viney said there were "still some gaping holes in our game plan" and Clarkson's efforts to fill them only led to "more meetings, more information and players … becoming a bit more confused".

The pair said a canvassing of the club, including players, revealed he no longer had the belief of enough people that he was the right coach to take the group forward.

"I hope he's okay," Brisbane Lions coach Fagan, who first worked with Clarkson at Melbourne in the late 90s before they joined forces at Hawthorn, said.

"I just hope that the feedback that was given at the press conference yesterday about him was given to him in person at some stage during this year, so that he had a chance to act on it.

" It was a pretty fierce press conference. The way that he was spoken about. I reckon probably an unfair description of the man that's done awful lot for footy. "

The 58-year-old's departure comes despite the Kangaroos's improved season in 2026, when they finished 14th and claimed nine wins.

"It was a big shock to me. I actually thought, 'That can't be right,'" Fagan said of the call.

"Under his guidance, North really started to improve. It just reminded me of how tough coaching can be.

"That when a bloke that's been as successful as him as a coach can be jettisoned as quickly as that."

Alastair Clarkson (left) and Chris Fagan were central figures in the investigation into racism at Hawthorn during their time at the club. (Getty Images: Adam Trafford/AFL Media)

The pair were central figures in Hawthorn's racism saga that was settled after two years of legal turmoil in 2024.

Clarkson took a mental health break in 2023 while Fagan, who has the Brisbane Lions in sight of a third-straight flag, admitted he came close to doing the same before opting to coach on.

Fagan, who has yet to speak to Clarkson, hopes his old mate is not lost to the game, and chuckled at the thought of him in a media role, given his typically frosty relationship with that industry.

"We go back a long way and we'll still be friends and still talk a lot about footy, and I'll still seek his advice, no doubt," Fagan said.

AAP

World.title: Current cricket schedule could hurt women's game, says Perry
World.content:
Ellyse Perry has called for Australia's women to be given regular cricket in the peak of summer, fearing the current schedule could stunt the game.

Australia will play nine white-ball matches at home this summer against Bangladesh and New Zealand, with all confined to October and March.

The Australian team has not played a game at home during the summer school holidays since January 2025, while the WBBL also now falls entirely during the school term.

Part of the issue for officials has been India's WPL moving to the January window, with a common fear it will eventually extend into most of February.

Australia's only home matches in the middle of summer under the current program, which runs until the end of 2029, are white-ball ones against Ireland in the first half of December 2028.
