Tech.title: DOGE Affiliate Asked for College Credits for Participating in Takeover
Tech.content:
Christopher Sweet, an affiliate of the so-called Department of Government Efficiency, requested college credit for his time in government, according to new documents obtained by a Freedom of Information Act request filed by Democracy Forward, a nonprofit legal organization.

Sweet was stationed at the Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD), and in emails between Sweet and Scott Langmack, another DOGE affiliate at HUD, it appears that Sweet was looking to frame his work at HUD as an independent study worth three college credits. Sweet joined HUD in the spring of 2025 as an undergraduate college student at the University of Chicago to work on building an AI tool that would crawl through the agency’s rules and regulations and flag them for rescission, or the cancellation of contracts. The tool, called SweetRex, was intended to be rolled out across the federal government.

WIRED has made this article free for all to read because it is primarily based on reporting from Freedom of Information Act requests. Please consider subscribing to support our journalism.

In an August 26, 2025 email titled “which of these should go to U Chicago,” Langmack wrote to Sweet saying, “I need to send them something that has specific framework of the different courses/credits we want them to give you.”

Documents attached to the email show that Sweet’s work was divided into four potential courses, “Advanced AI Prompt Engineering for Legal Reasoning,” “Applied Data Science for Federal Regulatory Analysis,” “Computer Programming for Scalable Al-Legal Systems,” and “Legislative & Regulatory Authority in AI-Driven Reform.” It appears these were meant to lead to a final proposed thesis focused on “the design, implementation, and impact of integrated AI, data science, software engineering, and legal authority analysis to rationalize outdated federal regulations.” The documents make clear that Sweet’s work was not an internship but, “graduate-level, multi-disciplinary research producing real-world outputs that are already influencing federal regulatory reform."

It appears that the final outline that was created to send to the University of Chicago for approval was created by AI. In an August 27, 2025 email, Langmack tells Sweet “I did the outline on ChatGPT.”

HUD and the University of Chicago did not reply to requests for comment. WIRED confirmed that Sweet did, in fact, graduate from the University of Chicago this June with a degree in economics, though it is unclear if credits from his time with DOGE contributed to the school’s requirements.

Langmack came to HUD from the property technology company Kukun—whose website describes it as being on “a long-term mission to aggregate the hardest to find data”—with zero experience in the federal government. He is now the executive director of deregulation AI at the Office of Management and Budget (OMB), according to his LinkedIn. Langmack did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

“These documents raise serious concerns about how one of DOGE’s unqualified employees has been entrusted to handle legal work, rewriting rules and regulations that affect millions of Americans, while attempting to count this work towards an undergraduate degree,” says Daniel McGrath, special counsel for oversight at Democracy Forward, describing the case as part of the “Trump-Vance administration’s relentless pursuit to cripple the important work of the federal government.”

Tech.title: These Meta Glasses Alternatives Found a Way to Last Longer With Snap-On Batteries
Tech.content:
Cameras on glasses have not been having a very good summer. The ongoing privacy concerns about Meta’s smart glasses have led to a reputation hit on the whole category, it seems, right as Google and Samsung are ready to launch their own versions of a similar idea. But more AI glasses are incoming, HTC’s new Vive Eagle among them. Previously available in Asia, they’re now on sale globally. In the US, they’re $499 and come in a range of colors and styles.

I‘ve been trying a pair of the camera-equipped AI glasses at home, minus the prescription lenses. It’s been a lot of squinting, but what I’ve really been curious about is how their camera and audio functions work compared to Meta’s. For the most part, the answer is similar: boomy music playback, comparable microphone quality for calls and serviceable 12MP wide-angle photos and videos that fall short of smartphone quality. However, HTC’s Ray-Ban–style glasses have a battery-boosting trick up their sleeve — one that could eventually make its way to Meta’s glasses.

The Vive Eagle’s separately sold Power Boost battery pack snaps onto the side of the glasses as you’re wearing them. Scott Stein/CNET

A separately sold $49 magnetic Power Boost battery pack — about the width of my thumb and half its length — snaps onto charging pins on one arm of the glasses, providing an instant boost when the built-in battery runs low after roughly four to five hours. By contrast, Meta’s glasses last four to eight hours per charge but must be removed and placed in their case to recharge.

This means you could keep HTC’s glasses running without taking them off, removing the battery pack to recharge it or swapping in extras — if you’re willing to buy them. In theory, you could use the AI and capture photos and videos almost continuously. Still, I’d worry about accidentally knocking off the magnetically attached battery pack.

The Vive Eagle looks very Ray-Ban-like, with similar camera placement (and an LED light that flashes when recording). Scott Stein/CNET

HTC’s glasses features aren’t as smooth as Meta’s, but the audio and microphones sound equivalent for phone calls and music. The AI service is powered by Google Gemini or OpenAI models, either of which can be selected in the glasses app. But it’s not the same as using actual Gemini or ChatGPT: Much like Rokid’s AI glasses, HTC is building its own AI chatbot that uses those models, and these glasses can’t tap into your own Gemini or ChatGPT accounts. (I had to use an HTC Vive account to connect to the glasses and HTC’s app.) The Vive Eagle glasses can also do live translation in 90 languages, but like all AI glasses, your phone’s app needs to be nearby and recently opened.

The build quality of HTC’s glasses seems sturdy enough, albeit thick and generic, like a knockoff pair of Ray-Bans. And they don’t do anything any differently, really, than what Meta already does (although you can skip connecting to Meta with these). There are privacy promises, with recording being blocked if the LED light indicator on the frame is covered (something Meta’s glasses just added an update to ensure), and photos and videos are kept locally on your phone and not shared to HTC’s cloud.

The Vive Eagle glasses have a case, but charge using a separate magnetic USB cable that snaps onto the side arm. Scott Stein/CNET

Also, these need a subscription, which costs $3 a month, but HTC includes two years of the service with the purchase of the glasses. I find the idea of subscription-required wearables disturbing, but it’s a growing trend, and I expect other companies are going to start imposing subscriptions more, too.

The most interesting thing, really, is the battery pack. And, as companies keep trying to find ways to make smart glasses and AI wearables do more always-on processing, battery solutions like this could pop up in more places.

Tech.title: One of Our Top Robot Vacuum Brands Is Diving into Pool Care
Tech.content:
Roborock, one of the flashiest home robot makers, is taking the plunge. The Beijing-based brand, known for its super-smart robot vacuums, including models with robotic grabbing arms and stair-climbing capabilities, has launched its first-ever robotic pool cleaner.

We saw it first at IFA Berlin.

On a crowded showroom floor, we got a look at Roborock’s small and colorful new pool cleaner. Dubbed the RockAqua P1, this autonomous underwater vacuum is engineered to clean pool floors, walls, waterlines and shallow platforms.

Roborock has entered the pool-care conversation with the launch of the RockAqua P1 at IFA.

Its adaptive cleaning path, a feature prominent in Roborock’s indoor vacuums, allows the robot to navigate pools of different shapes and depths. Vision-based obstacle avoidance identifies obstacles such as drain covers and steps, helping reduce interruptions during cleaning.

8 Best Robot Pool Cleaners, All Tested by CNET See at CNET

While obstacle avoidance is useful, the ability to track down debris in a pool using AI cognition, as our top-rated Aiper Scuba V3 does, is even more impressive. So far, it doesn’t look like Roborock’s entry into the pool-cleaner category offers a comparable debris-detection feature.

What the RockAqua P1 lacks in proactive leaf, bug, and stone hunting, it makes up for with a lot of suction power. The robot delivers a suction rate of 6,800 gallons per hour, placing it in the same class as some of the most powerful pool-cleaning robots from well-established brands. Still, our lab testing shows that raw power doesn’t necessarily translate to better cleaning.

Roborock’s first-ever pool vac can adjust its suction strategically to better capture debris. Tara Brown/CNET

One particularly interesting feature is the robot’s ability to adjust its suction depending on the situation. According to Roborock, when it encounters larger debris, the robot reduces suction to prevent the water flow from disturbing the debris and pushing it out of the cleaning path. As it gets closer, it increases suction to capture the debris.

Roborock’s first pool cleaner runs for up to 3.5 hours on a full charge, which is average for high-end models. When a cleaning cycle is complete, the robot rests on the water’s surface. That’s a useful touch, since some pool cleaners remain at the bottom and have to be hauled out manually. The surface-resting design should make the RockAqua P1 easier to retrieve for emptying and recharging.

As of now, the RockAqua P1 is set for release in the European market only, with a rollout to the US still in question.

Editor’s note: David Watsky’s travel costs for the IFA conference were covered by IFA. The judgments and opinions of CNET are our own

Tech.title: The Weirdest and Wackiest Tech We Found at IFA 2026
Tech.content:
Some tech at IFA was much more unusual than the rest. Here’s what caught our eye. Govee

IFA is in full swing, and the Berlin expo has gathered advanced tech from across the globe to show off, from all-new vacuum features to ultra-advanced AI ecosystems ready to help manage your home. Then there are the products that made us go, “…Huh.”

When tech companies are throwing everything they’ve got at IFA, things can get a little weird. Here’s the wackiest tech we spotted, what it’s supposed to do, and how useful we think it could be out in the real world.

Govee’s mood-reading sky light

Govee’s mood-interpreting light may not be as far-fetched as you think. Govee

Govee has long been at the forefront of strange home lighting creations, from literal curtains of light to spread across your garage to table lamps that look more like alien artifacts. Now Govee is showing off one of its oddest products yet: a dome-like ceiling light made to mimic the sky while being “mood-responsive.”

In this case, mood-responsive means you can use Govee’s AI to talk about your mood or how you’re feeling, and the Govee app will come up with ceiling light color schemes to match. But the light can also create a specific blue wavelength designed to evoke blue skies and natural daylight.

Too weird to work? Not as weird as you may think. I’ve tested Govee’s AI before, and you really can generate lighting patterns based on your mood or random musings. But Govee already has so many lighting scenes in its app that I didn’t find it very practical — although definitely fun. I wonder how well it will work with a full ceiling light.

SwitchBot’s AI shirt pin, the MindClip

SwitchBot’s AI clip sort of…spies on everyone around you. SwitchBot

If you thought AI was already in everything, just wait: SwitchBot is announcing the launch of its AI shirt device, the MindClip, at IFA. It’s made to clip onto your shirt pocket, collar, nearby strap or even belt. Once in place, it, well, essentially listens to everything that happens within a 3-meter radius for up to 20 hours and saves it for you.

The MindClip can recognize people by their voices and summarize conversations or events, ostensibly to help you with planning after a busy day. As far as AI goes, it’s no spying Meta glasses, but it is fairly invasive, especially for strangers you may be chatting with.

Too weird to work? Interestingly, this isn’t the first time we’ve seen an AI pin, although it is the smallest and least distracting version I’ve spotted. The problem is that none of them really took off, and some companies even pivoted to an entirely different product. So yes, it’s too weird to work for now, but maybe the rumored AI capabilities in Apple’s AirPods will be an exception.

The AI-powered companion doll from Lovense

Lovense’s updated AI companion doll also made an appearance at IFA. Lovense

Singaporean intimacy and sex toy company Lovense has brought the latest version of its AI “companion doll” to IFA, aiming to make it more lifelike than ever before. In addition to talking, remembering past facts and adjusting its personality, the silicone doll can blink, smile and look when called by its custom name. Users can also chat with the doll at a distance via a phone app and set up roleplay scenarios, if they prefer.

Too weird to work? Yes, the age of AI sex dolls is here. But it’s such an eclectic — and expensive (between $4,000 and $8,000) — proposition, this one is only for those with very specific tastes and a, ahh, particular relationship with AI. For others, Lovense also debuted several more conventional, AI-free toys.

A Eufy sensor that asks if you fell down

Eufy’s new sensor has a very, very specific purpose in the home. Eufy

When today’s home sensors can do nearly anything from recognizing when dogs bark to knowing when someone is tampering with a mailbox, it may sound strange to make a sensor specifically to say, “Oops, it looks like you fell down!” But that’s just what Anker’s Eufy brand has done.

There’s method behind this madness. The wall sensor uses a combo of algorithms and presence sensing with mmWave technology, no cameras necessary. It’s made to help those aging in place or living in rest homes without creating privacy concerns. The sensor even supports two-way audio, so family members or nurses can check in if they get an alert about a potential fall.

Quick note: As Anker consolidates its brand names, Eufy products are staying with us, but the Eufy name may not be around forever, so keep that in mind when shopping.

Too weird to work? In this case, not at all. I’ve already seen mmWave technology tap into Wi-Fi signals to help those aging in place, although Eufy’s sensor is the first I’ve seen that focuses on falls and enables two-way audio for a quick checkup. It’s a strong use of the technology.

Best DIY Home Security Systems of 2026: Install Them Yourself Dodge installation fees and take security into your own hands with these super smart security kits.

A smartphone for your pet

The Petphone certainly makes a lot of claims about AI pet powers. Petpogo

Ucloudlink has brought the newest version of its award-winning PetPhone to IFA this year, showing a world where cats and dogs have their own smartphone, too. Sort of.

The Petpogo PetPhone is technically a smart pet collar, and we’ve reviewed many of those. But this version comes with two-way audio to talk to your pet with an app and AI features that interpret behavior and motion so pets can theoretically initiate a call themselves, as well as emotion analysis of barks, meows and other actions. It also supports more traditional capabilities like tracking and geofencing, and it alerts pet parents to out-of-routine behaviors.

Too weird to work? No AI features can accurately interpret specific barks or meows into moods and feelings. That’s (currently) nonsense. And trying to get your pet to “call” you with specific behaviors sounds dubious at best. So most of the innovations here are too weird, but the underlying collar functionality looks usable.

These headphones that turn into a Bluetooth speaker

TDM’s Bluetooth speaker headphone hybrid is confusing. TDM

TDM is showing off its very unique Neo headphones, with a literal twist. In normal mode, they look like a typical pair of wireless headphones. But twist and collapse the earcups, and they form into a small Bluetooth speaker with up to 8 hours of music playback. The dual-device comes with an aux port, a USB-C charging port and a carrying case.

Too weird to work? When was the last time you saw someone with headphones and thought, “What a pleasant, private music experience that person is having, I wish there was a way for them to share it with all the people nearby?” Nope. No one likes it when you play music out loud in public spaces, especially when the same device could let you listen privately. I’m calling these headphones too weird to work.

A soundwave-creating smart bed

Amada’s acoustic mattress claims many different applications. Amada

Amada brought a fascinating mattress to IFA called the Soundwave Smart Mattress. Yes, it connects to a phone app. And yes, it really does produce soundwaves or at least a “vibroacoustic experience” with vibration modes for pre-sleep relaxation, meditation, focus and recharging. I’m not sure how vibration is supposed to help with those things, but CNET health expert Anna Gragert told me vibration therapy does have applications for recovery and disease treatment. The bed is made of polyurethane foam and polyester fabric, with a four-pin power connector.

Too weird to work? Well, Magic Fingers did have their day in hotel rooms across the US, but that day ended pretty fast. I don’t know if a bed with good vibrations is what the average home is looking for, but if you’ve tried it and it works for you, this could be a shakingly good upgrade.

Tech.title: These New Robot Vacuums, Mops, Mowers and Pool Cleaners Will Try to Convince Us They’re Maintenance-Free
Tech.content:
Roborock has offered some of the most unique and innovative robot vacuum models I’ve seen over the years. They’ve ranged from the arm-equipped Saros Z70, which I tested at home, to the stair-climbing Saros Rover we saw at CES earlier this year. At the 2026 IFA trade show in Berlin, the company is focusing on improving performance and perfecting the hands-free maintenance of the tried and true flagship robot vacuums, wet and dry mops, robot mowers and pool-cleaning robots.



The goal is to improve each model’s ability to handle the complexity of homes, yards and pools without requiring extensive human management and intervention to get over obstacles or self-clean.

“Our mission is about giving time back to our customers by automating and improving everyday tasks,” said Ricky Ma, president of Europe and Americas at Roborock, in a press statement. “Building smarter robots is just the means, not the goal. Every minute spent worrying about housework is a minute taken away from family, passions and personal well-being.”

I cover vacuums and home tech for CNET. While I’m here at IFA, I’m determined to seek out the most interesting tech that solves your most common cleaning problems. I’m excited to see the Saros 20 Neo, F25 Pro Turbo Combo and other devices in person on Wednesday. I’ll report back with my impressions later.

Saros 20 Flow Complete and Saros 20 Neo (Qrevo Edge 3 Pro in the US)

The Saros 20 Flow comes with Roborock’s key features and impressive obstacle avoidance. Roborock

The Saros 20 Flow Complete is Roborock’s newest top-tier robot vacuum with all the key cleaning features you’d expect. It has a powerful 36,000 pa of suction and lidar navigation. Naturally, it comes with AI, allowing it to recognize over 300 types of obstacles, and Roborock says it can navigate easily in both well-lit and dark environments.

It’s just 8.98 centimeters thick, which Roborock says makes it the slimmest robot vacuum on the market. The roller mop has 15 newtons of downward pressure, 240 rotations per minute and uses 16 pressurized water outlets to tackle tougher stains on hard floors. The pressurized water spraying is a feature I’ve seen on other robot vacuum models, as companies try to address the problem of dried stains in devices that aren’t suited for a lot of elbow grease.

Roborock

The robot also comes with dual-lifting side brushes to tackle edges. It has the AdaptLife system we’ve seen on other models, which allows it to cross double thresholds up to 8.8 cm. Like most flagship models. And it comes with a self-cleaning docking station that will wash and dry the mop, self-empty and dispense detergent.

The Saros 20 Neo, called the Qrevo Edge 3 Pro in the US, is similar to the Flow, but is designed specifically to tackle more complex home layouts without requiring you to rescue the robot. It comes with the AdaptLift chassis 3.0 to clear double-layer thresholds of 8.8 cm. It’s even slimmer than the Flow at 7.95 cm, letting it fit under low-clearance furniture. It has an extended battery life, which Roborock says is enough to clean 350 square meters (around 3,767 square feet) in a single run.

Roborock

In cleaning performance, it has 36,000 pa of suction and anti-tangle rollers to handle long pet hair. It also mops with 14 newtons of downward pressure and has a self-cleaning, self-emptying docking station.



Price and availability are yet to be confirmed, but Roborock says the Neo/Edge 3 Pro will be immediately available as of this writing. The Flow Complete is expected to launch in the US before October, with more details on price and availability to be shared later.

F25 Ultra Steam Gen 2 and F25 Pro Turbo Combo

Wet and dry mops may not be as exciting as robot vacuums, but they’re having their moment this year as Roborock continues to update its lineup. The newest models are the F25 Ultra Steam Gen 2 and F25 Pro Turbo Combo. The Gen 2 Steam outputs 2.5 times as much steam as the previous generation, letting it handle stains and more greasy messes faster. Once preheated, Roborock says it can output the steam at 180 degrees Celsius in 30 seconds.

It supports automatic cleaning adjustments for different flooring types, a feature I liked on the F25 Ultra. Roborock says it’s designed to fit under low furniture and has wheel assist to help you move it around smoothly. It has a robotic arm (not in the sense of the Saros Z70) that lets you get up against walls and edges and supports self-cleaning and drying.

The F25 Pro Turbo Combo is meant to be the company’s jack-of-all-trades. Roborock calls it a five-in-one because it combines a wet and dry vacuum with a cordless vacuum in a single unit, letting it tackle both hard flooring and carpet for wet and dry cleaning. It has 25,000 pascals of suction, assisted wheels, and a scraper that keeps hair from getting tangled in the brush. I’m generally a big fan of the combo vacuums; they save you from buying multiple devices, but I’ll be curious to see how it measures up in our lab tests.



The F25 Ultra Steam Gen 2 is expected to launch in the US on Sept. 28. We’re still waiting on details for the F25 Pro Turbo Combo.

RockNeo Q2 Lidar

Cunion

On the lawn care side, Roborock is coming with the RockNeo Q2 Lidar. It’s wire-free, with no need for a boundary wire or RTK beacon. Roborock says the lidar is sufficient to navigate diverse yards and surroundings and find its way through narrow areas. It can handle slopes up to 45% and passages as narrow as 60 centimeters. It has a three-blade cutting system that’s capable of 3 cm edge cutting. The mower itself is IPx6 waterproof.



The charging station has a built-in Wi-Fi amplifier, improving connectivity between the machine and the app and letting you manage mowing zones and cutting routines. There’s anti-theft protection built-in and support for Alexa and Google Home.



US availability and pricing for the RockNeo Q2 will be confirmed later.

RockAqua P1

Summer’s drawing to an end, but Roborock’s RockAqua P1 is the company’s newest pool cleaner for next season. Roborock says it’s the first robotic pool cleaner that’s built to clean not just the pool floor, but also the walls, waterline and shallow platforms. That’s a significant improvement from other pool robots we’ve tested that often struggle with more complex pools or require you to handle steps or the waterline yourself.

The P1 can handle more complex pool shapes, floor shapes and obstacles, like steps. It can clean platforms as shallow as 15 cm, and uses vision-based obstacle avoidance to identify drain covers and steps.

In capabilities, it can handle fine debris, sand and large leaves with 6,800 gallons per hour suction power, a 4-liter debris basket, and dual filtration with 180 μm and 70 μm filters. It can automatically adjust suction based on the debris it encounters, including reducing it to avoid disturbing debris as it approaches.

It has 3.5 hours of running time, letting it cover large pools and supports fast charging. US pricing and availability will be determined later.

Editors’ note: Ajay Kumar’s travel costs for the IFA conference were covered by Roborock. The judgments and opinions of CNET are our own.

Tech.title: I Was Disappointed by Miele’s Last Vacuums, but the New IFA Lineup Changed My Mind
Tech.content:
Miele is known as one of the most reputable brands for home appliances and cleaning, but when we lab tested the Miele HX2 cordless vacuum last year, we were a little let down by it — it performed poorly in sand tests for low and midpile carpet, and the design was a little finicky to use compared to lightweight competition from Dyson and Shark. It also cost $1,100 at full price, making it a hard sell.

With this in mind, when Miele showed me its new HX3 and HX3 Plus Aqua, I was skeptical it would be more than an incremental jump, but after spending some time using it at the Miele Experience Center in Manhattan prior to the IFA 2026 show in Berlin, I came away impressed by several of the changes.

To start with, while there hasn’t been a complete redesign, one of the big changes is rebalancing the weight distribution so that more of it is at the bottom, reducing the strain up top when you’re vacuuming. You can also change out where the motor and waste bin are, depending on how you attach the nozzles, so it’s up to you how you want the weight to fall.

A Miele representative showed me an example of how you might want it more top-heavy when you’re using it to clean the corners of ceilings and higher-up spots. You can also convert it fairly easily back into the self-standing vacuum mode, a traditional stick vac or a handheld.

There are also other quality-of-life tweaks, like push-button controls, easier dustbin emptying, finer particle capture, automatic flooring-type detection and the ability to stand upright. It offers 70 minutes of running time, which Miele says should be good enough to clean 1,700 square feet in a single charge, and some models have an extended battery included for even more juice. All key things that I value when vacuuming.

Miele

The big improvements come in performance. The HX3 has notably better pickup on both carpet and hard flooring. The Miele representatives even helpfully provided me with some condiments to imitate sand and pet hair to try to suction up from the carpet. While it wasn’t quite the same as CNET’s rigorous lab testing, the outcome of my vacuuming session offered solid results. The HX3 was able to remove most or all of the pet hair with a single back-and-forth motion, while the imitation sand was no challenge at all on hardwood (though that’s true of most vacuums and robot vacuums we test).

Overall, the HX3 seemed to do a great job of picking up dirt and debris from different floor types. There’s also a powerful Boost mode that can give you extra suction beyond even the highest setting, but it drains the battery the fastest, so it’s limited to just 10 seconds.

The HX3 Plus Aqua is basically the same as the regular HX3; it just comes with Miele’s first mopping attachment, the Aqua Twister Floorhead. It consists of dual spinning mop pads that are machine washable, a 300-milliliter water tank and a 360-degree light. I also took the mopping attachment for a spin, trying out its different modes on hard flooring to clean stains and dirt. Again, the results were impressive, with the amount of water being dispensed fully adjustable, allowing you to tackle bigger messes and spills. When the mopping head is attached, Boost mode also dispenses more water for 30 seconds, so it’s good to see the feature has been integrated into both cleaning heads.

Miele

While there are two distinct models, the HX3 and HX3 Plus Aqua, there’s a somewhat more consumer-friendly price spread: The base HX3 starts at $849, while the top-tier HX3 Aqua Plus, with all the accessories, including the mopping head, runs $1,249. There are a number of models in between, each with its own price and array of attachments, so I’m just going to lay them out in a list below, pulled from the specs sheet.

Triflex HX3 ($849) Included: MultiFloor XXL (SEB430), Accessory Set (dusting brush, upholstery tool, crevice nozzle, mounting clip), 1 Lithium-Ion Battery by Varta, Wall Mount with accessory storage

($849) Triflex HX3 Hardfloor (Amazon exclusive) ($949) Included: MultiFloor XXL (SEB430), Accessory Set (dusting brush, upholstery tool, crevice nozzle, mounting clip), Hardfloor Roller (HX-HC10), 1 Lithium-Ion Battery by Varta, Wall Mount with accessory storage

($949) Triflex HX3 Cat & Dog ($999) Included: MultiFloor XXL with headlight (SEB430), Accessory Set (dusting brush, upholstery tool, crevice nozzle, mounting clip), Electro Compact (HX-EC10), 1 Lithium-Ion Battery by Varta, Wall Mount with accessory storage

($999) Triflex HX3 Plus ($1,099) Included: MultiFloor XXL with headlight (SEB430), Accessory Set (dusting brush, upholstery tool, crevice nozzle, mounting clip), Hardfloor Roller (HX-HC10), 2 Lithium-Ion Batteries by Varta, Wall Mount with accessory storage

($1,099) Triflex HX3 Aqua ($1,049) Included: MultiFloor XXL with headlight (SEB430), Accessory Set (dusting brush, upholstery tool, crevice nozzle, mounting clip), AquaTwister Pro with 360 Light, Drip Mat, 2 Washable pads, FloorClean (17 fl.oz. bottle), 1 Lithium-Ion Battery by Varta, Wall Mount with accessory storage

($1,049) Triflex HX3 Aqua Plus ($1,249) Included: MultiFloor XXL with headlight (SEB430), Accessory Set (dusting brush, upholstery tool, crevice nozzle, mounting clip), Harfloor Roller (HX-HC10), AquaTwister Pro with 360 Light, Drip Mat, 2 Washable pads, FloorClean (17 fl.oz. bottle), 2 Lithium-Ion Batteries by Varta, Wall Mount with accessory storage

($1,249)

Miele also pointed out to me that the base specs and capabilities of each model are the same, so even if you buy the most basic model, you can pick up other attachments separately over time to build the vacuum you want. I’m looking forward to testing these at the CNET Lab, and we already have the Aqua Plus in hand for our next batch of tests. Expect to see results soon.

Editors’ note: Ajay Kumar’s travel costs for the IFA conference were covered by Roborock. The judgments and opinions of CNET are our own.

Tech.title: As a Pet Parent to 3 Asthmatic Cats, I’m Eyeing This New AAFA-Certified Vacuum at IFA 2026
Tech.content:
Anker has made some of our favorite and most innovative robot vacuums over the years, and recently, they’ve also been getting into robot lawn mowers, earning spots on our tested lists. The newest models they’re showing off at IFA Berlin 2026 include a robot vacuum and a robot mower, both with key improvements and features over previous generations.

Anker’s newest robot vacuum — and potentially the last one to keep the Eufy name (more on that below) — is the Omni E35, and it just might be what my three asthmatic cats need because it focuses on sterilization and disinfection. Anker describes it as “baby-grade,” meaning it’s TÜV Rheinland-certified for the “Maternal and Infant Cleaning Robot mark.” It can eliminate bacteria and dust mites, and it has low noise and high efficiency when it comes to cleaning and self-cleaning.

Anker says it’s the first and only robot vacuum to earn the Asthma & Allergy Friendly Certification from the Asthma and Allergy Foundation of America. This is especially interesting to me as someone who has the bad luck of having three cats diagnosed with asthma. The vet told me it was incredibly unlikely to occur naturally, so the cause is probably environmental — dust mites, dander, outdoor pollution, fragrances or smoke from the neighbors downstairs. At least a couple of those factors could be addressed by a robot vacuum capable of more thorough fine-dust pickup and sterilization, so I’m interested in seeing it in action and trying it at home.

Anker says the E35 Omni can clean your floors well enough for babies to play on. Anker

It has all the typical flagship features you’d expect from a top-tier model, including 35,000 pascals of suction and the Hydro Jet 2.0 self-cleaning roller mop. It also has a kitchen deep clean mode that uses an algorithm to determine how to tackle tougher stains, by saturating, soaking and then scrubbing.

The Omni E35 will be available starting Sept. 25, though pre-orders will start Sept. 4. It’ll cost $1,100 at MSRP, but if you buy it during the early bird pricing, you can get it for $900.

Eufy S2 Max

Anker

Also new in the robotics space is the Eufy S2 Max, Anker’s first robot mower developed entirely in-house. It has vision-based SLAM navigation and real-time 3D mapping, meaning no boundary wires or RTK beacons are required, which has become increasingly common in the robot mower market. It also has improved computing and full all-wheel drive, letting it handle terrain up to 80% slopes, a dual blade system and edge-to-edge cutting with an extendable trimming arm.

US availability and pricing are still to be determined, but it’ll be available in EU markets in May 2027 for 3,999 euros.

Anker is rebranding

Anker’s Eufy brand includes its lineup of robot vacuums and robot lawn mowers, as well as home security products. At IFA Berlin 2026, the company revealed that after 14 years of operation, it’s bringing all of its sub-brands, including Eufy and Soundcore for the audio products, under the Anker umbrella. In the future, all Anker products, no matter if they’re robot vacuums, robot lawn mowers, security cameras, smart doorbells or headphones, will be sold under the Anker brand.

The change isn’t immediate, and an Anker representative who briefed me prior to IFA said that for a time, consumers in different markets will still see the distinct branding across product categories, but the goal is to consolidate it under Anker. For now, the lineup announced at IFA 2026 will continue to use the Eufy or Soundcore branding. The announcement coincides with the opening of an official Anker Flagship store in Berlin on Sept. 5, the company’s first standalone retail store there.

I cover vacuums and home tech for CNET. While I’m here at IFA Berlin 2026, I’m determined to seek out the most interesting tech that solves your most common cleaning problems. I’m excited to see the Eufy Omni E35 and Eufy S2 Max. I’ll report back with my impressions later.

Editors’ note: Ajay Kumar’s travel costs for the IFA conference were covered by Roborock. The judgments and opinions of CNET are our own.

Tech.title: Anker’s Eufy Strides Into IFA With a New AI Ecosystem and Devices to Match
Tech.content:
Anker’s plans for home AI focus entirely on device algorithms. Anker

Anker and its home brand Eufy came to Berlin’s IFA event well prepared with major news, including an overhaul of how the company approaches home security, and the new capabilities it wants to give devices in the coming years. I’m no stranger to AI in home security, but Eufy’s approach is unique and has the potential to be particularly advantageous for customers.

Anker’s flagship announcement is an excellent example of what I’m talking about. We saw the company’s newest MindBase hub, a home AI enabler made to connect to many kinds of other Anker and Eufy products and process their data with AI algorithms, all entirely on-device. That means no connections to the cloud, few worries about how the company will use your private data for analysis and lower costs than most AI around the home.

Using Anker’s EasyOmni Link platform, the MindBase is supposed to connect to Anker’s security, energy, cleaning and audio devices. It also has Matter support, so devices that work with Apple Home, Amazon Alexa and Google Home are also on the table. The base uses an in-house-developed LLM running on an AI chip to accomplish much of what most companies need cloud help to do.

Eufy’s shiny new security tech sports the latest advances

Eufy’s new doorbell is pricey, but it has a 3K resolution and tracking. Anker Eufy

While Anker didn’t show off everything the MindBase is capable of, we did get some more advanced looks of its security capabilities thanks to Eufy’s new security line, set for the months to come.

The MindBase itself, which is still pending price and release date info, can tap into Eufy’s new Smart Security Shield sensor with radar to detect strangers and encrypted facial data that can recognize familiar faces from up to 30 meters away. The on-device approach to facial data could help Eufy escape the privacy lawsuits similar to those facial data technologies are facing in the US.

Eufy is also releasing a new wired video doorbell, notable for its 3K resolution and AI tracking technology (meaning it can keep delivery people in view for longer, etc.). It’s set for sale at $300 later this month.

For those who want a full security setup, Eufy is also launching an eight-channel NVR system with 2K security cameras. I’m not sure how many NVR features will need MindBase to function, but Anker says the wired, fully contained kit can handle auto framing, smart video searches, cross-camera tracking and 24/7 recording.

Eufy’s line is also expanding into two particularly interesting security devices. One is a presence-sensing wall sensor made to detect falls, especially for those aging in place. The detector can raise alerts and link loved ones using two-way audio, a feature combination I’ve never seen before. The brand is also releasing a new $70 window camera later this year, a small 2.5K device with a cup-like shield design to reduce glare so people can attach it to the inside of a window.

I’ve tested cameras like these this year from brands like Wyze, and they’re an interesting compromise fit for apartment windows (such as those looking over your carport) and similar situations where an outdoor camera isn’t feasible.

The big subscription question

I’ve seen the rise of window cams this year, now including Eufy’s. Anker Eufy

Anker’s Eufy brand has been one of my favorite options for no-subscription home security that still offers important features like human detection and local video storage without relying on the cloud. I’m not totally sure how the MindBase and new AI features will work, but there are promising signs.

For its new security cameras and sensors, Anker said, “The portfolio processes sensitive biometric data on-device … with no monthly subscriptions attached,” but added an important caveat that premium and optional features (not sure what those would be) may require a monthly fee, so there are a lot of questions for future details to answer.

For features like the MindBase’s MindSafe Memory, a local storage system that can perform AI searches through photos, videos and files, Anker didn’t mention any fee information, and I’m not sure if it will require a subscription. The same is true of the facial recognition features in the Smart Security Shield, although Eufy indicated earlier this summer that those features wouldn’t require a subscription, so I’m hopeful.

Anker also said it’s planning on adding new AI agents in addition to the security tricks, like an energy version to save power and a cleaning version to manage your robot vacuums, but I don’t have any info on whether those capabilities will require subscriptions.

A final important note about the Eufy brand

Anker showed up at IFA with plenty to test out in the coming year, as well as news about its branding plans. In the future, Anker has plans to congregate its brand names primarily under Anker. That means I may not be using the years-old Eufy name for too much longer.

Hints of this change were visible in Anker’s IFA showcases. For example, while the MindBase bears the Eufy name on the physical hub, Anker solely refers to it as the Anker MindBase in promotional materials, possibly a sign of things to come. I’ll keep you updated so the naming system doesn’t get too confusing when you’re looking for home security.

Tech.title: These Sleep Headphones Are My Best Redeye Flight Hack. They Just Got a Nifty Upgrade
Tech.content:
Last month, I took two back-to-back long-haul flights in economy that took me overnight from Asia to the UK. On paper, it sounded like a nightmare, and I was dreading it. But in the end, I managed to get a total of 7 hours of sleep — 5 of them on the first flight, which departed at 2 a.m.

I credit Anker’s Soundcore Sleep A30 earbuds, which drowned out all of the cabin noise around me and were also comfy enough to sleep in. I’ve been searching for this magic combination for a while now, and I finally found it in the A30s.

On Thursday at IFA in Berlin, Anker announced an upgrade to this holy grail product — the Sleep Earbuds 4 and Sleep Earbuds 4 Pro. The company says it’s made the earbuds even smaller, minimizing the 3D ergonomic design for even cozier sleeping. The Sleep 4 Pro also comes with a touchscreen case, allowing you to set alarms, play relaxing sounds and check insights all without touching your phone.

A key feature that sets the Pro model apart from the base model is what Anker calls a “track-assess-adjustment system.” This uses the headphones’ built-in sensors to measure various factors, including PPG, heart rate and HRV and adjust the audio to find the best sleep sounds for you to have the most effective sleep.

The Earbuds 4 will be available in October, with the Earbuds 4 Pro following soon after in November — though pricing is not yet available.

Anker’s sleek sleep speaker would look at home on my bedside table.

Anker is further building out its sleep ecosystem with a pair of stylish bedside speakers, which it also announced at IFA. The SleepLab will lull you to sleep with soft music and a nightlight, whereas the SleepLap Pro uses radar to track your sleep, heart rate and breathing, then play tailored audio to help you fall asleep and stay asleep — all with no wearables required.

The speakers feature a warm, circular lamp that almost appears to float within a wider cream circle. It looks like a thoughtfully designed piece of kit that I know I’d be happy to have on my bedside table. Anker isn’t sharing pricing or availability at this stage, but says no phone or subscription is required.

Anker headphones and a hearing aid

In May, Anker announced its first neural-net compute-in-memory AI audio chip called Thus, which it’s now put into a slew of new audio products.

Anker’s IFA headphone lineup is powered by its AI audio Thus chip.

The Anker Soundcore AeroClip 2 Pro is more than a pair of clip-on earbuds — the product is actually an AI note-taker that can capture online meetings and calls, transcribing them and providing summaries (not unlike the newly announced Plaud One headphones). There’s no launch date for the AeroClip 2 Pro right now, but there is a price — it will be $230.

Anker is really emphasizing clear call quality in its new audio device lineup. It’s listed as a major selling point of both the over-ear Soundcore Space 2 Pro and the Soundcore Liberty Buds 2. The Space 2 Pro comes with immersive adaptive active noise cancellation and 60 hours of listening time (30 hours with ANC on and 20 hours of talk time). The Libery Buds 2, meanwhile, pack six-sensor full-band ANC, which Anker promises will offer pure silence and block chaos so you can focus fully.

Both models will be available starting Sept. 22, with the Space2 Pro priced at $200 and the Liberty Buds 2 at $130.

The final audio product Anker unveiled at IFA is a little different and won’t be for everyone, but it will prove hugely useful to a select group. The Anker RIC Hearing Aids, also powered by the Thus chip, offer what the company describes as a clinical-grade hearing aid experience.

Anker’s hearing aid doesn’t have an on-sale date just yet.

The device will drown out unnecessary noise and amplify the voice you actually want to hear. Four beamforming microphones will lock onto the voice of the person you’re talking with, and the Thus chip will run 40 billion operations per second to isolate the sound.

There’s no pricing or availability details for the RIC Hearing Aids just yet, but it’s impressive to see Anker use its proprietary tech to develop an accessibility solution. The device will offer 12 hours of battery time, or 36 hours with the case, and 5 minutes of fast charging will give 2 hours of battery life.

Editors’ note: Katie Collins’ travel costs for the IFA conference were covered in part by Xiaomi. The judgments and opinions of CNET are our own.
